Supply chain data integrity becomes a priority when something breaks.

A cleanup gets launched. Parameters are corrected. Master data is aligned. Systems run better.

Then attention shifts.

A few months later, the same issues resurface.

Lead times don’t match supplier performance. Lot sizes and Minimum Order Quantities haven’t been revisited. Safety stock hasn’t been recalibrated. Overrides increase. New products introduced are missing required planning fields.

Frustration builds. “The system never works” becomes the narrative. Teams revert to old habits. Cross-functional trust weakens.

The problem usually isn’t the cleanup itself.
It’s that the structure to sustain it was never defined.

In practice, it comes down to four things:
𝟭. 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹
Define who has authority over planning logic and structural rules.
𝟮. 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽
Assign accountability for keeping those inputs current within the agreed rules.
Governance defines the rule. Stewardship maintains within it.
𝟯. 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲
Monitor material drift through normal operating forums and exception management, not a one-off project.
𝟰. 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗮𝗴𝗲
Connect data integrity to service, inventory performance, and cost.

One-time cleanups improve accuracy temporarily.
Operating discipline sustains trust.

If teams stop trusting the system, they will plan outside it and rebuild the very workarounds the cleanup was meant to eliminate.

#SupplyChain #SupplyChainPlanning #DataGovernance

🤔 Who decides? I got increasingly irritated with Microsoft Word of late. Why did every new document default to the “Aptos” font and double-spacing for the layout? This meant switching the font and spacing for every new document (I know, “Okay, Boomer”). 

That’s rework. (Finally) Googling the issue resulted in simple instructions on how to set formatting defaults in this 43-year-old (😲) application. Did the thing—now that’s done. No more rework. (Nice job, Boomer)

Which begs the question, where are we accepting defaults that fail to serve us? Apps drive a lot of it these days, so that’s a good place to start.

⏰ Another software-influenced default is the 1-hour meeting. It’s taken a few bold contrarians to declare 45- or 50-minute time slots as their norm. It still takes extra steps to alter the built-in 1-hour session, yet the practical and physiological realities beg for change:

- Calendars stacked with back-to-back meetings leave zero time for reflection, action, regrouping, preparation … and the list goes on.

- Cognitive neuroscience suggests the brain needs to switch tasks or rest frequently. The "50-minute rule" (ending meetings at 50 minutes) allows for decent cognitive breaks

I recently engaged a coach, and was immediately impressed when she announced that we’d be meeting for 50-minute sessions. We’ve only spoken once, yet this one construct made me think more of her. There are folks who offer 25- or 45-minute meetings on their calendar apps, so there’s a way to change that default. Yet most situations require extra steps.

Switching focus, we've also established some non-software-driven habits that may no longer serve us. 

🔄 What about: 
- Holding meetings when an email-update would suffice
Engaging in lengthy email exchanges when a phone call would be faster (using the rule of 3 helps—once there are 3 emails about a topic, time to pick up the phone)

- Scrolling through email first thing in the morning and wasting prime energy on administrivia instead of spending prime brain real estate on nailing a key task

These are defaults that warrant scrutiny, since even when we know better, it’s not easy to resist the thing in front of us. Some ways of operating seem easier, even though a bit of scrutiny proves us wrong. And some of our assumptions seem inevitable, although they’re not:

🤔 What about:
- Only recognizing people during annual reviews
- Assuming we’re “bad with names” (so it's okay to forget them)
- Figuring people know what they’re good at

Got any habits you’ve escaped from? It would be great to hear some of the “norms” others have challenged. I know there are more out there …

I promise to highlight the best ones in The Swan Dive. A monthly newsletter with cool tools, a little brain science, and good dose of constructive mischief.

I've spent some years working in supply chain. You get really good at your slice of it. Your tools, your process, your company's setup. You learn it deeply. But supply chain is enormous.

The decisions driving pharma distribution look nothing like what drives fast fashion replenishment. The way an automotive OEM thinks about supplier risk is a completely different problem to how a food manufacturer handles demand variability. Same concepts. Wildly different applications.

Working inside one company, one industry, one supply chain setup is limiting in ways that are easy to miss until you step outside it.

That's why I'm starting Shetty's Desk.

I want to stay close to how these concepts actually play out across industries. The real use cases out there, what worked and what didn't. The research sitting in Tier 1 consulting briefs and academic papers that most practitioners never get to, I aim to learn for me and share these insights with you. 

Supply chain drives more decisions than most people outside the industry realize. That's a gap I believe is worth closing because it affects everyone. Going through the actual research, building it into something readable.

The first one is on Nearshoring. The math most teams use to model it is incomplete, and the gap between what companies are planning and what they're actually executing is one of the more interesting problems in the industry right now.

80% of COOs plan to nearshore. 98% haven't moved. The carousel maps why: the 7-factor total landed cost model, the Mexico FDI picture, and the go/no-go framework that holds up when your CFO starts asking questions.

What's a supply chain topic you've wanted to go deeper on?

#ShettysDesk #SupplyChainIntelligence #SCM #Nearshoring #COO

👋 How critical is remembering names? I remember my chiropractor’s dog’s name, “Tibby,” by associating it with the tibia (assuming that's part of anatomy studies). Remembering a dog’s name might not matter that much (Depends on the person … and the dog), yet having a way to remember people’s names is key for a slew of reasons.

First, don’t berate yourself if you’re bad with names—we all are. Mainly because proper nouns get way less brain attention. Fifty percent of our brain’s processing is devoted to vision, so we’re far more interested in faces.

It’s worth developing techniques for storing names since both remembering and forgetting a person’s name—or mispronouncing it—have an immediate impact on a person and, by extension, organizational culture.

When people hear their names, they tune right in (think back to the chill of hearing a parent pronounce your full name—that got your attention). On the flip side, forgetting someone’s name triggers a feeling of exclusion and a sense of being unimportant. Not a good way to foster engagement and collaboration.

I know of a company with 1,200 employees where the CEO knows every person’s name. That tells you a lot about that culture without even knowing what they do. It also illuminates the role of intention in remembering names. 

My husband—self-proclaimed “bad-with-names” spouse—could remember everyone’s drinks when he was a bartender. His recall was so good that, after being rear-ended, he looked into the rearview mirror and called out, “Whisky Sour!” upon recognizing the driver. Both he and the CEO remembered because they wanted to—it was important to them.

Want to remember? A few tips:

👂Receive: Introductions can be full of distraction so focus when people say their name—easier said than done.

🔁 Repeat: Say the person’s name once or twice when you’re introduced to give your brain a shot at remembering—repetition is fundamental to retention.

🧠 Relate: Since names are contextless, give them context. “Ben” is a big guy, and “Big Ben” is memorable (the association can be random, quirky, and nonsensical, which is okay since you’ll never share it!).

✍️ Record: Write it down if you can. I just discovered that one of my clients took on a rescue donkey named Gladys to protect her baby goats from coyotes. What? There is no way I want to forget about Gladys.

Remembering names isn’t about talent—it’s about intention. And intention, repeated, becomes culture. If a CEO can know 1,200 names, and a bartender can remember every drink, the rest of us probably aren’t “bad with names.” We’re just deciding what matters.

Why is the world's second-largest shipping company buying warehouses instead of ships?

For decades, the shipping industry followed a single rule: build larger ships to drive down costs. Maersk is breaking that mold by moving away from a model centered only on the ocean and building an integrated system instead, over the past few years.

The main objective is to escape the commodity trap. Ocean freight is currently volatile and price-sensitive, with on-time rates often stuck between 50% and 60%. Maersk is creating a sticky service model focused on three pillars:
- Total control: They manage the journey from the factory floor to the front doorstep.
- Predictable growth: Logistics services provide steady growth that protects the company from market crashes.
- Reliability: Maersk is betting that premium brands will pay more for a guaranteed 90% on-time delivery rate.

To own these assets, they spent $3.6 billion on LF Logistics and $1.68 billion on Pilot Freight Services. They are moving beyond port-to-port logistics. It is a gamble on being the most reliable player in the market instead of just the largest.

How do you get a customer to visit your store 17 times a year without spending 1€ on traditional advertising? 

Zara’s supply chain could actually be their best marketing department. I’ve been dissecting the difference between efficiency and responsiveness. In a traditional supply chain, the goal is the lowest cost per unit. But Zara doubled down on an alternative idea: a cheap shirt that nobody wants is the most expensive item in the warehouse. 

While the rest of the industry was drowning in unsold inventory and 50% off clearance racks, Zara wanted to build on three pillars of strategic speed:
- The Intentional Scarcity Loop: By changing floor designs every 14 days, they’ve gamified the shopping experience. The "buy or bye" psychology allows them to sell 85% of their stock at full price.
- Physical speed : Utilizing "The Cube", underground monorails and airfreight they deliver to European stores in 24 hours and global markets in 48 hours.
- Wait-and-See Manufacturing: Zara only commits about 50% of its production before a season starts. By keeping their capacity liquid, they secure flexibility.

They prioritize agility over cost by using air freight, focusing on proximal logistics. It is their play on being the most responsive player in the market instead of just the cheapest. 

My take: The fast fashion approach has a huge impact on the environment, I believe we have lots of work to be done with promoting more eco-friendly practices. Nonetheless, an interesting study on agility and responsiveness.

When exceptions become the operating model, you don’t notice it right away.

The team adjusts. Then adjusts again. Over time, the workaround sticks. What was meant to be temporary becomes routine.

The issue isn’t that exceptions exist. Every business has them.

The issue is when structure gives way to constant correction.

At that point, performance depends more on effort than structure.

More energy goes in. Stability doesn’t improve. Predictability starts to decline. When predictability declines, performance eventually stalls, even if activity increases.

One simple signal: if the standard process is hard to clearly describe, it may already be gone.

The real question isn’t whether you have exceptions.

It's this: how would you know if they’ve become your default way of working?

1 error in every 16 million deliveries ≈ 99.999999% accuracy. 

Six sigma certification defines world class with a tolerance of 3.4 defects per million. 

The Dabbawalas of Mumbai do 200,000+ daily deliveries within a 30 minute delivery window. Whatever you think that costs to run, you're wrong. 

It's only $14 a month per customer.

The Dabbawalas run on constraints so tight there's almost no room for a decision to go wrong and they've been doing it since 1890.

What KPMG, Deloitte, and Philips found when they looked closely:
• Design for simplicity: The system was designed for workers who couldn't read. That constraint forced standardization so complete that the coding system still hasn't needed an upgrade or no requirement for software.

• Multiple hand-offs: Each tiffin box changes hands at least six times in each direction≈2.4 million handoffs daily. With only 40 seconds to loads hundreds of boxes onto trains and only 20 seconds to switch trains. 

• The 1993 Trust Test: During the Mumbai bombings, police frisked every commuter on the suburban railway except the Dabbawalas. A century of reliable delivery built that.

Supply chain complexity is expensive. The Dabbawalas didn't build a better tracking system, they built a system that doesn't need one. 

What's the variability in your network that you're managing with technology instead of removing with design?

February 28, 2026: US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

March 1: insurance underwriters withdraw Hormuz coverage.

March 2: 170 container ships. 450,000 TEUs. Zero movement.

The world's most critical energy corridor took 48 hours to close.

The insurance market closed the Strait of Hormuz before any naval blockade. At $750,000 per transit, no carrier can afford to move through a war zone. 

The 90-day cascade from that decision is already in motion.
• The chokepoint scale: 20% of global oil, one-fifth of LNG, and one-third of global fertilizer trade all transit a waterway 39 kilometres wide. Bypass infrastructure covers only 13% of that flow.

• The insurance mechanism: War-risk premiums doubled in a single session, pushing annualised transit costs to $150-200 million per vessel. 

• The petrochemical blind spot: Iran's feedstock capacity is driving a 15-25% cost spike in plastics, adhesives, and specialty chemicals. 

My take: the Hormuz story is not about oil prices only. It is about an efficiency model that removed lots of buffer from global supply chains and left a 39km waterway as one of the last unhedged structural risk which will have much wider consequences across industries.

What other consequences do you think the Hormuz strait blockade will have on the global supply chain?

96% of dry cargo containers. 

100% of refrigerated ones. 

All manufactured in one country.

China produces 1,015.1 million tons of crude steel annually. India is second at 149.4 million. The US, Japan, and Russia combined are no competition.

Steel accounts for 60% of the cost of a container. Because China produces more steel than the rest of the world combined, the geography of the raw material now dictates the geography of the container industry.

American manufacturing owned the standard in 1956. Today, three companies (CIMC, DFIC, and CXIC) are the Boeing and Airbus of the shipping world.

What a closer look at the industrial data reveals: 
• The Logistics Loop: Building a container in the West requires importing Chinese steel, paying tariffs, and then shipping the heavy, empty box back to China to pick up goods. The math fails at every step. 
• Black Light Factories: This is no longer a story of cheap labor. These are state of the art facilities using laser welding and AI quality control. They are designed to run in the dark. 
• Regulatory Survival: In 2017, a mandate for water based paints forced every small manufacturer out of business. Only the Big Three had the state backed capital to upgrade their factories and absorb the market.

India is now challenging this logic with almost a $1 Billion Container Manufacturing Assistance Scheme. The goal is to build an annual capacity of 1 million TEUs and reduce the import of 2 million empty containers every year. It is a massive strategic bet to reclaim a seat at the table.

Supply chain resilience is easy to talk about but expensive to build. When the raw math of steel and scale favors a single geography, diversification becomes a cost most companies simply cannot pay.

What other foundation of your business is built on a logic you no longer control?

Petrol prices have increased by approximately $0.27 to $3.25 per gallon in the United States, and €0.33 to nearly €2.00 per litre in the Eurozone. Natural gas prices have risen by about $0.15 to $3.02 per MMBtu in the US, while Eurozone prices have surged by roughly €6.08 to €15.58 per MMBtu.
Action: Review fuel hedging, diversify energy sources, and ensure contracts include price adjustment mechanisms.
• Shipping costs and lead times increasing
Last week, shipping a 40ft container (FEU) from the Far East to Europe via the Strait of Hormuz (Suez Canal route) cost approximately $2,844–$3,000. Current reroutes around the Cape of Good Hope have pushed costs to $7,000–$8,500 per container, adding 10–14 days transit.
Action: Secure alternative carrier capacity, negotiate risk-sharing clauses, and review buffer stock for critical SKUs.
• Raw material exposure
Metal, petrochemicals and fertiliser supply is threatened (although it is too early to tell if the rise in fertiliser prices will translate to higher prices on supermarket shelves).
Action: Dual-source away from high-risk regions and map supplier dependencies at least two tiers deep.
• Air freight volatility
Global capacity of air cargo has reduced by a fifth leading to increases in rates, for example, rates from China to US have increased by 15% and South Asia to Europe by 3%. This puts pressure on electronics, pharmaceuticals, and automotive components supply chains.
Action: Prioritise air freight for revenue-critical items and reassess safety stock levels.
• Third party risk management
Margin pressure and disruption may increase supplier insolvency risk.
Action: Run financial health checks on top 20 suppliers; activate dual-source strategies; review contracts, especially force majeure clauses.
For procurement leaders, this is a reminder that geopolitics is now a core supply chain variable.
#Procurement #SupplyChain #RiskManagement

The wrong assumption is not that tariffs are expensive. It is that a 25% tariff rate = a 25% landed cost increase; it does not.

Most procurement and supply chain teams are pricing goods on a model built before the tariff regime tripled. Running landed cost on 4-5 components when 11 exist; means your finance team is working with numbers that are wrong by a margin of 38-52%. Every mispriced PO compounds that error, and 18-32% of the tariff burden your company paid last year may already be recoverable.

This edition of Shetty's Desk maps the 11-component Total Landed Cost (TLC) model, the duty drawback audit, and the TLC Leader matrix for identifying where your tariff management program actually stands.

Three key takeaways:
- 11 components make up total landed cost. Most company models count fewer than 5.
- Nike maintained 43-46% gross margin across 2018-2023 while peers absorbed 200-400 basis points of tariff compression.
- 18-32% of apparent tariff exposure is recoverable for companies with formal TLC programs, drawback claims, and HTS audits in place.

Why a 25% tariff rate ≠ a 25% landed cost increase?
Buffer inventory, brokerage complexity, and compliance overhead are the secondary costs it triggers. They compound the impact, and most models miss all of them.

How complete is the Total Landed Cost model your organisation currently uses for sourcing decisions?

Why does the world's most recognised energy drink not own a single factory?

9 cents. That is what it costs Red Bull to make its drink. The can it comes in costs more. Here is why that number is the entire strategy.

Red Bull outsources everything. Rauch Fruit Juice mixes and fills the beverage. Ball Corporation makes the can. Both partners are collocated on the same footprint in Austria, with direct rail and highway access built into the site. The supply chain is not lean by accident.

Three things that make it work:
• The SKU discipline: Red Bull runs 17 product configurations. Monster Energy manages 150+. Fewer variants means Rauch and Ball can optimise every production run. No variety tax in the supply chain.

• The collocation model: Until 2021, two Alpine sites supplied every can sold globally. Same layout each time: Rauch plant, Ball plant, rail access, highway access. Red Bull replicated the exact model in Phoenix in 2021 for the US market.

•  The cost split: Of every roughly $3 can, 9 cents covers the drink. Around $1 goes back into marketing and athlete sponsorship. The supply chain efficiency is what funds the brand engine.

My take: Red Bull did not build a beverage company, it built a marketing machine and designed the supply chain to be cheap enough to leave $1 per can for everything else.

If you removed your brand budget and looked at what your supply chain architecture is actually enabling or constraining in your organisation, what would you find?

I got to see the river otter peek his head out of the ice this morning. Adorable? Yes, but I’m relaying this as part of a “causal gratitude” experiment. 

You may already have a practice of writing down 3 things you’re grateful for at the start or end of a day, and if so, you’re probably aware that counting your blessings makes you a happier person. What you may NOT know is that you can experience longer-lasting positivity and resilience if you include the root cause of the thing you’re grateful for.

A new study from American Psychologist characterizes the classic “List-3-things” approach as passive. As if you’re simply the lucky recipient of great stuff that happens to you, whereas the reality is that you’ve generally had a hand in those things. This reminds me of the quote, “You make your own luck” (generally attributed to a string of luminaries stretching from country-singing legend Loretta Lynn to Roman Philosopher Seneca). 

Based on the neurological research, you get more impact if you not only note the thing you’re grateful for, “The vendor just reduced their prices”, but you also reflect on the cause, “because I spent time and effort on maintaining a good relationship." Seemingly subtle, but it changes things. 

🧪 Results of the Experiment:
I spent last week adapting my morning habit to reflect “causal” gratitude, and the experience has been mixed. It takes longer, since you have to sit with the cause for a second, and you might not be able to connect it. The example of the otter was fairly straightforward:

“I’m got to see the river otter stick his head out of the ice this morning because I made it a point to live on a pond and put my desk in front of a window.”

Other attempts felt a strangely self-congratulatory:

“I got to have fabulous coconut chicken curry last night because I married a great cook.”

In general, the practice forced me to own my part in what’s going well. It puts the Gratitude Practice slightly more adjacent to the Small Wins Practice (big fan). And, no surprise, that rewires your brain in a good way as well. So far, it’s a keeper.

If you’re interested in a less-stressed, more positive brain, try it out. What are you grateful for, and what do you suspect is the cause?

In supply chain transformations, I’ve often found that a hybrid delivery approach works better than committing to either Waterfall or Agile.

Certain parts of a transformation benefit from a more predictive structure (Waterfall), while others work better with a more adaptive approach (Agile). That’s why many large programs end up blending the two.

From experience, I’ve seen transformations struggle when they lean too far in either direction. That said, the method chosen really depends on the type of work being done.

If everything is too rigid and structured, parts of the solution may already be outdated by the time they roll out. If everything stays too loose, the work can drift, scope creep sets in, and the program never really stabilizes.

The transformations that delivered the most value and adoption had both program discipline and the ability to adapt as the work took shape inside the business.

A hybrid approach helps maintain the structure needed to move the program forward while still allowing flexibility and value to show up along the way.

Have you found Waterfall, Agile, or hybrid more effective in supply chain transformations?

🏀 Metrics are tricky because for good or ill—they drive behavior. What about the balance of individual versus team metrics? Or team versus organizational? What about metrics that capture effort versus focusing only on “wins”?

My family-induced obsession with basketball has me immersed in individual and team metrics. Sports provide an abundance of analogies because they’re so stat-heavy. When comparing their metric saturation to that of the business world, they’re more like call centers with hold times, abandonment rates, and resolution rates, etc. There’s much to learn from hoops.

The most obvious basketball stat is buckets made, yet the NBA and the WNBA have developed ways to capture effort. Basketball stats have evolved to capture collaboration and the overall impact of each team member, as opposed to simply the number of baskets they make. There are rebounds (efforts that get your team the ball), assists (efforts to that led to a teammate scoring), blocks (efforts that keep the opponent from scoring), and, added in 2007, the confounding “+/-” score for each player.

The +/- is controversial stat that apparently has early roots in the NHL and was originally called “The Team Contribution Index” or TCI. The idea grew as coaches and players tried to get at the impact of a player that wasn’t captured in standard metrics. The way they set screens, whether they hustled on defense, passes they made that weren’t assists, along with their leadership and playmaking. 

AI Definition: The plus/minus (+/-) score in basketball measures a player's impact on the game by calculating the net difference between their team's points scored and allowed while they are on the court. A positive number (+10) means the team outscored the opponent during their time, while a negative number (-5) indicates they were outscored. Pretty straightforward.

I hear arguments for and against the +/- stat. Some point out that it’s a helpful aggregate score, rather than looking at individual games. I’m not QUITE as steeped in this to argue for or against it, I just appreciate that they’re trying to capture the whole player. If you focus mainly on baskets made, then you are encouraging what they call “iso” or isolation play. Meaning, if the main metric is baskets made, then I’m focused on getting myself to the basket. 

There are endless reports of star players hitting new highs in points, yet the team still loses. But if you focus on a balance of metrics that include effort and impact, then the player is more likely to focus on helping their teammates and the team. 

Unlike the NBA, we can’t watch film or count assists, and it’s unclear how to translate the +/- to the business world, yet we need better effort metrics because they drive good team behavior and therefore benefit the institution as a whole.

❓  What kinds of effort-based metrics have you heard of or used that drove good behavior?

6 links. 1 product. If any single one fails, it does not arrive. That is a supply chain.

I'm starting a series called Supply Chain 101. A simple, yet fundamental breakdown of supply chain building blocks and concepts made easy to understand and follow.

Both for experts and non supply chain folks! 

So, what is a Supply Chain?

A supply chain is not a single department or one organisation, it is the sequence of steps, people, and companies that turns raw material into something sitting on a shelf with a name on it. 

• The Source and the Supplier: The first 2 links determine what the product is made of and whether there is enough of it. Every shortage, substitution, and quality failure traces back here.

• The Factory and the Warehouse: Links 3 and 4 are where raw material becomes product and where most of the cost is locked in before a single order is placed.

• The Delivery and the Customer: They are the moment where 5 previous decisions either pay off or unravel at the final customer and how it is brought to them.

Which of these 6 links does your organisation understand the least? And.. is that the same one that keeps producing surprises for your supply chain?

Most supply chain leaders tracking Hormuz are watching oil prices. 

The more important signal is Urea. 49% of global seaborne nitrogen is stranded inside the Gulf, as the biological clock for Northern Hemisphere spring planting runs in real time.

The March/April application window for corn, wheat, and soybean opened March 1. Unlike freight costs, missed nitrogen application creates permanent yield damage that no delayed shipment is able to recover.

• The feedstock chain: Qatar is simultaneously the world's largest LNG exporter and a dominant urea producer. Hormuz halted both. Fertilizer plants in India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh are cutting domestic production too, because the gas feedstock for manufacturing their own supply is also blocked.

• The 30-day rule: Agronomists confirm nitrogen applied after the first 30 days of plant growth cannot recover stunted root development. Current 2026 models project a 12% global cereal yield loss if the blockade holds through May.

• Brazil and India: Brazil has secured only 30% of its next crop inputs, with May/June arrivals unconfirmed. India needs 10 million tonnes of urea for Kharif season in June. Both are currently stranded inside the Gulf with no confirmed replacement source identified.

My take: Oil is one part of the picture, but this shortage of urea will have a broader impact on food prices across the globe moving forward. 

Which other dependencies in your supply chain have been halted due to the Hormuz strait deadlock since February 28?

Not every challenge in life can be fought.
Not every situation can be avoided.
Some problems require something smarter — strategy.
I recently watched a short wildlife clip that left me thinking.
A wild animal had a cheetah sitting on its back, ready to attack.
Running away? Not possible.
Fighting back? Almost certain death.
Instead of reacting in panic, the animal did something surprising.
It slowly walked into a nearby pond.
But the pond had crocodiles.
The moment the cheetah realized the danger, it jumped off.
Within seconds, the crocodiles turned their attention to the cheetah…
and the animal calmly walked away to safety.
No fight.
No panic.
Just smart thinking.
The lesson?
In life and in business, strategy often wins over struggle.
In corporate life, many of us carry our own “cheetah” on our backs:
• Office politics from a colleague
• A project that constantly creates pressure
• A manager who blocks new ideas
• A client who delays payments endlessly
Most people respond the same way.
They work harder.
They argue more.
They complain louder.
Yet nothing really improves.
Because sometimes the issue is not effort — it’s the approach.
Smart professionals understand this.
They don’t try to fight every battle.
They redesign the situation.
They adjust the process.
They change the conversation.
They involve the right stakeholders.
And suddenly, the problem resolves itself.
In corporate life, strength helps.
But strategy changes the game.

This is what took the U.S from their shores to the Battlefront on the Middle Eastern waters.

During replenishment, every 90 seconds, a 5,200-pound load crosses 200 feet of open ocean between two ships doing highway speed(on water). The U.S. Navy runs this operation with no warehouse, no dock, and no fixed infrastructure. This is the Navy's Underway Replenishment.

Two ships that are pitching independently in the wide ocean. 

Here's what makes the Navy's Underway Replenishment unique:
• Stream stations: A single tensioned highline delivers 104 tons per hour, and a Nimitz-class carrier runs six or more stations simultaneously to push combined throughput past 1,200 tons per hour across fuel, ordnance, and provisions.

• Tolerance envelope: Helmsmen hold two ships within plus or minus 10 feet of lateral separation at 12 knots for eight consecutive hours, maintaining course within 2 degrees and speed within half a knot.

• Full evolution: A carrier strike group transfers 6,000 short tons of material in a single UNREP window of six to ten hours, with load sequencing driven by consumption priority and ship stability.

I find it interesting that the Navy started with the worst constraint, constant motion over open water, and engineered backward. That inversion is why their system works under pressure and most commercial ones don't. 

When was the last time your organisation stress-tested throughput assumptions?

Logistics moves it. Supply chain decides whether it should be moved at all, from where, and at what cost. Two words people use interchangeably. Two very different jobs.

This is episode 2 of Supply Chain 101. Last week we defined what a supply chain actually is. This week we separate it from the function it gets confused with most often: Logistics.

Think about your morning coffee - someone had to decide which country to source those beans from, which supplier offered the best balance of quality and price, and how much inventory to hold so your café never runs out. That is supply chain. 

Someone else had to get those beans from the port to the roaster, from the roaster to the warehouse, and from the warehouse to the café before opening time. That is logistics.

• Logistics is movement and storage. It answers: is the right product arriving at the right place, on time, and at the right cost?
• Supply chain is the architecture around that movement. It answers: are we sourcing the right product, from the right supplier, in the right quantity, for the right market?
• The relationship: logistics is a function inside supply chain, not a synonym for it. 

Here is the thing most people miss: when a company calls its logistics team 'supply chain', the planning and sourcing decisions often have no clear owner. And decisions without owners get made by default rather than by design.

What does your company call the team that decides which suppliers to use and how much inventory to carry? Is that team the same one managing the trucks?

In under 2 seconds, 22 humans execute 80 coordinated actions to swap all four tires on a car.  Red Bull's pit crew practices the same 1.8-second sequence over 1,000 times between races. 

Most operations leaders assume more hands on a task means more coordination chaos. F1 proved the opposite, the difference is one word: parallel process.

• The 70-year curve: F1 pit stops fell from 67 seconds in 1950 to 1.80 seconds in 2023, a 97% reduction achieved without adding a single robotic arm.

• The architecture shift: 22 crew members execute over 80 actions simultaneously because each wheel station runs 3 dedicated roles in parallel, making total time equal to the slowest corner, not the sum of all four.

• The hidden blocker: Most SMED projects stall at 40% improvement because the cost of serial changeover design is buried in OEE spreadsheets, while F1 teams can price every lost tenth of a second in championship prize money north of $100K.

I believe that the biggest changeover gains in manufacturing aren't locked behind capital equipment budgets. They're locked behind the assumption that one technician working a sequential checklist is 'lean' when it's actually the most expensive process architecture you can run.

When was the last time your organisation mapped a changeover not by step duration, but by how many steps are sitting idle waiting their turn?

We just passed 3,000,000 subscribers on YouTube.
10 years ago, some of my corporate friends made fun of me for starting a YouTube channel. 

Fair enough. 
Corporate people didn't really take YouTube seriously back then.

But here's what 10 years and 3 million people taught me:

#1 - Don't box yourself in
I deliberately never named my channel "Excel." 
I knew I didn't want to be stuck in one lane. But even then, it took me years to actually post something outside of Excel because I was scared my audience wouldn't approve.

Then last year, I posted something completely different. 
A Rubik's cube tutorial. 
Yes. A Rubik's cube! On an Excel channel.

That video now has 3,000,000 views. It's actually still our #1 most watched video. Hundreds of people have commented that they finally solved a Rubik's cube because of it.

I almost didn't post it. I teach tools like Excel and Power BI. But I realized, my main thing is helping people solve problems. It doesn't always have to be Excel. 
After all, I left corporate because I didn't want to be boxed in. It didn't make sense to create that box in my own business.

#2 - Do things you're passionate about and stop overthinking it.
The Rubik's cube wasn't a strategy. I just loved it. 
Not everything has to be strategy. What's the fun in work if you can't take some time and do things you love.

#3 - Know when to switch from "growth mode" to "sustainable mode."
For years, I posted every week. Then twice a week. There was a time I posted three times. I was terrified that if I stopped, everything would collapse.

Then I started getting stressed out. I was working on videos, courses, everything. And I had a YouTuber friend whose burnout got so bad he couldn't turn the camera on anymore. Beautiful channel. But he just couldn't do it anymore.

I took a month off. I didn't want to start hating what I loved.
Nothing collapsed. The channel was fine.

Your stats do go down when you post less. But you have to decide what matters more. I love teaching, and I want to keep doing this for a while. So I found a pace I can actually sustain.

It's like losing weight. You need the calorie deficit to get there. But at some point, you have to eat in a way you can live with. And only you know when that point is.

I'm grateful for 3 million. But that's just a number. What makes me happier is reading the comments below the videos from people sharing their wins. Whether it's solving a Rubik's cube or getting a promotion because they finally learned Power Query.

What's something you almost didn't do but are really glad you did?

Every time a delivery gets missed where I work, the first question is always the same: was that a planning problem or a scheduling problem? It sounds like semantics, but the fix for each is completely different

This is episode 3 of Supply Chain 101. Last time we separated supply chain from logistics. Now we are going inside the factory, where two words that sound interchangeable are very different.

Think of it like architecture and construction. 

• Planning is the blueprint: it decides how many units of which product you need over the next month, whether your lines have enough capacity, and which product families take priority. 
It works on the assumption that resources will be available when it is time to execute. 
That assumption makes planning useful, but it also makes it fragile, because the production floor does not operate on assumptions.

• Scheduling is the construction crew: It takes that blueprint and figures out the actual sequence: which order runs on which machine, when changeovers happen, what to do when Machine 3 is down for maintenance on Wednesday and the raw material for Batch 7 arrived a day late. 
These are not planning failures but floor realities that require a completely different kind of decision-making: trade-offs between competing orders, real-time sequencing, and working within whatever capacity is actually available right now.

• Where it breaks is the space between the two. If the planner hands over a monthly volume target without understanding what the floor looks like this week, the scheduler essentially starts from scratch every morning. And if the scheduler never feeds back what actually happened, next month's plan gets built on the same assumptions that already failed.

If you look at the bigger picture, this is one of the most underestimated gaps in manufacturing. 

So next time your production team misses a target: was the plan wrong, or did the plan just not survive contact with the floor?

She bombed in front of 100 executives.
Then she turned it into her superpower.

In her early 30s, Elisabeth Swan discovered improv comedy.
No script. 
No safety net. 
Just you, a stage, and whatever the audience throws at you.

She was also building a career in Lean Six Sigma, helping organizations solve problems and eliminate waste. On the surface, improv and process improvement seem like they belong in different zip codes.

But here's what she learned performing with ImprovBoston:
Improv IS problem solving. It just happens on stage.
You take unknown inputs. 
You build with what you're given. 
You say "yes, and" to move things forward. 
You listen, really listen, because your next move depends on it.

And the secret? 
Improv has structure. 
Rules. 
Rehearsal.
Structure sets you free.

That's also the heart of continuous improvement. 
PDSA, DMAIC, 5 Whys; they're not cages. 
They're launchpads that save you from the terror of the blank page.

So when Elisabeth led Starwood Hotels' Six Sigma transformation, 
she carried improv with her everywhere.

Then came Sardinia.
A gorgeous resort. 
Global leaders from Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. 
Four simulations running simultaneously. 
She'd been awake for 25 hours. 
Her partner was unprepared. 
A European leader torpedoed the exercise.

The simulation broke.

She was devastated. 
She'd gone from a Wall Street Journal write-up to a spectacular faceplant.

The next morning, a change management consultant dragged her out of her misery:
"Elisabeth, have you never bombed before?"
"No."
"Oh, PLEASE. Let me tell you..."
And one by one, they all shared their disasters. 
Their spectacular failures. 
Their human moments.

That day taught her something improv had been whispering all along:

Mistakes are gold.

Not because failure feels good. 
But because how fast you pivot from a misstep to a learning moment defines your trajectory.
And you can play a role in helping other people survive their faceplants.

Elisabeth worked with Starwood and Marriott for decades after that.

Years later, when a partnership collapsed at the start of COVID, those same improv muscles kicked in. 
Accept reality. 
Build with what you have. 
Keep moving forward.

She started writing weekly stories on LinkedIn. 
Sharing her faceplants. 
Drawing illustrations. 
Asking: How did YOU deal with this?

The response was overwhelming. 
It became an award-winning book (Picture Yourself a Leader). 
It opened doors to keynotes and speaking.

All from the same place improv taught her to operate: 
Say "yes, and." 
Listen deeply. 
Make others look good. 
When you fall, get back up. 
Then help the next person up, too.

When I asked Elisabeth what she wants her legacy to be, she said:

"She helped me see how capable I am.
She made learning and making mistakes fun.
She made me feel like I mattered."

After spending time with her, I believe she's already living that legacy.

Read the full conversation with Elisabeth in this month's Faceplant Files.

When strategic decisions get made with operational urgency, companies build warehouses they don't need. When operational decisions wait for strategic approval, customers don't get their orders. 

This is Episode 4 of Supply Chain 101. Last time we separated planning from scheduling. Today we're splitting planning itself into three layers, because treating them as one is where things start going sideways.

•  Strategic planning operates in years. It's about network design, market entry, and where to place capacity. The people in the room are the CEO, the VP of Supply Chain, and sometimes the board. These decisions shape everything downstream and they're expensive to reverse.

• Tactical planning operates in months to quarters. This is S&OP territory (which we'll cover in Episode 5). The question is: given the capacity we have, how do we allocate it across product lines and regions? Directors and senior managers own this layer, and the quality of their decisions depends entirely on whether the strategic layer above gave them clear guardrails.

• Operational planning operates in days to weeks. Which orders get prioritised? What do we produce on which line? This is where planners and schedulers live, and it's where most of the visible firefighting happens.


If you look a little closer, the problem isn't that companies don't plan. It's that they don't separate the layers. A five-year capacity question gets debated in a weekly operations meeting, or a daily prioritisation decision waits three weeks for a director's sign-off. Both cost money, both are avoidable.

Forecasting is not guessing — it’s structured decision making.

Choosing the right forecasting method can directly impact:
✔ Inventory levels
✔ Capacity utilization
✔ Customer delivery performance

Here are 4 widely used forecasting techniques every planner should know:

🔹 Naive / Simple Average
Best for stable demand with minimal variation. Quick and easy starting point.

🔹 Simple Moving Average (SMA)
Smooths fluctuations by averaging past ‘n’ periods. Ideal for moderate variability.

🔹 Weighted Moving Average (WMA)
Gives more importance to recent data (e.g., 0.5, 0.3, 0.2). Useful when trends are changing.

🔹 Exponential Smoothing
Applies a smoothing factor (α) to make forecasts more responsive. Best for dynamic and volatile demand.

No single method works for all scenarios.

 The real strength lies in:
👉 Understanding demand behavior
👉 Selecting the right model
👉 Continuously improving accuracy using MAPE, Bias & Tracking Signal

Sales says we'll sell 10,000 units. Operations says we can make 7,000. Finance has budgeted for 8,500. Somebody has to be wrong. S&OP is the process that figures out who, and what to do about it.

Today, we're onto Episode 5 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 4 we covered the three levels of planning. S&OP lives in the tactical layer, and it's probably the most talked-about process in supply chain that is also the most inconsistently executed.

S&OP stands for Sales and Operations Planning. It's a monthly cycle with five steps, and each one has a specific purpose:

• Demand Review is where the commercial side presents its forecast. What do we expect to sell, where, and when? 
• Supply Review is where operations responds with what's actually possible given current capacity, materials, and constraints. 
• Pre-S&OP is where the gaps between those two get surfaced and options are prepared. 
• Executive S&OP is where leadership makes the trade-off decisions (do we add a shift, delay a launch, or accept the shortfall?). 
• Implementation is where those decisions get translated into the operational and financial plans that everyone works from.

Here's the thing most people miss: the meeting itself is maybe 30% of the value. The other 70% comes from the preparation between meetings and the accountability that follows. Companies that treat S&OP as a monthly slide deck get monthly slide deck results. Companies that treat it as a decision-making rhythm get aligned execution.

If someone told you buying AI was like buying a cake, it might sound like an April Fool’s joke. Well, Jensen Huang of NVIDIA described AI not as a single tool, but as a “five-layer cake”.

For most procurement professionals, the focus is on the AI models and applications, but for the AI labs like Anthropic and the hyperscalers like Google, the supply chain in more complicated. The cake, or AI stack, includes:
- energy (e.g. Constellation Energy providing energy from nuclear reactors through long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs))
- compute (e.g. NVIDIA’s H100 GPUs are currently the industry standard for large-scale AI training and inference)
- cloud infrastructure (e.g. Amazon Web Services’ Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is one of the industry-standard, foundational service for cloud computing)
- AI models (e.g. Anthropic’s Claude model is often favoured for coding, creative writing and nuanced reasoning)
- applications (e.g. Cursor provides AI-native Integrated Development Environment (IDE) is a software application that provides an interface for developers to write, edit, test, and debug code efficiently)

Making a cake requires many ingredients as well as a variety of skills. Procuring the AI stack is no different. It involves multiple categories of spend, and a range of capabilities, from category management and strategic sourcing to procurement operations. In this respect, procurement is required to orchestration an entire ecosystem.

Like all categories of spend, procurement benefit from understanding not only the risk from first tier suppliers but the risk from second tier suppliers.

The most expensive supplier you have isn't the one charging you the most. It's the one your team is afraid to renegotiate with.
I've audited supplier relationships at six companies over 25 years.

The same pattern shows up every time.

There's always one or two vendors who've been "partners" for 10+ years. Long-tenured relationships. Senior contacts who maybe golf with someone at your company. Contracts that auto-renew because nobody wants to have the awkward conversation.

And almost without exception, those are the vendors who haven't had a meaningful pricing review in years.

The vendor you just onboarded last year? They got benchmarked, negotiated, and evaluated against alternatives. Their pricing is close to market.

The 12-year "partner"? Their margins are often 15-25% above market — protected by relationship, inertia, and the organizational myth that "the switching costs are too high."

Switching costs are real. I'm not dismissing them.

But the math on never having the conversation compounds year after year.

Here's what actually works:

Separate the relationship from the commercial review. "We value you as a long-term supplier. We also value market-rate pricing. Here's what comparable suppliers are charging."

Use data, not ultimatums. Show them where they sit against benchmark. Let the numbers do the talking so the conversation doesn't feel personal.

Give them the first chance to respond before going to market. Most long-term suppliers would rather reprice than lose the volume.

At Veza, we ran this exercise across our top 10 vendors. Achieved 4.6% cost reduction — without switching a single one of them.

The relationship survived. The pricing improved. Everybody left the table knowing where they stood.

When was the last time your longest-tenured supplier had a real pricing review?

The Army put me in charge of 46 soldiers, 15 vehicles, and $14 million in equipment when I was 23 years old. The Army had very high opinions of 23-year-olds.
Looking back, the most useful supply chain education I ever got wasn't my MBA.

It was the two years before it.

Some things the Army drilled into me that I still use managing multi-million dollar supplier networks today:

Logistics is leadership. In the field, when your supply line fails, the mission fails. Period. "We ran out" isn't a weather event — it's a planning failure. I brought that same standard to every procurement role I've had since. We don't run out. That's a decision, not a hope.

Plan for the worst case before it's the worst case. Military planning always starts with "what's the most dangerous thing that could happen" — and then works backwards. I do the same with supplier networks. If your most critical supplier called today and said they were shutting down: how long could you operate? If you don't know the answer, you haven't finished the planning.

Systems beat willpower. 46 people, 15 vehicles — I couldn't personally verify everything. I had to build checklists, accountability structures, and reporting systems that worked when I wasn't in the room. A supply chain that only works when the right person is watching it isn't a system. It's a dependency.

Communicate more than feels necessary. In the field, the most dangerous thing is someone who assumed instead of confirmed. I've watched million-dollar supplier problems start the same way — someone assumed a contract auto-renewed. Someone assumed the vendor knew about the spec change. Assume nothing. Confirm everything.

I've been out of the Army for 27 years. These four lessons still show up in some form every single week.

What's the most useful professional lesson you got from an unexpected place?

Why does IKEA build millions of bookshelves before anyone orders one, while Dell used to wait for your exact configuration before assembling a single laptop? 

Both were right. The difference is where each company draws the line.

This is Episode 6 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 5 we covered S&OP and how companies align sales ambition with operational reality. 

Today we're looking at the fundamental design choice underneath all of that: do you make before the customer asks, or after?

• A push supply chain produces based on what it expects to sell. Raw materials are ordered, products are manufactured, and inventory is moved into warehouses and stores before a single customer order exists. The upside is speed to the customer. The risk is overstock, markdowns, and waste when the forecast is wrong.

• A pull supply chain waits for actual demand. Nothing moves until a customer places an order. The upside is that you only build what's been bought. The risk is longer lead times and the possibility that customers won't wait.

But here's what makes this more interesting than a simple either/or: most supply chains are hybrid. They push up to a certain point (raw materials, components, semi-finished goods) and pull from that point forward (final assembly, customisation, delivery). 

That boundary is called the decoupling point, and where you place it determines your inventory, your lead time, and your responsiveness.

• Moving the decoupling point upstream makes you more responsive but requires better demand visibility.
• Moving it downstream makes you more efficient but slower to react. 

There's no universal right answer, only a right answer for your product, your customer, and your market. Where does the decoupling point sit in your supply chain? And did someone choose it, or did it just end up there?

Deloitte published a piece on the agentic supply chain worth reading if you’re in manufacturing or supply chain.

A few things that stood out:
• Agents support a more continuous planning approach through sensing, decision-making, and response instead of waiting on traditional planning cycles.
• This isn’t one agent doing everything. It’s layered across cross-functional, domain, and task-level agents working together across the flow.
• Dropping agents into existing workflows may miss the mark. Redesigning workflows around what humans and agents each do well provides more benefit.
• Humans still own oversight, judgment, and decision thresholds. Agents operate within those boundaries. Governance is treated as foundational, not something added later.

Deloitte also cited Gartner’s projection that ~50% of supply chain management solutions will include agentic AI by 2030. I can see this happening.

Lately I’ve been using Claude to run some simple agents with anonymized data. Things like checking planning data (lead times, purchase order dates, safety stock, etc.), flagging errors, and suggesting corrections based on defined rules or analysis. I’ve also been using it to run existing Python scripts against historical demand and generate forecast recommendations across different models for comparison and approval.

It’s still early, though the shift is noticeable from a productivity standpoint.

Sometimes it's hard to know what your boss expects. That's why I created a user manual for my team.
Your annual goals and company objectives should be crystal clear. You should be discussing them weekly in your one-on-ones with your boss, and they should be driving your day-to-day work.
But the real question is never about the big goals.
It's about the small decisions. The unplanned fire you need to put out. The gray area where you have to act but you can't check in on everything. What's your frame of reference?
I had a leader who asked their management team to create a few bullet points describing what they actually care about — not the HR version, but the real version. What would the team do if they had to make a decision with zero guidance? I've come to call it my "user manual."
These are the five critical behaviors I expect from my team:
·       Open, clear communication
·       Momentum Driven

How does a car manufacturer decide to build 50,000 vehicles before a single buyer walks into a dealership? And why would a yacht builder refuse to start without a signed contract and a custom specification? 
The answer is the production strategy.

This is Episode 7 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 6 we covered push vs. pull and the decoupling point. Today we're zooming in on what that looks like in practice, because the production strategy is essentially where your company has placed that line.

There are three main strategies, and the simplest way to understand them is by asking: where does the customer order enter the process?

• Make to Stock (MTS) means you produce finished goods before any customer order exists. The product sits on a shelf or in a warehouse, ready to ship. Think cereal, toothpaste, or IKEA furniture. The advantage is immediate availability. The risk is that you're betting your forecast is right, and when it isn't, you're sitting on inventory nobody wants.

• Make to Order (MTO) means production only starts after a customer places an order. Think custom furniture, industrial equipment, or a Dell laptop circa 2005. The advantage is no finished goods inventory and a product tailored to the order. The trade-off is a longer lead time that the customer has to accept.

• Engineer to Order (ETO) means even the design doesn't start until the customer commits. Think Boeing aircraft, offshore oil platforms, or bespoke machinery. The advantage is a product built exactly to specification. The reality is lead times measured in months or years and a supply chain built entirely around project management.

Here's the thing most people miss: the mistake isn't choosing the wrong strategy. It's running one strategy across an entire portfolio when different product lines need different approaches. Your commodity products and your custom products should not be on the same planning logic.

Which strategy does your highest-margin product line use? And was that a deliberate choice?

Procurement is full of brilliant people who can't get their ideas heard.

It's not a knowledge problem.

It's an influence problem. 👇

❌ They have the right answer but can't get buy-in. 
❌ They know what needs to change but lack the authority to change it. 
❌ They're seen as a support function. Not a strategic one.

But the best procurement leaders I've worked with?

✅ Decisions get made differently when they're in the room. 
✅ They get buy-in without forcing it. 
✅ They move organisations. Without a mandate.

Most of them couldn't even tell you what they do differently. But watch them closely and there's a pattern.

Here's what they unknowingly do:

1. The 4C's Framework 

↳ Competence: demonstrate your expertise 
↳ Care: show you want the best for others 
↳ Character: lead with integrity 
↳ Consistency: be dependable in your actions

You cannot influence without trust. These four build it.

2. The S-C-Q-A Framework 

↳ Situation: what's the current state? 
↳ Complication: what's the challenge? 
↳ Question: what needs to be solved? 
↳ Answer: present your solution

Confident, clear communication builds trust. And it speeds up buy-in.

3. The 3 Pillars of Influence 

↳ Ethos (Credibility): consistent, competent, trustworthy 
↳ Pathos (Emotion): connect emotionally, understand their needs 
↳ Logos (Logic): use facts and data to strengthen your reasoning

The best influencers integrate all three. Especially when they don't have the formal authority.

4. Prioritise alliances over short-term consensus 

↳ Map your stakeholders: decision-makers, influencers, those affected 
↳ Pre-align your idea one-on-one with key stakeholders 
↳ Align objectives, share quick-wins, and publicly share credit 
↳ Co-ordinate messaging so allies present a united front

Alliances create momentum. They turn strong ideas into action.

5. The Principle of Reciprocity 

↳ Give before you ask 
↳ Share helpful resources 
↳ Support others' goals 
↳ Recognise contributions

People back those who have backed them.

Here's what most people miss.

Influence has nothing to do with where you sit in the hierarchy. It never has.

A CPO who doesn't understand these principles will struggle. 

A junior buyer who does will outperform people three levels above them.

Anyone can build this. At any level. If they understand the principles.

Start applying it wherever you are.

Thoughts on the future of Supply Chain, driving forces and scenarios to manage 
 
The last three decades were built on one logic: 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲, 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲, 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁. That logic is being dismantled by five forces operating simultaneously: 
🎷 𝗴𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: The trade system is no longer just about tariffs,  sanctions, export controls, industrial policy, and AI access restrictions, turning network design into a geopolitical decision.
🎷 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗜: Industrial robots and agentic AI are becoming real operational tools, but we see a bottleneck in the organizations: curiosity to explore new ideas, data quality, process redesign, and the willingness to trust AI. 
🎷 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗯𝗼𝗻: Carbon pricing, shipping decarbonization mandates, and route disruptions (Hormuz,  Suez) make the cost of distance a strategic variable, not a logistics footnote. 
🎷 𝗰𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆: Three regions control 86% of the processing capacity for the materials that power electrification, AI infrastructure, and defense modernization simultaneously, and investment is not keeping up with demand
🎷 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗽𝘂𝘀𝗵 𝘁𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗰𝗶𝗿𝗰𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆: Regulation is forcing companies to design for end-of-life before they design for production. Reverse logistics networks required to comply do not yet exist at scale.

I use those forces to develop 4 possible scenarios and reflect on how the supply chain might look in 2030 and 2040:
🎷 𝗙𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 & 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘂𝘀 (most probable): The world splits into blocs, but automation and AI absorb the cost of that complexity
🎷 𝗚𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗻 & 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱: Carbon pricing and shipping decarbonization reshape the economics of distance before technology fully compensates. Supply chains shorten.
🎷 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗙𝗹𝗮𝘁 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱: Geopolitical tensions ease, and AI matures fast enough to make global networks smarter and cheaper than regional ones. The upside case.
🎷 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗻𝘁 & 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗱: Fragmentation deepens, automation stalls, and companies are left with brittle networks and no technology. The tail risk nobody wants to plan for, but should

Supply chain leaders need to work on 𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁, not the lowest total landed cost. A network designed for minimum reconfiguration cost builds optionality from the start. Companies may find they 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗵𝘆𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆

There are over 250 supply chain metrics in common use. SCOR organises them into 6 processes and 5 performance attributes. It's the closest thing supply chain has to a universal language, and it's been around since 1996.

This is Episode 8 of Supply Chain 101. We've spent the last few episodes building up the vocabulary of how supply chains plan, produce, and respond to demand. Today we're stepping back and looking at the whole picture, because SCOR is the framework that ties all of it together.

SCOR stands for Supply Chain Operations Reference. 
It was developed in 1996 and it does something deceptively simple: it says every supply chain on earth, regardless of industry, performs the same six processes.
• Plan sits at the centre. It's the process that balances demand and supply and coordinates everything else 
• Source is how you acquire what you need
• Make is how you transform it
• Deliver is how you get it to the customer
• Return handles anything that comes back 
• Enable is the foundation underneath all five: the rules, data, technology, and people that keep the system running

On the measurement side, SCOR gives you five performance attributes to evaluate how well those processes work: 
• Reliability (do you deliver what you promised?)
• Responsiveness (how fast?)
• Agility (can you flex when things change?)
• Cost (what does it cost to operate?)
• Asset Management (how efficiently do you use what you have?)

SCOR is misunderstood only as an academic exercise, but it's more of a benchmarking tool. 

A supply chain manager at a food company and one at an electronics firm can compare reliability scores because the definitions are standardised. That comparability is what makes it powerful, and it's what most internal KPI dashboards lack.

If you had to pick one of those five attributes your company is weakest on, which would it be?

After 30 days of deployment, you face one decision: scale, fix, or stop.

Most organizations skip this step. They assume deployment equals adoption.

Before you decide, run three checks.

Look for parallel processes. Who is running the old process alongside the new one "just to verify"? That person is not verifying. They are protecting themselves.

Watch what managers actually do. Not what they say in meetings. If the manager still asks for the old report format, the team reads that as a signal.

Check the corridor narrative. What do people say about the tool when you are not in the room? That is the truth about your adoption.

If adoption grows: scale to the next team.
If adoption is flat: fix the block before expanding.
If adoption declines: stop. Something fundamental is broken.

A project leader would move on at this point. A product leader stays and makes the call. That distinction decides whether the tool lives or dies.

DEMAND PLANNING (NEXT LEVEL)
Most people forecast. Few actually plan.
Everyone knows the basics: What • When • How Much
But real demand planning starts when you ask:
Why is demand changing—and what will it cost if I’m wrong?

1. Not all demand behaves the same 
Stable → optimize cost
Seasonal → manage timing
Trend → control scaling risk
Irregular → protect with buffers
Misclassification = wrong inventory, wrong decisions.

2. There is no universal forecasting model
Stop applying one method to all SKUs. Match model to behavior. Segment demand properly. Accept trade-offs (accuracy vs responsiveness)

3. Accuracy is incomplete without direction
MAPE tells you how wrong, Bias tells you where you’re leaning
High bias = overstock or stockouts
Low visibility = unstable decision

4. Forecast = business impact
Every number affects: Inventory investment, Service level, Lost sales or excess stock, this is not reporting, this is financial decision-making.

5. Discipline is what creates results
Before ordering: Validate trend vs noise. Check real demand drivers.
When issues happen:
Overstock → check bias
Stockout → check missed signals
And always: No adjustment without a reason. No decision without impact.
Bottom line, High accuracy alone is not success.
The real goal is balance: Service level • Inventory • Cost

That’s what separates a planner from a decision-maker.

A business student asked me for the single most important skill in procurement. I didn’t say negotiation. I didn’t say financial acumen. My answer surprised them.

I’ve been on the Penn State Behrend Black School of Business Advisory Board for a few years now, and every semester I get a version of the same question:

"What’s the most important skill I can have?"

My answer: Be able to drive who does what by when.

Not the answer they expect. But here’s why it’s the right one.

Procurement is at its heart a program management challenge. It doesn’t matter whether you’re timing in a new supplier, completing a new contract before the current one expires, or managing supplier compliance. Every one of these has gates and players that all need to move together.

That means leading internal and external stakeholders — making sure every one of them is talking to each other, establishing critical dates, and holding people accountable when those dates start to slip.

The best procurement leaders I’ve worked with aren’t the ones with the sharpest negotiation tactics. They’re the ones with clear systems to track commitments and the willingness to have the hard conversation when things fall behind. They’re velvet hammers — firm enough to keep the team moving at pace, skilled enough to do it without breaking relationships.

Without that discipline, nothing happens. The contract stalls. The qualification timeline drifts. The supplier misses a gate and nobody escalates until it’s a crisis.

When you drive the bus, you’re a lot less likely to be run over by it.

I tell the students: the skill isn’t the tactics. The skill is the willingness to keep people to their word.

The rest is just spreadsheets and phone calls.

• Procurement is the months of research: which brands, which features, which dealerships have the best reputation and financing terms.

This is Episode 9 of Supply Chain 101. So far we've covered the language of supply chain: planning layers, production strategies, and frameworks. Now we're moving into the mechanics. How supply chains buy, hold inventory, manage cost, and move goods. And it starts here, with the most commonly confused pair of words in the profession.

• Purchasing is operational and executional. It's the daily work of converting a need into a transaction: sending purchase orders, confirming delivery dates, managing invoices. 
• Procurement is strategic. It's the work of deciding who to buy from, where to source, at what terms, and under what quality standards. Procurement designs the supplier relationship before purchasing executes it. 

Here's the confusing part: when companies conflate the two, strategic decisions get treated like operational tasks. A supplier that should be evaluated on total cost, reliability, and alignment gets chosen because they responded to the RFQ fastest. And vice versa: operational orders that just need to go out get held up by strategic review they don't require.

Does your company have a procurement strategy, or just a purchasing department?

Why does the team buying raw materials for your product report to the VP of Supply Chain, while the team buying laptops, cleaning services, and travel reports to... nobody in particular?

This is Episode 10 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 9 we separated purchasing from procurement. Today we're splitting procurement itself into two categories, because the difference determines how much attention (and money) each one gets.

• Direct procurement covers everything that ends up in the finished product: raw materials, components, packaging. If you make cars, it's the steel, the electronics, the tyres. These categories get dedicated teams, supplier scorecards, and quarterly business reviews because the link between what you buy and what you sell is obvious.

• Indirect procurement covers everything the company needs to operate that doesn't touch the product: IT infrastructure, office supplies, facility management, travel, MRO (maintenance, repair, and operations), and professional services. These categories are often fragmented across departments, managed by whoever happens to need the service, and renewed on autopilot.

What I see is indirect spend is typically 15-30% of revenue, and in most organisations it has a fraction of the strategic oversight that direct spend receives. Not because the money is small, but because it's spread across dozens of categories with no single owner. And that fragmentation is exactly why it's where some of the easiest savings sit. 

The contrarian view is simple: if you've already optimised your direct material costs, the next lever isn't pushing suppliers harder. It's looking at the indirect side of the ledger where contracts auto-renew and nobody benchmarks.

Who owns indirect spend in your organisation?

📦 1) COGS (Cost of Goods Sold)

Meaning:
Direct cost of producing or purchasing the product you sell.

What’s included:

Raw materials / purchase price
Direct labor
Manufacturing costs (if applicable)

What’s NOT included:

Shipping to customer
Marketing, salaries, overhead
Import duties

Formula:

𝐶𝑂𝐺𝑆=𝑂𝑝𝑒𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝐼𝑛𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑜𝑟𝑦+𝑃𝑢𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑠−𝐶𝑙𝑜𝑠𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝐼𝑛𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑜𝑟𝑦

Or per unit:

𝐶𝑂𝐺𝑆=𝑈𝑛𝑖𝑡 𝑃𝑢𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑎𝑠𝑒 𝑃𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒+𝐷𝑖𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑡 𝐶𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑠

Example:
You buy a product for $100 and spend $10 manufacturing →
👉 COGS = $110

🚚 2) Landed Cost

Meaning:
The true cost of getting the product to your warehouse.

What’s included:

Product cost (COGS base)
Freight (international + local)
Insurance
Customs duties
Taxes
Port handling & clearance

Formula:

𝐿𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑒𝑑 𝐶𝑜𝑠𝑡=𝑃𝑟𝑜𝑑𝑢𝑐𝑡 𝐶𝑜𝑠𝑡+𝑆ℎ𝑖𝑝𝑝𝑖𝑛𝑔+𝐷𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑒𝑠+𝑇𝑎𝑥𝑒𝑠+𝐻𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑔+𝐼𝑛𝑠𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒

Example:

Product = $100
Shipping = $20
Duty = $10
Clearance = $5

👉 Landed Cost = $135

💡 This is the real cost per unit before selling

💼 3) TCO (Total Cost of Ownership)

Meaning:
The full lifecycle cost of owning or using a product—not just buying it.

What’s included:

Landed cost
Storage / warehousing
Maintenance
Operating costs
Downtime / risk
Disposal cost

Formula:

𝑇𝐶𝑂=𝑃𝑢𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑎𝑠𝑒 𝐶𝑜𝑠𝑡+𝑂𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝐶𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑠+𝑀𝑎𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒+𝐼𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑡 𝐶𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑠

Example:

Landed cost = $135
Storage = $15
Maintenance = $20
Loss/damage risk = $10

👉 TCO = $180

💡 This is critical for long-term decisions—not just pricing

| Metric          | Scope           | Use Case                   |
| --------------- | --------------- | -------------------------- |
| **COGS**        | Production only | Profit calculation         |
| **Landed Cost** | Up to warehouse | Pricing & import decisions |
| **TCO**         | Full lifecycle  | Strategic decisions        |

🧠 The Big Insight (Most people miss this)
COGS is accounting
Landed Cost is logistics reality
TCO is business strategy

If you price based on COGS only → you’ll lose money without noticing
If you ignore TCO → you might choose the wrong supplier or product

A supplier walked into our negotiation asking for a price increase. We pulled up their own website. It was bragging about record profits. You could see the color drain from their faces.

Here’s the full story:

When I was at GE, we negotiated electronic component pricing as an enterprise — consolidating volume across divisions to get the best deals. We’d meet with major manufacturers twice a year to set pricing for the next six months. Millions of dollars on the table every session.

One manufacturer came in asking for price increases across the board. Not a small ask — this would have cost us millions.

Their pitch was polished. Costs were up. Raw materials were squeezing margins. They needed capital investment to keep pace with production. The whole story sounded reasonable.

Then the lead negotiator on our side opened a laptop and pulled up the manufacturer’s own website.

Their investor page was celebrating record profits. Their press releases touted cost-cutting measures that had driven margins to all-time highs. They had glossy photos of the brand-new high-speed machines that had reduced their labor costs.

We asked them to square what was on the screen with what they had just told us.

There was nothing they could say.

The supplier agreed to a price reduction. Their own words had made the case for us.

The lesson: The best leverage in a negotiation isn’t volume or threats. It’s preparation. When you walk in with data — benchmarks, public filings, their own press releases — the conversation changes completely. You’re not arguing opinion against opinion. You’re presenting facts.

The negotiator who’s done the homework rarely has to raise their voice.

When has doing your homework given you an unexpected edge in a negotiation?

A 5% increase in consumer demand can become a 40% spike at the raw material supplier!?!

Each link in the chain over-orders to protect itself, and the further upstream you go, the wilder the swings get. This has had a name since 1961 and most supply chains today are struggling to solve for it.

This is Episode 11 of Supply Chain 101. We're following the mechanics of how supply chains operate. Today's concept is the bullwhip effect, and once you see it, you'll recognise it everywhere.

Procter & Gamble first documented this with Pampers nappies. Retail sales were remarkably stable, but upstream orders were swinging wildly. The supply chain was reacting to orders, not to demand, and the gap between those two things is where the bullwhip lives.

There are four root causes, and they all share a common thread:
• Demand signal processing: each tier forecasts from orders, not actual demand
• Order batching: companies order in bulk at intervals rather than continuously
• Price fluctuations: promotions and discounts create artificial demand spikes
• Rationing and shortage gaming: when supply is tight, buyers inflate orders to secure allocation

What I believe is that this isn't a forecasting problem. It's an information-sharing problem. The fix isn't better algorithms. It's making actual demand data visible further upstream so every tier works from the same signal instead of amplifying it.

How many tiers up does your actual demand data travel?

It is one of the most common questions heard in a boardroom after a supply chain crisis, and it is almost always asked by someone who, three months earlier, was sitting in a quarterly review that ended with the words "operations are running smoothly." The revenue was up, the new market entry was ahead of plan, and nobody had mentioned  Supply Chain because nobody needed to. When it works, it is invisible, and invisibility in that room feels like the highest possible endorsement a supply chain team will ever receive.

Then a single component goes on allocation somewhere in an overseas supplier network, and within days, the picture looks completely different. Shipments stop, customers escalate, and the CEO who was closing slides with quiet confidence is now standing in front of a crisis that seems to have appeared from nowhere. Except it did not appear from nowhere. The risk was visible in reports that nobody had read, in risk registers that nobody had requested, in the heads of planners who had flagged it quietly and moved on because nobody senior had ever thought to ask.

It was managed from a distance, measured on cost, and noticed only when something broke.
The companies that navigate disruptions best are not always the ones with the most sophisticated risk models. They are the ones where leadership understood, before any crisis arrived, that Supply Chain is the architecture of the business, not a support function whose importance is discovered only in a post-mortem.
