📦 Essential Logistics KPIs (With Formulas) — Track Smarter, Operate Better

Most teams track KPIs… but the real value comes when you understand, connect, and act on them.

Here’s a practical breakdown 👇

---

🚚 On-Time Delivery (OTD)
Measures reliability and customer trust
Formula:
OTD % = (On-Time Deliveries ÷ Total Deliveries) × 100
👉 Target: ≥ 95%

---

🧾 Order Accuracy
Ensures error-free fulfillment
Formula:
Accuracy % = (Correct Orders ÷ Total Orders) × 100
👉 Every mistake = cost + reputation hit

---

📊 Inventory Turnover
Reflects how efficiently inventory is managed
Formula:
Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory
👉 Low = overstock | High = stockout risk

---

🏬 Warehouse Utilization
Tracks effective use of storage capacity
Formula:
Utilization % = (Used Storage Space ÷ Total Capacity) × 100
👉 Sweet spot: 80–85%

---

📦 Freight Cost per Unit
Controls transportation expenses
Formula:
Cost per Unit = Total Freight Cost ÷ Units Shipped
👉 Track by lane, customer, and product

---

✅ Perfect Order Rate
Measures true service quality (on time + accurate + no damage + correct docs)
Formula:
Perfect Order % = (Orders with No Issues ÷ Total Orders) × 100

---

⏱ Cycle Time
Time from order receipt to final delivery
Formula:
Cycle Time = Delivery Date − Order Receipt Date
👉 Break it down: processing | picking | transit

---

📍 Dock-to-Stock Time
Speed of moving goods from receiving to storage
Formula:
Dock-to-Stock Time = Storage Time − Receiving Time
👉 Slow here = hidden stockouts

---

💡 The Real Insight (Don’t Miss This):

These KPIs are connected:

- Low OTD? → Check Cycle Time + Dock-to-Stock
- High Freight Cost? → Check Utilization + Consolidation
- Low Perfect Order Rate? → Check Accuracy + Warehouse Process

---

📈 Bonus KPIs to Level Up:

- Fill Rate = (Units Shipped ÷ Units Ordered) × 100
- Return Rate = (Returned Units ÷ Units Shipped) × 100
- Cost per Order = Total Logistics Cost ÷ Total Orders

---

🎯 Bottom Line:
Tracking KPIs is easy.
Understanding how they interact is what drives real operational excellence.

I gave my team full ownership of six AI projects. Some of them struggled with it.

Not because the projects were too hard. Because the freedom was too much.

When you tell experienced leaders "this is your domain, define the path yourself," two things happen. Some move immediately. They explore, test, start building. Others freeze. They ask for detailed instructions. They want examples of what the output should look like. They wait.

That second reaction is not a weakness. It is a product of decades in organizations that rewarded following instructions and punished independent decisions that went wrong.

This week's article is about what happens next. How to hold the line between support and micromanagement. Why I kept one project for myself to stay honest about what I am asking of them. And what it costs in the short term to build a team that thinks for itself.

This is not leadership theory. This is what I am going through right now, across six AI initiatives in a large supply chain organization.

Full article in the newsletter.

Like many people, I’ve been trying to get my head around AI in procurement. A post by Asmaa Gad this week really helped. Her Agentic AI Platforms Map (65 platforms, 10 categories, 2026 edition) brilliantly illustrates how crowded this space has become.

Given the number of platforms and categories, I wanted to step back and understand what they actually do. The discussion that followed provided the answer. AI platforms can broadly be viewed as operating across three layers:
- Orchestration: automating end-to-end procurement workflows (e.g. major Source-to-Pay suites such as Coupa, SAP Ariba, GEP)
- Domain Intelligence: generating insight within specific areas—spend analytics (Sievo, Rosslyn), contract intelligence (Icertis, Ironclad), supplier risk (Resilinc, Prewave)
- Data Access: the foundational layer—connectivity, supplier data, and infrastructure that everything else depends on (Palantir, E2open, One Network)

It’s worth noting that the major S2P platforms are increasingly bundling spend analytics and risk monitoring into their core offerings. So are these truly three distinct categories, or three overlapping capabilities? Perhaps the more useful question isn’t “which platform category do I need?” but “which capability will deliver the greatest improvement in performance?” For most teams, it’s the intelligence layer. The workflows already exist—genuinely understanding what you’re spending, with whom, and at what risk is where AI could close the gap first.

Safety stock exists because the future is uncertain. But most companies calculate it using averages, which assume the future behaves like the past. The very thing safety stock is meant to protect against is the thing the formula ignores.

This is Episode 12 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 11 we covered the bullwhip effect and how demand signals distort as they move upstream. Today we're looking at one of the most direct consequences of that distortion: how much extra inventory you keep as a buffer.

Safety stock is the cushion between your expected demand and reality. When your supplier delivers late, or demand spikes unexpectedly, safety stock is what keeps the customer from waiting. 

It sits below your regular inventory (called cycle stock) and above zero, and ideally you never touch it. But it's there so the business doesn't stop when something goes wrong.

The calculation depends on three variables:
• Demand variability: how much does customer demand fluctuate?
• Supply variability: how reliable are your supplier lead times?
• Service level target: what percentage of orders do you want to fulfil from stock?

If demand is stable and your supplier is reliable, you need less safety stock. If either one is volatile, you need more. And if your target service level is 99% instead of 95%, the buffer increases significantly, because that last 4% is expensive.

What most people do not realise is that reducing lead time variability is a better lever than tweaking the safety stock formula. A supplier that always delivers in 10 days needs less buffer than one that averages 10 days but swings between 7 and 15. 

When did you last recalculate your safety stock parameters?

We needed 3 lbs of powder coating material. Nobody on the continent had it. I found it in a lab in Germany.
My first battalion commander as a young Army officer had a rule for all leaders: "Ignore the first 5 'No's' when it comes to soldier welfare."
He expected us to leave no stone unturned when it came to taking care of the troops. That lesson stuck. I've carried it into every supply chain role since — for my team and for the customer. It's been behind a few miracles over 25 years.
Here's one of them:
We had an emergency takeover for a customer that was going to be held up by one part. A collar needed powder coating in a very specific color and grade. We needed 3 lbs to complete the run.
The powder coater didn't have it. Wasn't sure when he'd get it.
That's No #1. Most people stop here.
I got the powder coat sales company's contact info and called them. They were waiting on an update from their distributor. I got the distributor's number and called them directly.
No #2.
Distribution was waiting for a shipment from Germany. Best guess: 3-4 weeks. Nothing else in the pipeline at other coaters.
No #3.
I asked for the manufacturer's name, tracked down their headquarters in Germany, and made an early morning call across the Atlantic.
Everything was in transit. The coating wasn't scheduled to run for another 4 months.
No #4.
I asked about lab samples — we only needed a small amount. The contact said he'd check.
40 very tense minutes later, Germany called back. They had a 3 lb sample they could drop ship to the coater in 2 days. I gave them our small pack account, called the coater, called the customer, and the run stayed on schedule.
Everyone thought I was a miracle worker.
I thought it was just another day of ignoring the first 5 No's.
Here's the thing most procurement teams get wrong: they treat the first "no" like a wall. It's not a wall. It's a door to someone who might know the answer. And behind that door is another door. The people who solve the impossible problems are the ones willing to keep knocking.
Does your procurement team stop at the first No — or do they ignore the first five?

Why does your supplier say 6 weeks but the customer waits 10? Because supplier lead time is one of at least five lead times in your supply chain, and it's the only a portion most companies measure.

This is Episode 13 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 12 we covered safety stock and how lead time variability drives how much buffer you need. Today we're unpacking lead time itself, because most companies are only measuring a fraction of it.

When someone says "lead time," they usually mean supplier lead time: how long it takes from placing a PO to receiving the goods. But that's one segment of a much longer chain.

The full cumulative lead time breaks down into at least five components:
• Information lead time: how long it takes to identify the need, get approval, and enter the order into the system. This is pure decision speed, and it's often invisible.
• Supplier lead time: how long the supplier takes to produce or ship the goods after receiving the order.
• Manufacturing lead time: if you're transforming what you receive, how long does your own production take?
• Transportation lead time: time in transit from supplier to your facility, or from your facility to the customer.
• Receiving and QC lead time: time to unload, inspect, check quality, and make goods available in the system.

Add those up and you get the real lead time. In most cases I've seen, supplier lead time is less than half the total. 

While cutting 3 days of information lead time (faster decisions, fewer approval loops) often costs nothing. Cutting 3 days of transportation lead time might mean airfreight or a completely different logistics network. 


Have you mapped the full cumulative lead time for your top 10 SKUs?

The best executor on my team had the hardest time becoming a project owner.

The Army calls it a Hot Wash. Most companies call it a post-mortem. The difference? The Army actually does it every single time.

When I was an Army officer, we ran an After Action Report after every mission. Not just the ones that went wrong. Every. Single. One.

The format was simple: What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a gap? What do we do differently next time? Sometimes it was a brief as 3 ups, 3 downs.

No rank in the room during the debrief. The newest private could tell the commander what went wrong. That was the rule. Because the alternative — people staying quiet to protect egos — gets someone hurt next time.

I try to drive that same discipline into every supply chain role I’ve had since.

At one company, we had a supplier quality escape that shut down a production line for two days. Expensive. Embarrassing. The instinct was to fix it, move on, and pretend it didn’t happen.

Instead, we ran a Hot Wash. Got the procurement team, the quality team, and the production leads in one room. Walked through the timeline hour by hour.

What we found wasn’t a supplier problem. It was a receiving inspection gap — we’d changed the spec six months earlier and never updated the incoming inspection criteria. The supplier was building to the new spec. We were inspecting to the old one. The parts sat in quarantine for three weeks before anyone escalated.

That one Hot Wash led to a process change that prevented the same failure mode across every supplier in the network. Thirty minutes of uncomfortable conversation saved months of future downtime.

Here’s what I see at most companies: the crisis happens, everybody hustles to fix it, and then they wipe the sweat from their brow, congratulate each other, and move on to the next fire.

Nobody sits down and asks what actually broke. Or worse — they do sit down, but the meeting turns into a blamestorming session instead of a learning exercise.

The best procurement teams I’ve worked with have a system for this. Not a suggestion. A system. Every significant supplier issue gets a structured review within two weeks. Findings get documented. Changes get implemented. And the same mistake doesn’t happen twice.

Anyone can recover from a failure. What separates good companies from great ones is what happens in the 48 hours after.

When was the last time your team ran a real Hot Wash — not a blame session, but an honest debrief that actually changed how you operate?
#SupplyChain #Leadership #Procurement #StrategicSourcing

20% of your SKUs drive 80% of your revenue. That's the Pareto principle, and most supply chain teams know it. But revenue alone doesn't tell you how to plan them from an SC perspective. It is the second dimension, demand predictability, that changes everything.

This is Episode 14 of Supply Chain 101. In Episodes 12 and 13 we covered safety stock and lead time. Today we're looking at how you decide which SKUs deserve the most planning attention in the first place, because treating 10,000 SKUs the same way is how planners burn out and inventory gets misallocated.

ABC classification sorts your SKUs by value contribution:
• A items: the top 20% of SKUs that drive roughly 80% of revenue
• B items: the next 30% contributing around 15%
• C items: the bottom 50% contributing the remaining 5%
That's useful, but it only tells you what matters financially. It doesn't tell you how to plan it. That's where XYZ comes in.

XYZ classification sorts by demand predictability:
• X items: stable, predictable demand (low forecast error)
• Y items: some variability, often seasonal or trend-driven
• Z items: erratic, unpredictable, hard to forecast

Combine the two into a 3x3 matrix, and suddenly the planning approach becomes obvious:
• AX (high value, stable demand): automate replenishment, minimal manual intervention
• AZ (high value, erratic demand): your planner's full attention, manual review, tighter safety stock monitoring
• CZ (low value, erratic demand): seriously consider whether these should still be in your catalogue

The matrix doesn't just classify inventory. It classifies where human effort should go. And in most organisations, that effort is spread evenly when it should be concentrated.

How many SKUs fall in your CZ box, and does anyone review them?

Better models.
Better data.
Better numbers.

But experience teaches you something different:

👉 Accuracy alone doesn’t drive better decisions.

Because you can have:

✔ High accuracy
❌ But wrong direction (bias)

And that’s where problems start.

Over-forecast → excess inventory
Under-forecast → stockouts

The real question is not:

👉 “How accurate is the forecast?”

It is:

👉 “What is the impact if we are wrong?”

That’s why strong planning focuses on:

• Accuracy (how wrong)
• Bias (direction of error)
• Business impact

Because in the end—

👉 A slightly less accurate but unbiased forecast
is far more valuable than a “perfect-looking” but biased one

Forecasting is not about numbers.

👉 It’s about decisions.

What do you focus on more — accuracy or bias?

Why did your company choose the cheapest supplier and end up spending more? 

This is Episode 15 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 14 we covered how to classify SKUs by value and demand pattern. Today we're looking at how companies evaluate what they pay for those SKUs, because the number on the purchase order is only the tip of the iceberg.

Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) is what you actually pay when you account for everything beyond unit price. 

Think of it as an iceberg:
Above the waterline is the unit price. It's visible, it's on the quote, and it's what most procurement negotiations focus on.

Below the waterline is everything else:
• Transport and customs: freight, duties, insurance
• Quality costs: inspections, rejects, rework, returns
• Inventory carrying: safety stock buffers driven by lead time variability
• Administrative overhead: supplier management, communication, expediting
• Lead time costs: the cash tied up while goods are in transit or in buffer
• Payment terms: the financial impact of when you actually pay

In most cases, the below-waterline costs are 2–3x larger than the unit price itself. And they're spread across different departments (logistics, quality, finance, planning) so nobody connects them back to the original sourcing decision.

What often happens is in practice the supplier that's 15% cheaper on unit price is picked but has 3x longer lead times requires significantly more safety stock. That inventory costs money to hold, ties up working capital, and carries obsolescence risk. Run the full TCO calculation and the saving often disappears.

Does your procurement team evaluate on unit price or total cost?

"I am here when you need me" sounds like soft leadership. It is the hardest thing I do.

When a leader on my team hesitates, every instinct says step in. Fix it. Give the answer. That would solve today's problem and guarantee tomorrow's dependency.

The alternative: wait. Let them struggle. Answer when asked. Do not volunteer the solution before they have tried to find it themselves.

There is a specific moment when this works. A leader comes to me and says "I am stuck, here is what I have tried, what do you think." That is a productive conversation. They have done the thinking. They have a position. I can challenge or confirm it. Either way, they leave with a decision they own.

Compare that to "What should I do?" That conversation produces instructions, not ownership.

The cost is real. Sometimes my leaders take a direction I would not have chosen. Sometimes a week goes into an approach I knew would not work. I watch it happen.

But a leader who found the right approach on their own will defend it with conviction. Will troubleshoot it when problems appear. Will improve it without being asked. Because it is theirs.

That is worth more than three weeks of saved time.

At the same time, signals from the market are accelerating adoption. 2026 redundancy announcements across major tech firms include Oracle (up to 30,000 roles or ~18%), Amazon (~16,000 roles), and Meta (more than 8,000 roles) send a clear message that AI is replacing people. Loganix’s 2026 B2B AI Buying Behavior Analysis shows 73% of B2B buyers, including many in procurement, are already using AI tools.

The combination of limited governance and pressure to use AI is driving behaviour organisations may not see, or would not permit if they did. In procurement, this includes drafting RFPs using sensitive data, analysing confidential supplier pricing, providing feedback to suppliers as part of the negotiation process and making evaluation recommendations using approved tools like Copilot without appropriate governance, or shadow AI such as ChatGPT and Claude without approval.

I hope the “Mythos moment” is the point when governments, regulators, and boards come together to define clearer guardrails for AI use.

We'd used the same logistics provider for years. Everyone loved them. Great service. Quick to help. Subject matter experts.

Then we did a competitive bid. And found out what "good enough" was actually costing us.

At one company, we'd been with the same local 3PL for years. They were deeply integrated into our process. I'd lost count of the number of times they'd swooped in to save a shipment that was lost or hung up in customs. They earned the loyalty. I'm not dismissing that.
But as we continued to grow, I knew we had to benchmark what we were paying and what we were getting. Not because we were unhappy. Because nobody had ever looked. It was something that always just was.
So I built a market basket of our actual shipments and started meeting providers — small local firms and the 500-lb behemoths of the industry. I created a feature matrix comparing what our incumbent provided against what else was available in the market.
What I found surprised me.
Online freight tracking. Spend analysis tools. Integrated warehousing. These weren't exotic capabilities. They were standard offerings from multiple providers — and we'd been operating without them for years because we never asked the question.
After narrowing the field, I let the incumbent know their business was up for bid. Showed them the matrix. Asked about the gaps. Gave them every chance to respond.
They couldn't close the gap.
We moved the business to a larger local 3PL. The result: 27% annual freight savings, better visibility, better tools, and a flawless transition.
The incumbent wasn't a bad company. They were a good company that had never been challenged — and a good relationship that had quietly become an expensive assumption.
Every company has one of these. A vendor, a process, a cost line that nobody questions because it's always been that way and the relationship feels fine.
"Fine" is the most expensive word in procurement.
What's the assumption in your supply chain that's costing you more than you think?

A 1PL owns every truck and every warehouse whereas a 5PL owns nothing and manages everything. The further up the ladder you go, the less you physically control and the more you strategically coordinate. 

This is Episode 16 of Supply Chain 101. We've covered how supply chains buy, hold inventory, manage cost, and classify complexity. Today we're closing with how goods actually move, and specifically how companies decide who moves them.

There are five levels of logistics outsourcing, and each one represents a different trade-off between control and capability:
• 1PL: you do everything yourself. Own trucks, own warehouses, own drivers. Think of a local brewery delivering its own beer. Maximum control, but it only scales if logistics is your core business.
• 2PL: you outsource transport to a carrier or freight forwarder. They move your goods, but you manage the rest. This is the most basic form of outsourcing.
• 3PL: you outsource warehousing, transport, and fulfilment to a logistics provider. They handle operations on your behalf. This is where most mid-to-large companies sit today, and it's the level most people mean when they say "we use a logistics partner."
• 4PL: you bring in a partner that doesn't just operate. They manage your other logistics providers, optimise routes, and coordinate across the network. A 4PL is a strategist, not a truck operator.
• 5PL: the entire logistics function is managed as a platform or network service. Think large e-commerce platforms that orchestrate thousands of carriers, warehouses, and fulfilment centres through technology. This is logistics as a managed ecosystem.

The decision point isn't which level sounds most impressive. It's when your complexity outgrows your team's ability to coordinate, and that's the signal to move up.

What level does your logistics operation actually require?

You're not a rocket scientist 🚀, so stop being surprised that your latest forecast shit the bed again.

We are hearing increasingly that with "quantum leaps" (marketer words, not mine) in technology - in ML, in particular - that huge gains are there for the taking for savvy forecasters. Some bold/delusional solutions salespeople go so far as to promise 20 or 30% improvements in your forecast.

The problem is, you're not doing rocket science. You're trying to predict the outcome of something so much more complex that the vast majority of practitioners and tools give up on causality before they start and resort to auto-regression.

With over a hundred trillion neural connections in each human brain, it makes a credible argument for being the most complex structure in the universe. Multiply that by many humans in any market, and you have a system whose innate variability is so high that you will not have anything better than directional success except in very specific, controlled applications.

The issue isn't that you need stronger math. 😂 It is true we have many multiples more computing power now than we did when we last landed people on the moon. But we were able to do so with little more than a slide rule because the first principles equations we used were based on a solid EMPIRICAL understanding of the entirety of the system. That is, all of the variables at play. 

The residuals in many physics experiments are so small BECAUSE THE SYSTEM IS SO WELL UNDERSTOOD that they can be used to accurately account for minute seismic movements across the Pacific when observing waves lapping on the beach in California.

In real life, many companies are lucky to see 40% error margins at a meaningful granularity and horizon not because they need better software. Or consultants. Not because humans made their math-based forecast worse (although that happens a lot). But because the nature of their value chain is based on millions of conscious and unconscious decisions being made in real-time by humans whose motivations and behaviours at an individual level remain predictably elusive.

There are too many unknown unknowns to delude oneself into the misapprehension that we are doing hard science. People selling solutions hate the sound of that but it's true. It is why very few practitioners look at causality and even fewer have success using it predictively. 

We are at the end of the day giving up on the "why" and looking at the "what" and, with varying degrees of success, predicting that what happened before will happen again.

What does that mean?

1️⃣ Begin by understanding based on your value chain what is possible from forecasting.

2️⃣ Understand what the cost/benefit of forecast improvement is in your specific context.

3️⃣ Be realistic about what you can achieve through forecasting, and focus effort where ROI is the greatest (Supplier performance management, BOM consolidation/simplification, lead time variability reduction initiatives, etc.)

The most powerful thing you can do in a supplier negotiation is stop talking.
I mean it. After 25 years and over $150 million in contracts, this is the one tactic that has never once failed me.
Here's how it works:
You present your position. Your data. Your benchmark. Your ask.
And then you stop.
The silence feels unbearable. Every instinct tells you to fill it. To soften the ask. To explain yourself further. To offer a concession they haven't even asked for yet.
Don't.
The first person who speaks after a proposal has been made is the person who concedes ground. Almost every time.
I've watched experienced procurement professionals negotiate beautifully for 45 minutes — build the case, present the data, make a strong ask — and then give away 2% in the final ten seconds because the silence made them uncomfortable.
Two percent on a $10M spend is $200,000. That's the cost of not being able to sit quietly for 30 seconds.
Here's why it works: silence puts the pressure on the other party to respond to your position. The moment you keep talking, you're responding to your own position — and usually making it weaker.
The supplier is thinking. Let them think. That's the whole point.
I tell my team: after you make the ask, put your pen down. Take a sip of water. Look at your notes. Do whatever you need to do — just don't talk.
The answer will come. And it will almost always be better than whatever you were about to say to fill the gap.
What's the hardest part of negotiation for you — the preparation, the conversation, or the silence?

The answer to a bad forecast isn't a better forecast. It's recognising that forecasting was never meant to be the only tool. 

This is Episode 17 of Supply Chain 101. We're now moving into the Strategy of supply chains. We've covered the language and the mechanics. Now we're looking at the decisions that separate average supply chains from competitive advantages. 

And it starts with demand, because everything in a supply chain flows from what customers want, when they want it, and whether you can influence either.

• Demand planning is what most people mean when they say "forecasting." It uses historical data, market intelligence, and statistical models to predict what customers will buy months from now. It's essential, and it's also inherently limited, because the further out you look, the less accurate it gets. A 60-75% accuracy rate is considered normal, and that remaining 25-40% is where most supply chain pain comes from.

• Demand sensing is the short-term correction. It uses real-time signals (point-of-sale data, web traffic, order patterns, weather, events) to detect what's actually happening right now, not what the model predicted three months ago. It operates in days to weeks and typically achieves 80-90% accuracy because it's working with current information rather than projections.

• Demand shaping is the most underused of the three. Instead of predicting or detecting demand, it actively influences it. Pricing changes, promotions, product bundling, substitution offers, allocation decisions. Airlines do this constantly: dynamic pricing is demand shaping in its purest form.

My view on this is that most supply chains treat demand as something to predict rather than something to manage. Planning, sensing, and shaping aren't alternatives. They're layers, and the companies that run all three are working with a fundamentally different demand picture.

Does your supply chain team have a seat at the table when pricing decisions are made?

From Hoshin to Gemba: Japanese KMI → KPI → KAI in Action

In many companies, performance management quickly becomes a jungle of disconnected numbers. Japanese management philosophy offers a very simple and powerful cascade that solves this: KMI → KPI → KAI

✅ KMI (Key Management Indicator): 
The “WHY”
KMIs are the few strategic indicators owned by top management. They describe what really matters for business over the term such as:
🎯 Safety, Health & Environment
🎯 Customer Engagement & Quality
🎯 People & Culture
🎯 Asset Utilization
🎯 Cost & Profitability

Think of KMIs as the North Stars on your dashboard : there should be only a few

✅ KPI (Key Performance Indicator):
The “WHAT”
KPIs translate each KMI into measurable process metric. One KMI is usually supported by several KPIs, but total set should still be lean (10 max for site). Examples :

Safety, Health & Environment: 
 -TRIR, Days Without Incident, Emissions
Asset Utilization: 
 - OEE, Throughput, Capacity Utilization
Customer Engagement & Quality: 
 - RFT, Claims, OTIF
Cost & Productivity : 
 - Unit Cost, Inventory Turnover, COPQ, Energy Consumption
People & Culture :
 - eNPS, Absenteeism, Turnover, Suggestions

✅ KAI (Key Activity Indicator):
The “HOW”
KAI's are specific actions at shop‑floor level that move the KPIs. They are concrete and small enough to be owned by a team. Examples :

To improve OEE; KAIs could be:
- Setup time ↓
- # of Breakdowns ↓
- MTBF ↑
- Short stops # ↓
To improve TRIR, KAIs could be:
- Observations # ↑
- Safety audits # ↑
- PPE compliance % ↑
To improve Suggestions, KAIs could be:
- Ideas/FTE ↑
- Implementation % ↑
- Idea cycle days ↓

The KAI key is ‘Activity’, not a result.

Why KMI → KPI → KAI Cascade
1️⃣ Aligns strategy to Gemba
Everyone can see how today’s kaizens, suggestions, or project contributes all the way up to Safety, Customer, Cost, or People objectives
2️⃣ Clarifies target setting
You start with few KMIs, translate them into focused KPIs, then define KAIs, teams can influence every day
3️⃣ Enables performance management, not just reporting
Reviews can follow simple logic: KMI trend ↓ → which KPI is off? → which KAI needs to improve/change?
4️⃣ Drives Continuous Improvement
KAI's become natural funnel for Kaizens: If KPI is red, teams propose and track more Kaizens until it turns green.

How to implement
✅ Start by agreeing on 4–5 KMIs that truly define success for your site 
✅ Limit yourself to max 10 KPIs, clearly owned, each mapped to one KMI
✅ For each KPI, define 2–3 KAIs, specific activities you want teams to execute
✅ Review regularly KMI → KPI → KAI on the same page, as in visual, so everyone sees connection

When you get this right, you create a clear line of sight:
KAI improves KPI → KPI improves KMI → Every team, Every shift, Every individual, Every improvement contributes directly to the company’s success.

Offshoring saves money on labour. Nearshoring saves money on speed. Reshoring saves money on control. All three are true and all three are incomplete. The real comparison isn't unit cost, it is the total landed cost, and most companies miss the whole truth

This is Episode 18 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 17 we covered demand planning, sensing, and shaping. Today we're looking at one of the most debated strategic decisions in modern supply chain: where should you manufacture?

There are three options, and each one optimises for something different:
• Offshoring means manufacturing far from your end market, typically in low-cost countries. The advantage is lower unit cost. The trade-offs are longer lead times, higher inventory requirements, shipping costs, customs complexity, and less direct oversight of quality and operations.

• Nearshoring means manufacturing closer to your end market, though not necessarily in the same country. Think Mexico for US companies, or Turkey and Eastern Europe for Western European companies. The advantage is shorter lead times and easier coordination. The trade-off is higher unit cost than offshoring, though not always by as much as people assume.

• Reshoring means bringing manufacturing back to your home market. The advantage is maximum control, minimal lead time, and the simplest supply chain. The trade-off is typically the highest unit cost, though automation is closing that gap in some industries.

Here's the thing most people miss: the comparison should never be unit cost alone. 

Total landed cost includes freight, duties, inventory carrying costs, quality failure rates, lead time buffers, management overhead, and the opportunity cost of slow response. When you add those factors, offshoring's advantage often shrinks significantly, and in some cases flips entirely. 

Has your org run a total landed cost comparison, or is the decision still based on the number on the supplier quote?

Asakai : What Gets Managed Daily, Improves Continuously

Daily Management System (DMS) or in Japanese Asakai is a structured approach to managing day-to-day operations that focuses on continuous improvement and loss (muda) reduction.

Asakai is a set of practices and tools that enable companies to:
1️⃣ Monitor performance daily
2️⃣ Identify areas for improvement
3️⃣ Take corrective actions quickly
4️⃣ Align KPI’s with execution
5️⃣ Standardize processes
6️⃣ Establish standard work
7️⃣ Foster a CI culture

Asakai is typically executed through a tiered structure:
➡️ Tier 1 (Team Level):
- Daily huddles (5-15 minutes) at the start of each shift
- Review of key performance indicators (KPIs)
- Discussion of issues and quick problem-solving
➡️ Tier 2 (Supervisory Level):
- Daily meetings (5-15 minutes) with team leaders
- Review of escalated issues from Tier 1
 - Coordination of cross-functional problem-solving
➡️ Tier 3 (Management Level):
- Daily meetings (15-20 minutes) with supervisors and managers
- Review overall performance and strategic alignment
- DMS/Asakai Actions follow up
- Review and decision making for escalated issues from Tier 1-2 
- Resource allocation and improvement initiatives follow up

Key components
✅ Visual management boards displaying KPIs and action items
✅ Standard work for leaders at each level
✅ Gemba walks to observe processes and identify improvement opportunities
✅ Problem-solving methodologies (Root Cause Analysis)
✅ Escalation processes for unresolved issues

☑️ Improves overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) through daily monitoring and rapid problem-solving
☑️ Reduces unplanned downtime by promoting proactive maintenance

4 Competitive Zones: Where Operational Excellence Really Wins and Where It Wastes Time

Most companies still try to “be better at everything” – and then wonder why their Operational Excellence program feels busy but not strategic.

A more honest and useful lens is the 4 competitive zones – with a different OpEx playbook for each one.

1️⃣ Winning Zone – Where You Must Double Down
This is the sweet spot where:
- You are genuinely strong
- Customers truly care
- Competitors can’t easily match you
🎯 Here OpEx is about scaling and protecting your edge: World Class Manufacturing, standard work, rock‑solid OEE, a zero‑defect mindset and a relentless Kaizen engine. Every 1% improvement here compounds your competitive advantage.

2️⃣ Battleground Zone – Where Execution Decides the Winner
Everyone is playing here: you, your competitors and the customer.
- Use Value Stream Mapping to remove waste end‑to‑end
- Run focused Kaizen projects on the critical CTQs
- Shorten lead times, reduce breakdowns, tighten delivery reliability
🎯 Here OpEx focus shifts to speed, stability and cost. Whoever executes faster and more consistently wins the battleground.

3️⃣ Losing Zone – Where You Can’t Afford to Stay
The customer cares, but the competitor outperforms you.
Here you need ruthless clarity:
- Do we fix this (and how fast)?
- Do we partner or exit and focus elsewhere?
🎯 Here OpEx brings structure: gap analysis, structured problem solving, and focused improvement. The goal is not cosmetic change; it’s closing a survival‑critical gap or consciously walking away.

4️⃣ “Who Cares” Zone – Where Waste Likes to Hide
Both you and your competitors invest here, but the customer barely notices.
This is prime territory for:
- Complexity reduction
- “Stop‑doing” lists
- Reallocating resources into the Winning and Battleground zones
🎯 OpEx here is about freeing capacity, not polishing non‑value‑adding work.

When you look at your OpEx roadmap through these four lenses, priorities become painfully clear:
✅ Less “project shopping”

I made $60K+ with this pricing system:

Everyone wants to make money with AI workflows,
but pricing is the part nobody teaches you.

How do you define the value?
How do you justify the number?
How do you say the price with confidence?

Charge for the outcome instead.

↳ Saves money (cuts costs)
↳ Saves time (frees up hours)
↳ Reduces errors (prevents expensive mistakes)

The faster you build, the less you make.

2️⃣ The 2 core pricing models
↳ Value-based project pricing (based on business impact)
↳ Monthly retainer (for ongoing maintenance and optimization)

Most freelancers only use one.
The best ones use both.

3️⃣ The 10x ROI rule
This is the number that makes pricing obvious.

Price at 10% of annual savings.

Example:
↳ Workflow saves €12K/year
↳ You charge €1,200

That's a no-brainer for any business owner.

4️⃣ How to price retainers
Simple formula:
↳ Estimate your monthly cost
↳ Apply a 50% margin (double it)

No undercharging.

Lead with what changes for them.
Define what "done" looks like before you say the price.

Never discount your price.

If the budget is tight:

↳ Phase the project

Your price signals your value.
The moment you discount, you signal the opposite.

Every project is a door to a retainer.

Offer:

One client. Multiple invoices.

The largest contract negotiation I ever led was $50 million over six years. Here’s the one thing that made the difference between a good deal and a great one.

GE Transportation needed motors. Millions of dollars of motors annually.

They’d always built them internally. This was the first time they were going external.

That meant finding a supplier willing to commit to six years of production and invest in the tooling to support it — while entering a commercial relationship with a customer who had massive volume leverage but also the accountability of a long-term dependency.

We came into that negotiation having done something most procurement teams don’t do: we spent three months before the first meeting building a detailed benchmark of what this motor supply should cost, what the tooling amortization should look like, and what the realistic cost reductions over the contract period were achievable.

We didn’t walk in with "we want the lowest possible price."

We walked in with the math.

Here’s why that matters: the supplier couldn’t argue with the benchmark. They could argue with our number — and they did — but they couldn’t argue with the methodology. We weren’t making up a target. We’d built the model.

The final contract: $50 million, six years, with $5.9 million in scheduled cost reductions built into the agreement.

The lesson I’ve carried from that negotiation:

The negotiator who walks in most prepared rarely has to fight hardest. The preparation does the work. The meeting is almost a formality.

What’s the most preparation you’ve ever done for a supplier negotiation?

Just-in-Time was the greatest supply chain innovation of the 20th century. Just-in-Case was the lesson of 2020. 

This is Episode 19 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 18 we covered the nearshoring decision and total landed cost. Today we're looking at one of the most misunderstood debates in supply chain: should you run lean or should you hold buffer?

• Just-in-Time (JIT) is an inventory philosophy that originated at Toyota. The idea is simple: materials arrive exactly when they're needed in production, not before. The benefit is minimal waste, lower inventory costs, and a faster, more responsive operation. But it requires extremely reliable suppliers, consistent quality, short replenishment cycles, and stable demand. When those conditions exist, JIT is powerful. When they don't, it's fragile.

• Just-in-Case (JIC) is the opposite instinct: hold enough inventory to absorb disruption. The benefit is resilience. The cost is tied-up capital, warehouse space, and the risk of obsolescence. After 2020, many companies swung hard toward JIC, adding weeks or months of buffer stock across their entire portfolio.

But here's what makes this more nuanced than a binary choice: the right approach depends on the product. 

• A high-value, critical component with a single supplier in a volatile region probably needs a JIC buffer. 
• A low-cost, widely available commodity with three local suppliers can run JIT safely.

My view on this is that the mature answer is portfolio segmentation. Not every product line needs the same inventory strategy. The companies that segment, applying JIT where conditions support it and JIC where the risk demands it, are managing cost and resilience simultaneously rather than trading one for the other.

Which items in your supply chain run JIT by default rather than by design?

---

Found this useful? Follow Poornajith Shetty for more supply chain insights and save/repost this for the next time someone debates JIT vs. JIC as if it's a binary choice.

“We want a new system… but can it still do what the old one did?”

20+ years and I still hear this in almost every project.

It starts full of ambition:

That slightly awkward process

New system projects aren’t really about replacing software.

Operational Excellence Periodic Table: Your Toolkit for Continuous Improvement

The attached illustration, "Operational Excellence Periodic Table," is a visual representation of the tools and methodologies that drive Operational Excellence across industries.

What’s Inside the Table:

🔵 Basic 7 QC Tools:
Check Sheet (CS), Histogram (Hi), Control Chart (CC), Flow Chart (FC), Pareto Chart (PC), and more. These foundational tools are essential for monitoring and improving process performance.

🔴 Root Cause Analysis Tools:
Fishbone Diagram (FB), 5 Whys (WW), Fault Tree Analysis (FTA), and Root Cause Tree Diagram (RTD). Perfect for identifying and eliminating the root causes of inefficiencies.

🟢 Process Improvement Techniques:
Value Stream Mapping (VSM), Process Mapping (PM), SIPOC, and Design of Experiments (DOE). These tools streamline workflows and optimize processes for maximum efficiency.

🟣 Product Design Tools:
Quality Function Deployment (QFD), House of Quality (HK), Voice of Customer (VOC). Essential for aligning product design with customer needs and expectations.

🟤 Problem Solving Methods :
12 Step Kaizen, 8D, A3, DMAIC. Guiding you in a systematic way for problem solving.

🔴 Improvement Methods / Philosophies :
TPM, Lean 6 Sigma, TPS, TQM.

🟠🟣 Advanced QC Tools & Statistical Analysis:
Hypothesis Testing, ANOVA, Bayesian Analysis, Matrix Data Analysis, and more. Ideal for tackling complex problems with data-driven precision.

Why Does These Matter
Whether you're solving a recurring issue on the shop floor or designing a new product, these tools empower teams to:
 ✅ Identify inefficiencies 
 ✅ Solve problems systematically 
 ✅ Improve quality sustainably 

From the simplicity of 5 Whys to the sophistication of TPM and Lean Six Sigma, this table is a reminder that there’s a tool for every challenge and mastering them is the key to operational excellence.

The Operational Excellence Periodic Table isn’t just a collection of tools,methods and techniques; it’s a mindset shift toward continuous improvement.

Non-tech company research can be a useful antidote to AI hype. PwC’s latest AI performance study is a good example, while PwC clearly has an interest in AI adoption, the report is written for buyers and builders of AI in large organisations, not by AI labs thinking about the next round of funding. The study finds that the most "AI-fit" companies deliver 7.2x higher AI driven financial performance than the rest.

The report opens with a familiar scene: a room full of people, a PowerPoint presentation packed with AI pilots, and plenty of questions on deployment, scaling, and business cases. But very few answers.

The report goes on to describe "AI-fitness" as the ability to point AI at what matters, build fit-for-purpose foundations, and embed AI throughout the enterprise, quantified through a nine-category index covering strategy, governance, data, technology and more. Data and technology, for example, is described as "the degree to which a business has modern, scalable platforms and trusted varied data sources accessible to everyone". 

Anyone who completed the London Marathon a fortnight ago knows fitness is built over months and years, not in a weekend bootcamp. AI is the same, anyone expecting to become AI fit overnight is setting themselves up for disappointment, without targeted, sustained effort, rooms full of AI pilots and too little measurable impact will persist.

My favourite part of the report is the ideas in motion section (case studies by any other name). John Deere’s "See & Spray", really gets into the weeds (pun intended), showing how AI can create new revenue opportunities while delivering tangible environmental benefits, not just prettier dashboards.

For anyone interested in or already deploying AI, this report is well worth a careful read (see comments for the link).

Single-sourcing gives you leverage through volume. Multi-sourcing gives you resilience through options. 

The decision isn't about risk tolerance. It's about which risk you prefer to carry: the risk of dependency or the risk of complexity.

This is Episode 20 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 19 we covered JIT vs. JIC and the idea that inventory strategy should be segmented by product. Today we're applying that same logic to supplier strategy, because the number of suppliers you use for a category is one of the most consequential decisions in procurement, and most companies make it by default rather than by design.

• Single-sourcing means one supplier for a category. The advantages are real: concentrated volume gives you negotiating leverage, deeper relationships, simpler quality management, and often better pricing. The risk is equally real: if that supplier fails, you have no immediate alternative.

• Dual-sourcing means two suppliers sharing volume. It's the most common risk mitigation approach because it provides a built-in backup without excessive complexity. The trade-off is that neither supplier gets your full volume, which can dilute your leverage and may mean neither prioritises you as highly.

• Multi-sourcing means three or more suppliers. The advantage is maximum optionality and redundancy. The trade-off is significant management overhead: more contracts, more quality audits, more relationship management, and diluted volume across all of them.

Here's the thing most people miss: the number of suppliers matters less than three underlying factors. 
• Supply risk: how likely is disruption? 
• Spend volume: is there enough to split meaningfully? 
• And criticality: what happens if this component is unavailable? 

A low-risk, high-volume commodity might be fine with a single source. A high-risk, critical component with limited alternatives needs at least two, and they should not be in the same geography.

For your top 5 spend categories, can you name a tested alternative?

The 8 Pillars of TPM (WCM): Your Blueprint for Operational Excellence

As many practitioners think TPM, (once called Total Productive Maintenance, NOW named Total Productive MANAGEMENT) is NOT a maintenance program. It is a full Operating System designed to achieve ZERO LOSSES by turning all employees into co‑owners of equipment & processes.

Also known as World Class Manufacturing (WCM) or World Class Operations Mahagement (WCOM); TPM stands on 8 powerful pillars:

1️⃣ Autonomous Maintenance
Operators clean, inspect, lubricate, and detect abnormalities so machines never “surprise” with failures
2️⃣ Focused Improvement
Cross‑functional teams attack chronic losses with structured methods for hard, measurable gains
3️⃣ Planned Maintenance
From firefighting to predictive and prescriptive; breakdowns become rare exceptions, not the norm
4️⃣ Quality Maintenance
Defects are prevented at source by controlling critical conditions, not just caught at end of line
5️⃣ Early Management
New products and equipment are designed for reliability and quick vertical start‑up with extensive design reviews
6️⃣ Training & Education
Skills are built systematically, replacing “belted heroes” with capable, multi‑skilled employees
7️⃣ Safety, Health & Environment
Risk is engineered out so safe  processes become default
8️⃣ TPM in Administration
The same mindset is applied to planning, logistics, offices etc eliminating information and decision losses

Why it is so powerful 
✅ Holistic Integration
TPM integrates equipment reliability, employee empowerment, and safety as foundation. It ensures machines, processes, and people all work to achieve zero losses
✅ Focus on Maintenance
TPM emphasizes proactive and predictive strategies. This ensures equipment uptime and reliability for industries where downtime leads to significant losses
✅ Employee Engagement
TPM empowers all employees to take ownership of their machines and processes. This creates culture of accountability and continuous improvement at every level
✅ Structured Loss Elimination
TPM systematically identifies and eliminates losses in relentless loops using loss intelligence systems & multiple tools. This approach delivers solid and sustained results.
✅ Quality at the Source
TPM ensures defects are prevented than detected. By controlling critical process parameters, TPM achieves consistent quality.
✅ Transformation
TPM integrates Change Management, Hoshin, and Shingo Model to create a culture of excellence that is sustainable. It’s not only reducing losses, it’s about transforming the whole organization.
✅ Structural Excellence  
The eight pillars are steered by a cross-functional Steering Committee that ensures alignment, regular assessments, and synergy across functions. This structure makes it not just a program but an enterprise-wide management system for excellence.

Why did some companies recover from 2020–2025 disruptions in weeks while others took years? 

Not because they predicted the events. Because they had categorised the risks, and the framework told them where to look first.

This is Episode 21 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 20 we covered sourcing strategy and the trade-offs between single, dual, and multi-source. Today we're zooming out to look at the broader question: how do you systematically think about everything that could go wrong, without trying to predict the unpredictable?

The starting point is a 2x2 risk matrix: probability on one axis, impact on the other. Every potential disruption gets plotted. 

Within that matrix, supply chain risks tend to fall into five categories:
• Geopolitical: trade wars, sanctions, regional conflicts, regulatory changes
• Supplier: financial collapse, capacity loss, quality failure, single-point-of-failure
• Demand: sudden shifts, customer concentration, market collapse
• Operational: cyberattacks, IT failures, labour disruption, internal capacity loss
• External: pandemics, climate events, infrastructure failures, currency shocks

Here's what's important to remember: you don't need to predict the next pandemic, the next ship-stuck-in-a-canal, or the next regional conflict. You need to know which of these five categories your operation is most exposed to right now, and have a documented response for each. The framework isn't a crystal ball. It's a map of where to look first when something changes.

The two levers that consistently separate companies that recover from those that struggle are visibility (do you know what's happening upstream and downstream as it unfolds?) and optionality (do you have alternatives ready, or do you have to scramble to find them?).

Does your supply chain have a documented risk register?

Prevent Before it Happens : Proactive Safety & Health Risk Assessment for Zero Accidents

Safety & Health Risk Assessment is a systematic process of identify workplace hazards, evaluate their risks, and implement control measures to minimize or eliminate potential harm. It ensures compliance with safety standards while fostering a culture of proactive risk management.

How to Perform*
1️⃣ Identify Hazards:
Walk through the workplace to identify potential hazards related to activities, equipment, materials, or processes.
2️⃣ Evaluate Risks:
Use a Risk Matrix to assess each hazard’s probability and impact. Assign a Risk Score based on likelihood (e.g., very likely to very unlikely) and severity (e.g., negligible to catastrophic). CATHASTROPHIC here is used for magnitute of the consequence is fatal.
3️⃣ Decide on Mitigation Actions:
For each hazard, define specific mitigation actions to reduce risk. For high-risk hazards (e.g., scores of 16-25), immediate actions like engineering controls or process redesign are recommended.
4️⃣ Assign Responsibilities and Deadlines:
Allocate tasks to responsible individuals and set deadlines for implementing mitigation measures. So close the loop.
5️⃣ Reassess Residual Risks:
After implementing mitigation actions, reassess the risk probability and impact to ensure the residual risk is either Low or Very Low, which could be acceptable until you mitigate all Cathastriphic, High and Medium risks.
6️⃣ Document Findings:
Keep detailed records of hazards, risk scores, mitigation actions, and outcomes for future reference.
7️⃣ Review and Update Regularly:
Periodically review the analysis to ensure it remains relevant as workplace conditions change.

Why to Perform
✅ Proactive Hazard Management: Identify and address risks before they cause harm.
✅ Improved Compliance: Ensure adherence to safety regulations and standards.
✅ Enhanced Decision-Making: Use data-driven insights to prioritize safety interventions.
✅ Continuous Improvement: Foster a culture of ongoing safety enhancement.
✅ Increased employee morale because of improved workplace safety standards

S&H Risk Assessment is not a compliance exercise, it’s the foundation of proactive safety culture.

Safety is a journey, not a destination - every step you take today builds a safer, more resilient workplace for tomorrow.

* For simplicity and reference only. There are models like HIRA, JSA, HAZOP etc that you can use.

Two of the most expensive words in ocean shipping:
Demurrage and Detention.

Most teams know they’re expensive.
Far fewer understand the difference.

Both charges occur when containers exceed the carrier’s free time...typically 3-7 days depending on the port and carrier.

Here’s the difference operators need to know:

➝ Demurrage
Container stuck inside the port
- Clock starts when the container is discharged from the vessel
- Applies while the container remains in the terminal
- Common causes: customs delays, paperwork issues, or no truck arranged

➝ Detention
Container stuck outside the port
- Clock starts when the container gates out
- Applies while the container is being unloaded or awaiting return
- Common causes: slow unloading or delayed empty return

A simple way to remember it:
Demurrage = Port storage problem
Detention = Equipment return problem

Both exist for one reason: Carriers need containers moving, not sitting.

Ocean shipping doesn’t end when the vessel arrives.
For many teams, that’s when the cost clock actually begins.

➜ Supply Chain VPs: how is your team tracking demurrage and detention risk before charges hit?

Safety Walks : A Practical Guide - Embedding Safety in Daily Routine

Yesterday, I explained Safety Risk Assessment, today we'll go through another very important activity : Safety Walks - A systematic and disciplined approach to ensuring a safe working environment by observing, analyzing, and addressing potential risks.

🚨 What is a Safety Walk
A Safety Walk is a proactive measure where managers, supervisors, safety officers together with OPERATORS; tour the workplace to identify potential hazards and risks. It involves observing practices, interacting with employees, and promoting a safety culture.

How to Plan
1️⃣ Determine the Path : 
Determine checkpoints with a special Focus on high-risk areas or processes with recent incidents.
2️⃣ Select a Diverse Team: 
Include safety managers, supervisors, and frontline workers for diverse perspectives.
3️⃣ Develop a Checklist: 
Use detailed templates for PPE, equipment inspection, and facility conditions (example in illustration).

How to Conduct
👣 Briefing: 
Explain the purpose and review the checklist.
👣 Document Findings: 
Note hazards, non-compliance, and opportunities for improvement. Taking pictures and attaching them to report is highly recommended. A picture is worth thousand words.
👣 Interact with Employees: 
Gather insights on safety protocols and concerns.

Reporting and Actioning
1️⃣ Debriefing Session: 
Analyze findings, prioritize issues, and plan corrective actions.

Safety Dashboard : Turning Safety Data Into Decisions That Save Lives

Previous two days I talked about Safety Risk Assessment and Safety Walks. Today, I want to introduce another important Visual Management tool : Safety Dashboard. 

Most companies talk about safety.  
Very few can see their risks before someone gets hurt.

What if you could see exactly:
🎯Where incidents and near misses happen,
🎯Which sites, shifts or contractors are most exposed,
🎯Which body parts are most often injured…  
and fix them before the next accident?

That’s what a Safety Dashboard does.  It is a single, visual platform that shows your critical safety metrics in real time and turns raw data into clear actions. 

It helps leaders monitor performance, spot patterns and prioritize the controls that actually reduce harm.

Key metrics I propose:
1️⃣ Total Recordable Incident Rate (TRIR) – all recordable injuries per 200,000 hours worked.  
2️⃣ Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate (LTIFR) – injuries with lost time per 1,000,000 hours worked.  
3️⃣ Near Miss Reporting Rate – how actively people are reporting hazards and close calls.  
4️⃣ Training Completion Rate – % of employees who completed mandatory safety training.  
5️⃣ Safety Compliance Rate – % of compliant items vs all applicable legal/standard items.  
6️⃣ First Aid Case Rate – first aid cases vs all injury cases.  
7️⃣ Mostly injured body parts – where to focus PPE and task redesign.  
8️⃣ Average time to close incidents/actions – how fast you respond and fix root causes.  
9️⃣ Safety perception scores – how safe employees feel, not just what the stats say.

Why Dashboard matters:
✅ Proactive risk management instead of reacting after accidents.
✅ Better compliance and easier audits.
✅ Sharper, data‑driven safety decisions.
✅ Stronger safety culture through visibility and accountability.

This creates a very different environment for procurement leaders than even a year ago.

In this week’s episode of the pod, I speak with Gordon Donovan, Vice President Research - Procurement & External Workforce, SAP, to unpack what this most recent data tells us about the newest challenges facing procurement.

Procurement leaders are being asked to navigate both pressure and possibility… at the same time. The organizations that move forward will be those that are willing to rethink how they operate, rather than relying on approaches that were designed for a different environment.

#procurement #confidence #savings Art of Procurement

Supply chain leaders who can't talk in O2C and P2P language get treated as operators, not strategists. The decisions you make every day (lead times, inventory, supplier terms) directly drive the metric your CFO actually cares about: cash conversion.

This is Episode 22 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 21 we covered risk management. Today we're connecting supply chain to the two financial cycles that determine how cash actually flows through the business, because every decision you make about lead times, inventory, and supplier terms is shaping these cycles whether you realise it or not.

• Order-to-Cash (O2C) is the cycle from the moment a customer places an order to the moment the cash hits your bank account. It includes order management, fulfilment, invoicing, and collection. The metric that summarises it is Days Sales Outstanding (DSO): on average, how many days does it take to collect payment after a sale? Lower is better.

• Procure-to-Pay (P2P) is the mirror image. It runs from the moment you identify a need to buy something, through purchasing, receipt, invoice approval, and payment to the supplier.  The metric is Days Payable Outstanding (DPO): on average, how many days do you take to pay after receiving goods? Higher (within reason) is better for cash flow.

The gap between these two, plus the time inventory sits in between, is the Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC). DSO + Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) - DPO = CCC. It's the metric your CFO actually watches, and it's almost entirely shaped by supply chain decisions: how much inventory you hold, how fast you fulfil orders, what payment terms you negotiate.

Supply chain leaders who frame their work in CCC terms get heard in the boardroom. The same decisions, framed as service levels or fill rates, sound operational. Framed as working capital impact, they sound strategic.

Can you calculate your company's CCC?

Most factories try to manage performance in dozens of scattered meetings and slides. An Obeya Room does the opposite: it brings everything into one big visual room.

What is an Obeya ?  
An Obeya (“big room” in Japanese) is a dedicated physical or digital space where teams meet align on goals, priorities; track progress; prevent, fight with and solve problems. It is often called the “brain of Continous Improvement” because it concentrates goals, KPIs, problems, and actions in one visible place.

What does it do
✅ Aligns everyone on the same goals, priorities, and constraints
✅ Makes performance, risks, and bottlenecks visible at a glance

🎯It is strategically situated at the heart of operations for easy access
🎯The walls (or screens) show KPIs, SQDCP, plans, Kaizens, risks, actions, and owners.
🎯Cross-functional teams stand up in short, rhythmic meetings (daily, weekly, monthly).
🎯Every routine follows a simple flow: review goals, review metrics, see gaps, escalate issues, assign actions, follow up
🎯Problems are surfaced visually and solved using structured methods instead of long email chains.

Key benefits of Obeya
🚩Faster, better decisions because all information and people are in one place.
🚩Stronger collaboration across functions, less silo thinking.
🚩Earlier detection of deviations and real-time course correction
🚩Higher accountability: everyone sees commitments, owners, and progress every day
🚩Clearer link from strategy (Hoshin) to daily execution and problem solving

In simple terms: an Obeya room turns your factory from “managing by scattered PowerPoints, Excels and email” into “managing by facts, visually, together, every day.” 

It is headquarters of a Visual CI Operating System

If your site already has Daily Management System, Boards and Asakai, the Obeya is the natural next step: One room where the whole story of your factory becomes visible.

How to shift procurement to strategic. Free Guide 🎁 

Perception is built on evidence. But the evidence the business sees every day is tactical.

Let's look at the transformation step by step:

1️⃣ Signs the business sees you as tactical

↳ They only involve you AFTER a supplier has been chosen 
↳ Stakeholders treat procurement as a box-ticking exercise 
↳ You're only measured on cost savings 
↳ You spend more time on POs than influencing decisions 
↳ Nobody invites you to early planning conversations 
↳ Your reports go to Finance, not the boardroom 
↳ The business regularly goes around procurement entirely

If 3+ are true, you're seen as purchasing. Not procurement.


2️⃣ The 5 shifts to close the gap

(i) From Price to Value 
↳ Stop leading with "we got 10% off" 
↳ Start showing total cost of ownership, risk reduction, supplier reliability

(ii) From Reactive to Proactive 
↳ Stop waiting to be briefed after decisions are made 
↳ Start building relationships that get you upstream

(iii) From Process Enforcer to Business Partner 
↳ Stop saying "you need to follow the procurement process" 
↳ Start saying "let's figure out how to get you the outcome you need"

(iv) From Tactical KPIs to Strategic Metrics 
↳ Stop reporting PO cycle times and savings vs budget 
↳ Start reporting supplier risk, value delivered, market benchmarks

(v) From Departmental to Cross-Functional 
↳ Stop talking only to direct budget holders 
↳ Start building relationships with Finance, Legal, Operations, and the C-suite


3️⃣ Change how you speak

Instead of: "You should have involved us earlier" ❌ 
Try: "At what point did the supplier conversation start?" ✅ 

Instead of: "That's not the procurement process" ❌

Instead of: "We need 3 quotes" ❌ 
Try: "Here's what the market looks like. Let me show you the options" ✅ 

Instead of: "I can't approve that supplier" ❌

Instead of: "We saved £200K this quarter" ❌

4️⃣ The perception checklist

↳ Do stakeholders involve you before supplier decisions?

↳ Can you articulate procurement's value beyond savings? 
↳ Do you bring market intelligence, not just process? 
↳ Does the business know what it costs to bypass procurement?

INVENTORY DOESN’T SOLVE SUPPLY CHAIN PROBLEMS.
It only hides them temporarily.

Too much inventory often means:
• Poor forecasting
• Unstable supply
• Long lead times
• Weak coordination
• Slow decision-making

But too little inventory?

That creates:
• Stockouts
• Expediting costs
• Service failures
• Production disruption
• Lost sales

That’s why inventory management is not about keeping MORE stock.

Strong supply chains focus on:

✅ Which items create the highest business risk
✅ How fast inventory moves
✅ How variability impacts stock levels

The best planners understand one important truth:

Inventory is a business decision —
not just a warehouse number.

Every extra pallet affects:
• Cash flow
• Service levels
• Working capital
• Operational flexibility

And in today’s volatile environment:

The companies that manage inventory intelligently
respond faster than competitors.

Because supply chain advantage is no longer built only on cost.

Kaizen, Lean, and Six Sigma are often put in the same bucket.
But they are not the same thing.

Kaizen is the daily habit of improvement.
 Small changes. Operator involvement. Better work every day.

Lean is the operating system.
 Remove waste. Improve flow. Create value with less chaos.

Six Sigma is the precision tool.
 Reduce variation. Use data. Attack defects with discipline.

The mistake is choosing one like it is a religion.

The better question is:

What problem are we solving?

If the floor is chaotic, start with Lean.
 If people are disengaged, start with Kaizen.
 If defects are repeating, bring in Six Sigma thinking.

Tools do not fix factories.

People using the right tool for the right problem do.

A system will never tell you that your S&OE process should change. 
It will tell you the optimal plan, given yesterday's data. 
That's the difference between a tool and a strategy.

The best Supply Chain Directors aren't looking for AI that thinks for them. 
They're looking for AI that gives them better questions to ask themselves. 
The rest is marketing.

Value is rarely created in the planning cycle.

That may sound provocative in a world of IBP, complex systems, and endless dashboards. But after years in Pharma Supply Chain, this is one of my strongest observations:

Strategy only creates value when it changes real-world decisions.
In complex organizations, this is often where the gap starts. 

We invest heavily in planning processes and governance, but the real test comes when the plan is no longer enough:

🔹 When supply is constrained.
🔹 When demand shifts unexpectedly.
🔹 When launch assumptions change.
🔹 When working capital, service, and growth pull in different directions.

For me, planning excellence is about building a leadership system that helps organizations make better decisions under pressure.

The next evolution of IBP in Pharma will not be driven by more reporting.
It will be driven by clearer trade-offs, better scenario thinking and stronger ownership of decisions.

I’m looking forward to sharing these reflections at PSIP 2026 in Basel and discussing how supply chain planning can move closer to actual business value creation.

Because in the end, value is created in the moments where organizations decide, prioritize, and adapt.

Looking forward to the conversations in Basel.

The more I try to get my head around AI, the less convinced I am by the “jobpocalypse” narrative applies to procurement and supply chain.

John Burn-Murdoch in the Financial Times recently referenced the Jevons paradox. When technology makes something more efficient, we often end up using more of it, not less. My favourite example is LED lights. They dramatically reduced the cost of lighting, which led to an explosion in overall use and ultimately wiped out a significant portion of the intended savings. I just need to look at my kitchen ceiling to know it’s true.

I think procurement and supply chain could experience the same effect.
AI will reduce the cost of sourcing, forecasting, optimisation and supplier analysis. But after COVID exposed the fragility of global supply chains, and with continued geopolitical uncertainty in Eastern Europe and the Middle East, organisations are demanding more resilience, optionality, and scenario planning, not less.

That probably means:
• more sourcing to align with the market 
• more suppliers and greater diversity 
• more multi-sourcing strategies to mitigate risk 
• more product variation to align with demand 
• more live data to enable real-time decision making

To manage these additional demands and the evolving AI landscape, entirely new roles will emerge. A couple of months ago, I shared Gartner’s view that new roles will include Business Ontologists, AI Product Managers, Agentic AI Portfolio Managers and Procurement Business Architects.

Historically, firms simplified operations because complexity was expensive. AI may fundamentally change that equation. The future of procurement may not be smaller teams. It may be teams managing far greater complexity than was previously possible. Procurement may be heading for its own lighting moment.
Not a few bulbs in the centre of the room but thousands of LEDs illuminating every corner of the supply chain.

I was part of the first team at Finish Thompson to source directly from India. Here's what I wish I'd known before we started.
We qualified two Indian suppliers. First direct India sourcing the company had ever done. A lot went right. A few things were harder than expected. Here's the honest version:
What went well: The quality, once the suppliers understood our standards, was excellent. The suppliers we worked with were technically sophisticated, responsive, and genuinely interested in building a long-term relationship. India's manufacturing capability is often underestimated by companies that haven't been there. The pricing was competitive — not always dramatically lower than other Asian sources when you include freight and lead time, but competitive with the quality level we needed.
What was harder than I expected: Lead times are longer than China. Not dealbreaker-longer, but plan for it. Buffer inventory matters more here. Communication rhythm took adjustment. Not a capability issue — a time zone and process issue that smoothed out after the first few months once we'd established a regular cadence. First article qualification took longer than comparable processes with more experienced export suppliers. Build the extra time into your project plan and don't treat it as a problem — it's just the front-loaded investment in a relationship that pays off later.
The bottom line: India sourcing is real and it works. It's not a magic solution to tariff pressure, and it's not a backup you can stand up in 90 days. But as part of a diversified global supply strategy, done properly, it delivers. If you're looking at India as part of a China diversification strategy — I'm happy to share more about what the qualification process looked like. It's more accessible than most companies think.

You don't need 50 metrics, you need 10 that map to SCOR's 5 performance attributes. Two per attribute - one for the boardroom, one for the floor. 

Most SC dashboards have the inverse: hundreds of operational numbers and almost nothing the CEO can actually use.

This is Episode 23 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 8 we covered SCOR as the universal supply chain language. Today we're using its five performance attributes as the structure for cutting a bloated KPI list down to the ten that actually matter.

The five SCOR attributes are: Reliability, Responsiveness, Agility, Cost, and Asset Management. For each attribute, you need two KPIs: one strategic (the boardroom number that tells leadership if you're healthy), and one operational (the floor number that tells the team what to act on today).

• Reliability:
Strategic: Perfect Order Rate (% of orders delivered complete, on time, undamaged, with correct documentation)
Operational: On-Time Delivery (% of orders shipped by promised date)

• Responsiveness:
Strategic: Order Fulfilment Cycle Time (average time from order to delivery)
Operational: Manufacturing Lead Time (production cycle time per unit)

• Agility:
Strategic: Upside Supply Chain Flexibility (% volume increase deliverable in 30 days)
Operational: Forecast Accuracy (forecast vs. actual at SKU level)

• Cost:
Strategic: Total Supply Chain Cost as % of Revenue
Operational: Cost per Order Shipped (or per unit)

• Asset Management:
Strategic: Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time (your CCC from Episode 22)
Operational: Inventory Turns (revenue / average inventory)

The mistake isn't picking the wrong metrics. It's reporting strategic metrics to the warehouse and operational metrics to the board. Both audiences need different numbers because they're solving different problems. Two scorecards, not one bigger one.

Which of these ten does your organisation track today, and how many of them actually shape decisions?

Most people think supply chains run on ERP systems 🖥

They don’t.

They run on a 3-layer 🌐planning engine.

And whether you manufacture products, distribute them, or simply procure and resell them…

the logic is fundamentally the same.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📊 LAYER 1 — DEMAND PLANNING
“What is likely to happen?”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

This layer senses and predicts demand using:

✅ Historical trends
✅ Promotions & pricing
✅ Market intelligence
✅ POS / downstream signals
✅ Seasonality
✅ AI-assisted forecasting
✅ Scenario planning

The goal is NOT perfect forecasting.

The real goal is:

⚡ Faster decision-making under uncertainty.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
⚙️ LAYER 2 — SUPPLY PLANNING
“How will the network respond?”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

This is the orchestration layer.

Depending on the business model, this may involve:

🏭 Manufacturing planning
📦 Inventory planning
🚚 Replenishment planning
🌐 Deployment planning
🛒 Allocation planning
🏢 Capacity planning

This layer balances:

⚖️ Service levels
⚖️ Capacity
⚖️ Inventory
⚖️ Lead times
⚖️ Cost
⚖️ Flexibility

This is where most supply chain trade-offs are made.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📦 LAYER 3 — EXECUTION PLANNING
“What exactly needs to happen?”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

This layer converts plans into execution:

✅ Purchase orders
✅ Supplier schedules
✅ Production orders
✅ Warehouse replenishments
✅ Transportation movements
✅ Inventory deployments

This is where instability gets amplified if upstream signals are weak.

And this is exactly why small demand changes often create massive upstream disruption.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🚨 WHY MANY PLANNING ORGANIZATIONS STILL STRUGGLE
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Because these layers often operate in silos.

Demand planners forecast.
Supply planners firefight.
Procurement expedites.
Warehouses react.
Finance questions inventory.

Everyone optimizes locally.
The network suffers globally.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🚀 WHAT LEADING ORGANIZATIONS ARE DOING DIFFERENTLY
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Modern supply chains are shifting toward:

✅ AI-assisted planning
✅ Real-time replanning
✅ End-to-end visibility
✅ Scenario simulations
✅ Constraint-aware planning
✅ Demand sensing
✅ Multi-echelon inventory optimization
✅ Integrated Business Planning (IBP)

The future of planning is no longer:

Forecast → Plan → Execute

It is becoming:

📡 Sense → Simulate → Decide → Adapt

Continuously.

And the companies that master this loop will build the fastest, smartest, and most resilient supply chains of the next decade.

𝟏. 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬: Solve the problem before picking the tech.
