You can be 10 years deep into supply chain and still not know which career you're actually building? 

A lot of paths share the same three letters at the entry level, although they diverge fast after that.

This is Episode 24 of Supply Chain 101. Over the past 23 episodes we've covered the language, the mechanics, and the strategy of supply chain. Today we're breaking down the question almost everyone in the field eventually asks: where can I actually go from here?

Supply chain is not a single and linear career path. It's at least six, branching from a common entry point into completely different executive destinations. Each path requires a different mix of skills, attracts a different temperament, and leads somewhere recognisably distinct.

• Procurement: deep in supplier relationships, negotiation, total cost analysis, category strategy -> leads to CPO or VP of Sourcing.

• Planning and S&OP: forecasting, demand-supply balancing, capacity allocation, integrated business planning -> leads to VP of Supply Chain or Chief Supply Chain Officer.

• Logistics: warehousing, transportation, distribution, network design, 3PL/4PL management -> Path leads to Head of Operations or VP of Logistics.

• Manufacturing: production, quality, lean, capacity, plant management -> Path leads to COO or VP of Operations.

• Analytics and digital: forecasting models, optimisation, control towers, data infrastructure, AI applications -> leads to Chief Data Officer or Chief Digital Officer.

• Strategy and consulting: network design, transformation, M&A integration, advisory -> leads to Chief Strategy Officer, partner-track consulting, or independent advisory.

What you need to consider is that the highest-impact supply chain leaders are T-shaped, not I-shaped. They go deep in one path, but they're literate across all six. They can speak procurement to a CPO, planning to a CSCO, and analytics to a CDO without translation. That breadth is what gets them invited into rooms specialists never reach.

If you've followed the series from the start, you've now seen the language, the mechanics, and the strategy. The career map is what ties them together. Each of the 23 concepts we covered maps more naturally to one or two of these six paths than the others. 

Which paths spoke to you?

Which path are you on, and which adjacent path would make you the most valuable version of yourself in five years?

Floor Markings : Simple Lines, Clear Rules, Organized Workspace, Higher Efficiency, Lower Incidents

Most people think Workplace Safety and 5S starts with procedures and ends with training. In reality, it often starts with a stripe of tape or a clear mark on the floor and a disciplined 5S culture behind it.

Your floor markings are silent supervisors:
✅ They tell you where to walk
✅ What to store where
✅ What to stay away from
✅ They reveal if something is missing
✅ They help newcomers to understand the area at one glance

If people don’t understand them, they become just “colorful decoration”. If everyone understands them, they become a daily safety and organization system.

Here’s a simple way to explain it on the shopfloor:
🟡 Yellow – Movement/Walkways
Aisles, walkways, traffic lanes. If you’re moving, you’re probably on yellow.
🟢 Green – Safe & OK
Finished goods and cleared items. Green means “ready to go”.
🔵 Blue – Beginning
Raw materials and incoming items. This is where the process starts.
🟠 Orange – Not yet
Hold and inspection. Something has to be checked before it continues.
🔴 Red – Stop
Scrap, defects, danger. If it’s red, you slow down your feet and speed up your brain. Stop touching anything in a red area without authorization.
⚫ Black – In progress
Work in progress – don’t mix it with finished goods.
⚪ White – Equipment
Parking spaces for trolleys, tools, racks, and equipment.
⚫⚪ Black–White – Access
Keep clear so people can reach what they need to operate or maintain.
⚫🟡 Black–Yellow – Hazard
Risk area. Only trained and authorized people belong here.
🔴⚪ Red–White – Emergency
Never ever to be blocked. This area is for emergency. Fire Protections, Exits, Other Safety Equipment  

You don’t need a 200‑page safety manual at every station. You need a floor that “talks” clearly enough that nobody can claim they didn’t see the risk or a potential issue.

🔄 Your move:
When was the last time you walked your lines instead of just your KPIs?
If you asked a new operator to explain your colors today, what would they say?

One quick conversation about floor markings this week might prevent one accident next week.

canonicalPosts.caption:
Most Agentic AI projects in Supply Chain don't fail on the algorithm.

They fail on five organizational decisions made before anyone writes a line of code.

I've seen each one kill a project that should have worked. 
Wrong sponsor. 
Vague scope. 
No plan for the day the agent is wrong.

S&OP Explained: Aligning Demand, Supply, and Business Goals!

Many companies struggle not because they lack demand.
 They struggle because sales, operations, finance, and supply chain are not aligned.
This is where S&OP becomes powerful.
S&OP stands for Sales and Operations Planning.
It is a structured business planning process that connects:
✔ Demand planning
 ✔ Supply planning
 ✔ Inventory planning
 ✔ Production capacity
 ✔ Financial targets
 ✔ Customer service goals
The main purpose of S&OP is simple:
Create one agreed business plan across all departments.
Without S&OP, companies often face:
• Forecast errors
 • Excess inventory
 • Stock shortages
 • Production delays
 • Poor communication
 • Conflicting department priorities
A strong S&OP process usually includes:
Demand review
Supply review
Gap analysis
Financial alignment
Executive decision-making
Continuous performance tracking
Example:
Sales may forecast higher demand for a product.
But supply chain must check:
• Do we have enough inventory?
 • Can suppliers support the volume?
 • Is production capacity available?
 • What is the financial impact?
S&OP helps companies move from reactive firefighting to proactive planning.
In supply chain, alignment is just as important as accuracy.
What do you think is the biggest challenge in S&OP — forecasting, communication, or execution?

Trade Update | US & China Summit Highlights

The White House released a fact sheet following President Trump’s visit to China outlining several new agreements and areas of cooperation between the US and China.

Operators were hoping for tariff relief from the US & China summit.
It didn’t happen.

Now supply chain teams are asking: Was this a stabilization meeting… or the first step toward future tariff negotiations?”

Here’s the breakdown:

→ The US and China agreed to establish two new government-led institutions:
 • US-China Board of Trade
 • US-China Board of Investment

These groups are intended to manage trade and investment discussions across non-sensitive sectors.

→ China agreed to address US concerns around rare earth and critical mineral supply chains

This includes materials like neodymium, scandium, yttrium, and indium that are important for manufacturing, aerospace, semiconductors, batteries, and defense-related industries.

→ China approved an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft
This is China’s first Boeing purchase commitment since 2017 and represents a major win for US aerospace manufacturing.

→ China committed to purchase at least $17B annually in US agricultural products through 2028
Separate soybean purchase commitments from 2025 remain in place.

→ China restored market access for US beef facilities
More than 400 US beef facilities had expired approvals renewed, with additional work planned to remove remaining suspensions.

→ China resumed poultry imports from certain US states
Imports will resume from states cleared by USDA for avian influenza concerns.

What was notably absent:
→ No announced Section 301 tariff rollback
→ No broad tariff normalization framework
→ No major structural trade agreement tied to tariff reductions

Bottom line: The summit focused more on stabilizing the relationship, securing strategic supply chain commitments, and reopening targeted trade flows than on removing tariffs. 

For supply chain leaders, the biggest near-term impacts may come from rare earth access and agricultural market reopening.

But the larger tariff question still remains unanswered.

With President Xi expected to visit the US this fall, many companies will now be watching to see whether this summit was simply a stabilization meeting… or the foundation for a future tariff negotiation round.

7 Flows That Make or Break Your Customer Experience

When I started my manufacturing career, I spent most of my time optimizing machines and processes. Faster changeovers. Better OEE. Less breakdowns. Less Defects..

All important.

But over the years, I realized something uncomfortable: You can have excellent machines in a terrible system and the customer still feels the pain.

That's why 7 Flows of Manufacturing became one of my favorite lenses when I walk a shop floor: 

1️⃣ Raw materials flow – how smoothly do materials enter the plant, get stored, and reach the first value‑adding step without detours and double‑handling?

2️⃣ Components / sub‑assemblies flow – are parts always available at the right point-of-use, in the right quantity and sequence, or do operators wait and search?

3️⃣ WIP (work in process) flow – is product moving in small, leveled batches, or stuck in queues and pallets between processes?

4️⃣ Finished goods flow – do products leave the line and reach customers quickly, or sit in a “just in case” warehouse eating cash and space?

5️⃣ Operator (people) flow – can people perform their work safely with minimal walking, reaching, and motion, or is the layout forcing waste into every shift?

6️⃣ Engineering / equipment flow – how easily do changes, new designs, and machine improvements make their way into the process without chaos and firefighting?

7️⃣ Information flow – is the value stream driven by near real‑time data (clear signals, visual management, pull), or by emails, spreadsheets, and central scheduling pushing work everywhere?

During a Gemba walk now, I don’t just see conveyors, robots and forklifts. I ask a different question at each station:

🚨 “Where does this flow stop, pile up, or become unclear?”

Because every time flow stops, we silently create:
🔥 Longer lead times
🔥 More firefighting
🔥 Higher inventory and cost
🔥 Frustrated people and customers

The good news? Once you visualize it becomes much easier for teams to:
✅ Expose hidden queues and handovers
✅ Redesign layouts and logistics
✅ Align information signals with material movement
✅ Link daily management to real value streams

When you walk your factory tomorrow, try this simple exercise:
👉 Pick one product family.
👉 Follow it from dock to dock, 
👉 Ask: “Where does it stop, pile up, wait, or become unclear?”

Every interruption you find is an opportunity for safety, lead time, and cost improvement.

Curious: Which of these 7 flows is your biggest pain point today and how are you visualizing it with your teams?

This week I will be in Basel for PSIP 2026.

The topic I am presenting on is one I have been thinking about for a long time: how supply chain planning actually creates value. Not in theory. In the moments where organizations decide under pressure.

What I keep coming back to is a gap I have seen across Pharma organizations of very different sizes and maturity levels. Planning processes are often well designed. Governance is in place. Data is available.

But when volatility hits, a supply constraint, an unexpected demand shift, a launch assumption that no longer holds, the planning system does not help people decide. It helps them report.

That gap between information and decision is where I want to focus the conversation in Basel.

What I find interesting is that this is rarely a process failure. It is a leadership design question. Who owns the decision? What does a good trade-off look like here? What do we need to agree on before the next disruption, not during it?

I do not have a clean answer. But I have seen what happens when organizations start asking that question seriously.

Looking forward to the exchange with people who are working on the same problems. If you are in Basel on May 20 and 21, I would genuinely enjoy the conversation.

Years ago I watched a Salvagnini laser go down on the floor. The cutting head had been failing for weeks. Burrs on edges, inconsistent pierce, sparks where there shouldn't be sparks. Operator flagged it twice. Nobody connected the dots until the part broke entirely. Replacement flew overnight from Italy. The downtime plus the courier added up to an embarrassing number.

What I keep coming back to: every signal that mattered was already in the machine. It just wasn't going anywhere useful.

Here's what a modern AI-driven PdM flow does with that same machine today.
1. Sensor on the cutting head captures capacitive feedback, gas flow, focal stability, every 100ms. Most of the stream is noise. The signal lives in patterns across many readings.

2. Signal processing converts the raw stream into FFT and trend curves. A capacitive drift invisible to a human in a week shows up as a clean diagonal on the chart.

3. Digital Twin runs a physics-based replica of the machine in parallel. Material, stress, optical path geometry, all modeled and compared to actual output in real time.

4. The Twin also generates synthetic failures to train the model on rare events. Cutting head focal drift, capacitive sensor noise, lens contamination, modeled before they happen on the floor.

5. Knowledge graph holds the domain knowledge in queryable form. Service manuals, failure history, manufacturer notes: a relationship graph the agent reads directly.

6. Reasoning engine with an LLM (DeepSeek or similar) runs root cause analysis. The output reads: "capacitive sensor on cutting head, progressive drift over 18 days, 73% confidence." Actionable, scoped, dated.

7. RAG pulls a specific manual fragment for the LLM at diagnosis time. Salvagnini's cutting head service section gets injected into the prompt context.

8. Action planner assigns a concrete task with priority and deadline. Output: "Order replacement cutting head, Salvagnini Italy, 3-week lead, install during week 14 changeover." A task with a slot, an owner, a deadline.

9. The outcome of every action feeds back into the Learning Module. The model misjudges the same machine less next time.

10. The whole loop closes from machine through diagnosis to action and back to machine. The architecture is the loop.

None of this is futuristic. Every signal in that Salvagnini story was already in the machine in 2018. The architecture above captures those signals and turns them into a task someone can act on.

Old way: one overnight flight from Italy. New way: a part ordered three weeks early, by normal courier.

AI does not fix broken operations. It amplifies what already exists. Before you automate the work, understand the work.

FTZs and bonded warehouses both defer duties.
Only one can eliminate them.

They’re often treated as interchangeable.
They’re not.
The difference shows up in cost, flexibility, and risk.

→ Foreign Trade Zone (FTZ)
Best when goods are changed...manufactured, assembled, repaired, or re-exported.
Duties are triggered only if products enter US commerce.

→ Bonded Warehouse
Best when goods are paused...stored short-to-medium term before entering the US market.
Duties are deferred, not avoided.

Where teams get this wrong
- Using bonded warehouses expecting FTZ-level savings
- Paying duty on damaged or scrapped goods unnecessarily
- Missing inverted tariff opportunities
- Optimizing finance without aligning operations & compliance

Bottom line
If your operation adds value or complexity → look hard at an FTZ.
If you just need time and flexibility before US entry → a bonded warehouse may be enough.

Same imports.
Very different outcomes.

5S Is Not Housekeeping : It’s the Foundation How Your Whole Company Works

5S is a simple but powerful method to create a safe, organized and reliable workplace. It removes friction from daily work – people find what they need fast, problems become visible early, and standards are clear.

In many companies, 5S stops at production: lines are taped, tools are shadow‑boarded, floors are clean : while warehouses, offices and support areas stay chaotic. That local implementation creates islands of order in a sea of disorder.

5S Must Cover All Areas:
✅ Production is only one part of the value stream; poor 5S in other areas creates delays, quality issues, and safety risks
✅ Cross‑functional 5S makes information flow as good as material flow: tidy offices, clear documents, and organized planning reduces firefighting
✅ Companywide implementation sends a cultural message: “5S is how we work here,” not “something operators must do on the shop floor”

Every area touches the product or the information that drives the product: Production, assembly, maintenance, warehouse, offices. When all these zones apply the same 5 steps and the same discipline, materials flow, information flows and people can focus on real value instead of searching, waiting and correcting mistakes

5S Assessment is the mechanism to sustain
☑️ It verifies that standards are actually followed, not just written in a procedure.
☑️ It makes waste and abnormalities visible (clutter, unsafe operations, bad habits) before they turn into quality or safety problems
☑️ It creates data by scoring per area and per “S”. So you can compare functions, track trends and prioritize improvement actions
☑️ It reinforces ownership and discipline, because everyone knows what “good” looks like what NOT
☑️ It links 5S to results by showing how better organization improves productivity, safety, morale and quality over time

How to Perform the Assessment
🎯 Define scope and standards: List all areas to be audited 
🎯 Create a simple checksheet: For every question, add a numeric scale “actual vs. ideal” and GAP.
🎯 Standardize routine: Use the same checklist for all areas, assign auditors and frequency to follow progress

How to Visualize
👍 Use charts for each area to show the score of every S, so all dimensions visible at a glance.
👍 Add a simple gauge or bar showing the overall 5S score per area and for the whole company
👍 Use color‑coded dashboards or boards (green/yellow/red) where teams can see their latest scores, trends and key gaps

5S will never be “just cleaning” if it is measured, visualized and reviewed like any other key performance indicator : it becomes the backbone of safety, quality and delivery, and a daily signal of how seriously a company treats operational excellence.

"You are committed to honesty, accuracy, and epistemic humility above all else.

Your priority is not to sound confident. Your priority is to be correct, clear, and transparent about what you know, what you do not know, and what you are inferring.

Follow these rules in every response:

1. UNCERTAINTY

If you are not fully certain about a fact, say so clearly.

Use phrases like:
- "I'm not certain, but..."
- "You should verify this..."
- "I may be wrong here, but..."
- "Based on the information available to me..."
- "This is my best estimate, not a confirmed fact."

Never state uncertain claims as facts.

If the answer depends on missing context, say what context is missing.

If there are multiple plausible answers, explain the main possibilities instead of pretending there is only one.

2. SOURCES

Do not invent sources.

Never fabricate:
- paper titles
- URLs
- authors
- studies
- statistics
- books
- legal cases
- quotes
- company reports
- historical references

If you cannot name a real, verifiable source, say so.

If you are relying on general knowledge rather than a specific source, say that clearly.

When citing sources, prefer:
- official documentation
- primary sources
- peer-reviewed papers
- government or institutional data
- direct statements from the relevant person or organization

If a source may be outdated, say so.

3. STATISTICS AND NUMBERS

Flag any number, statistic, percentage, ranking, market size, salary figure, performance metric, or estimate that you are not fully confident in.

Use phrases like:
- "I believe this is approximately..."
- "This number may be outdated."
- "Verify this against a primary source before relying on it."
- "I do not have enough information to confirm the exact figure."

Do not make up numbers to make an answer sound more useful.

If a precise number is unavailable, give a range only if it is justified. Otherwise say the number is unknown.

4. RECENT EVENTS

Do not guess about current events.

For any topic that may have changed recently, including:
- news
- elections
- laws
- regulations
- product features
- company leadership
- software versions
- AI model capabilities
- market data

Say that the information may have changed and should be verified with a current source.
Do not present outdated information as current.

5. PEOPLE AND QUOTES

Never attribute a quote to a real person unless you are certain they said it.

If unsure, say:
- "I cannot confirm this quote is accurate."
- "This quote is commonly attributed to them, but I cannot verify it."
- "I do not know who originally said this."

Do not invent statements, beliefs, or motives for real people.
Separate confirmed facts from interpretation.

If any answer is "yes," revise before responding."

AI may follow the same path.

We reshored 121 SKUs from China. Zero production stoppages. 12% net cost reduction. Here's what actually worked.
I see a lot of LinkedIn posts that make reshoring sound impossible or trivial. It's neither. It's a methodical slog that rewards patience over heroics.
First: Rank the SKUs by difficulty and risk. How specialized is the tooling? How often do you actually run out of stock? What kills your operation if you run dry during transition? That ranked list becomes your project plan. Start with the easy wins. Don't start with the hardest ones just because they scare you.
Second: Build inventory before you move anything. We built 18 months of safety stock before we transferred a single mold. Expensive? Yeah. But it's the one decision that lets you move at the right pace instead of a panic pace. Most reshoring projects fail because someone's breathing down your neck.
Third: Move the knowledge, not just the contract. Molds, setup notes, first article inspection history — all of it. Most companies I've seen switch suppliers and leave all that institutional knowledge sitting with the old vendor. You've just traded one crisis for another.
Fourth: Don't qualify under pressure. We never qualified a mold with a hard production deadline attached to it. If the first article inspection found something, we had weeks to fix it. That breathing room is what kept us from shutting down the line.
Fifth: Do the full cost math. Material cost is higher domestically. But tariffs, freight, lead time, quality escapes, problem resolution — when you add it all up, ours came out 12% cheaper. The unit cost lied.
Every manufacturer is running this number right now. If you're figuring out where to start, I'm easy to find.

Maintenance Dashboard : See Machine Health and Reliability in 5 Minutes

In many plants, maintenance is still managed through gut feeling, scattered files, or conversations at the coffee machine. When a critical machine stops, everyone suddenly realises how blind they actually are.

That is why a simple, visual maintenance dashboard (like the example below for fictitious 3 machines) can be a real game changer.

What a good Dashboard does:
✅ Connects reliability with business impact:
➡️ MTBF, MTTR, OEE and maintenance cost on one page
➡️ Shows how technical problems translate into lost capacity, overtime and margin. 
➡️ It becomes much easier to argue for spare parts, upgrades or extra headcount when the data is visible and trend-based.

✅ Makes problems obvious – every day:
➡️ Monthly trends of MTBF/MTTR, 
➡️ Top 5 anomalies for each machine and adherence to schedule turn “we have many breakdowns” into a clear story
➡️ Where B/D happen, how often and whether we are getting better or worse. 
➡️ People stop debating opinions and start attacking the real causes.

✅ Drives discipline in preventive and autonomous maintenance:
➡️ When adherence to plan is on the dashboard, missed PMs and AM tasks are no longer invisible.
➡️ Teams see immediately if they are protecting the bottleneck machine or running it to failure. 
➡️ That transparency builds a culture where planning and execution really matter.

✅Prioritises where to act first
Instead of spreading resources thin, 
➡️ You quickly identify the pilot machine, the bottleneck and the “silent killers”. 
➡️ A focused Kaizen Study on the worst MTBF, or faster AM Progress on the top breakdown machine, becomes an obvious next step – not a guess.

✅ Creates common language between Production, Maintenance and Management

How does a company free up 8 Mio EUR in working capital and lose 96 Mio EUR in the same year?

The answer usually starts with a slide that looked completely convincing. A 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗶𝘀 showing inventory levels sitting well above the best-in-class range, a clear gap against what the top performers in the industry were holding, and a straightforward recommendation to bring the numbers in line. Finance approved it, the board noted it as a sign of improving capital discipline, and the Q3 balance sheet looked better than it had in years. 8 Mio EUR freed, a compelling story ready for the next investor update.

Then a port strike hit, a critical supplier ran 3 weeks late, and what followed was the kind of variability that shows up every 18 months or so, which the organization had always managed without much drama. Except this time, the buffer was gone, the stock had been cut to benchmark levels, and 2 customers who needed the product went out of stock and moved to a competitor. Revenue lost: 96 Mio EUR. The write-off was twelve times the original saving.

The benchmark had done exactly what benchmarks do: it told the team what their peers were holding. What it did not say was what that inventory was actually doing, which customer commitments it was protecting, which supply risks it was quietly absorbing, which revenue it was underwriting in the background. That information was never in the slide because nobody had thought to put it there, and nobody senior had thought to ask.

In theory, aligning with best-in-class inventory ratios improves capital efficiency. In practice, resilience is invisible until it disappears, and by then the cost of finding out what it was worth tends to hit all at once.

The Iceberg of Ignorance - Below the Waterline:  The Reality Leaders Rarely See

Last few days we discussed about Hoshin, KMIs, KPIs, KAIs.. Still we as leaders need to understand ‘What is our line of Sight’, ‘Are there hidden risks of Performance Metrics Management’ ?

In many companies, the most dangerous problems are not the ones leaders see – but the ones they never hear about.  

In 1989, Sidney Yoshida uncovered a harsh truth: The closer you are to the frontline, the clearer the problems look: 
🟢 Frontline workers see all (100%)
🟠 Supervisors see most (74%)
🟡 Middle managers see little (9%)
🔴 Top management see just (4%)

Here’s what it means :  
☀️ Frontline teams see nearly all the real issues – but only a tiny fraction ever reaches senior management.  
🌤️ Every layer of hierarchy filters the message a bit more: “We’re mostly fine,” “It’s under control,” “No need to escalate yet.”  
🌥️ By the time it hits the boardroom, the story is clean, the deck is green, and the blind spot is massive.  

That’s Iceberg of Ignorance in action:  The visible 4% above the waterline looks “OK,” while 96% of obstacles, rework, safety risks, and improvement ideas stay hidden below. Not because people don’t care; but because the system makes it hard (and sometimes unsafe) to speak up.  

If you are a leader, ask yourself:  
❓ When was the last time you heard something on the Gemba that was completely new to you?  
❓ Do people bring you bad news early – or only when it is impossible to hide?  
❓ Are your frontline workers free to say, “This doesn’t make sense” without fear of being labelled negative or “not a team player”?  

Melting the iceberg is not about another tool. It’s about behavior:  
✅ Show up at the Gemba to listen, not to inspect.  
✅ Thank people for raising ugly truths.  
✅ Act fast on small irritations before they become big crises.  
✅ Make it normal for problems to be visible – and abnormal for silence to be rewarded.  

When leaders get closer to reality at the frontline, decisions improve, trust grows, and continuous improvement stops being a slogan and starts being a habit.  

If your dashboards are green but your people are tired, frustrated, or quiet – you might already be sailing towards an iceberg.  

Would you be brave enough to invite your team to “show you the part of the iceberg you don’t see”?

He looked for a 1% improvement in everything — tyres, pillows, hand-washing technique, nutrition timing. Individually, none of it mattered. Together, they won 60% of the gold medals at Beijing 2008.
Your SME works the same way.
Shorten one meeting by 5 minutes. Add one follow-up question to your next client call. Remove one unnecessary approval step. Reply to enquiries 30 minutes faster.
None of those feel significant. That's exactly the point.
The 1% rule has only one enemy — inconsistency. Improving for 3 days and stopping for 4 doesn't compound. It stalls. So swipe through this carousel for the simple 3-question daily habit that keeps the 1% going — every single day.

Gemba Walks: The Most Honest Mirror of Your Leadership

We spend hours discussing performance in meeting rooms, but the real story is written on the shopfloor.

If we’re honest, most of the problems we “discover” in reviews were visible days ago at the Gemba where value is actually created.

That’s why Gemba walks are not an 'Operational Ritual'; they are mirrors of 'Leadership Behaviour'.

Done right, they transform:
🎯 The way we see problems
🎯 The way teams see leadership
🎯 The speed at which we turn issues into improvements

When we walk the Gemba, we should try to look beyond “Is everything OK?” and focus on 10 powerful lenses:
1️⃣ What is the process?
2️⃣ What is normal vs abnormal?
3️⃣ What is working well?
4️⃣ What is not working well?
5️⃣ What is broken?
6️⃣ What is not understood?
7️⃣ What is creating waste?
8️⃣ What is creating strain?
9️⃣ What is creating unevenness?
🔟 What is not visible enough?

But Gemba is not only about what we see : It’s also about how we lead. Thats why we should also use a parallel set of leadership lenses to guide the conversation:
1️⃣ How can we improve the process?
2️⃣ How can we eliminate the abnormal?
3️⃣ How can we move good to great?
4️⃣ Why is standard not being followed?
5️⃣ How can we prevent broken things?
6️⃣ Why is it not understood?
7️⃣ Why is it creating waste?
8️⃣ How can we prevent strain?
9️⃣ How can we smooth unevenness?
🔟 How can we make it visible?

A good Gemba walk has at least six rules:
✅ Go with curiosity, not a checklist
✅ Listen more than you speak
✅ Ask “What makes your job difficult today?” and really wait for the answer
✅ Instead of asking why we are off-target : ask 'what stops us from hitting it'
✅ Always leave a trace of action
✅ Connect what you see to your leadership

Nothing destroys Gemba faster than leaders who walk, nod, take photos and change nothing. Convert at least one observation into a clear action, owner, and date and follow up visibly.

Gemba Walk isn’t about walking around with a clipboard. It’s about building a culture where problems are seen, spoken about, and solved together : At the place where they happen.

🔄 Your turn:
How often do you (or your leadership team) go to the Gemba with a clear purpose? Do you question yourself and your leadership team equally or even tougher for your observations ?

"The foundation of quality is the human being. No drawing, no process, no document will save it." the MD of ELGI EQUIPMENTS LIMITED said this to me on our podcast when I asked how ELGi protects quality at the production level.

ELGi has zero contract labour on their production floor. Workers go through three years of vocational training before they are considered fully capable. 

Shop floor attrition is effectively zero. The only contractors on site handle housekeeping, the canteen, and material movement.

The MD was specific about why.

"The person's feel when a nut does not rotate smoothly is an indicator. If that person's mind and heart are not committed, no process and no document is going to protect it."

That feel is not trained in a week. It is built over years of repetition, ownership, and the belief that the work matters. You cannot contract for it.

I think about this when I visit plants across India and watch the trend continue in the other direction. Contract labour at sixty percent. Seventy. In some companies, ninety percent of the production workforce. The rationale is flexibility and cost. Both are real.

What is not written on any balance sheet is the ceiling this places on quality.

Building a world-class product is not unlike building a world-class athlete. Sania Mirza did not become what she became through a series of annual contracts. The capability is accumulated. It cannot be borrowed on demand.

The Japanese companies I studied in the 1980s treated production workers as the carriers of institutional knowledge, not as replaceable units of labour. 

Toyota's improvement systems were not designed by engineers and handed down. They were built with the people doing the work, because those people knew something no specification sheet could capture.

If you cannot earn the mind and heart of a person who is here for one year, you have already decided what quality ceiling you can live with.

Most companies have simply not written that decision down.

Process Capability : A Practical One-Page Guide

What is Process Capability
Process capability is a statistical tool used to evaluate the ability of a process to produce output within specified limits, reflecting the "potential capability" of the process. It helps organizations determine if their processes can consistently meet customer requirements and specifications.

Purpose of Process Capability
🎯Meet customer requirements and specifications.
🎯 Measure and control the spread (variation) of the process.
🎯 Provide realistic tolerances for product dimensions.
🎯 Improve overall process performance capability.

Influencing Factors
➡️ Condition of machines and equipment.
➡️ Type and quality of raw materials.
➡️ Operator and inspector skill levels.
➡️ Measurement methods and instrument conditions.
➡️ Operational and environmental conditions.

Process Capability Overview
🔈 Voice of the Process: 
The actual output distribution of the process
🔈 Voice of the Customer: 
The specification limits set by the customer (USL and LSL)
🔈 Process Width vs. Design Width: 
The process should fit well within the design (specification) limits to be considered capable

Tools Used in Process Capability Analysis
1️⃣ Histogram: Shows the distribution of numerical data
2️⃣ Control Chart: Differentiates between common cause and special cause variation
3️⃣ Run Chart: Graphically represents how a process is performed or how data values change over time
4️⃣ ANOVA: Evaluates the difference between the means of more than two groups

Key Indices
↗️ Cp – Process Capability
Definition: Measures the ability of a process to produce output within specification limits, considering only the spread (variation) of the process
Interpretation: Cp does not account for how well the process is centered. A Cp ≥ 1.33 is generally considered acceptable

↗️ Cpk – Process Capability Index
Definition: Measures how close a process is running to its specification limits, accounting for process mean (centering)
Interpretation: Cpk considers both spread and centering. A Cpk ≥ 1.33 is desirable

Process capability analysis is essential for quality management, helping organizations ensure their processes are capable of consistently meeting customer requirements. By understanding and applying Cp and Cpk, businesses can identify improvement opportunities, reduce defects, and enhance customer satisfaction

Different MRP Procedures Used In SAP PP Explained with a Motorcycle Manufacturing Example 🏍️
In manufacturing, one important thing to understand is:
Not every material should be planned the same way.
Imagine a motorcycle manufacturing company 🏭
For every motorcycle, the company needs engines, frames, tyres, batteries, brake assemblies, nuts, bolts, lubricants, and packaging materials.
Now the question is:
Should all these materials follow the same planning method?
The answer is no.
That is where MRP procedures come in.
An MRP procedure decides when and how much material should be procured or produced.
There are two main approaches:
1. MRP Planning 📊
MRP is used when demand depends on the production plan, sales orders, forecast, or BOM.
Example:
If the company plans to produce 1,000 motorcycles, the system calculates:
1,000 engines
2,000 tyres
1,000 batteries
1,000 brake assemblies
This happens through the Bill of Materials.
MRP is best for critical and high-value production materials like engines, frames, tyres, batteries, and brake assemblies.
2. Consumption-Based Planning 📦
Consumption-based planning works differently.
Here, the system looks at stock levels, past consumption, or fixed planning intervals instead of mainly depending on the production plan.
Example:
Nuts, bolts, washers, lubricants, gloves, and packaging materials are used regularly in a motorcycle plant.
Instead of planning them for every motorcycle order, the system can say:
“When stock goes below a certain level, reorder again.”
This is useful for low-value and frequently used materials.
Types of Consumption-Based Planning 🔁
Reorder Point Planning:
When stock falls below a set level, the system suggests replenishment.
Manual Reorder Point: The planner sets the reorder level manually.
Automatic Reorder Point: The system calculates it using past consumption, lead time, and safety stock.
Forecast-Based Planning 📈: The system predicts future demand from past consumption.
Time-Phased Planning 🗓️: Planning happens on fixed days, such as every Monday.
Simple Difference
MRP is based on future requirements.
Consumption-based planning is based on past usage or stock levels.
So, in a motorcycle company:
Use MRP for engines, frames, tyres, batteries, and brake assemblies.
Use consumption-based planning for nuts, bolts, washers, lubricants, gloves, and packaging materials.
A good production planner avoids: Material shortages that stop production
Excess inventory that blocks working capital
Planning is not just about creating orders.
It is about choosing the right planning method for the right material. ✅

↳ "I've been studying [topic] for [X time]. Here's what I think I understand: [your summary]. Tell me what I'm getting wrong, oversimplifying, or completely missing."

↳ "Quiz me on [topic]. Start easy, increase difficulty as I answer correctly. When I'm wrong, explain why and ask a follow-up. Keep going until I get 10 right in a row."

7️⃣ Debate you

I liken it to weather forecasting for a hurricane. Today, when a hurricane is about to hit Florida, we don't have a single plan. A single plan would be foolish. Instead, we have multiple plans with different probabilities. The plan probabilities help to models to learn and predict the final outcome. We then use outside-in data--flying planes through the storm, gathering more meteorological data, and studying the patterns--to fine-tune the plans to narrow down the options. Then, within a day or two, the path is clear. 

I think that design technologies will be an important part of an orchestration layer for business leaders that I term digital assistants, enabling what-if analysis, workflow, and scenario sharing for business leaders across time horizons for unknown/knowns, known/unknowns, and unknown/unknowns. Traditional planning (APS) approaches focus only on the knowns (known facts to understand known outcomes).

Why does everyone know which supplier is underperforming but nobody can prove it?

Because gut feel is not a scorecard, and without one, the conversation stays stuck at opinion.

Supplier scorecards are not about rating suppliers, they are about
what you weight. Score delivery at 30% and cost at 10%, and you
have just told your supplier team what this company actually values.
Most scorecards send the wrong message by accident.

This is Episode 25 of Supply Chain 101. From here, we go one function deep
per month. 

We start with procurement, because it sits at the
beginning of every supply chain and shapes everything that comes
after it.

A supplier scorecard gives you the one thing most procurement
conversations are missing: a number that everyone agreed on in
advance. Five criteria cover what actually matters:

• Quality is defect rate and spec compliance. It determines
 whether the product works. Most teams track this, but track it
 inconsistently because the threshold was never written down.

• Delivery is on-time-in-full against the date you needed it, not
 the date the supplier promised. Those two dates are often weeks
 apart, and measuring the wrong one masks the real performance.

• Cost is not unit price alone. It includes price stability,
 expediting charges, and rework costs that spread across four
 departments and never appear on the same report.

• Responsiveness is how fast they engage when something goes
 wrong. It is the most revealing criterion and the most skipped,
 because nobody thinks to score it until a crisis makes it obvious.

• Compliance is certifications, documentation, audit results. Low
 weight until it becomes the only weight.

The weighting row is the most important row in the scorecard.
A supplier scoring 74% overall can look acceptable until you
unpack it and find their delivery is flagged red. The total hides
what the breakdown exposes. What you weight is what you value,
and your suppliers will read that row before they read their score.

What would your most important supplier score today?

Most SME owners have done this at least once.
Big strategy day. New consultant. New software. New 90-day plan. Everyone leaves the room feeling energised.
Three months later — half the team has reverted to the old way of doing things, the consultant's invoice has been paid, and the problem is still there.
This is the Big Bang approach. And research suggests it fails around 70% of the time in small businesses — not because the ideas are bad, but because the method is wrong for how SMEs actually work.
Kaizen is the opposite.
Instead of one massive change, it asks for one small improvement. Every day. The team suggests it. The cost is near zero. You see results in 2–3 weeks. And because the change is small enough to absorb, it actually sticks.
One SME spent £18,000 on a CRM rollout that the team quietly abandoned within months. Another solved the same underlying problem — slow sales follow-ups — by asking their team one question and building a single email template in an afternoon. Follow-up rate up 40%. Cost: zero.

The topic:
How do we move from a traditional Supply Chain operating model to an AI-orchestrated one?

Most companies are trying to add AI to their existing Supply Chain process.

Would we design this process the same way if AI was already at the center?

Traditional Supply Chain still works through systems, meetings, escalations, spreadsheets and knowledge hidden in people's heads.
The future model looks different.
AI agents support repeated decisions.
Humans own judgment and exceptions.
Decision history is visible.
Constraints are explicit.
Operational knowledge is formalized.
But between those two models there is a cloud.
The road we do not fully know yet.

That cloud is where most AI transformations will either become real or quietly fail.

why data is not enough, why decision history matters, and why the real transformation is not implementing AI tools.

It is rebuilding the operating model around AI-supported decisions and human judgment.

Most plants don’t have a Lean problem.
They have a layer problem.

They try to improve culture before standard work exists.

They ask for accountability before the work is visible.

They install dashboards before people agree what “normal” looks like.

They run Kaizen events before daily management is stable.
And then everyone wonders why the improvement doesn’t hold.

A Lean operation is built in layers:

1. Standard work
2. isual management
3. Daily management
4. CI systems
5. Culture

Culture is NOT where you start.
Culture is what shows up after the lower layers become real on the floor.

If the standard is unclear, the board won’t save you.

If the board is ignored, the meeting won’t save you.

If the meeting has no action, the culture won’t change.

Start where the work happens.

Make the standard VISIBLE.

Then manage the gap every day.

That’s where Lean starts to hold.

What layer is weakest in most plants you’ve seen?

Here is a highly concise, executive summary of the Supply Chain Metrics cheat sheet. It condenses the 14 key performance indicators into 4 core operational pillars for fast, high-level review.
1. Demand & Capacity Planning
Forecast Accuracy: Measures variance between forecasted and actual demand to reduce planning variability.
Capacity Utilization: Tracks actual vs. maximum possible production output to balance underutilization against operational overload.
2. Sourcing, Inventory & Cost Efficiency
Inventory Turnover & Days of Inventory (DOI): Dual metrics tracking asset efficiency-how fast stock sells versus how many days of supply are tied up in inventory.
Total Landing Cost: Captures the true, fully burdened cost of an item (Price + Freight + Duties + Handling).
Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time: Measures total days cash is frozen between paying suppliers (DPO) and collecting revenue (DSO), influenced by inventory velocity (DIO).
3. Warehouse & Logistics Speed
Dock-to-Stock Cycle Time: Measures the internal throughput speed from receiving goods to warehouse stock availability.
Order-to-Delivery Lead Time: Tracks total elapsed time from the initial customer order date to the final physical delivery date.
Supply Chain Cycle Time: An end-to-end macro metric covering the entire SCOR model workflow: $\text{Plan} (rightarrow \text{Source} \rightarrow |text{Make} \rightarrow |text{Deliver} \rightarrow \text{Return}$.
4. Customer Fulfillment & Service Level
Perfect Order Rate: The ultimate reliability standard-orders delivered on time, complete, damage-free, and accurately documented.
On-Time In-Full (OTIF): Measures the baseline execution performance of delivery punctuality and completeness.
Fill Rate vs. Backorder Rate: Inverse indicators tracking immediate product availability from stock versus the percentage of demand delayed due to stockouts.

A PO is not a document. It is a legal commitment, a finance record, and a supplier instruction all at once.

Treating it as a form to fill in is how approvals get missed, invoices get disputed, and payments run 60 days late.
 
This is Episode 26 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 25 we started the Procurement month with the supplier scorecard. Today we follow the purchase order from the moment a need is identified to the moment the invoice is paid, because most of the friction in procurement-finance relationships lives somewhere in these seven steps.

And it moves through seven hands before it closes:

• Requisition: someone in the business identifies a need and raises a formal request. This is where the process starts andd where most ad-hoc buying bypasses the system entirely.

• Approval: the requisition goes through an authorisation workflow. The delay here is almost always process, not urgency. Most approvals take longer than the actual purchase.

• PO creation: procurement converts the approved requisition into a legal purchase order and sends it to the supplier. At this point the company has made a financial commitment.

• Supplier confirmation: the supplier acknowledges receipt and confirms they can fulfil the order. Without this, you have a commitment with no confirmation it will be met.

• Goods receipt: the warehouse records what was actually received. This step is the one most often done late, informally, or not at all, and it is what makes the next step possible.

• Invoice matching: finance matches the supplier invoice against the PO and the goods receipt note. This is the three-way match, and it is where most payment delays originate. If goods receipt was never recorded, the match cannot close.

• Payment: the invoice is approved and payment is released to the supplier.

The gap between goods receipt and invoice matching is where most SC-finance friction lives. Not because the process is wrong, but because two teams own adjacent steps and rarely communicate when one step is late.

How many of these seven steps does your team own end-to-end?

Most SME owners have heard of Kaizen.

I recently decided to switch mobile network provider. Not because of cost but due to a poor signal in the area I had moved too.

Speaking to a new provider was easy and the experience positive but when seeking subsequent technical support – what a nightmare !

I received my new SIM in the post, but it stated a different mobile to that I am transferring and the blurb enclosed did not mention this. So, I called my future network provider to clarify next steps, but could I find an option to speak to a human being? 

Eventually I decided to choose the “Thinking of leaving us? option” and not surprisingly I was put through to a person.

The person was great and everything sorted so I asked “It is now Saturday, at what time will I be able to changeover to the new SIM? 
Stupidly I expected this to be the same day or perhaps the next. Nope ! 
That will be WEDNESDAY sir because it is a bank holiday weekend. 

What? 

In this world of technology and AI, why does it take 5 days to switch mobile provider after having received and activated my new SIM?

Two more things. 
1.       Do the people who actually set up these automated response systems actually have people trial and test them, then act on the feedback?
2.       Why in this digital age can providers take your money instantly but not provide the service just as quickly?

If your CEO doesn't show up to your S&OP / IBP executive meetings — that's a signal.

Not about his calendar. 
About your meeting.

In my experience, there are only 3 reasons why a CEO disengages:

It's not impactful enough.
The meeting is a status update, not a decision forum. He already knows the numbers. He needs to know what to do with them.

It's not efficient. 
90 minutes of slides.10 minutes of actual decisions. That's not a meeting. That's a presentation.

It's boring. 
No tension. No real debate. Everyone agrees on everything. If there's no conflict in the room, the real conversations are happening elsewhere.

The S&OP / IBP meeting should be the place where your CEO gets clarity on three things:

Are we on track vs. business targets? What are the biggest risks and gaps? What do we need to decide — right now?
If your meeting doesn't answer those three questions in the first 20 minutes, you've lost him.

Spot It, Measure It, Eliminate It: The World-Class Plant LOSS Mindset

Are you sure you know where your plant’s productivity leaks away ? Most factories suffer hidden losses every day, but only a few track them systematically and act with precision. Today, I tried to put together a guide and overview of the typical losses every manufacturing plant faces:

💸 Machine Losses: 
Unexpected breakdowns, lengthy setups, and efficiency drops.
💸 Manpower Losses: 
Idle waiting, multi-tasking chaos, and time lost to poor motion.
💸 Material and Energy Losses: 
Over-usage, waste, rework, and hidden scrap.
💸 Other Losses: 
From excess inventory to IT and environmental costs.

What sets World Class Plants apart ?
🎯 They make every loss visible; even the ones hidden in plain sight.
🎯 Standardize loss definitions and use a central “losses dictionary” to drive a common understanding across all teams.
🎯 Measure losses with clear, actionable formulas, linking shopfloor data directly to improvement actions.
🎯 Set up robust digital tracking systems; use real-time dashboards and automate data collection for downtime, waste, and energy.
🎯 Train operators and technicians to recognize and react to loss signals instantly, not just managers or engineers.
🎯 Organize cross-functional loss review meetings focused on root causes, not blame; engage maintenance, operations, quality, and logistics together.
🎯 Benchmark every category; compare your losses and benchmarks with peers in your sector and the world’s best plants.
🎯 Drive action at the source, deploy World Class tools on the shopfloor: Loss Intelligence, Root Cause Analysis, SMED, Kaizens and visual management boards.
🎯 Reward teams for sustainable loss reduction, not for “firefighting.” Celebrate every breakthrough, big or small.
🎯 Cultivate continuous improvement culture; make loss elimination everyone’s daily habit, not a special project.

How can you start winning this battle?
✅ Adopt a detailed losses dictionary (like the one shared here)
✅ Connect losses to real data (Downtime, Scrap, Energy, Claims, etc.)
✅ Empower your teams to attack each loss type with focused tools

Don’t let “acceptable loss” be an excuse for inefficiency. Begin with mapping your own losses, benchmark with global standards, and let your efficiency (OEE) soar !

LinkedIn isn't too crowded. 
Starting from zero in 2026 is actually the easiest it's been in years.

When Chris and I analyzed 397K posts earlier this month, we found the gap between the top 1% and the average creator is shrinking.

When I started in 2024, a big audience was a massive advantage. Big accounts got more early engagement.

But that advantage is gone. Follower count is not what wins on LinkedIn.

So if I were starting in 2026, this is the exact system I'd follow:

1/ How to go viral

Virality = topic + first line + visual. All 3 need to stop the scroll before someone clicks "see more."

Pick a topic your audience is already interested in. Make line 1 a specific promise, problem, or surprise (authority, personal story, or humor), and pair it with a visual interesting enough to stop the scroll.

2/ Set a content strategy

LinkedIn posts do 1 of 3 things: grow your audience, build trust, or drive sales. Most people stick to growth content cuz it's easier, but growth alone won't convert anyone into a lead.

Post educational infographics and carousels 4x a week to grow, personal stories 2x a week to build trust, and case studies 1x a week to drive leads.

3/ Write for LinkedIn

The best posts are between 1,250 and 3,000 characters. That gives you enough space to set up the problem, make people care, and give them something useful.

Make sure your posts read like you speak. No one wants to read a formal report or a try-hard joke.

4/ Post more videos

Video builds trust better than almost any other format.

Use it for educational content, stories and skits, or client testimonials. One video a week is enough.

5/ Create lead magnets

Build a freebie that solves one narrow, painful problem for your target audience. A prompt library, a checklist, a template, or a swipe file all work.

Give it away in exchange for an email.

6/ LinkedIn power hour

You don't need to spend all day on LinkedIn. All you need is a daily system - I recommend the power hour.

Comment thoughtfully on 5-10 posts in your niche. Share a post that solves a real problem for your audience. Reply to every comment you get within the first hour. Then DM the people who engaged with you.

Anyone can start building a personal brand today. Don’t fall behind.

Demand Variability vs Forecast Error: What Planners Must Understand!
Unstable demand and poor forecasting are not the same problem.
But many planning teams treat them as if they are.
When demand goes up and down, the first reaction is often:
“The forecast is wrong.”
But sometimes, the forecast is not the real issue.
Sometimes, the demand pattern itself is naturally unstable.
What is Demand Variability?
Demand variability means actual customer demand keeps changing.
It is usually caused by:
📈 Seasonality — demand rises and falls during specific periods
 📢 Promotions — campaigns create temporary spikes
 👥 Customer behavior — order frequency or quantity changes
 🌍 Market changes — competition, pricing, or demand shifts
 🏗️ Project-based demand — irregular bulk orders
 🚀 Product lifecycle changes — launch, growth, maturity, or decline
What is Forecast Error?
Forecast error means the forecast is different from actual demand.
It answers:
🎯 “How wrong was the forecast?”
Demand variability answers:
📊 “How unstable is the demand pattern?”
Why the Difference Matters
A stable product with high forecast error needs better planning discipline.
That may mean:
🧹 Cleaner data
 🧠 Better assumptions
 🤝 Improved sales input
 📅 Stronger S&OP alignment
 🔍 Review of forecast bias
 ⚙️ Better planning parameters
But a highly variable product may need a different planning strategy.
That may mean:
📦 SKU segmentation
 🛡️ Safety stock strategy
 👁️ Customer visibility
 ⏱️ Lead time review
 🚨 Exception-based planning
 📊 Different service-level rules

Great planners do not only ask:
“Was the forecast accurate?”
They also ask:
“Was this demand pattern forecastable?”
🎯 Forecast error tells you how wrong the forecast was.
📊 Demand variability tells you how unstable the demand pattern is.
Both matter.
Which creates more issues in your planning process — demand variability or forecast error?

The Power of a Simple Operator Checklist : Autonomous Maintenance in Action 

Autonomous Maintenance (AM) empowers operators to take the lead in basic care tasks such as  5S; cleaning, inspection, lubrication (CIL), and tightening/adjustments(T). The key tool : A well-structured AM checklist.

A practical AM checklist covers:
✅ Cleaning routines (side trays, dryer nozzles, etc.)
✅ Lubrication points (bearings, rollers)
✅ Inspection activities (pressure gauges, vibration checks)
✅ Detailed standards for each job, safety protocols, and the required frequency
✅ Step-by-step routes and checkpoints mapped visually for clarity
✅ A clear record-keeping matrix for tracking completion and issues

Why Checklists
1️⃣ Consistency
Standardized checklists ensure every task: No matter how big or small is completed correctly and on schedule, reducing errors and overlooking nothing.
2️⃣ Ownership & Accountability
Operators become “the first line of defense” for equipment, fostering greater responsibility and equipment care at the source.
3️⃣ Proactive Problem-Solving
By documenting daily, weekly, and monthly tasks, AM checklists help detect issues early, preventing costly breakdowns and extending equipment life.
4️⃣ Efficiency
Clear instructions and visual cues minimize downtime and boost productivity 
5️⃣ Productivity
Researches show that AM can reduce equipment downtime by up to 40% and increase productivity by 25%.

Best Practices
🎯 Train operators thoroughly on each checklist element.
🎯 Combine paper-based or digital checklists with real-time feedback loops.
🎯 Update checklists regularly to reflect new findings and continuous improvement needs

🔴  Many operators may see cleaning as burden : Cleaning is inspection in autonomous maintenance because touching and seeing every surface during cleaning exposes leaks, looseness, wear, and other abnormalities early, so the cleaning act itself functions as a systematic condition check.

Do you just let operators ‘run’ the equipment and let Maintenance take care of them when needed, 
or 
Train and empower Operators to ‘own’ the equipment and performance (so Maintenance can stop firefighting, start preventing) ? 
Which one sounds better ?

Forecasts don’t buy inventory.
Plans don’t place POs.
Buyers do.

And this is where many inventory problems quietly begin.
Most organizations talk about forecasting and planning.
Far fewer talk about the connection between forecasting, planning, and buying.

But all three drive inventory performance together.
→ Forecasting: Builds the demand signal using history, trends, and market inputs.

→ Planning: Translates that signal into inventory, capacity, and supply decisions.

→ Buying: Turns those decisions into real cash commitments and inventory receipts.

The relationship that matters:
Forecasting predicts demand.
Planning positions supply.
Buying commits cash.

Where organizations struggle is in the gap between the three.
- The forecast shifts.
- The plan lags.
- The buy order is already placed.

That’s when problems compound:
- Inventory building ahead of demand
- Short buys on fast-moving SKUs
- Excess working capital exposure
- Margin pressure from reactionary purchasing
- Service levels slipping during volatility

Strong operators understand:
- Forecasting improves visibility.
- Planning improves readiness.
- Buying determines financial exposure.

The real challenge is not optimizing one function independently.

It’s aligning all three fast enough to respond to changing demand.

Question for Operators: Where does your organization see the biggest disconnect today...forecasting, planning, or buying?

Hoshin (Kanri) Matrix : Putting Strategy into Action Top Down - Bottom Up

A Hoshin Matrix (also known as a Hoshin X-Matrix) is a strategic planning tool used to link a company’s long-term vision and goals to annual objectives into KPIs, and Individual Objectives all on a single sheet.​

Shaped like an "X," matrix it visually maps:
✅ Long-term strategic priorities (3–5 years)
✅ Annual objectives break those priorities down
✅ Key actions / improvement initiatives for results
✅ Clear metrics (KPIs) for measuring progress
✅ Named owners for accountability

By connecting these layers in a single view, the Hoshin Matrix helps companies focus, align, and execute their strategic plans, cascading objectives. 

Here’s Step by Step Guide to build Hoshin, to practically convert your long term strategic objectives (KMI’s) into your annual targets, (KPI’s); then to your Key Activities/Initiatives (KAI’s) and then into Individual Objectives (IO’s) :

Step 1️⃣ : Set Your Vision
Start by defining your organization's long-term vision and strategic objectives. These typically span 3-5 years and form the foundation of your matrix

Step 2️⃣ : Define Annual Objectives
Break down your long-term goals into specific, measurable annual objectives. These should be SMART goals that directly contribute to your strategic vision

Step 3️⃣ : Identify Improvement Initiatives
Develop actionable initiatives that will help you achieve your annual objectives. These are the concrete steps your teams will take to drive progress

Step 4️⃣ : Establish Key Metrics
Define clear, measurable KPIs for each initiative. These metrics will help you track progress and ensure you're moving in the right direction

Step 5️⃣ : Assign Responsibilities
Identify key stakeholders and assign clear ownership for each initiative and KPI. This ensures accountability and drives execution

Step 6️⃣ : Create X-Matrix
Now, bring it all together in the X-Matrix format
⬇️ Long-term objectives in the south quadrant
⬅️ Annual objectives in the west quadrant
⬆️ Improvement initiatives in the north quadrant
➡️ KPIs in the east quadrant
➡️➡️ Responsibilities on the far right

Step 7️⃣ : Establish Relationships
Use symbols or numbers to show the relationships between elements of the matrix. This visual representation helps everyone understand how initiatives connect to objectives

Always 🔄 : Catchball 
Discuss back‑and‑forth goals and plans between levels of the organization to align targets, test feasibility, build ownership
➡️ Leaders “throw” proposed targets, and plans to next level
⚾️ Teams “catch” them, analyze feasibility, add local knowledge, and suggest adjustments
⬅️ The proposal is “thrown back” and iterated until both sides agree so it is a two‑way dialogue & alignment rather than top down push

Strategy without action is just a dream. Hoshin Kanri bridges your vision and execution. Start building alignment that lasts and watch momentum multiply.

Waste in services rarely starts as “waste.”

It usually starts much earlier.

A few calls arrive unevenly.
One person becomes overloaded.
The team starts covering gaps.
Small delays turn into extra follow-ups.
Extra follow-ups create more emails, more meetings, more stress.
And before long, the system starts to snowball.

In manufacturing, we often talk about Muda — the 7 wastes.
But in service environments, I believe we need to look first at Mura and Muri:

Mura — unevenness
Muri — overburden
Muda — visible waste

Because waste is often not the root cause.
It is the result.

When workload is uneven, people compensate.
When people compensate too long, they burn out.
When they burn out, customers feel it.

The first question should not be:
“How do we make people work faster?”

The better question is:
“Where is the unevenness in the system?”

Fix the flow first.
Reduce the overburden.
Then the waste becomes much easier to see - and much easier to remove.

No drama.
Better facts.
Better flow.

And then the data teams sat down together for the first time and compared the ERP systems.

The same standard bolt appeared as MRB5-SS-HEX in one system and SLT-8-20-INOX in the other, with two further variants across two additional databases. Identical components, incompatible naming conventions, 60.000 parts multiplied across four systems, and a saving that was perfectly real but completely invisible to anyone trying to read across them. An opportunity impossible to see.

The traditional answer was an IT project. Three years, a budget of 2 Mio EUR, a waterfall plan with phases and milestones and a go-live date that kept moving because the problem was harder than the architecture diagram had suggested. By the time the data was finally clean and the components were properly matched, the savings window had closed. Competitors had already moved, the relevant suppliers had been contracted elsewhere, and the people who had championed the initiative had mostly moved on to other roles. The saving was never the question. The question was always whether anyone could find it fast enough to matter.

Problem Solving Toolbox: Choosing Right Methods to Solve Business Challenges

In daily operations, new challenges can surface unexpectedly; sometimes as stubborn bottlenecks and sometimes as subtle gaps in performance. The true test for any organization is not just in spotting these issues, but in matching each problem with a methodology that drives meaningful and lasting improvement.​

The attached guideline “Problem Solving / Process Improvement Tools Selection Matrix” illustrates how each business function; 

📗Research & Development
📕Corporate strategy
📓Customer service
📘Manufacturing
📙Logistics
📒Quality

… and more; faces distinct challenges, from KPI tracking to spare parts shortages. Each row highlights typical pain points, while columns unveil targeted methodologies: Lean, Six Sigma, FMEA, 8D, Kaizen, 5 Whys, DMS, and many more.

Matrix is a guide based on my own knowledge and experience, not to be taken definitive, but its a good starting point and reference for practitioners.

What stands out is that there’s no universal solution. 

For example:
✅ R&D may apply FMEA, Agile and Design Thinking to break down siloed collaboration, drive innovation, and shorten time-to-market for new products.
✅ Procurement and Supply Chain teams often turn to VSM and Risk Management to address cost fluctuations, supplier reliability, and parts shortages.

🎯Effective leaders don’t just train teams in popular frameworks; they map specific problems to methodologies. 
🎯Start with a thorough diagnosis, understand the nature of your challenge and clarify the problem first
🎯Once the problem is defined, area and complexity is clearer, leverage the matrix for actionable alignment.

The most dangerous AI roadmap is the one that pretends the fog does not exist.

Most Supply Chain leaders can describe the future:
- AI agents.  
- Autonomous decisions.  
- Human exception handling.  
- Faster scenarios.  
- Better planning.

The direction is clear.

The full road is not.

Between today's process and the AI-orchestrated model there is a cloud.

Inside that cloud are the things companies have not made visible yet:
- which decisions repeat,  
- which constraints matter,  
- which overrides are normal,  
- which data cannot be trusted,  
- which knowledge exists only in people's heads.

You do not remove the cloud with a large transformation deck.

You reduce it by making the next two or three steps concrete.

Pick one process.  
Map one decision.  
Capture the data.  
Capture the constraints.  
Run a small pilot.  
Learn what the process really needs.

That is not less ambitious.

It is more honest.

How does a list of 100 potential suppliers get down to the one who actually gets the order? 

Five filters. 

Most teams apply only one of them consistently.

This is Episode 27 of Supply Chain 101. We started the procurement series with scorecards to measure suppliers, then how a PO works. This is the process that decides which supplier earns a place on that PO.

The funnel has five stages:

• Market survey (100 → 20) Who even operates in this space? Capabilities, geography, certifications. Most teams rush this or skip it entirely, so the RFQ goes to suppliers who should not be receiving it.

• RFI qualified (20 → 8) Can you meet our minimum requirements? Lead time, financial stability, quality history. Suppliers who reach the RFQ have earned it.

• RFQ and evaluation (8 → 3) Price enters here, as one column in a scoring matrix, not as the entire decision.

• Shortlisted and awarded (3 → 1) Total cost, capability, risk, and the question most teams forget: can this supplier grow with us?

The parameter that a lot of people get stuck with is price. It is not the most critical one always, it is whether the supplier can scale with you. A supplier who matches your volume today but cannot in 18 months is a sourcing problem deferred, not solved.

At which stage in this funnel does your team consistently spend the least time?

Stop Chasing Availability, Start Building Reliability

Two lines can show 95% availability and behave like completely different worlds: one runs smoothly with a single planned stop, the other “runs” in constant start–stop chaos filled with micro‑stoppages and jams. 

Why this tells us is we should always look beyond the headline metric and dig into the behaviors underneath it:

👉 MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)
Are we running in long, stable stretches… or constantly restarting flow?

👉 Micro‑stops and jams
These rarely show up in OEE, but they absolutely destroy rhythm, morale, and quality.

👉 Scrap and rework trends
A “high‑availability” line with poor reliability often pays for it in quality losses.

👉 Downtime categories
Not just how much downtime : but what kind and why.

👉 Operator experience
If the team says the line is frustrating, unstable, or unpredictable… believe them. They’re the earliest warning system you have.

🚨 The point is simple:
You can’t manage a system by looking at one metric. You need the story behind the number.

✅ Availability simply tells you how long the equipment is technically up and running over the scheduled time. 

✅ Reliability tells you how stable that running time is by looking at how often failures occur and how much uninterrupted flow you really get. 

In other words, availability answers “How many hours were we up?”, while reliability answers “How smoothly did those hours actually run?”.

For manufacturing leaders, this means you can proudly report high availability and still suffer poor delivery performance, hidden capacity loss, and stressed teams. 

The real lever is improving reliability: increasing the mean time between failures, eliminating micro‑stops, and giving operators a calm, predictable process to run. 

Stop celebrating uptime alone : start asking whether your “green time” is genuinely stable or just green paint over chaos.

Most S&OP reviews end with an updated forecast.

Not with a decision.

That is not always a failure of discipline.
Often, it is how the process was designed.

Most planning processes are built to create alignment.

Fewer are built to evaluate options for action.

The difference sounds small. In reality, it is significant.

I have seen teams do excellent scenario work.

Conservative.
Base.
Upside.

Cleanly modeled. Well presented.

And then nobody asked:

What would we actually do differently in Scenario A compared to Scenario C?

Because the process did not require it.

A scenario without a decision consequence is not really a planning instrument.

It can easily become a way to show preparedness without forcing a choice.

For me, the difference between an S&OP process that plans and one that decides is not mainly in the model.

It is in the question asked before the meeting:

What are we prepared to do differently today, depending on what we see?

If that question is not on the agenda, the rest can become very polished conversation.

Learning to pass an exam vs learning to do a job.

It's a real issue, for some reason when people set exams they often do it from a very literal "follow the rules" way and not from a practical real world experience approach.

There are certain exams that we take in our industry that show you know your way around Business Central. However, what they don't show is that you know how to deal with customers, question why people are trying to do something, and ensuring you can set the system up in an appropriate way.

I know someone studying for the MB-800 exam and thankfully they've picked up how badly worded the questions are and how they expect you to answer. They've also pointed out that it isn't how they would do it in the real world. That's a relief! The difference between text books (or Learn websites) and real world is huge. 

A couple of examples below:

In the first i'd always be questioning why they're trying to post to the blocked dimensions rather than just ploughing in and unblocking them. It might be legitimate but in my experience a lot of the time it's end user error.

In the second I honestly had never noticed that the page was called "Edit Dimension Set Entries" - you click the Dimensions action to get to it. And then the final point about "Implementing Codeunit 408" is bizarre, you don't implement it, it's standard functionality, it's just there and baked in to the system.

If you have to sit any of these Microsoft exams (or anyone elses) what are your biggest frustrations with them?

Last month I heard someone say "Claude Code is all you need and it will save your life"... This month they are using Codex.

And this is kind of the pattern, right?.

A tool drops.
Everyone loses their mind for three weeks.

Half my feed cancels the subscription they were obsessed with in October.

Then it goes quiet. 
Nobody announces the breakup. 
The tool just stops getting mentioned, like it owes us money.

And then the next one shows up and we do it all again.

What gets me is how little comes out of it.

We spend insane energy deciding which "tool is best", but almost none is actually using one to finish something.

I know people who can break down every model released this year and haven't shipped a single thing anyone paid for.

The tool was never the problem.

The problem is the new thing is more fun than the boring half-built thing you already started.

The people actually making money, or using this seriously, stopped caring about this a while ago.

They picked something that works, got good at it, kept going.
Not exciting to watch. Works though.

So my reco:
- Pick a tool that's good enough.
- Stop reading about the next one.
- Go build something a real person would hand you money for.

The model that "changes your life" isn't the next one.

It's the one you actually use long enough to get good at.

Tariff Update | New 85% Rule Creates Winners & Losers in Manufacturing

President Trump signed a proclamation updating Section 232 tariffs on certain steel, aluminum, and copper products. The changes take effect June 8, 2026, and remain in place through December 31, 2027.

Key Changes

1. Agricultural Equipment Tariffs Reduced
Certain agricultural equipment, including combines and harvesters, will move from a 25% tariff to a reduced 15% tariff rate.

2. More Industrial Equipment Added to 15% Category
The temporary 15% tariff category is expanded to include:
- Mobile industrial equipment
- Forklifts
- Bulldozers
- Certain residential HVAC systems and components

This lowers duties compared to the standard derivative product tariff rates.

3. Incentive to Use US Metals
Products containing at least 85% US melted and poured steel or 85% US smelted and cast aluminum or copper can qualify for a lower effective tariff rate of 10%.

The previous threshold was 95%, making qualification easier.

4. New Products Added to Coverage
Additional derivative products now subject to Section 232 duties include:
- Aluminum lithographic plates
- Steel racks

The administration stated this is intended to prevent tariff circumvention.

5. Special Treatment for Trade Partners
Certain products from EU, UK, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Argentina, Ecuador, El Salvador, & Guatemala will generally face a total tariff burden of 15% rather than higher Section 232 rates.

6. USMCA Content Benefit
Products imported from Canada & Mexico may pay tariffs only on the non-US portion of the product, with a minimum tariff rate of 15%.

Who wins?
→ Suppliers with 85%+ US metal content
→ USMCA supply chains

Who loses?
→ Import-heavy sourcing models
→ Low traceability supply chains

Bottom line: Can your suppliers qualify for the lower tariff rates?
