Trade Update | Customs Compliance Just Moved Into the Boardroom

President Trump has directed a sweeping overhaul of customs enforcement, importer accountability, and trade compliance requirements.

Within 180 days, CBP is expected to implement major importer accountability reforms, making this one of the most significant customs enforcement changes in years.

Most headlines will focus on enforcement.

The bigger story is supply chain visibility.

Companies selling in the US will be expected to understand who is bringing goods into the country, how those goods are being declared, and where compliance risk exists across their network.

Key changes include:
→ Higher customs bond requirements
→ More importer ownership disclosures
→ Expanded supply chain reporting requirements
→ New "good standing" requirements for Importers of Record (IORs)
→ Increased audits and enforcement
→ Tougher penalties for non-compliance
→ Greater scrutiny of undervaluation, transshipment, & forced labor violations

One area that deserves particular attention is customs bonds.

For years, many companies viewed customs bonds as a routine administrative requirement.

That may no longer be the case.

As bond requirements increase, customs bonds become a working capital issue, a financial planning issue, and potentially a growth constraint for some importers.

Higher bond requirements could mean:
→ Increased collateral requirements
→ Greater scrutiny of importer financial strength
→ More CFO involvement in customs decisions

Another area many companies should evaluate is DDP purchasing.

If you buy goods Delivered Duty Paid, that means you may have limited visibility into:
→ Customs declarations
→ Valuation methods
→ Country-of-origin reporting
→ Duty payment practices
→ Supply chain compliance documentation

The legal responsibility may sit with the IOR.
The operational risk does not.

If shipments are delayed, seized, audited, or disrupted, your customers still expect product availability.

From a COO perspective, this Executive Order is not simply about customs enforcement.

It's about understanding how your goods enter the US, who is accountable for compliance, and where hidden supply chain risks may exist.

Questions every supply chain leader should be asking:
→ Who is our Importer of Record?
→ Is our customs bond sufficient?
→ How much DDP exposure do we have?
→ Can we support our supply chain documentation if CBP requests it?

The biggest risk may not be the tariff. It may be discovering you don't actually understand how your goods enter the US.

The result? It takes so much longer to actually get good.

The teams that win with AI aren't the ones who demanded excellence from day one. They're the ones who gave their people room to experiment, fail, and iterate on low-stakes work first.

This is true whether you're leading a team or learning on your own.

The people who look effortless at this right now? They've been at it for years. And they were bad at it at first too.

So if you're a leader watching your team's early AI output and feeling anxious about the quality: that's the wrong metric. The right metric is, are they building the habit? Are they getting reps in?

I just had one of the most rewarding experiences an author can hope for.

At the New England Society of Association Executives (NE/SAE) Annual Meeting at Margaritaville Resort Cape Cod, I had the chance to join a Book Club discussion built around 𝙋𝙞𝙘𝙩𝙪𝙧𝙚 𝙔𝙤𝙪𝙧𝙨𝙚𝙡𝙛 𝙖 𝙇𝙚𝙖𝙙𝙚𝙧. Over the past several months, this group of emerging leaders had been meeting regularly, working through the discussion prompts and assignments together.

What struck me most wasn’t just that they read the book. It was how thoughtfully they applied it.

They shared examples like:
• Using “the pause” to stay present during difficult conversations and heated meetings

• Resisting the urge to solve problems for others so people can build confidence and capability themselves (Reminds me of Billy Ray Taylor’s famous quote: “If you fight their battles, you steal their victories.”)

• Helping people understand the "why" behind change efforts.

• Moving from blanket invitations to more intentional outreach by personally inviting people and letting them know how their expertise would strengthen a panel or leadership group.

• Using self-awareness and active listening to navigate the uncertainty and complexity that come with mergers and organizational change

Listening to them connect these ideas to real leadership challenges was both educating and energizing. (I learned a whole new category of techniques to stay present).

Books are strange things. You write them alone, hoping the ideas will eventually become useful in someone else’s world. Getting to sit in a room and hear how these leaders are actively applying the concepts was an incredible reminder of why I wrote Picture Yourself a Leader in the first place.

Many thanks to Jenna Tarabelsi, QAS of PINE (Printing Industries of New England) and everyone involved in organizing the session and creating such a thoughtful learning experience. And thank you to this impressive group of leaders for your openness, insight, and generosity in sharing your takeaways.

This was a good reminder that leadership development doesn’t happen through inspiration alone. It happens through reflection, discussion, experimentation, and practice.

A lot of plants learn lean backwards.

They start with what's visible. 5S. Kanban. OEE. Boards. Events. Labels. Tools.
Then the floor does what the floor always does.

The board gets ignored by Tuesday. The standard gets bypassed when orders run late. The hero fixes the same problem nobody wrote down. The schedule pushes work that creates rework before production starts. The OEE number looks fine while flow gets worse.

This visual collects 10 of those moments. Most plants will recognize at least half.

The pattern under all of them is one fact: a tool only works when the behavior around it is managed every day.

I learned this from a supervisor named Fausto. The sandwich station was running low on glue. The next bucket was a five-minute walk away. The old way: operators run out, stop, search, lose twenty minutes, nobody calls it a problem. The new way: Fausto saw it coming, walked the glue over before it ran out. The line never paused. Nobody noticed.

That's the whole job. Watch the flow. Remove friction before it stops the line.

Fausto left the plant five years after me. After him, lead times drifted back to three weeks. Same layout. Same tools. No one left to watch the flow.

These aren't tool failures. They're behavior gaps the tools were supposed to close.

If a tool doesn't change what happens on Tuesday afternoon, it's decoration.

Less heroics. More system.
Stability first. Everything else follows.
The floor tells the truth.

It can take a one-off exception and quietly turn it into a new rule.

Which is terrifying if you’re using AI for actual business processes.

For brainstorming? Great.

For personalization? Maybe useful.

For production workflows?
I want the AI following the playbook... not guessing what I “probably” want based on something it saw yesterday.

The source of truth should be the playbooks, not the AI tool's memory.

This is one of those AI ops lessons that feels small until it breaks something.

Memory can make AI feel more human. But in operations, I don’t want more human.

I want more reliable.

Most people use "AI Agent" to describe everything AI does.

That's a problem.

Because non-agentic AI, agentic AI, and AI agents are three completely different things.

and if you want to learn how to build and sell all three,
check this: https://lnkd.in/d5nE_Fuc

Here's the breakdown:

1️⃣ Non-Agentic AI
↳ One input. One output.
↳ No memory. No reasoning. No tools.

User types a prompt → model responds once → done.

No checking its own work.
No context retained after.

Use cases: summarizing reports, rewriting emails, generating headline variations.

Fast. Cheap. No setup.
But it can't handle multi-step work.

2️⃣ Agentic AI
↳ AI that plans, executes, critiques, and repeats on its own.

You set a broad goal → system breaks it into sub-tasks → connects to tools and APIs → evaluates results → loops to improve.

Use cases: research + market analysis + slide deck in one run, managing ad campaigns, generating and testing onboarding flows.

Handles complex projects.
Integrates with tools and memory.
More reliable than single prompts.

But it's slower, more expensive, and still needs human guardrails.

3️⃣ AI Agent
↳ A single-task worker that automates one repetitive job reliably.

You define one clear responsibility → agent connects to 1-2 tools (CRM, email, calendar) → executes → outputs result without human guidance.

Use cases: pull pipeline data from HubSpot weekly, draft FAQ replies and send via email, generate expense reports from accounting software.

Easy to test. Easy to refine. Reliable in its lane.

But it can't handle broader projects, and breaks with unclear inputs.

The confusion between these three is why people overpay for the wrong solution, or underbuild when the problem needs more.

Know what you're building before you build it.

90% of a viral LinkedIn post depends on 1 thing.

Get it wrong, and the whole post could flop...

The hook determines whether people engage with your post or move on.

I've written hooks across 100s of accounts.

After 1,000+ posts tested across multiple brands, 
The formats winning 12 months ago aren't getting reach anymore.

In 2024, curiosity hooks dominated.
They were vague and clickbait-adjacent. 
"You won't believe what happened next" energy.

In 2026, authority hooks win.
And the algorithm prioritises content that gets read by the right people.

Your hook needs to do 2 things at once:
Stop the scroll, and signal who the post is for.

Here's the complete hook writing playbook for 2026:

1️⃣ How To

Lead with a powerful statement and drop the "how to" on line 2.

↳ Best for: Top of funnel reach and saves.
↳ Example: Delegation is the most underrated leadership skill. Here's how to do it properly:

2️⃣ How I

Lead with a specific result and a timeframe.

↳ Best for: Trust building and conversion content.
↳ Example: How I generated 23,000 leads in 30 days. Without running a single ad:

3️⃣ Contrarian

Make a strong, polarising claim.

↳ Best for: Reach, comments, and challenging bad advice.
↳ Example: Most LinkedIn advice is making your content worse. Here's what to do instead:

4️⃣ Shocking Stats

Lead with a number that stops the reader cold.

↳ Best for: Awareness content and broad reach.
↳ Example: 95% of LinkedIn posts get fewer than 1,000 impressions. Here's why yours is one of them:

5️⃣ Open Promise

Make a bold promise based on a credible result. Add a timeframe.

↳ Best for: Mid and bottom of funnel content.
↳ Example: This one change grew a LinkedIn account by 400% in 3 months. Here's exactly what changed:

Hook formats evolve, but the formatting rules never do:

Line 1: 62 characters maximum.
Line 2: 50 characters maximum.

No bold or italics in the hook, ever.
1 clear idea per hook.

Authority, specificity, and ICP relevance are doing more work in 2026 than shock alone.

Ask yourself this after every hook you write:
Would this stop me from scrolling?

If the answer isn't an immediate yes, rewrite it.

Hooks are the highest leverage skill on LinkedIn right now.
1 line can double your reach, or kill it entirely.

Start treating them like they matter that much.

Your supplier's price increase lands on your desk 48 hours before the meeting. How much of it can they actually justify?

Most category managers walk in with last year's price and a margin assumption from memory. The actual cost build stays on their side of the table: raw materials, labour, overhead, and the margin layer sitting on top of all of it. The negotiation opens with their number and you respond to it.

A should-cost model changes that

Last week, we reviewed we broke down the RFQ on episode 27, now we focus on cost modeling. You give ChatGPT the product specs, the bill of materials in whatever form you have, and the key cost drivers. ChatGPT structures the cost model: separates the four layers, sizes each one proportionally, and returns a should-cost range with the margin layer visible. 

Now you know which layers are structural (commodity costs, labour rates, fixed overhead) and which one you can actually move.

How to do it:
• Open ChatGPT. Paste your product specs and any BOM data you have.
• Prompt: "Build a should-cost model for [product]. Components: [list]. Key drivers: [materials, labour region, annual volume]. Show each cost layer as a percentage of total and as an absolute value. Where does supplier margin typically sit in this category?"
• Cross-reference the output against any commodity data you have. Adjust one assumption. You have a credible anchor.
• Walk into the meeting with it.

ChatGPT works here because this is a structuring and calculation task: multiple input types, proportional cost layers, margin separated out.

And one honest limitation: if the product has proprietary inputs the supplier will not disclose, the model becomes directional rather than precise. Use it to anchor the conversation, not to challenge line by line.

What you get: a cost breakdown by layer with percentages and a should-cost range, ready before they present their number.

Try this before your next supplier price review.

Cost Avoidance: The Procurement Achievement That Often Goes Unnoticed!
In procurement, everyone celebrates cost savings.
✅ Negotiated 5% discount
✅ Reduced supplier price
✅ Consolidated spend
✅ Lowered purchase cost
These are easy to see.
But one of the most valuable procurement contributions is often ignored:
Cost Avoidance.
Cost avoidance is the cost increase that procurement prevents before it hits the business.
It may not always appear as direct savings in the P&L.
But it protects margin, budget, continuity, and customer service.
Examples of cost avoidance in procurement:
🛡️ Preventing a supplier price increase
📦 Avoiding emergency freight by planning early
🌍 Reducing tariff exposure through alternate sourcing
📉 Avoiding material cost escalation through fixed-price contracts
🏭 Preventing production downtime by qualifying backup suppliers
✅ Avoiding quality failures through better supplier evaluation
⏱️ Reducing delay risk through improved lead-time agreements
💰 Avoiding extra inventory cost through better MOQ negotiation
The challenge?
Cost avoidance is often invisible.
When procurement prevents a problem, people may not notice because the crisis never happened.
But that does not mean value was not created.
In fact, preventing cost is sometimes more powerful than reducing cost.
Because cost savings improve today’s numbers.
But cost avoidance protects tomorrow’s business.
Procurement should not only report:
“We saved this much.”
Procurement should also report:
“We prevented this much cost exposure.”
For example:
A supplier announces a 12% price increase.
Procurement negotiates, validates market data, reviews alternate suppliers, and limits the increase to 4%.
The visible saving may not look dramatic.
But the avoided cost is real.
That 8% prevented increase is a procurement achievement.
The same applies to avoiding:
❌ Stockouts
❌ Expedite charges
❌ Supplier failure
❌ Rework cost
❌ Contract leakage
❌ Tariff impact
❌ Poor payment terms
❌ Unplanned price escalation
In today’s volatile supply chain environment, procurement is not just a buying function.
It is a value protection function.
The best procurement teams do not only chase discounts.
They protect the business from hidden cost exposure.
Cost saving gets attention.
Cost avoidance deserves recognition.
Because the best cost is often the one your business never had to pay.

Inventory Turnover: Are You Moving Stock or Just Storing It?
Inventory is not just stock in a warehouse.
It is cash locked inside boxes.
One of the simplest ways to check whether inventory is healthy is through:
Inventory Turnover - This metric tells how many times a company sells and replaces its inventory during a period.
In simple words:  How fast is your inventory moving?
Main Formula:
Inventory Turnover = COGS / Average Inventory
Average Inventory = (Beginning Inventory + Ending Inventory) / 2
Example:
COGS = $1,000,000
Beginning Inventory = $200,000
Ending Inventory = $300,000
Average Inventory = $250,000
Inventory Turnover = 1,000,000 / 250,000 = 4 times
This means inventory was sold and replaced 4 times during the period.
Why It Matters?
Low inventory turnover may mean:
❌ Overstocking
❌ Slow-moving items
❌ Poor demand planning
❌ Cash tied up in stock
❌ Higher storage cost
Very high turnover may mean:
⚠️ Stockout risk
⚠️ Low safety stock
⚠️ Missed sales
⚠️ Replenishment pressure
So the goal is not always the highest turnover.
The goal is the right turnover.
Read It with Other KPIs
Inventory turnover should be compared with:
✅ Service level
✅ Stockout rate
✅ Gross margin
✅ Forecast accuracy
✅ Carrying cost
✅ Slow-moving inventory
Inventory turnover is not just a finance metric.
It is a supply chain health signal.
Inventory that moves too slowly hurts cash.
Inventory that moves too fast without control hurts service.
The real target is: Right stock. Right speed. Right service. Right margin.

Demand Sensing: Using Real-Time Signals Before It’s Too Late!!

They happen because the business reacted too late.
Traditional forecasting often asks:  “What happened last month?”
Demand sensing asks:  “What is demand starting to do now?”
That difference matters.
Because markets move faster than monthly planning cycles.
Demand can shift when:
🔹 Customers change buying behavior
🔹 Competitors launch promotions
🔹 Online demand suddenly spikes
🔹 Supplier delays affect availability
🔹 Sales teams notice early market signals
🔹 Warehouse dispatches increase before reports are reviewed

But early in the month:
⚠️ Competitor goes out of stock
⚠️ Online searches increase
⚠️ Retailers order more
⚠️ Sales reports faster movement
⚠️ Warehouse dispatches rise
Potential demand moves toward: 28,000 units
If the team waits until month-end, the result may be:
❌ Stockouts
❌ Lost sales
❌ Expediting cost
❌ Emergency procurement
❌ Poor customer service
The issue is not only forecast accuracy.
The issue is weak demand sensing.
🔍 What to Monitor
Demand sensing works when planners connect signals such as:
📦 Sales orders
🛒 POS data
💻 E-commerce demand
⏳ Backorders
📞 Customer inquiries
📢 Promotion plans
🏁 Competitor activity

The goal is not to chase every signal.
The goal is to identify which signals matter for each product category.
✅ Better Approach
Use demand sensing practically:
🔹 Segment SKUs using ABC/XYZ
🔹 Track early demand deviation
🔹 Connect sales, inventory, procurement, and logistics data
🔹 Use exception-based planning
🔹 Validate changes through S&OP

Demand sensing is not only about technology.
📊 Dashboards can detect signals.

Demand sensing does not replace forecasting.
It improves the forecast before it becomes outdated.
The best planners do not only explain forecast error after it happens.

Root Cause Analysis: 5 Whys vs Fishbone Diagram
Most quality problems come back because we fix the symptom, not the root cause. 🔁
A defect happens.
A machine stops.
A customer complains.
A shipment is delayed.
The quick reaction is usually:
✅ Rework it
✅ Replace it
✅ Expedite it
✅ Apologize
✅ Close the complaint
But if the root cause is still there, the problem will return.
That is where Root Cause Analysis helps. 🔍
Two simple but powerful tools are:
1️⃣ 5 Whys
Use 5 Whys when the problem has a clear path.
Example: Packaging damaged
➡️ Why 1: Carton was damaged
➡️ Why 2: Packaging was too weak
➡️ Why 3: Wrong specification was used
➡️ Why 4: Old product spec was copied
➡️ Why 5: No packaging validation checklist existed
🎯 Root cause: Missing validation process.
5 Whys helps you go deeper.
2️⃣ Fishbone Diagram
Use Fishbone when there are many possible causes. 🐟
It helps you analyze the issue across the 6M categories:
👷 Manpower — training, fatigue, skill gap
⚙️ Machine — calibration, breakdown, maintenance
📦 Material — supplier variation, wrong specification
📋 Method — unclear SOP, no checklist, poor standard work
📏 Measurement — wrong gauge, late detection, missing data
🌡️ Environment — dust, temperature, layout, lighting
Fishbone helps you see the bigger picture before jumping to conclusions.
Best Practice 🧠
Don’t choose only one.
Use them together:
Fishbone → Pareto → 5 Whys → Corrective Action → Control Plan
Because the goal is not to blame people.
The goal is to improve the process. ⚙️
A label defect may look like operator error.
But the real cause may be:
❌ No setup checklist
❌ No calibration standard
❌ Poor changeover control
❌ Weak training process
❌ Missing first-piece approval
RCA is not a blame exercise.
It is a process improvement discipline.
And when quality improves, the whole supply chain improves. 🚚
Because quality issues do not stay in the factory.
They move into:
📦 Inventory
🗓️ Planning
🚛 Logistics
🎧 Customer service
💰 Cost
⭐ Brand reputation

Demand Planning Mistake: Treating Last Year as the Future!!
One common forecasting mistake is assuming last year will repeat itself.
It rarely does.
Last year’s sales data is useful, but it only tells us:
• What happened?
• Not always why it happened?
• Not always whether the same pattern will happen again?
A planner may say:
“Last Season we sold 15,000 units, so this year we should plan the same.”
But this year may be different.
🔸 Prices changed
🔸 Competitors launched promotions
🔸 Customers shifted behavior
🔸 Supplier lead times changed
🔸 Some SKUs had availability issues
🔸 Sales focus moved to another category
So the forecast may look logical, but still fail.
The problem is not using historical data.
The problem is using historical data without challenging the assumptions.
📊 A Simple Example
Last year’s demand: 15,000 units
This year’s actual demand: 10,500 units
Forecast gap: 4,500 units
Why did the gap happen?
⚠️ Competitor promotion
⚠️ Price increase
⚠️ Supplier delays
⚠️ Customer shift to cheaper alternatives
⚠️ Different sales priorities
The forecast missed because the business copied the past instead of reading the present.
✅ Better Approach
Use history as a baseline, not the final answer.
Before finalizing the forecast, ask:
• What changed in the market?
• Were last year’s sales affected by promotions or stockouts?
• Are customers behaving differently?
• Are competitors influencing demand?
• Do sales, supply, procurement, and finance agree on the assumptions?
Good demand planning is not about copying last year.
It is about:
🔹 Understanding the past
🔹 Reading current signals
🔹 Preparing for what may happen next
The best planners do not ask only:
“What did we sell last year?”
They ask:
“What changed since then?”
#DemandPlanning #Forecasting #SupplyChainPlanning #SOP #SupplyChain #InventoryManagement #LeanSixSigma #BusinessPlanning #SupplyChainAnalytics

Forecast Bias: The Silent Planning Error!
Forecast error tells you how much you missed.
Forecast bias tells you whether you keep missing in the same direction.
That difference matters.
When forecasts are consistently too high, the result is:
📦 Excess inventory
⏳ Aging stock
💰 Cash blocked
🏷️ Markdown pressure
🏭 Warehouse congestion
When forecasts are consistently too low, the result is:
🚫 Stockouts
📉 Lost sales
🚚 Emergency buying
❌ Poor OTIF
🤝 Lost customer trust
A forecast can look “acceptable” on accuracy reports but still damage the business if it keeps leaning high or low.
That is why demand planning teams should track bias separately from accuracy.
Forecast Bias % = (Σ Forecast − Σ Actual) ÷ Σ Actual × 100
Positive bias = over-forecasting
Negative bias = under-forecasting
Near zero = balanced planning
To tackle forecast bias:
✅ Compare statistical forecast vs sales input vs final forecast
✅ Clean demand history from stockouts, promotions, bulk orders, and abnormal demand
✅ Review bias by SKU, customer, category, and region
✅ Set bias control limits
✅ Discuss bias monthly in S&OP
Forecast bias is not just a planning metric.
It is a warning signal that business assumptions are drifting from reality.
The best teams do not only ask:
“How accurate were we?”
They also ask:
“Are we consistently wrong in the same direction?”
What do you see more often in your organization — over-forecasting or under-forecasting?
#DemandPlanning #Forecasting #SupplyChainPlanning #SOP #InventoryManagement #SupplyChain #LeanSixSigma #DataAnalytics

Most processes don’t slow down everywhere!
They slow down at one critical point: The bottleneck.
A bottleneck is the step that limits the speed, capacity, or output of the entire process.
In supply chain and operations, bottlenecks often appear as:
🔴 Queue buildup
🔴 Long waiting time
🔴 High utilization but low output
🔴 Repeated expediting
🔴 Rework loops
🔴 Downstream teams waiting
How to identify it?
✅ Map the full process flow
✅ Measure cycle time at each step
✅ Check where work piles up
✅ Compare demand vs capacity
✅ Observe the process at Gemba
✅ Use Pareto analysis to find the biggest delay drivers
Example:
A procurement team may think buyers are the problem.
But data may show the real bottleneck is approval waiting time.
So instead of pushing people harder, the solution could be:
✔ Clear approval matrix
✔ Delegation rules
✔ Escalation triggers
✔ Dashboard visibility
Lean Six Sigma insight:
Don’t optimize every step equally.
First fix the step that controls the flow.
Then check where the next bottleneck appears.
The fastest way to improve a process is not always to work harder.
It is to find what is slowing everything down.
Where do you see the biggest bottleneck in your process — approvals, systems, people, suppliers, or data?
#LeanSixSigma #ProcessImprovement #OperationalExcellence #ContinuousImprovement #SupplyChain #RootCauseAnalysis #LeanManagement #ProcessOptimization #OperationsManagement #SupplyChainExcellence

The cheapest supplier is not always the safest supplier.
In procurement, choosing suppliers only by price can create hidden risk.
A low-cost supplier can quickly become expensive when they cause:
❌ Late deliveries
❌ Quality issues
❌ Emergency freight
❌ Stockouts
❌ Production delays
❌ Customer complaints
That’s where the Kraljic Matrix helps.
It classifies suppliers based on two factors:
📌 Profit Impact
How much does the item affect cost, margin, or operations?
📌 Supply Risk
How difficult is it to source if the supplier fails?
The matrix gives 4 supplier categories:
🔴 Strategic Items
High profit impact + high supply risk
➡️ Build partnerships, backup plans, and risk monitoring.
🟠 Bottleneck Items
Low profit impact + high supply risk
➡️ Increase safety stock and qualify alternate suppliers.
🟢 Leverage Items
High profit impact + low supply risk
➡️ Use competition, negotiation, and volume consolidation.
🔵 Routine Items
Low profit impact + low supply risk
➡️ Automate, simplify, and reduce manual effort.
The key lesson?
Procurement should not ask only:
“Which supplier is cheapest?”
Procurement should also ask:
“What happens if this supplier fails?”
Because supplier selection is not just about saving money.
It is about protecting cost, continuity, and customer service.
Right classification. Right strategy. Lower risk. Higher value.
#Procurement #StrategicSourcing #SupplierRisk #KraljicMatrix #SupplyChain #VendorManagement #RiskManagement #CostOptimization #LeanSixSigma

I think we should all stop measuring accuracy at Month +2 or +3.
Cumulative accuracy is what really matters.

And if you really want to stick to measuring accuracy for a specific horizon, take Month+0 - that's the most important one.

Launching a new product is one of the most complex planning moments in Pharma.

Not because data is missing. But because the trade-offs are real and costly, and everyone in the room has a different stake in the game.

I remember sitting in a launch alignment meeting where this exact friction escalated. Demand Planning wanted a 6-month safety stock because patient availability is non-negotiable. Finance saw millions in cash tied up in inventory that would expire if regulatory approval delayed by just two weeks.

Classic dead-end. The room was tense: not because people did not want to decide, but because the consequences of getting it wrong were visible to everyone.

What changed the game was not a sharper forecast. It was mapping out the trade-off explicitly before the vote.

Instead of fighting over who had the better crystal ball, we ran three scenarios side by side: conservative, base, upside. Each with its financial and operational consequences attached. Suddenly we were not debating assumptions. We were looking at what the business was actually prepared to accept.
That shift took the emotional pressure out of the room. It turned a standoff into a structured decision.

Scenario planning is not a methodology to me. It is a way to stay honest about uncertainty without letting it paralyse your operations.

Still refining the playbook. But when it clicks, the speed of execution is worth it.

Everyone says 'give your AI more context' but nobody shows you what that actually means.

Here's the specific thing I do.

Before I start any AI task, I ask myself: if I asked the AI a question about the background information I assume it knows, would it get it right?

If I'm not sure, I just ask it directly.

For example: 'List out our current products, what they cost, and who they're targeted to.'

That's it. One simple prompt reveals exactly what your AI knows and what it doesn't.

Maybe it has the right products but outdated pricing. Maybe it has no idea what that internal acronym means. Maybe it's working with information from six months ago.

You won't know until you check.

This takes 30 seconds and saves you from generating outputs that are confidently wrong about your own business.

AI doesn't tell you what it doesn't know. So you have to ask.

Test your context before you assume it's there.

How To Build Stakeholder Alignment Before You Decide

We had an incumbent vendor. Bad pricing, poor design, late delivery. The list was endless.
As the procurement leader, I knew I needed better options. But I didn't make that decision alone. I got the stakeholders in a room: Engineering, Manufacturing, Sales, Finance.
We built a scorecard together. Critical dimensions of what a perfect supplier would deliver. Weights for each dimension. Thresholds for selection. Most importantly — we agreed on what success would look like before we ever bid the market.
Then we went out, bid the commodity, and found something interesting: the incumbent was still the best fit.
But we had data for where they were falling short. We knew exactly what their competitors offered that they didn't.
This led to a frank conversation with the incumbent. "Here's where you're not meeting the market. Here's what we need from you." They came back with a price reduction, dedicated engineering resources on site, and a redesigned delivery system.
We got a better supplier and a better deal without switching vendors or spending six months on a transition.
Here's why this matters: when everyone in that room helped build the scorecard, they all had skin in the game. When the incumbent improved, they all saw it as a win. There was no second-guessing in the hallways.
Stakeholder alignment before the decision is harder than making it alone. It takes longer. It requires uncomfortable conversations with people who see the world differently. But it's the difference between a procurement decision and a company decision.

Every procurement team has a process, although many never wrote it down. The ones that did outperform the ones that didn't.

This week on Supply Chain 101, Episode 29 we dive deep into the journey of a need to a PO.

There are seven steps between a sourcing need and a signed purchase order.
In a reactive team they run out of sequence, some get skipped entirely, and
the process rebuilds from scratch each time a new category comes up. In a
planned team the same seven steps run in order, and each one feeds the next.

• The foundation (Steps 1 to 3): Identify the real requirement, define
specifications clearly, and survey the supplier market before making contact
with anyone. These three steps take the most time, generate the most leverage downstream, and get cut most often when the team is under pressure.

• The market cycle (Steps 4 and 5): Issue the RFQ with the foundation complete and you get comparable, evaluable responses. Evaluate on total cost, lead time, and quality record, not price alone. A team that jumps to price at Step 5 undoes every hour invested in Steps 1 to 3.

• The close (Steps 6 and 7): Negotiate with a benchmark. Award and issue the PO with a written record of why this supplier was selected.

One of the key things that people miss out on: reactive purchasing and planned procurement use the same seven steps. The difference is whether your team reaches Step 3 before or after they have already committed to a supplier in their mind.

At which step does your procurement process most often stall?

The 8 Pillars of TPM (WCOM): Your Blueprint for Operational Excellence

As many practitioners think TPM, (once called Total Productive Maintenance, NOW named Total Productive MANAGEMENT) is NOT a maintenance program. It is a full Operating System designed to achieve ZERO LOSSES by turning all employees into co‑owners of equipment & processes.

Also known as World Class
 Operations Mahagement (WCOM); TPM stands on 8 powerful pillars:

1️⃣ Autonomous Maintenance
Operators clean, inspect, lubricate, and detect abnormalities so machines never “surprise” with failures
2️⃣ Focused Improvement
Cross‑functional teams attack chronic losses with structured methods for hard, measurable gains
3️⃣ Planned Maintenance
From firefighting to predictive and prescriptive; breakdowns become rare exceptions, not the norm
4️⃣ Quality Maintenance
Defects are prevented at source by controlling critical conditions, not just caught at end of line
5️⃣ Early Management
New products and equipment are designed for reliability and quick vertical start‑up with extensive design reviews
6️⃣ Training & Education
Skills are built systematically, replacing “belted heroes” with capable, multi‑skilled employees
7️⃣ Safety, Health & Environment
Risk is engineered out so safe  processes become default
8️⃣ TPM in Administration
The same mindset is applied to planning, logistics, offices etc eliminating information and decision losses

Why it is so powerful 
✅ Holistic Integration
TPM integrates equipment reliability, employee empowerment, and safety as foundation. It ensures machines, processes, and people all work to achieve zero losses
✅ Focus on Maintenance
TPM emphasizes proactive and predictive strategies. This ensures equipment uptime and reliability for industries where downtime leads to significant losses
✅ Employee Engagement
TPM empowers all employees to take ownership of their machines and processes. This creates culture of accountability and continuous improvement at every level
✅ Structured Loss Elimination
TPM systematically identifies and eliminates losses in relentless loops using loss intelligence systems & multiple tools. This approach delivers solid and sustained results.
✅ Quality at the Source
TPM ensures defects are prevented than detected. By controlling critical process parameters, TPM achieves consistent quality.
✅ Transformation
TPM integrates Change Management, Hoshin, and Shingo Model to create a culture of excellence that is sustainable. It’s not only reducing losses, it’s about transforming the whole organization.
✅ Structural Excellence  
The eight pillars are steered by a cross-functional Steering Committee that ensures alignment, regular assessments, and synergy across functions. This structure makes it not just a program but an enterprise-wide management system for excellence.

How strong is your OpEx program ? Still using tools, belted superheroes to hold it tight or already its standing on its own strong pillars?

For 15 years, I didn't know what was happening to my body.

Doctors told me to eat less. Run more.
I was playing softball five nights a week, so that wasn't exactly the problem.

So I covered my legs. Stopped wearing dresses. And stopped going back.

That decision cost me years.

Eventually, I learned I had lipedema - a chronic condition that affects 11% of women and almost no one has heard of.

Since then: two surgeries, full-body compression suits, and more complicated feelings about my body than I can count.

But the part I can't get over? I didn't have the self-worth to keep pushing back. 

And that silence made everything harder.

I write about this in my memoir, but the lesson I keep coming back to is bigger than one condition:

The way we advocate for ourselves (or don't) has real consequences.

Not just in business. In our own health. In our own lives.

Self-worth isn't a 'soft skill.' It's what keeps you in the room when every room is telling you to leave.

Why does every cost reduction programme start with a conversation and end with a spreadsheet nobody agrees on?

We started with a need to PO journey on Supply Chain 101, earlier this week. Now we jump into Episode 30.

A spend analysis maps all organisational spend by supplier, category, and
business unit to show where the money actually goes. It is not a cost
reduction programme. It is the picture that makes one possible.

The Pareto principle holds across almost every organisation that has run a
proper spend analysis. Twenty percent of spend categories account for eighty percent of total spend. 

The strategic categories are usually visible because someone manages them. The problem is the tail: fragmented spend across dozens of smaller categories where no one has clear ownership and the per-unit cost is consistently higher than it needs to be.

• Direct spend is usually managed: Someone negotiates the materials that go
into the product, tracks the suppliers, and monitors performance. The data is
imperfect but the visibility exists.

• Indirect spend is a different story: Facilities, IT, professional services,
travel, MRO. In most organisations this runs between 15 and 30% of revenue.
Almost none of it is managed strategically because no one has mapped what is actually being spent and with whom.

My view on this is that cost reduction programmes stall not because the
savings are not there, but because the spend is not visible enough to know
where to start. A spend analysis does not find the savings, it finds the
categories where savings are most likely to exist.

Does your team know which category holds the most unmanaged spend in your organisation right now?

The 4 Answers That Win Crisis Credibility

At GE, everyone had their number. One metric that determined whether you'd make your goals. For sourcing, it was cost savings — deflation. You'd plan a target and build the roadmap to get there. Then something would derail the plan.
You needed to recover. But you also needed to tell management in a way that inspired confidence instead of panic. Every plan hits roadblocks. The question is whether you can present that roadblock and your response clearly enough to drive action and keep leadership aligned.
I found that having these four answers, delivered crisply in two minutes, was highly effective:
What's the root cause? Tell management why you're in this situation. Did the supplier short ship? Are they demanding a price increase? Did engineering change a design? You don't need to go down to the smallest detail, but you need to put the problem in context. Someone else may have seen this before. If you can't define the issue clearly, management can't trust you to solve it.
When will we feel it? Everyone needs to understand the timeline. Will this hit the production line tomorrow at start-up, or is it a problem for next quarter? How much runway do you have to fix it? This drives resource allocation and gives everyone a deadline.
How much will it impact? Will the line shut down or will it be a hiccup? Will you miss your number by $5k or $500k? Let management know what they can expect if nothing gets fixed. Make sure they understand this is worst-case — you're already working on mitigation.
What's the plan? Your recovery doesn't need to be super-detailed, but you need to clearly spell out what you're doing. Is there another source? Are you escalating to their CEO? Who else is engaged? Without a recovery plan, you're just dropping a hot potato on someone else's lap.
When you can deliver these four data points clearly, you're well on your way to solving the problem. The tone matters as much as the content. Practice saying these cleanly so you sound strong in what you're saying. The more "ums" and "ahs," the less confident management feels in your ability to handle it.
Senior leaders have told me that once these four things are answered, they can't ask too many more questions. They're paying you to lead these issues. When you state your issues, the impact, your recovery plan in a firm, clear voice — you're assuring them their trust is well founded.
#SupplyChain #Leadership #Procurement

Spirits CEOs say it's a storm. Beer CEOs say it's a sea change. One of them is wrong.

Greg Hughes and the spirits consensus — Suntory Global Spirits — are calling this cyclical. Input costs, post-COVID normalization, discretionary spending compression. The playbook is: hold price, manage inventory, wait it out.

Rahul Goyal at Molson Coors Beverage Company is not waiting. His language around this moment is structural — a "defining moment" for the category. Beer has been losing share for two decades. A cyclical framing doesn't fit that math. Opposite end is Michel Doukeris over at Anheuser-Busch, AB InBev

Then there's Heaven Hill Brands. Kate Latts made a point that doesn't fit either camp cleanly: as a family business, they measure in decades, not quarters. It's a different decision framework entirely. And the long view has an advantage when you are not worried about public markets. 

The structural vs. cyclical read has real stakes. If it's cyclical, you cut costs and protect margin until the volume comes back. If it's structural, you reposition now or you don't reposition at all.

My read: spirits is cyclical. Beer is structural. The problem is that spirits and beer are increasingly fighting for the same consumer.

The Financially Conflicted Middle [Consumer Sentiment Series] 1 of 5

What the heck is Middle?

First, there is no formal definition. Almost no one agrees on what “the middle class” actually means. Especially politicians…

Pew Research Center arguably has the best definition of “middle-income” households as those earning between two-thirds and double the national median, adjusted for household size thats roughly $57,000 to $170,000 for a household of three. By that definition, about half of American households qualify.

That half, used to be a very clear majority in 1971. 61% of U.S. households were middle-income. 

Forward to 2023, it was 51%. 

The middle has thinned out over five decades  with some households moving up but WAY more feeling left behind (just look at recent consumer sentiment)

But there is more to it. The bigger problem is that “middle-income” no longer tells you whether someone feels middle class. 

Two households can earn the exact same paycheck and live in completely different economies and the other underwater. Income is just the first tollgate in the conversation. 

That gap between what the middle earns and how the middle feels is the whole point of what I am going to attempt to convey. Started as a deep dive for work but is worth breaking up and sharing. 

Over the next four posts I’ll get into where it actually comes from: assets, age, timing, and behavior.

Data: Pew Research Center.

85% of leaders regretted a major decision last year.

I've coached 650+ CEOs.
Every one of them has been there.
And I have too, of course.

The decision that keeps you up at 2am.
The one you overthought until the window closed.
The one you rushed when you should have slowed down.

The gap between a good call and a costly one is preparation.

The best CEOs pick their decision tool before the pressure hits.

7 decision frameworks worth keeping close:

1/ The Eisenhower Matrix
→ Sort by urgency and importance
→ Do it, schedule it, delegate it, or delete it

2/ The OODA Loop
→ Observe, Orient, Decide, Act
→ Built for fighter pilots. Works for fast markets.

3/ One-Way vs. Two-Way Doors
→ Reversible? Move fast.
→ Irreversible? Slow down.

4/ The ICE Method
→ Score options by Impact, Confidence, and Ease
→ Pick the highest score. Stop debating.

5/ The SPADE Framework
→ One person decides. Everyone else is heard.
→ Kills the "who's actually in charge" problem.

6/ The Premortem
→ Assume the decision already failed
→ Work backward. Fix it before you commit.

7/ The 10/10/10 Rule
→ How will you feel in 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years?
→ Strips the emotion out of the decision.

That last one is the one I lean on most.

10 minutes in, you're scared.
10 months later, you're glad you did it.
10 years later, you've made that call 20 times.

You're bulletproof.

« Ok, but that’s only like 1% of our orders. »
  
I spent most of my time discussing data quality with my clients in workshops. And, quite often, as we start digging down into specific weird orders or business practices, someone would say, “Ok, that’s not good, but it’s only 1% of the total.”
 I’d say that as long as data isn't 100.00% clean, it’s not clean enough.
 Overlooking data problems because “it’s just a few cases” comes with two main issues, 
  
1. At SupChains, we automate all our data cleaning routines and store inconsistencies in reports. If you’re used to seeing a report with 1000+ inconsistent orders, you won't pay attention the day you get another 20. If you're used to seeing 0 errors, the day you see 20, you know something popped up – and you should take a look.

2. Being 1% wrong on average for all your products/clients is “relatively” ok. But usually, that’s *not* how data errors are spread. Most of your customers/products will be 100% correct, and some will be 50% wrong – this will have real consequences in terms of inventory and service level
Your AI is only as smart as your instructions.

Landing at #YVR last night with my youngest son, we wanted to grab a quick drink before the car ride back home.

Lee's Donuts now has a location in Domestic Arrivals and at this time of evening, had the market cornered on a place to get a drink. They were also contending with their leftover inventory from the day and were offering donuts at 50% off. How many we bought is not the point of this post. 😆

The gentleman working there volunteered that his manager had overbought inventory that day based on expectations of increased volume from the FIFA World Cup kicking off in Vancouver (and cities across North America) last night.

And this, to me, underlines the fundamental limitation in the definition of "Demand Planning" as presented by people selling you software and quick Forecast Accuracy fixes.

Forecasting is not Demand Planning. At all. It isn't a plan, for starters.

Software isn't going to tell a new retail location selling donuts during a once in a generation event how many donuts to buy.

Extrapolating intrinsic demand patterns from history to (ultimately naively, though not always incorrectly) assume that the future will look like a version of it is something computers can do reasonably well. And humans don't typically add a lot of value here.

But that is not Demand Planning. That is time series forecasting. And it often counts for exactly zero in the real world.

Demand Planning is the work that Manager at Lee's Donuts did to use the information they had available and to derive a reasonable range of demand values for the day. Executing against that plan weighed the upside benefit of the high end against the downside cost of the low end and determined a plan that met their risk tolerance.

At ten minutes from closing I addressed 20% of their inventory issue at a price that was probably still profitable on a per unit basis, and two employees happily went home with the small balance of the inventory resulting from the demand call.

Your 5% defect rate isn't a quality control issue. It is a ₹2 Crore hole in your annual EBITDA.
Most plant directors accept a baseline of scrap, rework, and equipment downtime as the standard cost of doing business. This is a critical strategic error.
When you isolate shop-floor data from boardroom financials, you blind yourself to the actual cash bleed.
Let’s look at the real math. A defective unit does not just cost you raw materials.
It burns energy, machine time, and operator wages.
It demands secondary labor for inspection, sorting, and rework.
Most dangerously, it traps capital that should be circulating in your cash flow.
In a plant doing ₹50 Crores in revenue, an "acceptable" 5% defect rate easily scales into the Crores in lost profit margins.
Lean Six Sigma is not a theoretical exercise meant to keep your quality department busy. It is a rigorous, mathematical business strategy designed to protect your margins and scale your operations.
By applying statistical process control and eliminating root-cause variations, you do not just improve a metric on a clipboard. You permanently seal the leaks in your cash flow and release trapped capital back into your business.
You cannot scale a plant's profitability if the operational foundation is leaking cash.

AI-Ready Process Checklist

Before you automate a Supply Chain process with AI, check if the process is actually ready.

Not technically ready.

Operationally ready.

Ask seven questions:

1. What decision repeats often enough to matter?
2. What data is used to make it?
3. Who owns the outcome when the decision is wrong?
4. Which constraints must never be violated?
5. What human knowledge is used but not written anywhere?
6. When should the AI act and when should it ask for review?
7. How will we know after 30 or 60 days that the process improved?

If you cannot answer these questions, the issue is probably not the AI tool.

The issue is that the process is not yet legible enough to automate.

That is not a failure.

It is the work.

Make the process visible first.

Then automate one decision flow.

Then redesign the next one.

This is how AI transformation becomes real.

Not by jumping from today’s process to full orchestration.

By rebuilding the process decision by decision.

One way to see this story is that Coke is falling short on beverage innovation, but if the two companies want this 70-year partnership to last, they need to collaborate on execution as well as product development and marketing.

Supplier co-innovation sounds great - and it IS great - when done well.

SOP: Turning Best Practice into Daily Practice!
A process is not stable if every person performs it differently.
Without a clear SOP:
🔸 One person checks documents first
🔸 Another checks quantity first
🔸 Someone skips damage inspection
🔸 Someone delays system entry
🔸 Someone labels the material differently
The result?
❌ Delays
❌ Errors
❌ Rework
❌ Inventory mismatch
❌ Poor handoffs
That is where an SOP becomes powerful.
An SOP is a Standard Operating Procedure - is a step-by-step guide that explains how a task should be performed consistently.
It turns:
✅ Tribal knowledge into shared knowledge
✅ Individual habits into standard practice
✅ Random execution into repeatable performance
In simple words:
An SOP is the written version of the best-known way to do the work.
Example: in warehouse receiving, a good SOP defines the correct sequence:
📄 Verify delivery note
📦 Check physical quantity
🔍 Inspect packaging and damage
💻 Record receipt in the system
🏷️ Attach standard label
🚚 Move goods to staging
⚠️ Escalate discrepancies
Now the process becomes:
✅ Consistent
✅ Trainable
✅ Measurable
✅ Auditable
✅ Easier to improve
But here is the common mistake:
Many companies create SOPs only for audits.
📁 They sit in folders
⏳ They become outdated
🚫 Operators do not use them
🎓 Training is not linked to them
🔎 Supervisors do not audit them
That is documentation.
Not standardization.
A good SOP should be:
📌 Clear — simple language
🖼️ Visual — screenshots, photos, icons, flow steps
⚙️ Practical — reflects the real process
📍 Accessible — available where work happens
🔄 Updated — reviewed when the process changes
Because SOPs do not remove flexibility.
They remove avoidable variation.
Key takeaway:
If Standard Work defines the best method, SOP ensures that method is understood, documented, and repeated.

Make-or-Buy Decision: It’s Not Just About Cost 
In supply chain, one of the most strategic decisions is whether to make internally or buy from an external supplier.
Many companies make the mistake of comparing only:
Internal production cost vs supplier price 
But the real decision should include:
✅ Total cost of ownership
✅ Quality control
✅ Supplier reliability
✅ Internal capacity
✅ Lead time flexibility
✅ Risk exposure
✅ Strategic importance
✅ Long-term business value
Make internally when control, quality, confidentiality, stable demand, or core capability matters. 
Buy externally when suppliers have better expertise, lower investment is needed, demand is uncertain, or flexibility is more important. 
A low supplier price can become expensive if it creates delays, defects, stockouts, or dependency.
A strong internal process can become costly if capacity is low, demand is unstable, or investment is too high.
The best make-or-buy decision is not the cheapest option.
It is the option that gives the best balance of:
Cost + Quality + Control + Flexibility + Risk + Strategy 🎯
Make-or-buy is not only a procurement decision.
It is a supply chain strategy decision.

🏭 Manufacturing Is More Than Just Machining!

Many people associate manufacturing only with CNC Turning, Milling, and Drilling. However, a complete manufacturing ecosystem consists of dozens of interconnected processes that transform raw materials into finished products.

A comprehensive manufacturing process chain includes:

✅ Casting Processes
✅ Forging & Forming Processes
✅ Sheet Metal Operations
✅ CNC Machining Processes
✅ Laser Cutting & Water Jet Cutting
✅ Welding & Joining Technologies
✅ Heat Treatment Processes
✅ Surface Finishing & Coating
✅ Additive Manufacturing (3D Printing)
✅ Non-Conventional Machining (EDM, Wire EDM, ECM, etc.)
✅ Molding Processes
✅ Inspection & Quality Control Systems

Every process has a direct impact on: 🔹 Product Quality
🔹 Manufacturing Cost
🔹 Lead Time
🔹 Tool Life
🔹 Production Efficiency
🔹 Customer Satisfaction

The most successful manufacturing organizations don't focus on a single process—they optimize the entire value chain from raw material procurement to final inspection and dispatch.

The Procurement Health Check
Most procurement self-assessments are built to make you feel good. This one isn't.
I kept walking into manufacturers — $50M to $500M, the companies I work with — and hearing the same line. “Our procurement is fine.” Then we'd pull the spend data. Tail spend nobody owned. Single-source dependencies nobody had mapped. A CEO who couldn't name one procurement KPI.
Fine is a feeling. I wanted a number.
So I built one. Thirty questions. Eight minutes. It's anchored in the two frameworks the Fortune 500 companies actually uses to score themselves — the ASCM SCOR Digital Standard and the ISM Capability Model — adapted down for what a mid-market manufacturer actually deals with. The questions are behavioral, not aspirational. Not “do you value supplier relationships.” Do you share a scorecard with your top suppliers every quarter. Yes or no.
That's the part that matters. Sandbag the score to feel better and you've thrown away the one thing the tool was going to give you — the gaps.
It scores six categories. Strategic Alignment. Sourcing & Supplier Management. Spend Visibility & Master Data. Process Discipline. Risk & Resilience. People & Capability.
Each one gets a subtotal. Add them up and you land in one of four maturity bands — Reactive, Functional, Strategic, Best-in-Class. Then the tool flags your three lowest categories. That's not a list of what you're bad at. That's where the money is. Most teams I work with are stronger than they think in one or two areas and quietly bleeding in another they've never measured.
A 60% in Risk & Resilience isn't a verdict on your team. It's a starting line. Manufacturers can move two full maturity bands in a category inside 90 days — mostly from finally agreeing on what “good” looked like and going after the gap.
Over the next nine posts I'm breaking the whole thing down. One category a day. The actual questions, and the trap each one is built to catch. Then the scoring, the bands, and where to start.
If you run procurement — or you're the CEO who signs off on it — follow along. By the end you'll score your own function without me in the room.
One question to start. Can your CEO name two or three procurement KPIs right now, from memory? Curious where people land on that one.

Many inventory problems happen because companies react too late.

🎯 Service level targets

✅ Reduced manual PO work

Half my feed says AI is going to collapse lean manufacturing...

I don’t buy it....

The Toyota House has held for 70 years and it still is the right structure.

Stability.
Just-in-Time.
Jidoka.
Standard work.
Kaizen.
Flow.

AI doesn’t remove those layers.

It puts new sensors, cameras, advisors, and feedback loops inside them.

Start with stability.

IoT sensors can read vibration, temperature, current, pressure, cycle drift, and motor behavior before the machine stops the line.
That turns maintenance from “call someone when it breaks” into... “this asset is drifting, check it before Friday.”

Same house.
Stronger foundation.

Now look at Jidoka...

A smart camera reads the station and the flow through it. Not just the person. The process itself.

After a while, people stop performing for the camera. You get closer to real behavior.

Then you define what value-added work looks like.

The camera classifies motion, waiting, walking, searching, rework, handoffs, and downtime against that definition.

At the end of the shift, the plant manager gets:
“Station#15. 17% NVA activity - Kaizen needed.”

Science fiction?

I don’t think so...

The pieces already exist. The hard work is defining VA and NVA clearly enough that the number means something.

Same with 5S.

A camera can take dozens of frames per minute at a workstation...

- Tools missing.
- Bins out of place.
- Material outside the marked zone.
- Shadow board gaps.
- Blocked aisle.

The 5S audit stops being a monthly theater exercise and becomes a live condition.

Then come the advisors.

A supervisor asks a SOP advisor how to handle a setup issue.
A lead asks a safety advisor what to check before restarting a cell.
HR answers policy questions without pulling the plant manager into every small issue.
A business advisor helps connect today’s floor problem with cost, lead time, and customer risk.

Even the brake operator starts using plain language with the press brake...
- “What bend sequence should I check first?”
- “Why is this program throwing an error?”
- “What changed from the last job?”

That’s where this gets real.

AI won’t save a chaotic floor.

It will just make chaos move faster.

But on top of clear standards, stable flow, and visible problems, AI becomes another layer of the operating system.

The technology is coming.

The question is simple:

Will we bolt it onto broken processes, or will we finally define the system clearly enough for AI to help?

Where would you start first?

Smart cameras for VA/NVA?
IoT sensors for preventive maintenance?
5S vision checks?
Supervisor AI advisors?

🏭 Lean Manufacturing Excellence starts with understanding every motion.

Many organizations focus on machines, automation, and technology to improve productivity. However, one of the biggest opportunities for improvement lies in the way people perform their work.

This is where PMTS (Predetermined Motion Time System)plays a vital role.

PMTS is an Industrial Engineering technique that breaks a task into basic human motions such as Reach, Grasp, Move, Position, and Release, assigning a standard time value to each motion based on scientific data.

📊 Why PMTS matters?

✅ Establishes accurate standard times
✅ Eliminates unnecessary motions and waste
✅ Improves productivity and line balancing
✅ Supports capacity and manpower planning
✅ Reduces dependency on subjective performance ratings
✅ Strengthens Lean Manufacturing Excellence

Example:

Task: Pick and Place a Component

🔹 Reach = 8 TMU
🔹 Grasp = 3 TMU
🔹 Move = 12 TMU
🔹 Position = 6 TMU
🔹 Release = 1 TMU

Total = 30 TMU

Since 1 TMU = 0.036 seconds,

⏱ Standard Time = 30 × 0.036 = **1.08 seconds**

The real value of PMTS is not just in calculating time—it is in designing better methods, eliminating waste, and creating sustainable productivity improvements.

💡 Every unnecessary motion is a hidden cost. Eliminating it today improves performance tomorrow.

A forecast is only valuable if it leads to the right purchasing decisions.
Forecasting helps us understand future demand, but inventory norms are what turn those insights into action. Factors such as Safety Stock, Reorder Point, Lead Time, MOQ, Service Level, and Inventory Coverage guide when to order, how much to buy, and how much inventory to keep on hand.

When demand forecasts and inventory policies work together, businesses can:
* Reduce stockouts and lost sales opportunities
* Avoid excess inventory and unnecessary carrying costs
* Improve cash flow and working capital efficiency
* Maintain better product availability for customers
* Respond more effectively to changes in demand

Good inventory management isn't about keeping more stock it's about keeping the right amount of stock at the right time. By combining accurate forecasting with well-defined inventory norms, organizations can make smarter purchasing decisions and build a more resilient supply chain.

Forecast → Inventory Norms → Purchase Order → Product Availability

A simple process, but one that has a significant impact on operational performance and customer satisfaction.

This is the most hilarious thing I've seen in a while... And it's a perfect analogy for AI Agents.

A Chinese robot recently tried to moonwalk at a tech showcase.

Impressively nailed the first few steps.

Then hit a stair.

Went face-first onto the stage.

The owner had to drag it off by hand.

The crowd's silence was deafening 😅

(The music just keeps going and going...)

Here's the takeaway:

→ AI-supported tech is genuinely remarkable.  What it did before the stairs? Jaw-dropping. Don't let the fall fool you.

→ On a clear path, it performs brilliantly.  No obstacles = no problems. The results can look magical.

→ But it's GUESSING.  Most fields of AI are statistics-based. They predicts the most likely next move based on objective and pattern dataset ("skills"). It's not great with novel problems (e.g. stairs)

→ Your job isn't to be amazed. It's to catch the robot before he falls. It's to remove the stairs ahead of time. And/Or to include the stairs in the dataset for next time.

Guardrails. Human review checkpoints. Edge-case testing. Exception handling. Escalation logic.

That's the real work in the Era of AI...

Getting intimate with the work, as I call it.

The robot didn't fail because it's bad technology.

It failed because nobody mapped the stage.

AI *simulates* human intelligence.

There will be skill level variations (and stupidity) just like with all of us 😅!

It's important never to forget that.

Before you deploy an AI Agent in your procurement process, make sure you're also using showcases (testing!)

And I hope your testing phases provide as many laughs as this video 😂

Step 2: Sourcing & Supplier Management
Most companies think they manage suppliers. What they actually do is place orders and hope.
Real supplier management means a scorecard. A real one, shared with your top suppliers every quarter, with on-time delivery, quality in PPM, and responsiveness on it. If your supplier has never seen the numbers you keep on them, you're not managing the relationship. You're just buying from it.
The trap in this category is the top-20 list. Most teams have one — by spend. Almost nobody has the second list, by criticality. Those are different suppliers. Your biggest invoice and your biggest risk rarely share a name. The $40K-a-year machine shop that makes the one part nobody else can make will hurt you worse than the million-dollar vendor with three backups.
When I ran a $63M book across 43 suppliers at GE Transportation, the ones that kept me up at night weren't the largest. They were the single-source specialists buried in the middle of the spend.
Pull your top 20 by spend. Now pull them by criticality. How much overlap did you actually get?

A 2% rework rate isn't a quality issue. It is a ₹50 Lakh annual tax you are voluntarily paying for ignoring process variation.
Most plant directors write off minor rework as standard operational variation. They treat it as an unavoidable cost of doing business. This mindset actively destroys your working capital.
Let's break down the true Cost of Poor Quality (COPQ). When a component fails inspection, you do not just lose the raw material.
You pay the operator to build it. You pay the inspector to catch it. You pay secondary labor to fix it. And you pay the penalty of delayed shipping.
The financial impact compounds daily. If you apply the DMAIC methodology (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) to stabilize just one critical machine, the math is undeniable. Reducing that 2% variation to a controlled 0.1% routinely returns ₹50 Lakhs directly to your annual EBITDA.
Lean Six Sigma is not about filling out quality checklists. It is a strict financial discipline designed to eliminate the invisible taxes draining your profit margins.

Periodic Counting vs Cycle Counting!
Inventory accuracy is not built only during year-end stock count.
It is built every day through disciplined warehouse transactions, clean master data, and strong process control.
There are two common approaches:
🔹 Periodic Counting
🔹 Cycle Counting
Both are useful, but they serve different purposes.
📌 Periodic Counting
Periodic counting means counting the full inventory at fixed intervals.
It is usually done:
📅 Monthly
📅 Quarterly
📅 Half-yearly
📅 Yearly
📅 During audit or financial closing
✅ Best when:
🔸 Full stock validation is required
🔸 Warehouse size is small
🔸 SKU volume is low
🔸 Operations can stop temporarily
🔸 Finance needs inventory valuation
⚠️ Main challenge:
Errors are often discovered late.
If the mistake happened months ago, finding the real root cause becomes difficult.
📌 Cycle Counting
Cycle counting means counting selected SKUs, bins, or locations continuously throughout the year.
It can be based on:
🔹 ABC classification
🔹 Fast-moving items
🔹 High-value items
🔹 Critical spare parts
🔹 Problem SKUs
🔹 Specific warehouse locations
🔹 Stock variance signals
✅ Best when:
🔸 SKU volume is high
🔸 Inventory moves daily
🔸 Warehouse cannot stop operations
🔸 Stock accuracy is critical
🔸 ERP/WMS data must be reliable
⚠️ Main challenge:
It requires discipline, proper scheduling, trained people, and strong follow-up on variances.
✅ Best Approach
The best approach is not choosing one and ignoring the other.
Use both.
🔹 Cycle Counting for daily inventory accuracy
🔹 Periodic Counting for audit and financial validation
Periodic counting answers:
“What is our inventory balance now?”
Cycle counting answers:
“Is our inventory control process working every day?”
Periodic counting confirms inventory.
Cycle counting controls inventory.
The best warehouses do not wait until year-end to discover stock problems.
They build inventory accuracy into daily operations.
Because wrong stock data leads to wrong planning, wrong purchasing, wrong service decisions, and unnecessary cost.

Step 3: Spend Visibility & Master Data
You can't negotiate what you can't see. And most mid-market manufacturers can't see their own spend without a two-day fire drill.
This category sounds like an IT problem. It isn't. It's a money problem wearing an IT costume. Dirty master data — duplicate suppliers, miscoded categories, three spellings of the same vendor — hides leverage. You think you have four suppliers in a category. You have one, billing you under four names, and you've been negotiating against yourself.
The test is simple. Can you pull a clean spend report by category, supplier, and buyer in under an hour? Not a clean-it-up-over-the-weekend report. An hour. If the answer is no, every sourcing decision you make is running on a guess.
The quiet killer here is tail spend — everything under $10K a transaction. It's usually a third of your supplier count and almost none of your attention. Ignored tail spend is where maverick buying lives.
Time yourself this week. Clean spend report, by category and supplier. How long did it actually take?

The board wants AI.

Supply Chain wants clarity first.

That is the part many companies underestimate.

AI does not enter a clean process.

It enters the real operating system:

2. local Excel logic
3. overloaded planners
4. unclear ownership
5. decisions hidden in meetings

Then everyone is surprised that the pilot looks better than daily work.

This is not only a Supply Chain problem.

It is a management problem.

If the decision flow is unclear in planning, it is usually unclear somewhere else too.

Before starting the first AI use case, ask one question:

Which repeated decision are we trying to improve?

If the answer is vague, the pilot will probably become vague too.

Start smaller.

Pick one decision.

Define the owner, data, rule, exception and KPI.

Then test AI there.

AI is not the strategy.

It is a stress test for operating discipline.

Question:

Which repeated decision in your operation would be the best first test?

One common mistake in warehouse design!!
Designing racks first and process flow later.
This creates congestion, long travel distance, poor picking productivity, weak staging control, and unsafe movement.
A better approach is to design the warehouse in this sequence:
🔹 Define business requirements
🔹 Analyze SKU and order behavior
🔹 Map inbound-to-outbound process flow
🔹 Segment products using ABC, FSN, and XYZ
🔹 Design receiving, QC, storage, picking, packing, and dispatch zones
🔹 Select storage systems and material handling equipment
🔹 Validate capacity for peak demand
🔹 Build WMS/ERP transaction logic
🔹 Measure performance using KPIs
Warehouse layout is not only about space.
It is about movement.
Before asking “How many racks can we fit?”
Ask: “How will goods move?”
Because every unnecessary movement becomes cost, delay, damage, or error.

In my early 20s, I was part of a sting operation.

Not a metaphor. ACTUAL authorities. ACTUAL criminals. One of them had a knife.

I was working at a warehouse when a shipment of drugs came through - hidden in cargo. 

The police set things up. I was there when the men came back with the customs stamp at the back of the dock. They were taken into custody.

After that, their colleagues (truck drivers who knew what had happened) would walk past me in the warehouse and say, "We know what you did."

Customs later asked me to testify at trial. The guys disappeared before the date, so I never had to go.

But I've never forgotten what that felt like.

Crime in supply chain isn't theoretical. It never was.

I was talking to Robert Strenk at SecurSpace recently, and he said something that stopped me:

"Criminals are staying a step ahead, and AI accelerates that."

That's not a line you can ignore.

But here's the part that gave me hope ... Bobby also said:
"We're at a point where people understand the importance of working together to solve the problem."

THAT shift - from competitive silence to collective action - is what actually moves the needle.

The leaders I keep seeing pull ahead aren't protecting their playbooks. They're sharing them.

Most Lean transformations fail because companies install the tools before they build the system.

You can put 5S on the wall.

You can run Kaizen events.

You can create boards, labels, kanban cards, standard work sheets, and daily huddles.

But if the floor still doesn’t know what matters first, what problem to surface, who owns the next action, and how learning gets captured, the same chaos comes back.

That’s why I like the Toyota House.

It shows Lean as a system.

The roof gives direction.
The pillars hold the operation.
The PDCA wheel keeps the system learning.
The principles guide behavior.
The tools support execution.

When Lean fails, the tools usually aren’t the problem.

They were just bolted onto an unstable operation.

The real test is simple:

Can the supervisor use it tomorrow?
Can the operator see the standard?
Can the team spot the abnormal condition?
Can the next action happen without a meeting?

That’s where Lean thinking becomes real.

The floor doesn’t need more decoration.

It needs structure people can actually use.

I could stop running the business, go full-time creator, and probably make great some great cash. I'm staying in the operator seat anyway.

My personal brand brings in around 50 inbound meetings a month. ColdIQ is at $550 MRR. So the obvious move is to let someone run the business, create full-time, and let the brand compound on its own.

It's the trade every founder-creator hits at some size. Hormozi made the call a few years back and Leila joined him last year. Plenty of others have too, and for some of them it's the right call.

Here's what I think it costs.

Your content is only as credible as what you're operating right now. The day you stop running the business, the content you make starts to be more and more high level. Your best stories start to be things you did a while ago, and people can feel it fast.

Hormozi spent years as one of the best business creators alive, and he earned it by actually building. The risk at this stage: you move from operator to commentator without noticing.

Most days I'm in 1:1s with the leadership team, on client calls, reading the numbers before anyone writes a post about them. That's the part that makes the content worth reading. Hand it off and I'd just be writing about a company I used to run.

Running a business is the best source material, and I haven't found a better way.

If that ever changes, you have my permission to stop reading me.

Yesterday, my wife asked me to help predict World Cup match results so she could beat her colleagues in their prediction league.
 
I am not really into football. But I am into predictive models.
Here's the prompt I would use to generate a predictive model 


"
- Build a dataset of international football matches from the last 15–20 years.
- Train a model, for example with LightGBM, to estimate the probability of each possible scoreline, from 4–0 to 0–4.
- Use features such as:
 • Goals scored and conceded by each team over their last 10 matches
 • Estimated total market value of each team when the game starts
 • Team stability, measured as the percentage of players changed over the last 10 games
 - Backtest the model on the 2022 World Cup.
 - Compare it against a simple benchmark: the historical probability of each scoreline in international competitions after 90 minutes.
 - Then create a final prediction by combining the model output with the benchmark."

How would you do it?

Using one AI tool for everything limits what you get.

Know what each tool is weak at, and you'll know which one to use.

- Claude: Catches its own errors better than others (26.4% vs 36.2% confidence-contradiction rate). Use it when being wrong costs you.

- ChatGPT: Strongest for everyday productivity, creative writing, and general tasks across the board. 

- Perplexity: Leads on citation accuracy by 37%—every answer comes with sources you can actually verify. 

- Grok: Built for real-time social conversations and fast-paced interactions, especially on X for catching emerging trends. 

- Notion: Built directly into your workflows. Use it when you're already inside Notion for notes and tasks.

- NotebookLM: Everything comes cited. Use it for learning and studying because sources matter.

The Claude-Perplexity pair is structurally complementary; use them together for research that needs both precision and verification. 

Pick based on what the task actually needs. That's it

Half of all consumer spending now comes from the top 10%. So  what are they buying?

Big stuff…and a very specific kind of big-ticket.

Federal Reserve Bank of New York  (Liberty Street Economics — Chakrabarti & Pham) tracked real spending growth by income since 2023.

- Middle: +3%
- High earners (over $125K): +7.6%

Look at “recreational goods and vehicles” the Bureau of Economic Analysis polite term for boats, RVs, motorcycles, e-bikes, high-end gear. Basically, expensive toys. 

Real spending in that one category went from about $654B in 2021 to $819B in 2025. That’s +25% in real terms… while overall real spending barely budged.

Add the rest of the durable good like new cars, furnishings, jewelry, watches + luxury goods, high-end dining and entertainment, and you’ve got the actual shape of “the resilient consumer.” 

It’s actually a discretionary, big-ticket, top-heavy story.

Issue is durable and toys are the most cancellable category in the entire economy. Nobody NEEDS a new boat (though we would all like one). That spending only happens when people feel rich and people only feel rich when their assets are up.

We are not looking at a sturdy consumer.

Picking delays don’t always mean your team is slow.
Sometimes, the picking method is the real problem.

A picker walks the same aisle again and again.
→ That is wasted movement.

Orders wait because one zone is overloaded.
→ That is poor flow.

Teams pick fast, then spend too much time sorting.
→ That is hidden rework.

Dispatch gets delayed because orders were not released in the right sequence.
→ That is a planning problem.

This is why the right picking method matters.

Not every warehouse needs the same approach.

𝗣𝗶𝗲𝗰𝗲 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ Best when order volume is low and orders are simple.
𝗕𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ Best when many orders share the same SKUs.
𝗭𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ Best when the warehouse is large and SKUs are spread across different areas.
𝗪𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ Best when dispatch timing, carrier schedules, or shipping cut-offs matter.
𝗖𝗹𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ Best when small e-commerce orders need to move fast without getting mixed up.

The mistake is not choosing a “bad” method.

The mistake is using the wrong method for your workflow.

Most efficient warehouses combine methods based on:

→ Order volume
→ SKU spread
→ Warehouse layout
→ Team size
→ Dispatch pressure
→ Sorting accuracy

The goal is simple:

Reduce walking.
Reduce waiting.
Reduce sorting mistakes.
Keep orders moving toward dispatch.

Save this cheatsheet for your next warehouse picking review.
