Step 4: Process Discipline

Process discipline is invisible when things are calm. Then a line goes down at 4 p.m. on a Friday and you find out exactly how much of it you have.
The tell in this category is expedites. In a disciplined shop, an expedite gets approved before the supplier is authorized to ship. In an undisciplined one, the buyer makes the call under pressure, the freight bill shows up later, and finance asks who signed off. Nobody did. That's not a decision. It's an invoice you already owed.
Same story with contracts. If you've ever been surprised by an auto-renewal, you don't have a contract process — you have a drawer. Central tracking with renewal alerts costs almost nothing and saves you from negotiating with a gun to your head 30 days out.
Discipline isn't bureaucracy. It's what lets you move fast without breaking things, because everyone already knows the approval thresholds and the escalation path before the pressure hits.
When a supplier issue can't be solved at the buyer level, does everyone know exactly who it goes to next?

Direct procurement always gets a worse deal than indirect procurement. That's just the way it is.

When it comes to procurement technology,

I see these 2 mistakes constantly:
 
1) Direct manufacturers buy and end-to-end S2P suites built for indirect-only teams.

Why?

It seems easier than trying to fix the ERP processes... A shortcut!

But it's a mistake in most cases...
 
2) Indirect-only companies running procurement in an ERP with a poor user experience...

When there are such better options out there to get desired benefits.

Seems like a way to save money on applications... But it creates cost elsewhere.
 
Both of these mistakes are expensive ways to create more problems than you solve.
 
Here are the default rules for foundational procurement platforms (even though yes, there are exceptions):
 
→ No inventory, materials or MRP (indirect only)? Put end-to-end procurement in a dedicated platform.
 
→ Inventory, materials and MRP (some direct)? Put P2P inside your ERP. Augment around the edges. Yes, even for indirect spend.
 
Why the second rule surprises people:
 
Your ERP already owns production planning, maintenance, supplier confirmations, and the data manufacturing depends on.
 
Fragmenting purchases across system types doesn't reduce risk. It multiplies it.
 
Even a "bad" ERP beats a disconnected best-of-breed stack if your business runs on inventory and materials.
 
The fix is making the ERP (and the experience around it) better.

A few examples:
 
→ Catalog management integrated with requisitioning
→ Supplier PO confirmation workflows that sit on top of ERP
→ A UX layer that doesn't fight the system underneath it
(or copy database tables...)

A 15-minute daily machine jam does not show up on your monthly P&L. But it is quietly stealing ₹25 Lakhs from your bottom line every year.
Walk across any shop floor, and you will see operators dealing with "minor" issues. A sensor trips, a conveyor jams, or a feeder needs manual adjustment.
Because it only takes a few minutes to clear, it never gets logged as downtime. The operator just deals with it. This normalization of micro-stoppages is a silent EBITDA killer.
Let's do the math on a single bottleneck machine: A 15-minute stoppage per shift. Across 3 shifts, that is 45 minutes of lost production daily. Over 300 working days, you have lost 225 hours of pure manufacturing capacity.
If that line generates ₹10,000 of product per hour, that "minor annoyance" is costing you over ₹22 Lakhs in lost revenue, plus the cost of wasted operator wages and utilities.
You cannot scale profitability if your baseline process is bleeding time.
Lean Six Sigma stops treating these jams as operator tasks and treats them as engineering failures. By applying root-cause analysis and implementing robust poka-yoke (mistake-proofing), you eliminate the stoppage permanently.
You do not need to buy a faster machine to increase your revenue. You just need to stop the one you have from stopping.
Are you ready to fix the root cause and get that ₹25 Lakhs back?

The skills that make you a great Director won't make you a great VP.
And the skills that make you a great VP won't make you a great C-level executive.

Many leaders assume the next level is simply a bigger version of their current role. It isn't.

The job changes.
The focus changes.
The leverage changes.

The strongest organizations understand this: 
Each leadership level creates value in a different way.

- Directors build scalable systems, processes, and teams.
- VPs align functions, resources, and priorities to deliver results.
- C-level executives make company-wide decisions that impact growth, culture, risk, and long-term strategy.

As leaders move up, success becomes less about personal execution and more about decision quality.
Less about solving problems yourself.
More about ensuring the organization can solve them.

At the executive level, much of the work happens through:
Capital allocation
Strategic prioritization
Risk management
Executive alignment
Customer, investor, and partner relationships

This is why the calendar of a C-level executive often looks very different from the calendar of a Director.
- The scope of responsibility is different.
- The consequences of decisions are different.
- The time horizon is different.

When organizations fail to recognize those differences, problems appear quickly:
- Directors get trapped in tactical firefighting
- VPs become consumed by operational details
- C-level leaders get pulled into decisions they shouldn't be making

That's usually when:
Execution slows
Priorities conflict
Accountability blurs

The organization becomes reactive instead of intentional

One thing I've learned over the years in operations and supply chain:
Every leadership level matters.

Great companies aren't built because everyone does the same work.

They are built because every leadership layer focuses on the work only they can do.

S&OP vs IBP: Many companies use the terms together, but they are not exactly the same.
🔹 S&OP = Sales & Operations Planning
It helps the business balance demand, supply, inventory, capacity, and service levels.
🔹 IBP = Integrated Business Planning
It goes one level higher by connecting strategy, finance, commercial plans, operations, and business goals.
📌 S&OP asks: Can we deliver the demand plan?
📌 IBP asks: Is this the right plan for the business?
✅ A strong S&OP process includes:
📊 Demand review
🏭 Supply review
📦 Inventory review
💰 Financial review
👥 Executive decision-making
🚚 Execution tracking
✅ A strong IBP process adds:
🎯 Strategic alignment
💵 Financial integration
📈 Scenario planning
⚠️ Risk visibility
🧩 Portfolio decisions
🏢 Enterprise-wide ownership
The biggest mistake?
Many companies call it IBP, but they are only running a monthly supply chain meeting.
True IBP is not just about balancing supply and demand.
It is about connecting business strategy with real operational capability.
In simple words:
🔁 S&OP manages the plan.
🚀 IBP manages the business through the plan.

Non Value Added Analysis: Stop Improving Waste!
Most supply chain processes are not slow because people are lazy.
They are slow because too much time is spent on activities that do not create customer value.
Busy does not always mean value added.
✅ Real Work = Value Added
Activities that move the customer forward:
✅ Picking the right item
✅ Packing safely
✅ Replenishing stock
✅ Delivering on time
✅ Producing actual demand
This is work that improves service, accuracy, availability, or speed.
🚨 Hidden Waste = Non Value Added
Activities that consume time and cost without adding value:
❌ Waiting
❌ Searching
❌ Rework
❌ Duplicate entry
❌ Extra movement
❌ Unnecessary reports
❌ Emergency fixes
This is where lead time, cost, and frustration hide.
🟡 Business Required Work
Some work is necessary, but should still be controlled:
🛡️ Quality checks
🛡️ Customs documents
🛡️ Invoice matching
🛡️ Compliance approvals
The goal is not always to remove it — but to simplify it.
🔍 Simple Lean Filter
Before improving any process step, ask:
🔹 Does the customer benefit?
🔹 Does it improve product, service, or availability?
🔹 Is it required for risk or compliance?
🔹 Is it caused by an earlier mistake?
🔹 Can it be removed, simplified, combined, or automated?
⚠️ Common mistake
Many teams try to:
❌ Automate waste
❌ Speed up broken flow
❌ Standardize unnecessary steps
But Lean thinking says:
✅ See the waste
✅ Classify the activity
✅ Remove what is unnecessary
✅ Improve what truly adds value
🎯 Key Takeaway
Do not improve waste. Remove it.
The biggest gains often come from removing what should not exist in the first place.

It was 1999. My first job, at a staffing agency. A major Dutch car factory put their staffing contract out to tender. 10 agencies invited to pitch, round one.
 
That got cut to 6, for round two.
 
Then 3 of us, for a final round: half a day of negotiation, brainstorming, and presentations to convince them we should be their primary supplier.
 
All human to human. Three rounds. Months of work. Not a single piece of it done online, no digital research, no shortlisting mechanisms, nothing like that.
 
That's how B2B used to work. People met people, and the best relationship-builder usually won the deal.
 
Fast forward to last week, when I watched two AI agents negotiate a vendor contract.
 
No human in the room. No human in the loop until the final sign-off. Pricing, terms, back-and-forth, all handled machine-to-machine, in about 4 minutes.
 
Same fundamental task as that car factory tender. Completely different world.
 
We've spent 25 years optimizing GTM for human attention (better copy, better design, better funnels, better "personalization.") All of it built on one assumption: a person reads it, feels something, decides.
 
That assumption is starting to break.
 
→ Discovery is moving from search and ads to protocol-native distribution agents can parse 
→ Trust is moving from brand and design to machine-readable reputation 
→ Funnels are becoming autonomous journeys, no human required to move stage to stage 
→ CRMs are turning from systems of record into systems of action 
→ Revenue itself is becoming a recursive execution loop, not a quarterly motion
 
Most of us are still optimizing for a buyer who reads, feels, and decides like I did in that boardroom in 1999.
 
The next buyer might not read at all.
 
I'm not saying humans disappear from B2B as high-stakes decisions still need someone accountable for them. I'm saying the 𝘱𝘢𝘵𝘩 to that decision is being rebuilt by agents, right now, while most of us are still A/B testing subject lines.
 
If that unsettles you a little good. 
It should have unsettled me too, watching that demo.
 
I'm an advisor/ambassador for Hard Skill Exchange, and they're hosting a free virtual summit on exactly this shift: Agent-to-Agent GTM, June 23–25. I'll also be speaking at one of their future summits.

Turn the people engaging with your LinkedIn posts into booked meetings.

Here's the 7-step workflow that got our team 120 meetings last month.

1/ Post for your ICP

We use Taplio to spot trending topics before we write, and to see which of our own posts pull the most attention. Then we double down on what's working.

2/ Pull everyone who engaged.

Someone who reacts to a post about outbound automation is telling you what they care about. We use Apify to export a clean list of every profile that liked, commented, or reposted.


3/ Enrich the list in Clay.

We push the list into Clay and layer in company, role, seniority, and firmographics. Now it's a real prospecting dataset instead of a list of names.

4/ Score and tier by ICP fit.

Not everyone who engages is a buyer. We rank each account in Clay. 
Tier 1 is a strong match on role, company size, and industry. Tier 2 and 3 fit, but with lower urgency. 
This keeps us from burning touches on people who were never going to buy.

5/ Find verified emails with a waterfall.

We run the enrichment in sequence inside Clay: Wiza, then Prospeo, then LeadMagic, then FullEnrich. 
If one tool misses the email, the next one catches it. Coverage stays high and you never overpay a single provider.

6/ Add buying signals before you write anything.

This is where relevance comes from. Before reaching out, we pull live context in Clay: active hiring, tech stack, team growth. 
A company hiring SDRs is a completely different conversation than one that isn't.

7/ Reach out based on tier.

Tier 1 gets a LinkedIn DM through Instantly.ai or Expandi, more personal and higher intent. 
Tier 2 and 3 get an email sequence through Instantly, scaled but still personalized with the signals from step 6.

The one rule we never break: no pitch on the first touch. We open with something useful instead, a relevant lead magnet, a quick insight, or the results we got for a similar company. We show we understand their situation before we ask for anything.

Engagement is just the top of the funnel. This workflow is how you turn it into pipeline.

The most commonly cited growth statistic in US spirits gets misread.
7.5x growth in active distillery permits from 2012 to 2024 reads as a boom. The mechanism that produced it is not what a boom looks like.

New permit issuance has held steady at 350 to 500 per year for the entire decade. Issuance didn't accelerate. The base compounded because closures stayed near zero.

That distinction matters....acceleration would show as a curve bending upward. This curve is a flat line of new entrants laid on top of a base that kept growing because almost nobody left.

Steady issuance plus near zero attrition is what late stage market expansion looks like in any industry. The 12 year curve is dramatic because of math, not because of velocity.

Day 6 — Step 5: Risk & Resilience

There are two ways to find your single points of failure. On a spreadsheet, on a quiet Tuesday. Or on the floor, when the line stops and nobody can say why.
Resilience isn't a binder you write after an audit. It's whether you can name your top five supply chain risks right now, today, and point to a plan for each one. Most teams can name one — usually the one that already bit them.
The deeper miss is sub-tier visibility. You know your direct suppliers. Do you know who supplies them? The part shortage that stops your line often starts two tiers down, with a sub-supplier you've never heard of, in a country you didn't know you were exposed to.
I held 98.7% inventory availability through COVID while competitors went on allocation. That wasn't luck or a bigger checkbook. It was knowing where the single points of failure were before the world found out the hard way, and having moved on them first.
Tariffs are doing the same thing right now to companies that mapped exposure at the country level and stopped there.

One 2x2 grid, drawn in 1983, still decides how the best buyers spend their time.

This month on Shetty's Desk we're on procurement; in episode 31 we dig underneath comparing quotes sits a bigger idea: you can't manage every supplier the same way.

In 1983, Peter Kraljic drew a simple 2x2 in Harvard Business Review. 

Plot everything you buy on two questions, how much it moves your profit and how hard it is to source, and where it lands tells you how to behave:
• Leverage items are big spend but easy to find, so you make suppliers compete on price. 
• Strategic items are critical and hard to replace, so you build the relationship and protect it. 
• Bottleneck items are cheap but single-source, so the job is to secure supply before it bites. 
• Routine items are the small stuff, so you automate them and stop spending attention there.

The common instinct is to negotiate hardest where it's easy. The matrix tells you to put your energy where both the stakes and the risk are high. Which of your suppliers are you treating as routine when they're quietly strategic?

Transportation Cost % of Sales: A Logistics KPI That Shows Profit Pressure!
Many companies track transportation cost.
But the better question is:
How much of our sales revenue is being consumed by transportation?
That is where this KPI becomes powerful.
Formula:
Transportation Cost % of Sales = Transportation Cost ÷ Net Sales × 100
Example:
Transportation Cost = $50,000
Net Sales = $1,000,000
$50,000 ÷ $1,000,000 × 100 = 5%
This means 5% of sales revenue is consumed by transportation cost.
Why does it matter?
Because a company can have lower total transport cost but still perform worse if sales are low.
Example:
Company A:
Transport Cost: $80,000
Net Sales: $2,000,000
Transport Cost %: 4%
Company B:
Transport Cost: $50,000
Net Sales: $500,000
Transport Cost %: 10%
Company B spends less in total, but transportation is consuming a bigger share of revenue.
This KPI helps reveal hidden issues like:
🚚 Underutilized trucks

🛣️ Poor route planning

Transportation cost is not just a logistics expense.

Cooking dinner or ordering in is the same call companies make on everything they sell?

We're on procurement episode 32 at Shetty's Desk, and this is the decision that quietly shapes the whole business: do you make something yourself, or buy it from a supplier?

It feels like a price comparison, but it isn't. Two ideas sit underneath it. 

Transaction cost economics says make it in-house when dealing with the market is too costly or risky, and buy when the market does it cleanly. The core-competence view says keep what makes you different and outsource the rest.

So you weigh both sides on more than cost:
• Make gives you control and builds your own capability, but you carry the fixed cost and own every defect. 
• Buy rents a supplier's expertise and flexes with demand, but adds dependency and hands them the margin.

And the honest comparison is total cost of ownership, not the price per unit. The cheap quote that ties up your critical know-how can be the most expensive call you make.

To make this quite: buy what the market makes better and cheaper, and make what makes you, you.

Where have you outsourced something that turned out to be core?

Book research question for you:

Have you ever been praised for doing something, but the praise was vague, so you ended up repeating the wrong behavior?

Maybe a manager told you, "Great job!" after a presentation, so you doubled down on the animation, graphics, and transitions when what they actually appreciated was your simple summary matrix at the end that helped them make a decision.

Maybe a colleague said, "Nice work leading that meeting.", so you started taking charge, talking more and directing conversations. But what they actually valued was that you listened carefully and drew quieter people into the discussion.

One of the ideas I'm exploring in my next book is that praise teaches. Whether we intend it or not, people often treat praise as a clue about what matters, what is valued, and what they should do again.

We had a client paying $50,000 a year for ZoomInfo, nobody on their team ever logged in.

They didn't buy a bad tool. They bought a tool with no one driving it.

The license that you purchase is not the outcome, the outcome comes from a person doing the work with it.

And right now everyone is making the same mistake with AI.

Founders buy an agent, point it at the whole GTM motion, and wait for pipeline. It doesn't come. Replies go silent, copy sounds like a robot wrote it, and they decide AI doesn't work.

AI works. It was just never going to run the whole thing on its own.

We've run outbound for 276+ companies now. We use the same rule on every one. I call it 10-80-10.

You own the first 10%. Who we go after, what a good lead looks like, the angle to take. That's judgment, and no model makes that call for you. It's also the part people often skip.

AI runs the middle 80%. The research, the data, the first drafts, the follow-ups. Hundreds of accounts in a night, across the tools you already pay for. We build our own software on top so it keeps getting better at that 80%.

Then you own the last 10%. You read the work before a prospect ever does. You catch what the model got wrong, cut what's weak, and decide what goes out.

We've never let an agent run a play end to end. There's always a human on both ends of it.

I don't think AI is coming for your team. I think it makes a good team faster, and it does close to nothing for a team that couldn't tell good work from bad in the first place.

Once AI can do the 80% for everyone, doing the work stops being the edge. The 20% that decides what's worth chasing and what's good enough to send becomes the whole game.

That 20% is what clients pay us for. It's the reason this still needs people.

The tool you pick determines how fast you finish a task.

Half of the slowness comes from fighting the wrong tool. 
Once you stop doing that, everything becomes much faster.

Here's how I use them:

1. Comments backing up
I use Wispr Flow to comment faster. I finish in half the time instead of typing each one out.

2. Need visuals in 10 minutes
I send ChatGPT my previous posts and my visual style as reference. 
Type it what the new post needs and then I drop it into Canva and edit the infographic. 

3. Planning a month ahead
Claude breaks down the content pillars and themes. 
Then Notion holds the calendar and I use Notion AI to organize batches.

4. Find what's trending in my niche
I go to subreddits in my space. Filter by top this month or this year and that tells me what people actually care about. 
Grok also catches conversations early before they blow up everywhere.

5. Turn one video into five posts
One YouTube video becomes five different LinkedIn posts. 
NotebookLM pulls the key points, and Notion organizes them by angle. 

6. Writing posts
I use Wispr Flow to give me a rough voice draft of what I want to say. 
I paste that into Claude and it adapts it to my actual voice and makes it sharper. One back-and-forth and it's ready.

7. Sanity check claims
I use Perplexity to fact-check before posting. 
It pulls sources so I'm not guessing if something is true.

8. Visual inspiration
I reference what works visually on Pinterest and Reddit. 
See what resonates in design, color, layout and apply those elements to my own work.

Start doing this with one task. 
You'll notice the difference immediately.

Most people let their AI infer context about them randomly. I actually tell mine exactly what to know.

I call it a personal README. And it's one of the highest-leverage things I've done to get better AI output.

Here are the 6 things I include:

1. Who I am
Basic background. Not a bio, just enough context to ground everything else.

2. How I think
Do I make fast decisions or deliberate ones? Do I optimize for simplicity or first principles? Do I care more about reducing risk or moving fast? This one changes how the AI frames every piece of advice it gives me.

3. My actual work
The types of tasks, responsibilities, and domains I operate in. Without this, AI defaults to generic. With it, everything becomes specific.

4. How I work with others
How I want to show up in different situations. Meetings, feedback, leadership moments. Useful any time I'm asking for help navigating a people situation.

5. Mental models, frameworks, and mentors I admire
This is where it gets interesting. When AI knows which thinkers and frameworks I already trust, its advice actually fits my worldview instead of contradicting it.

6. A glossary of key terms
Every industry and every person has their own language. I define mine so I stop repeating myself and the AI stops misinterpreting me.

The last two have given me the most leverage by far.

If you're using AI heavily in your work and you haven't built something like this, you're essentially starting from scratch every single conversation.

Curious if anyone else has done something similar. What would you add to the list?

Reaction Plan: A Signal Without a Response Is Only Decoration 🚨
Many operations teams have dashboards, alerts, control charts, scanners, and inspection points.
But when something goes abnormal, one question often remains unclear:
What should the team do next?
Common abnormal situations:
🔴 Wrong SKU scanned
⚖️ Packing weight mismatch
🚨 Machine alarm triggered
❌ Defect found during inspection
📊 KPI crosses the control limit
If the only response is “inform the supervisor,” the process is still weak.
A Reaction Plan defines the exact response when abnormality happens.
It answers:
✅ What triggered the reaction?
✅ What must stop immediately?
✅ Who owns the response?
✅ How should the risk be contained?
✅ When should it escalate?
✅ When is it safe to restart?
✅ What must be documented?
Example: Packing weight mismatch 
Weak response:
❌ Operator checks again manually
❌ Decision depends on experience
❌ Issue may move forward
❌ Root cause may not be recorded
Strong Reaction Plan:
✅ Stop the carton
✅ Re-scan the SKU and order
✅ Verify quantity
✅ Check for wrong or missing item
✅ Quarantine if unclear
✅ Record the reason
✅ Release only after confirmation
A good Reaction Plan protects the process before the problem reaches the customer.
It works well with:
📊 Control Charts
🛡️ Poka-Yoke
🚨 Andon
🔍 5 Whys
⚠️ FMEA
📘 SOP
✅ Control Plan
Lean lesson:
Detecting a problem is not enough.
The team must know exactly how to react.
🚨 Detect the abnormality
🛑 Stop the process
🛡️ Contain the risk
🔍 Find the cause
▶️ Restart with control

But we are completely ignoring the real management challenge of the next decade: What happens when an agent and a human actually work on the same team?

Consider the friction points:
How does a critical handover work at 2 AM?
Who owns the outcome when an agent prepares a recommendation, but a human approves it?
What happens when algorithmic logic and human intuition point in different directions?
And how do you give feedback to a system that might repeat the exact same mistake at scale?

My view: We need to stop treating agents as just another software feature.
Not because they are employees. They are not. But because they require the exact same management discipline we expect when onboarding a new team member:

A clear role, defined responsibilities, decision boundaries, structured supervision and continuous feedback.

Because agents will make mistakes. They will work with incomplete information, misread context, and occasionally produce an answer that looks entirely convincing but is completely wrong.

The real test will not be whether an organization can avoid every failure. It will be whether it notices early enough, responds responsibly, and improves the system afterward.

That is why agentic AI is fundamentally an organizational design question.
Technology determines what an agent can do. Leadership determines what it should do, who remains accountable, and how humans and agents improve together over time.

The next decade is not just a race for better tech. It’s a test of whether our organizations are mature enough to work with it.

Where are you already seeing this tension in practice? Let’s discuss in the comments. 👇

Inventory Carrying Cost: The Hidden Cost of Holding Stock
Inventory is not free.
Even when stock is sitting quietly in the warehouse, it is still costing the business money.
Every extra unit needs:
📦 Space
💰 Capital
🛡️ Insurance
👷 Handling
⚠️ Damage control
⏳ Expiry monitoring
📉 Obsolescence risk
That is why Inventory Carrying Cost is one of the most important inventory KPIs.
Formula
Carrying Cost % = Total Holding Cost / Average Inventory Value × 100
Example:
Total Holding Cost = $75,000
Average Inventory Value = $500,000
Carrying Cost % = 15%
This means the business spends 15% of average inventory value just to hold inventory.
Related Formula
Holding Cost per Unit = Total Holding Cost / Average Units Held
Example:
$75,000 / 25,000 units = $3 per unit
Why It Matters
High carrying cost may signal:
❌ Overstocking
❌ Slow-moving inventory
❌ Poor demand planning
❌ Excess working capital
❌ High storage cost
❌ Expiry or obsolescence risk
❌ Weak replenishment control
A product may look profitable on paper.
But if it stays too long in storage, holding cost starts eating the margin.
How to Reduce It
✅ Improve demand forecasting
✅ Reduce slow-moving stock
✅ Review safety stock levels
✅ Use ABC/XYZ analysis
✅ Set stock aging alerts
✅ Review minimum order quantities
✅ Improve warehouse space utilization
✅ Liquidate dead stock early
Inventory carrying cost is the price of keeping stock before it becomes sales.
Too little inventory can hurt service.
Too much inventory can silently drain profit.
The real target is:
Right stock. Right quantity. Right time. Right cost.

🏭 Lean Manufacturing Excellence starts with understanding work at the motion level.

Many organizations focus on improving output, but sustainable productivity improvement begins with understanding how work is actually performed.

This is where MTM (Methods-Time Measurement) and MOST (Maynard Operation Sequence Technique) become powerful Industrial Engineering tools.

📊 Both are Predetermined Motion Time Systems (PMTS) used to establish standard times without relying solely on stopwatch studies.

🔹 MTM – Methods-Time Measurement

MTM analyzes basic human motions such as:
✅ Reach
✅ Grasp
✅ Move
✅ Position
✅ Release

It provides highly accurate standard times and is ideal for detailed method improvement and workstation design.

🔹 MOST – Maynard Operation Sequence Technique

MOST focuses on motion sequences rather than individual motions.

Benefits include:
✅ Faster analysis
✅ Easier implementation
✅ Suitable for high-volume manufacturing environments
✅ Effective for process planning and capacity estimation

🎯 MTM vs MOST

🔹 MTM = Higher Accuracy + Detailed Analysis
🔹 MOST = Faster Application + Practical Implementation

Both methods help organizations:

✔ Establish standard work
✔ Improve line balancing
✔ Reduce cycle time
✔ Optimize manpower utilization
✔ Improve productivity
✔ Support Lean Manufacturing Excellence

💡 You cannot improve what you cannot measure.

Understanding motion, eliminating waste, and standardizing work are the foundations of world-class manufacturing.

🚀 Manufacturing Excellence is achieved when every motion adds value and every process is continuously improved.

Your S2P platform will never replace your ERP if you do direct purchasing...
 
And yet, I keep seeing companies try.
 
Here's why it never works:
 
Direct purchasing is tied directly to your operations:
 
→ Bills of Materials (BOMs)
→ MRP production schedules
→ Inventory replenishment
→ Engineering change orders
→ Supplier quality management
 
Every one of these lives inside your ERP (or should).
 
Your S2P platform doesn't know what your production line needs next Tuesday.
 
Your ERP does.
 
This is why the "one platform for all procurement" pitch collapses the moment direct spend enters the room.
 
Direct and indirect have different masters:
 
→ Indirect answers to Finance
→ Direct answers to Operations
 
S2P tools were mostly built for indirect.

Making a ProcureTech roadmap in a direct procurement business is a COMPLETELY different game than businesses without:

→ MRP

Companies that accept it do the hard ERP optimization work and build stacks AROUND ERP that actually work.

Day 9 — Maturity Levels: The Four Bands
 
Your score isn't a grade. It's a position on a map. Four bands, and the point of knowing yours is seeing what the next one looks like.
Reactive, 0 to 30%. Procurement is overhead. Decisions happen after something breaks. Single-source dependencies are a surprise, every quarter.
Functional, 31 to 60%. You have a defined role and basic KPIs, but procurement isn't part of strategy yet. Things work — until they don't.
Strategic, 61 to 85%. Procurement reports to a C-level. Goals tie to margin, growth, and working capital. Leadership consults you before the big moves. This is where most of my clients want to live.
Best-in-Class, 86 to 100%. Sourcing decisions shape pricing, product, and competitive position. Procurement is a profit center, not a cost center.
Most teams don't sit in one band. You might be Strategic in spend visibility and Reactive in risk. That spread is useful — it tells you exactly where to spend the next 90 days.
A good manufacturer can move two full bands in a single category in 90 days, mostly from agreeing on what good looked like and going after the gap.
Which band fits you today — and which one do you want to be in by year end?

Beer companies are buying spirits brands. Spirits companies are launching canned cocktails. Distributors are laying off hundreds.
Is beverage alcohol still three categories — or is it becoming one?

Molson Coors Beverage Company and Rahul Goyal are not waiting for beer to recover — they're moving into adjacent occasions. The Boston Beer Company has been doing this for years. Campari Group is tightening the portfolio while the category is wide open. Suntory Global Spirits is betting on premiumization as a long cycle, not a short one. AB InBev and Brown-Forman are navigating the same structural pressure from different positions on the board...may even be fully merged into Pernod Ricard

The distributor tier is already consolidating around this reality. Reyes Beverage Group, Republic National Distributing Company, Southern Glazer's Wine & Spirits are not building infrastructure for three neat categories. They're building for throughput across occasions.

The three-tier system was designed for a world where beer, wine, and spirits were distinct. That world is going away. The consumer has already moved — ready-to-drink, hard seltzer, canned cocktail, non-alc. The channel is following. The supplier tier is the last one still debating categories as if they're fixed.

The hardest part of AI adoption is not convincing people that AI works.

It is helping them accept that the current process does not.

I have seen this pattern many times in large operations.

The first discussion is usually about the tool.
* Which model?
* Which platform?
* Which data source?

But after a few hours, the real questions appear.

* Who can override the recommendation?
* Who owns the exception?
* Which KPI wins when service and inventory conflict?
* Who explains the tradeoff to finance?
* Who decides when the plan is good enough?

This is where AI becomes useful.

Not because it answers everything.

Because it makes weak decisions harder to hide.

For many teams, that is uncomfortable.

A spreadsheet can absorb unclear ownership for years.

An AI agent cannot.

It needs a decision path.

If the path does not exist, the project slows down.

The lesson is clear for me.

Before asking whether your supply chain is ready for AI, ask whether your planning process is ready to be questioned.

That is usually the better test.

A supplier wants +9%. Before the meeting, have Claude build a should-cost model that shows how much of it actually holds up.

On epsiode 34 we review the moment that tests one: the price conversation, where they've prepped for weeks and you've had a day.

A "+9%" is really a stack of claims, and each one only moves the slice of cost it actually touches. So instead of arguing a position, you build a model.

In Claude Code you don't just talk it through, you build the thing. Point Claude at the quote and the last PO: split the price into material, labour, energy, overhead and margin, tie each line to a public index, and apply new price = base times current over base index, weighted by that line's share. 

It writes the model, sums it, and lands on what's defensible. In my example that was about +5.6% against a +9% ask, which turns a vague argument into a specific 3.4% gap they have to justify. Here's how to do it:

Own Fleet vs 3PL Decision
🚚 Own fleet gives control.
🤝 3PL gives flexibility.
But the right logistics model should not be chosen only by freight cost.
The real question is:
Which model supports your business reality better?
Own fleet works well when:
✅ Delivery volume is stable
✅ Routes are dense and repetitive
✅ Service control is critical
✅ Product handling needs special care
✅ Fleet utilization is consistently high
But it also brings:
❌ Maintenance cost
❌ Driver dependency
❌ Fuel and insurance cost
❌ Idle truck risk
❌ Empty return trips
❌ Compliance burden
A truck that is owned but underutilized becomes a fixed cost burden.
3PL works well when:
✅ Demand is variable
✅ Geographic coverage is wide
✅ Seasonal peaks are common
✅ New region expansion is needed
✅ Specialized logistics support is required
But 3PL also has risks:
❌ Less direct control
❌ Hidden charges
❌ Visibility gaps
❌ Service dependency
❌ Inconsistent delivery experience
A 3PL is only effective when KPIs, contracts, systems, and communication are clear.
Simple Decision Rule
✅ High volume + dense routes + strong service control
➡ Own fleet may work better.
✅ Variable demand + wide coverage + peak flexibility
➡ 3PL may work better.
✅ Stable core routes + variable overflow demand
➡ Hybrid model is often the best option.
Key Takeaway
The best logistics model is not the cheapest one.
It is the one that gives the right balance of:
✅ Cost
✅ Control
✅ Flexibility
✅ Service level
✅ Scalability
✅ Risk management
Own fleet gives control.
3PL gives flexibility.
The right choice depends on your operating reality.

Cleopatra, the last queen of ancient Egypt, lived closer to the iPhone than to the building of the pyramids.

It sounds strange, but the math checks out. Cleopatra lived from about 70 BCE to 30 BCE. That's 2,037 years before the iPhone was released in 2007. 

The Great Pyramid at Giza (center of the picture below) was completed 2,580 years before Cleopatra was born. It seemed as ancient to her as it does to us today. At some point, ancient is just ancient.

Technology is advancing so quickly day by day and week by week that it is hard to conceive of what anything will look like 2,000 years in the future. Even the AI revolution we are experiencing now will just be a blip. 

Which is why Cleopatra is so interesting. 

I'm not sure anyone will be talking about the iPhone in 2,000 years, but most people know her story. The Great Pyramid still stands, serving as its own evidence, but for a person to have that kind of staying power is amazing... it puts everything we are focused on today into perspective.

Then again, she was not exactly a rules follower (well-behaved women rarely make history, right?), which acts as a preservative to this day. 

The real question is, which person alive today will be remembered in 4026?

Your warehouse layout was decided
before you were hired.

And it is probably costing you
more than any process ever will.

Most managers inherit a floor plan
and never question it.

→ They optimise picking.
→ They fix slotting.
→ They redesign packing stations.

But the flow itself?
Nobody touches it.

Here is the problem:

A bad layout taxes every single movement.
Every pick. Every putaway. Every pallet.
All day. Every shift. For years.

Three layouts exist.
Each one solves a different problem:

— U-Shape puts receiving and shipping on the same wall. One dock crew, fast cross-docking, short travel for your top movers. Best when space is tight and volume is moderate.

— I-Shape runs a straight line from receiving to shipping, opposite ends. Zero cross-traffic, clean linear flow. Best for high-volume operations that need total separation.

— L-Shape bends the flow around a corner, receiving and shipping on adjacent walls. Best when the building shape forces it, or you need moderate separation without the cost of two full dock setups.

The layout nobody chose on purpose
is quietly deciding your cost per order.

I mapped all three side by side
with the trade-offs and a comparison table
in one cheatsheet (below).

Save it for the next time someone says
"we just need to fix the picking."

Save this cheatsheet for your next warehouse performance review.

The higher you move in leadership, the fewer tasks you own and the more meetings you attend.

There is a reason for that.

Many employees look at executive calendars and think: 
"Why are they in meetings all day?"

Most leadership calendars revolve around 7 types of meetings:

→ Alignment & Status Meetings
Daily huddles, check-ins, stand-ups, and status reviews.
These meetings help teams coordinate work, surface roadblocks, and maintain momentum.

→ Problem-Solving Meetings
Focused discussions to address operational challenges, customer issues, risks, or unexpected obstacles.
The goal isn't to discuss the problem.
It's to determine the best path forward.

→ Project & Initiative Meetings
System implementations. Network expansions. 
New product launches. Cost reduction programs.
Major initiatives often require cross-functional alignment and regular reviews to keep execution on track.

→ Financial & KPI Reviews
Revenue. Margins. Cash flow.
Customer service. Operational performance.
Leaders review results, identify trends, and determine where attention is needed most.

Every decision eventually shows up in the numbers.

→ Strategy & Planning Meetings
Leaders evaluate long-term goals, business priorities, investments, and future opportunities.
These conversations shape where the organization is headed.

→ All-Hands Meetings
Company-wide communication designed to create transparency, reinforce priorities, celebrate wins, and keep employees connected to the mission.

→ Executive Leadership & Board Meetings
Discussions focused on governance, organizational performance, risk management, capital allocation, and long-term strategy.
Few decisions have a larger impact on an organization's future.

One thing I have learned over the years in Operations & Supply Chain:
Most organizational problems are not execution problems.
They are alignment problems.
And alignment rarely happens by accident.

When alignment is strong:
- Decisions happen faster
- Resources follow priorities
- Teams move in the same direction
- Execution accelerates

When alignment breaks down:
- Effort gets wasted
- Priorities compete
- Decisions stall
- Execution slows

The best leaders are not managing tasks.
They are creating alignment.
And alignment is what turns strategy into execution.

A product recall is not only a quality issue - it is a full supply chain test!!
When a defective, unsafe, mislabeled, or non-compliant product reaches the market, the real challenge is not just removing it.
The real challenge is knowing:
✅ Which batch is affected
✅ Where the stock is located
✅ Which customers received it
✅ How fast it can be blocked
✅ How much can be recovered
✅ How to prevent it from happening again
This is where traceability becomes critical.
Strong traceability helps companies move from panic to control:
📦 Batch / lot tracking
🔍 Barcode & QR scanning
🏭 Supplier batch linkage
🧾 Delivery & invoice records
🟢 ERP / WMS visibility
🔁 Mock recall testing
🛠️ CAPA and root cause action
Without traceability, recalls become wider, slower, and more expensive.
With traceability, recalls become targeted, faster, and safer.
Product recall guidelines control the crisis.
Traceability prevents the crisis from becoming uncontrollable.
Recall readiness is built before the crisis - through accurate data, disciplined warehouse operations, batch control, and system visibility.

🏭 Master the Manufacturing Flow: Is Your Bottleneck Running You?
 
In manufacturing, a system is only as strong as its weakest link. If you aren't actively managing your constraint, that constraint is managing your entire plant's output.
 
To transition from local "efficiencies" to global system excellence, the Theory of Constraints (TOC) provides a proven roadmap for the shop floor:
 
🚀 The Five Focusing Steps for Continuous Improvement:
 
Identify the system constraint.
Exploit the constraint (ensure not a single minute of bottleneck time is wasted).
Subordinate everything else (align all non-constraints to support the bottleneck's pace).
Elevate the constraint (invest in more capacity only after steps 1-3 are exhausted).
Repeat (don't let inertia become the next constraint).
 
📊 The Three Key Measures of Success: Traditional cost accounting can be misleading. TOC simplifies your focus into three manufacturing-specific metrics:
 
Throughput (T): The rate at which the system generates money through sales (Revenue minus raw material costs).
Inventory (I): All the money tied up in raw materials, work-in-process (WIP), and finished goods.
Operating Expense (OE): All the money spent turning inventory into throughput (labour, utilities, etc.).
 
⚙️ Execution & Scheduling:
 
Drum-Buffer-Rope (DBR): The "Production Engine" that synchronizes the plant's pace to the constraint, using time buffers to protect the flow and a "rope" to pull work only when the system can handle it.
Throughput per Constraint Minute (T/CM): The "Scheduling Brain" that prioritises jobs based on how much global profit they generate per minute of bottleneck time, rather than just per-unit margins.
 
Stop chasing 100% efficiency on every machine and start focusing on the flow that matters. 🚀

🏭 Line Layout Types: U-Shape vs Straight vs Modular
Which layout delivers the best production efficiency?

There isn't a single "best" layout—the right choice depends on your product, order size, and production strategy.

🔹 1. Straight Line Layout

✅ Best for high-volume, repetitive production
✔ Easy to manage and monitor
✔ Simple material flow
❌ Longer walking distance for supervisors and helpers
❌ Less flexible for style changes

🔹 2. U-Shape Layout

✅ Best for Lean Manufacturing
✔ Shorter material movement
✔ Better communication between operators
✔ Faster problem-solving
✔ Reduced WIP and improved line balancing
📈 Often delivers higher efficiency in balanced production lines.

🔹 3. Modular Layout

✅ Best for small batches and frequent style changes
✔ Multi-skilled operators
✔ High flexibility
✔ Faster response to customer demand
❌ Requires skilled teamwork and cross-training.

📊 Example (Denim Pants Production)

A factory producing 1,200 denim pants/day compared three layouts:

🔸 Straight Line → 72% Efficiency
🔸 U-Shape → 82% Efficiency
🔸 Modular → 87% Efficiency (after operator training)

Key Lesson:
The highest efficiency doesn't come from the layout alone—it comes from proper line balancing, standard work, operator skills, and continuous improvement.

Procurement ROI: Is Procurement a Cost Center or Value Creator?
Procurement is not just about creating POs, negotiating prices, or following up with suppliers.
The real question is:
For every $1 spent on procurement, how much value does the business get back?
That is where Procurement ROI matters.
Formula:
Procurement ROI = Savings Generated ÷ Procurement Operating Cost
Example:
Savings Generated = $500,000
Procurement Operating Cost = $100,000
Procurement ROI = 5:1
That means every $1 spent on procurement generated $5 in value.
But procurement value is not only cost savings.
It can also come from:
✅ Cost avoidance
✅ Better contract compliance
✅ Reduced maverick spend
✅ Supplier consolidation
✅ Lower emergency buying
✅ Improved payment terms
✅ Process automation
✅ Reduced supplier risk
The key is not to report inflated numbers.
Procurement ROI must be:
✔ Finance-validated
✔ Business-linked
✔ Measured consistently
✔ Separated between savings and avoidance
Procurement is not a cost center when it proves measurable value.
Better sourcing = measurable savings
Better compliance = reduced leakage
Better analytics = better decisions

So we left. Bags half-packed, I booked a hotel room without hesitating. And I loved myself for it.

Sure, I had the money 5 years ago too. But I'd have thought twice. Then talked myself out of it.

Back then, that Thursday would've looked like me:

- Sweating in a 35°C flat, telling myself to toughen up.
- Stressing about the time I wasn't spending working.
- Counting which "favors" I'd have to cut that month.

Because back then my body wasn't mine to protect. A boss decided when I worked. A startup swallowed €80K of my unpaid work.

Losing control isn't abstract for me. I've lived it. At school, at work, in rooms where being wired differently got punished.

So when the heat hit and my chest closed up? The panic wasn't about the weather. It was the old feeling. Trapped, without an exit or a say.

I built a business that runs on my rules. And that business booked two scared, overheating people into a cold room without flinching.

That's the freedom nobody writes about on LinkedIn. You book the cold room when your body needs it. Because you can.

My fiancée and I both slept that night. Breathing.

And I remembered I built this so my body would always be mine to protect.

PS: That cold hotel room was paid for by posts. If you want the 3 that booked me clients while I slept, I'll break them down in my €1 workshop tomorrow.

Your LinkedIn profile ranks your posts now.
Every section on your profile feeds into how your posts get distributed.

LinkedIn's algorithm indexes your headline at 5x the weight of any other field on your profile. 
Optimized headlines get 40% more profile views. 

That means your banner, headline, featured content and experience all feed into whether your posts get shown to 100 people or 10,000.

Here's how mine is set up:

1. Banner communicates what I do and whom I help in one line without any clutter or extra visuals getting in the way.

2. Headline uses 150+ of the 220 characters LinkedIn gives you. Every unused character is a keyword you're not ranking for.

3. Featured section gets updated monthly with posts, resources, and offers that reflect current positioning.

4. Experience shows impact with numbers like revenue, results, and scale. Recruiters spend 6 seconds scanning, and numbers are what they stop on.

A strong profile makes every post work harder.

Posting every day is bullshit.

Here's why:

I see LinkedIn coaches telling their clients to post daily, minimum five times a week, if they want their account to grow.

That makes your content calendar look productive. 
But frequency without clarity is just noise.

Posting every day doesn't work unless you know:

- Who you actually want to talk to
- What problem keeps them up at 3am
- Why they'd choose you over the 50 other people in their feed

I know a lot of top creators post every day.

But that's because it's their job or they have a ghostwriter doing it for them.

If you're a founder without that luxury, focus on making sure every post has a purpose.

If you want leads and authority and to be the only person your ICP thinks of when they have the problem you solve.

Then you need to know exactly who you're talking to before you write a single word.

Know the pain.
Know the objection.
Know what makes them stop scrolling.

Consistency matters. 
I’m not saying it doesn’t of course it does. 

But consistency without knowing who your audience is pointless.

That's why when I coach people, I never say you have to post X amounts per week.

I ask: how many times can you realistically post a week while still providing real value for [insert target audience].

If that's every day, go for it…

But I need at least one day off. 


What’s one piece of LinkedIn advice you followed that never worked?

Distillery Starts vs Stops: 9 distillery closures in 2012. 123 in 2024. A 13x increase in 12 years, in a regulatory category where shutting down requires actively surrendering a federal permit.

The growth in closures has compounded steadily, not in a single bad year. 35 closures in 2018. 75 in 2021. 123 in 2024. The trend line is unambiguous.

The issuance side has stayed remarkably stable across the same period. 350 to 500 new permits per year, every year, since 2012. Net additions are still positive only because of delta: 411 new entrants in 2024 minus 123 closures gives 288 net.

Project that forward. If closures continue compounding at the current rate and issuance holds steady, net additions turn negative inside 36 months.

Most personal brands are forgettable.
The memorable ones have 4 things figured out:

1/ Their niche
2/ Their profile
3/ Their content mix
4/ They actually talk to the people who show up

Start doing this and in 30 days, the right people will remember you.

Here is the exact plan:

1/ Fix your profile

- Use a high quality, close-up photo with a solid background.
- Write your headline: who you help + how you help + proof.
- Use bullets in your About section to be clear what you can offer your audience, then end with a call to action.
- Put your lead magnets, like templates or courses, in your Featured section.
- Direct your custom button to your main offer. This will show on EVERY post.

The goal: people should know within seconds why they should follow you.

2/ Find your niche

- Write down your skills, your experience and the results you can drive.
- Pick one type of person who would benefit from that knowledge.
- Choose one painful problem they need solved.
- Name the clear solution only you can offer them.
- Put it together: "I help [who] solve [problem] so they can [result]."
- Use that sentence as a north star in your content.

"Career advice" is easy to forget. "Helping mid-level professionals land more interviews" is memorable.

3/ Create your content mix

- Share news from your niche and explain why it matters.
- Write about a common problem and show a new perspective.
- Teach one useful lesson people can apply that day.
- Tell stories from your life that have a valuable takeaway.
- Share useful resources like how-to guides and carousels people will want to save.
- Answer the objections that stop people from buying.

Some posts help new people find you. Some give them a reason to trust you. And some convince them to buy from you. No post should do all 3.

4/ Build your network

- This takes about 60 minutes a day.
- Comment on 5–10 posts in your niche before your post goes live.
- Add a real thought, example or question to each one.
- Once your post is live, reply to every comment.
- Send a short, personal message to the people who regularly engage.
- Connect with creators at your level in your niche.

This is probably the most important piece - creating real connection with your audience is the fastest way to become memorable to them.

Everyone reinforces the wrong clause.

When a supply contract hits the negotiation table, most of the energy goes to one thing: liability. 

Who pays when something goes wrong. It has been the single most-negotiated term in commercial contracts since 2007, and that makes sense, because nobody wants to be the one left holding the bill.

This is Episode 35 of Supply Chain 101, where I break down one supply chain idea at a time, in plain language, for people inside the field and outside it.

A supply contract really rests on six clauses, not one:
• Price and indexation: what you pay, and how that price is allowed to move.
• Scope and specification: what you actually agreed to deliver.
• Delivery and lead time: when and how it shows up.
• Quality and SLA: the standard it has to meet.
• Liability and remedies: who carries the risk when it breaks.
• Term and exit: how the relationship starts, and how it ends.

And here is the twist. 77% of contract disputes do not start at liability at all. 

They start at scope, the clause about what was actually promised, because two parties read the same words and walked away with two different pictures of the job.

So teams armour the clause that rarely cracks, and leave the one that quietly does the most damage half-defined.

My view on this is that a contract is not won in the clause you argue hardest. It is won in the clause you make impossible to misread.

Which clause in your last supplier contract turned out to be the one nobody could agree on afterwards?

My sensei Gary said something years ago that I still come back to.

“Accepting Lean is like changing religion. And how often do people actually change religion?”

That line explains more about failed Lean transformations than most maturity models I’ve seen.

You can teach someone 5S in an afternoon.

Standard work.
Value stream mapping.
Kaizen events.
Visual boards.

The mechanics are simple.

The belief underneath is the hard part.

That problems are normal and worth surfacing.

That the person closest to the work knows something the org chart doesn’t.

That stopping the line to fix a defect is strength.

That daily improvement matters more than the perfect rollout plan.

That’s a worldview.

And worldviews don’t change because someone ran a workshop.

I’ve watched plants put up the boards, run the huddles, hang the templates, and change almost nothing.

The methodology was borrowed.

It never became how the operation actually worked.

So what moves people across that line?

Proof.

Someone tries one small change.
It holds.
Their day gets easier.
The problem comes back less often.

Then the belief starts to move.

One person at a time.

Slower than any rollout plan wants. But much stronger when it sticks.

Most transformations install the tools and wait for belief to follow.

I think it works the other way around.

The proof comes first.
Then belief follows...

🏭 Lean Manufacturing Excellence starts with measuring work accurately.

In manufacturing, productivity is not improved by working faster—it is improved by establishing the right standards and continuously improving them.

One of the most important Industrial Engineering metrics is SMV (Standard Minute Value).

📊 What is SMV?

SMV is the standard time required for a qualified operator to complete one unit of work using the defined method under normal working conditions.

🔹 Components of SMV

✅ Observed Time (OT)
✅ Performance Rating (PR)
✅ Normal Time (NT)
✅ Allowances (Personal, Fatigue & Delay)
✅ Standard Time (ST)

🔹 Typical Allowances

👤 Personal Allowance: 5–7%
💪 Fatigue Allowance: 8–12%
⏳ Delay Allowance: 3–8%

Typical Total Allowance = 15–25%

🔹 SMV Formula
SMV = Normal Time × (1 + Allowance %)

Where:

Normal Time = Observed Time × Performance Rating

🔹 Why is SMV Important?

✔ Production Planning & Scheduling
✔ Capacity Planning
✔ Manpower Planning
✔ Line Balancing
✔ Cost Estimation
✔ Productivity Measurement
✔ Incentive Calculations

💡 Example

Observed Time = 70 sec
Performance Rating = 110%
Allowance = 20%

➡ Normal Time = 1.284 min

➡ SMV = 1.541 min/unit

This means a trained operator following the standard method should take 1.541 minutes to produce one unit.

🎯 Key Insight

Without an accurate SMV:

❌ Capacity calculations become unreliable
❌ Production targets become unrealistic
❌ Manpower planning becomes inaccurate
❌ Productivity measurement loses meaning

Accurate SMV is the foundation of Lean Manufacturing Excellence, enabling organizations to balance resources, improve efficiency, and make data-driven decisions.

🚀 You cannot improve productivity unless you first establish the standard.

One question that is being asked is; how do we cost effectively change to a ‘Just In Case’ stock model to improve supply to our customers, as material and product supplies are so unreliable, erratic and costly?
.
.
.
The answer is that you are not.

The good news 🌞  is that there are many actions that can be taken to try and address this difficult situation many are facing right now. I will mention a few actions you could do now, but I have many thoughts on addressing this conundrum.

1.	Stop panic buying 🛒 : A reaction is often to buy more right now because we don’t know when there will be more available. ‘Toilet paper’ is all I say on this! Do your due diligence and homework. Some businesses use the strategy to sell more by creating panic to suit their own agenda.

2.	Carefully analyse your stock data 📋 : What parts or materials are the showstoppers and what is their current stock position and availability, even if at a higher price.

3.	Call your premium customers 🌟 : If you are not getting a regular forecast, it may be sensible to speak to those customers that you rate highest, determine their current situation and expectations for more product.

4.	Turn old stock into cash 💷 : Many businesses have a fair chunk of materials etc that have gathered dust for some time. Some of this stock has a real cash value. Perhaps those that you purchased it from originally may love to buy it back for another customer they have. It may be sensible to turn this dusty old stuff into cash and use that to buy stock you really need.

5.	Look at your supply contracts 🔎 : It may be both in your interest and that of your supplier to have a stocking agreement or call off arrangement. Don’t ask, don’t get. Don’t make assumptions. Sometimes suppliers will ringfence certain stock for you and not charge if you do not take it. It may be a regular standard item that they can sell easily to someone else.

6.	Re-assess your safety stock levels 📦 : I have seen safety stocks that were appropriate years ago still enforced. The situation is changing all of the time so it is surprising how irregularly stocking parameters are left static and unchecked.

These are just a few suggestions. 

Is your business doing the above? 

As a business owner, are you running the numbers 🏃‍➡️ or hoping that someone on your team is doing it 🙏 ?

Purchasing and Supply Chain professionals should be doing this and much more as their day job. If you cannot afford to employ one, how are you bridging 🌉 the gap?

A few years back, I managed a supply shortage on a blockbuster drug that dragged on for almost two years.

The supply issue itself was a headache, but what actually drained everyone was the politics. Every country wanted maximum supply, every sales team had a different priority, and because we lacked a shared decision structure, we were essentially renegotiating the rules of engagement every single Monday morning.

We finally broke the cycle by forcing three workstreams in parallel: one for manufacturing capacity, one for network safety stock, and one to manage the demand planning.

We didn’t do it because it was some brilliant strategy. We did it just to stop the fighting. Once the structure was there, the negotiation about the rules stopped, and the work of actually allocating supply began. The logic itself was secondary; what mattered was that the logic existed and everyone knew the game we were playing.

I’ve seen the same pattern everywhere since, not just in pharma. When supply gets tight, the bottleneck is rarely the effort or the capability. It’s almost always the absence of a decision architecture that everyone can point to.

It turns out that when things get chaotic, a clear set of rules is worth more than a perfect forecast.

Status Tagging in Warehouse Explained!
Not all stock inside a warehouse is available stock.
This is one of the biggest mistakes in inventory control.
A system may show:
1,000 units in stock
But the real situation may be:
 ✅ 600 units available
 🟡 150 units under quality hold
 🔴 100 units damaged
 ⛔ 80 units rejected
 🔒 70 units reserved for customer orders
So the question is not only:
“How much stock do we have?”
The better question is:
“How much stock is actually usable?”
That is where status tagging becomes critical.
Warehouse status tagging is the process of clearly identifying the condition, usability, and control status of inventory.
It tells the warehouse team whether stock can be picked, moved, issued, sold, inspected, returned, or blocked.
A zone color tells the team:
📍 Where should this stock physically stay?
🚦 What movement rule applies in this area?
✅ Is this a free movement zone or a controlled zone?
The biggest mistake is assuming:
Stock in warehouse = stock available
Example:
A yellow hold tag should not be in the green available zone.
A rejected pallet should not sit near pickable inventory.
A reserved pallet should not appear as free stock.
A near-expiry pallet should not be hidden behind fresh stock.
When tag, zone, and system do not match, warehouses create false availability.
And false availability leads to:
❌ Wrong picking
❌ Wrong dispatch
❌ Quality risk
❌ Expiry loss
❌ Customer complaints
❌ Inventory mismatch
A controlled warehouse should know more than quantity.
It should know:
✅ What is usable
✅ What is blocked
✅ What is damaged
✅ What is reserved
✅ What must move first
✅ What must never move
Physical quantity tells what is present.
Status tagging tells what is allowed.
Zone color coding tells where it belongs.

Your WMS says FIFO.
Your floor says otherwise.

I've walked into warehouses
where the system says rotation is perfect.

Then I check the back of the lane.

Dust. Faded labels.
Stock that hasn't moved in months.

The system didn't fail.
The floor did.

Stock rotation is not a setting you pick
and forget about.

It's a discipline you verify
every single day.

Three methods exist.
Each one protects something different:

→ FEFO: earliest expiry leaves first. Protects compliance.
→ FIFO: oldest received leaves first. Prevents aging stock.
→ LIFO: newest leaves first. Only works when expiry doesn't matter.

Here's where most warehouses go wrong:

→ Expiry date missing from WMS. Team picks by arrival instead. Product expires on the shelf.
→ New stock placed in front because putaway is faster. Old stock buried behind it for months.
→ Perishables stored in LIFO racking because that's what was available. Audit risk ignored.

The fix is not in the system.
The fix is on the floor.

Walk the lane.
Check the back of the shelf.
If old stock is gathering dust,
your rotation has already failed.

I mapped all three methods side by side
with the mistakes and floor checks
in one cheatsheet (below). Save it.

Major cheat code for productivity: Not every task on your to-do list needs maximum effort.

Most people get this backwards.

They treat every task like it's the most important on your list.

The email. The doc. The slide nobody will read twice.

All of it gets polished.

And it feels productive.

But here's what's actually happening:

You're spending your best energy on work that barely matters. 

Only about 20% of what you do drives real returns.

→ That's the work where extra effort compounds. Where the difference between good and great is the difference between a quiet month and a record-breaker.

The other 80%?

→ Quick wins. Stuff where extra effort adds no extra value. Where the first draft, the AI one-shot, the "good enough" version is genuinely good enough.

So here's the playbook:

Go through your list. One task at a time.

Ask yourself 1 question:

"Does this need my maximum effort?"

If the answer isn't a HELL YES, it's a no.

Be ruthless. 80% should be 'no'.

Effort isn't free. Every ounce you pour into the 80% is an ounce stolen from the 20% that actually moves you forward.

Protect your energy above all else.

The old playbook: One central fulfillment node. Simple, clean, easy to manage.

The new playbook: Expand into multiple nodes. Get closer to your customer. 

The smarter playbook: It actually depends — and getting it wrong is expensive either way. 


Here's what I've seen play out recently with two CPG brands in the health and wellness space: 

Brand A came to me operating out of two fulfillment locations. On paper it made sense. 

In practice? 

They were a wholesale-driven business with a leaner team, and the complexity was quietly killing them. Inventory split across two nodes meant they couldn't optimize levels at either one — which led to chronic stockouts that were frustrating their retail partners. 

The fix was consolidating to one central node. 

Simpler inventory management, lower carrying costs, fewer headaches for a team that didn't have the bandwidth to manage the complexity. 


Brand B was the opposite story. A DTC-first business shipping from one central location — with over 30% of their orders traveling to zones 6-8. 

They had the team, the right logistics partners, and the volume to justify a second node. 

The projected savings? $250K annually just in outbound shipping costs. 

Same industry. Completely different answers.

 I believe the brands that win in the next era of fulfillment won't default to "one node" or "many nodes" — they'll ask better questions first. 

What does my channel mix look like? Where does my customer actually live? What can my team and partners realistically support? 


Network design is a lever for better performance and cost savings and knowing when to pull it in either direction leads to better outcomes in the long run.

Who carries the cost when the work runs over?

This week on Supply Chain 101 we are staying inside the contract on episode 36. 

The earlier post looked at what actually lives in one. This one is about how it is priced, because once the clauses are set, the pricing model is what quietly decides who absorbs the risk when costs move.

Here is the simple version. Imagine the same job, agreed at the same number, hit by the same surprise: it runs over budget. Three contracts, three very different outcomes.

• Fixed-Price: you agree one number up front and the supplier delivers for that, whatever happens. If costs rise, the supplier absorbs it, and you pay for that safety in a premium baked into the price from day one.
• Time and Materials: you pay for the hours worked and the materials used. When the job runs long, the bill grows with it, so the risk is shared, but it leans toward you.
• Cost-Plus: you reimburse the supplier’s actual costs and add an agreed fee on top. If the work overruns, you carry it, and the supplier still earns their margin.

The lowest number on paper is often the one that quietly hands you all the risk.

So if a key supplier contract ran 20% over next quarter, which pricing model are you on, and would that surprise land on you or on them?

If you’ve ever wondered how much and how often you should order, the EOQ formula (Economic Order Quantity or Wilson Formula) is your answer.
The Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), also known as the Wilson formula, helps you pinpoint the ideal inventory order size.
The goal is to strike a balance between two cost drivers:

👉 Holding Costs: The inventory storage cost increases as the order quantity grows.
👉 Ordering Costs: The transaction cost of placing orders decreases as the order size increases because fewer orders are needed to meet demand.

These costs create two opposing curves.
The Total Cost curve, the sum of Holding and Ordering Costs, reaches its minimum where the two costs are equal.
This intersection represents the EOQ, the optimal order quantity that minimizes total costs.Do you want to implement EOQ?

Do every demand spike needs a reaction?
One common mistake in supply chain planning is treating every demand movement as a signal.
Sales increase?
Raise the forecast.
Demand drops?
Cut the plan.
One customer orders extra?
Build more inventory.
But many demand changes are just normal variation.
The real challenge is knowing the difference between:
🔹 Normal noise
Small ups and downs that naturally happen in demand.
🔹 Real signal
A meaningful change caused by promotion, seasonality, market shift, customer behavior, or disruption.
When teams react to every movement, the result is usually:
❌ Forecast instability
❌ Excess inventory
❌ Stockouts
❌ Expediting
❌ Supplier pressure
❌ Bullwhip effect
This is where Six Sigma thinking helps.
Instead of asking, “Why did demand change this week?”
Ask:
“Is this change outside the normal pattern?”
Tools like control charts, demand segmentation, forecast bias review, and root cause analysis help planners separate real signals from random noise.
A good planner does not react to every fluctuation.
A good planner understands variation before changing the plan.
Because in supply chain:
Reacting too fast can be just as costly as reacting too late.

Good "hooks" matter.

The first line of your post = 80% success.

Charlie Hills has summaized the difference between a "good" & "bad" hook brilliantly here.

👉 Good hooks have:

1. Specificity:
☒ "Here's how to grow on LinkedIn" 
☑︎ "LinkedIn changed. Your strategy should too."

2 - Engagement:
☒ "AI is changing everything"
☑︎ "ChatGPT changed. Most people didn't notice."

3 - Value Proposition
☒ "Let me share some tips"
☑︎ "I rebuilt my LinkedIn strategy from scratch. (How I went from zero to 115k+ in 494 days)"

4 - Action-Oriented Language
☒ "You might want to try this"
☑︎ "How to make a landing page in 5 minutes. Using AI and your LinkedIn profile."

5 - Relatability
☒ "Here's what I learned"
☑︎ "My AI outputs were trash for 6 months. Then I discovered these 8 prompting styles."

👉 Bad hooks have:

1 - Vagueness: "Pretty interesting topic, right?"
 
2 - Generic Questions: "Looking to grow your following?"
 
3 - Clichéd Openings: "In today's fast-paced world..."
 
4- Tentative Language: "This might work for you..." "
 
5 - Missing Value: "I have a secret to share..."

👉 Hook formulas that work:

Pattern 1: Contrast Reality "Most people [common mistake]. But [tool/method] can help you [better result]."

Pattern 2: Platform Shift "[Platform] has completely changed. The old tactics don't work anymore."

Not every SKU deserves equal attention.

10-20% of your SKUs

But most warehouses treat them all
like they matter equally.

Same cycle counts.
Same prime locations.
Same reorder logic.

That's not discipline.
That's wasted effort on the wrong things.

ABC classification fixes this:

→ A items: few SKUs, highest value. Count often. Best locations. Tight control.
→ B items: moderate value. Standard reorder rules. Routine review.
→ C items: many SKUs, lowest value. Simplify. Lower-touch storage. Count less.

But here's what most people stop at.

ABC tells you what matters.
It doesn't tell you how predictable it is.

That's where XYZ comes in:

→ X: steady demand. Automate replenishment.
→ Y: variable demand. Review periodically.
→ Z: unpredictable demand. Buffer stock and watch closely.

Combine them and you get a 3x3 matrix
that sets your stock policy per SKU.

AX gets automated.
CZ gets questioned: should you even carry it?

Walk your floor tomorrow
and ask one question:

Are your A items in the best locations,

they don't deserve?

- The more specific your message is for your ICP, the harder it hits.

We were watching inventory drop day by day.


(And a supplier shortage meant it could turn into a sales problem fast.)

One thing I wish I knew earlier in my career about contingency planning:

The relationships you maintain when you don’t need them are the ones that save you when you do.

Earlier this year, a primary supplier hit an unexpected materials shortage and we were running dangerously low on inventory—the kind of low where you’re doing the math daily and hoping your timeline holds.

The thing that saved us was a former co-manufacturer we’d worked with for two years before switching to another provider.

We hadn’t given them a PO in a while—but we stayed in touch, kept the relationship warm, and treated them well on the way out.


One phone call later, they moved quickly to source materials and get our production scheduled.

We got inventory out the door in time.

If that relationship had gone cold, we would’ve been starting from scratch in the middle of a crisis—vetting someone new while the clock was ticking.

Your contingency plan is only as strong as the relationships behind it.

Secondary suppliers, backup co-mans, alternative logistics providers—they’re not just names on a list. 

They’re relationships that need attention even when everything is running smoothly.

The Third Space Is Not Coming Back: 

A third place is any space that isn't home and isn't work. The bar. The diner. The bowling alley. The golf club. Sociologist Ray Oldenburg argued in 1989 these aren't amenities. They are the physical infrastructure through which communities maintain themselves.

That infrastructure is contracting. And the data tells us why.
What the numbers show:
- Americans spent 43 minutes per day socializing in 2014. By 2019, before any pandemic, that had already fallen to 38 minutes. By 2024 it sits at 35. No recovery.

- The lost time didn't move to other social activities. It moved to household tasks (+14 min/day), sleeping (+13 min/day), and screens.

- In 2014, Americans watched TV for 3.9 minutes for every 1 minute socializing. By 2023 that ratio was 4.7 to 1.

- Bars and nightclubs lost 1,371 establishments from 2014 to 2023. Annual declines starting four years before COVID.

- Bowling centers down 13%. Golf courses down nearly 400 locations.

- Coffee shops grew 53% in units. Starbucks now runs 70% of sales through drive-thru and mobile. More locations, fewer gathering occasions.

Three Major Attributed Drivers...
- Smartphones (no surprise) optimized for content consumption replaced social exchange. 

- Car-dependent development removed the conditions for incidental gathering. Made worse with the pandemic shut down of pulbic transit and forcing many to purchase vehicles to get to work (seperately, this drove much of the used car market). 

- On-premise economics made the cost of going out hard to justify when the social outcome is available at home for free.

This is not a pandemic story. The behavioral shift was already running at 1.1 minutes per year before 2020. COVID compressed five years of trajectory into eighteen months.

Six Sigma doesn't care what you manufacture.

Spend time around manufacturing clusters in Maharashtra — auto-component units, foundries, specialty chemicals plants, pharma API facilities, seafood export units, pump and bearing manufacturers — and one thing becomes obvious: the same DMAIC framework applies to completely different problems:

→ An auto-component press shop battling changeover downtime → A foundry fighting casting rejection rates → A specialty chemicals plant chasing batch-to-batch consistency → A pharma API facility tightening GMP documentation and yield → A seafood export unit protecting cold-chain integrity and cutting processing waste → A pump and bearings manufacturer improving OEE on ageing machine lines

Different industries. Different defects. Same discipline: define the problem in numbers, measure what's actually happening (not what people assume is happening), find the root cause, fix it, and build a control system so it doesn't come back.

The manufacturers who move fastest aren't the ones with the newest machines — they're the ones who build a culture where every operator is trained to spot variation and fix it at the source.

That's the real value of Lean Six Sigma: not a training certificate on the wall, but a plant floor that gets a little better every single day.
