🏭 Performance Rating – The Heart of Accurate Time Study

In Industrial Engineering,
measuring time alone is not enough.

Two operators may complete the same task in different times due to differences in skill, effort, experience, and working methods. This is where Performance Rating (PR)becomes critical.

📊 What is Performance Rating?

Performance Rating is the assessment of an operator's working pace compared to a qualified worker performing at a normal speed.

Its purpose is to convert Observed Time (OT) into Normal Time (NT)and establish fair, realistic, and achievable standards.

🔹 Why Performance Rating is Important?

✅ Eliminates bias from fast or slow operators
✅ Establishes realistic standard times
✅ Improves capacity planning accuracy
✅ Supports manpower planning
✅ Enables accurate SMV calculation
✅ Improves productivity measurement
✅ Strengthens Lean Manufacturing Excellence

🔹 Typical Rating Scale

🔹 80% – Slow
🔹 90% – Below Normal
🔹 100% – Normal
🔹 110% – Good
🔹 120% – Fast
🔹 130% – Very Fast

🔹 Factors Considered During Rating

✔ Skill
✔ Effort
✔ Working Conditions
✔ Consistency

🔹 Components of SMV

1️⃣ Observed Time (OT)
2️⃣ Performance Rating (PR)
3️⃣ Normal Time (NT)
4️⃣ Allowances
5️⃣ Standard Time (ST)
6️⃣ SMV (Standard Minute Value)

🔹 Typical Allowances

👤 Personal Allowance = 5–7%
💪 Fatigue Allowance = 8–12%
⏳ Delay Allowance = 3–8%

Total Typical Allowance = 15–25%

🔹 SMV Formula

Normal Time (NT) = OT × PR / 100

Standard Time (ST) = NT × (1 + Allowance %)

SMV = Standard Time

🔹 Example

Observed Time = 70 sec

Performance Rating = 110%

Allowance = 20%

➡ Normal Time = 77 sec

➡ Standard Time = 92.4 sec

➡ SMV = 1.54 min/unit

🎯 Key Insight

Without proper Performance Rating:

❌ Standard Times become inaccurate
❌ Capacity calculations become unreliable
❌ Production targets become unrealistic
❌ Productivity measurements lose credibility

A stopwatch records time, but Performance Rating converts that time into a meaningful standard.

🚀 Accurate standards lead to accurate planning, and accurate planning drives Manufacturing Excellence.

Can a part pass inspection and still be a defect?

Yes...

A part can be inside the tolerance and still miss the target.

That’s the uncomfortable lesson behind Genichi Taguchi’s quality thinking.
Most quality systems ask:

“Is it in spec?” - Useful question.

But not enough.

The better question is:

“How far is it from nominal?” - Because the customer doesn’t feel your tolerance chart.

They feel the fit.
They feel the noise.
They feel the assembly issue.
They feel the rework that shows up 3 operations later.

A part sitting at the edge of tolerance may pass inspection.

But it’s already telling you something.

The process is drifting.
Variation is too wide.
The system is accepting loss because the part is still “good enough.”

That’s where Aristotle connects to the floor.

Excellence isn’t one good part.

It’s the habit of hitting the target so often that variation starts to shrink.

Same principle, different century:

→ Every deviation carries a cost.
→ On-target beats barely in-spec.
→ Variation is the real signal.
→ Habits set the mean.
→ Quality starts before inspection.

Most operations still reward “inside the limit.”

The best ones chase the target.

Ask your floor this week:

Do you measure parts against the limit, or against the target?

Hit the target.
Shrink variation.
Cut the loss.

#Lean #Quality #ContinuousImprovement #Manufacturing #Operations #LeanManufacturing #OperationalExcellence

Many SME Manufacturing and Engineering companies are feeling acute pain 🤕 . Some are asking:- "How can we renegotiate commercial terms with our suppliers and customers before our margins disappear?"

I get it, it is not easy. You are being squeezed from all angles, but there are actions that you can take.

1.	Establish where you are achieving margin and where not: Many companies do not drill into their data and know what money they are earning by product and customer. If you don’t know its time to get your finance person on the case. Not all customers are the same. Some may be more open to and capable of absorbing price increases than others. Do you know who are which?

2.	Stop 🛑  uncontrolled and unnecessary discounting: Some discounts are given away too easily and often become a quick way of trying to win orders however they can have a massive impact on your margins and profitability. 

3.	Check your supply and customer contracts 🗒️ : Look at sections regarding price variation, MOQ’s, delivery terms, payment terms, force majeure etc. What wiggle room is there, or not? Don’t take anything for granted.

4.	Challenge price increases 🫸 : Not all price increase requests are reasonable and supported by evidence. Have you asked for the evidence, have you checked their facts, can they effectively demonstrate every penny of the price increase, are you checking against published indices, are their competitors doing the same, what is happening to your competitors? 5.	Are other terms of business an option rather than price ❓ : In negotiations price is not always the most important factor. Maybe it’s the payment term? Are other trade-offs possible that would be better for your business?

Not every supplier risk deserves the same response!
Some suppliers only need monitoring.
Some need improvement.
Some need a backup plan.
Some need immediate escalation.
That is why procurement and supply chain teams need a Supplier Risk Decision Matrix.
A simple way to assess supplier risk is by looking at two factors:
Impact:
How serious is the business damage if the supplier fails?
Probability:
How likely is the supplier to delay, fail, underperform, or disrupt supply?
When these two factors are combined, supplier decisions become clearer:
🟢 Low Impact + Low Probability
Monitor normally.
🟡 Low Impact + High Probability
Improve communication, follow-up, and corrective actions.
🟠 High Impact + Low Probability
Build a contingency plan, backup supplier, and buffer stock.
🔴 High Impact + High Probability
Escalate immediately, reduce dependency, and activate risk mitigation.
Supplier risk should not be judged only by price or relationship.
It should include:
✅ Delivery reliability
✅ Quality performance
✅ Lead time stability
✅ Capacity availability
✅ Financial strength
✅ Single-source dependency
✅ Geographic and logistics risk
✅ Responsiveness
A supplier may look stable today, but if one delay can stop production or affect customer orders, the risk is much bigger than it appears.
Strong procurement teams do not ask only:
“Is this supplier giving us the best price?”
They ask:
“What happens if this supplier fails?”
Because supplier risk management is not about reacting after disruption.
It is about protecting the business before disruption happens.

↳ Read it out loud. Cut what you would not say to a friend. If a line feels stiff, it is.

Mine is 114 lines now. Took an afternoon to write. It saves me an edit pass on every post since.

The file is the asset, whatever tool you paste it into. Your voice, written down once.

2. Deleting posts hurts more than it helps.

Got a typo, wrong visual, or just underperforming content? Unless it's truly off-brand, let it live. Try to resuscitate it. Deleting doesn't erase it from your history; it signals instability to the algorithm.

3. Your connections are dragging down your reach.

Want to grow fast? Build followers. But be ruthless about who you connect with. If they don't post, don't engage, and sit outside your topic fingerprint, they'll quietly tank your distribution.

4. Spamming DMs is killing your visibility.

If people keep ignoring your messages, LinkedIn notices. Low response rates on your outbound DMs signal spam behavior, and the platform will suppress your profile and content. Honestly, I'm cheering for this one.

5. Comment-and-run is getting penalized.

Leave 30 comments and disappear? LinkedIn now tracks whether you follow up. If someone replies to your comment and you ghost them, our data shows your comment reach can drop by 35%. Your relevance ranking tanks.

The algorithm rewards behavior that looks like genuine participation.
Performative tactics are quietly dying, and honestly, that's a good thing!

The reason your last implementation ran late has a name. And it's not the consulting partner's name 😅

Bent Flyvbjerg studied 16,000+ different types of projects across 136 countries.

Only 8.5% finished on time and on budget.

Add "delivered the promised benefits" to that bar, and it drops to 0.5%.

IT projects fall squarely in this distribution...

The culprit isn't incompetence.

It's a cognitive pattern Flyvbjerg and Daniel Kahneman call the planning fallacy.

Most timelines get built from the "inside out".

List the tasks. Assign durations. Add a 15% buffer.

This ignores how similar projects actually performed in the past.

The fix is Reference Class Forecasting.

Start from the historical record, not your project plan.

→ Find deployments comparable to yours in scope
→ Pull actual outcome data, not vendor reference calls
→ Position your project in that range, adjust at the margins

Do that, and you'll have much better data about how long your project will take.

There's also a second problem: your RFP process rewards the vendor who lowballs the timeline.

(which inevitably gets you into trouble)

Everyone knows it. Everyone plays along anyway.

Most warehouses don’t need more storage.
They need better flow.

Cross-docking is one of the simplest examples of this.

Instead of receiving goods, storing them, picking them again, and handling them multiple times, the product moves from inbound to outbound with minimal storage time.

Inbound truck
 → Sorting / staging
 → Outbound truck

That sounds simple.

But cross-docking only works when the operation is disciplined.

It needs reliable suppliers, clear dock scheduling, accurate sorting, proper staging, and strong coordination between inbound and outbound teams.

Without that, cross-docking becomes dock congestion with a fancy name.

There are three common types:

→ Flow-through: goods move straight from receiving to shipping.
 → Consolidation: small shipments combine into one full load.
 → Deconsolidation: one large shipment breaks into smaller deliveries.

The goal is not to remove storage completely.

The goal is to remove unnecessary storage.

Because some products should flow fast.

And some products should stay controlled.

Save this cheatsheet for your next warehouse flow review.

The book was written before COVID-19 reshaped global supply chains. It was written before generative AI and ChatGPT entered the mainstream. Yet it remarkably explains many of the forces that have shaped, and continue to shape, our economy and our supply chains. Or, as Sean might say, the journey from Steam Engines to Search Engines.

What strikes me most is how well the book connects technology, economics, complexity, and human behavior into a coherent picture of the world we're living in today.

Some of the themes that continue to resonate include:

▶ The transition from the Industrial Age to a new era driven by data, networks, and intelligence.
▶ Why exponential technologies create nonlinear change that traditional management approaches struggle to address.
▶ How increasing complexity makes prediction more difficult and adaptability more valuable.
▶ Why organizations must shift from optimizing individual functions to thinking in terms of interconnected systems.
▶ The growing importance of resilience, collaboration, and trust over efficiency alone.
▶ How emerging technologies should augment human decision making rather than simply automate existing processes.

As someone who spends a great deal of time thinking and writing about Supply Chain 5.0, I have to acknowledge that many of the ideas I've been exploring are anticipated in this book.

If you want to understand the bigger picture behind what's happening in today's supply chains, I would consider Transition Point required reading.

Inventory accuracy does not start with counting!!
It starts with identifying inventory correctly.
If your items are not clearly identified, the system may show stock available — but the warehouse may still face:
❌ Wrong picking
❌ Duplicate item codes
❌ Poor stock visibility
❌ Expiry losses
❌ Weak traceability
❌ Inaccurate ERP reports
That is why inventory identification methods are so important.
Key methods include:
✅ SKU Identification — unique code for each product variant
✅ Barcode / QR Code — faster receiving, picking, and dispatch
✅ Batch / Lot Tracking — traceability for quality and recall control
✅ Serial Number Tracking — unit-level control for high-value items
✅ Expiry Date Control — supports FEFO and reduces write-offs
✅ Location Coding — improves put-away, picking, and cycle counting
✅ FIFO / FEFO / Specific ID / Weighted Average — controls stock flow and valuation
Good inventory identification improves:
📦 Inventory accuracy
🎯 Picking accuracy
🔍 Traceability
📊 ERP / WMS reliability
💰 Financial accuracy
🚚 Service level
🛡 Audit control
The simple truth:
You cannot manage what you cannot identify.
Right item. Right quantity. Right location. Right batch. Right value. Right decision.

Sales overforecasts.

Many times for political reasons.

I have listed 7 red flags to challenge a sales forecast, and what to do:

1. A spike with no story
The forecast suddenly jumps, but nothing explains it: no promotion, no launch, no market event
↳ Compare against the last 12 months
↳ Ask what changed
↳ Request the supporting assumptions

2. "It comes from the customer"
A customer number is treated like confirmed demand
↳ Ask if it is an order or a forecast
↳ Verify the source
↳ Plan based on how firm it is

3. Seasonality ignored
The forecast does not match the historical seasonal pattern
↳ Compare with the last 2–3 years
↳ Look for exceptions
↳ Challenge unexplained deviations

4. It does not match the AOP (Annual Operating Plan)
The forecast tells a different story from the plan the business signed off on
↳ Quantify the gap
↳ Reconcile with Sales and Finance
↳ Align on one set of numbers

5. A target dressed as a forecast
The sales target becomes the demand forecast
↳ Ask if it is the commit or the stretch
↳ Separate targets from expected demand
↳ Plan supply against reality

6. Finance disagrees
The financial plan and the sales forecast do not align
↳ Compare both plans
↳ Bring Finance into the discussion
↳ Resolve the differences before planning

7. The metrics are warning you
Forecast accuracy and bias have been off for multiple cycles
↳ Review accuracy and bias by SKU
↳ Identify recurring patterns
↳ Change the forecasting approach

OCR isn't Accounts Payable Automation. It's one-sixth of it.
  
Ask ten people what "AP automation" means and you'll get ten different answers.
  
Most stop at "scanning invoices instead of typing them in."
  
That's OCR. It's a feature, not the system.
  
It's also why so many AP automation projects deliver less than half of what the sales call promised.
  
Real AP automation is six steps, not one:
  
→ Invoice receipt
→ Data capture
→ Coding
→ Matching (2-way or 3-way)
→ Approval routing
→ Payment and reconciliation
  
The automation isn't any single step.

It's the invoice moving from step one to step six without anyone re-typing anything along the way.
  
Here's the part vendor demos never show you:
  
PO-based invoices are the easy 80%.

A PO already exists, so the system matches and flags discrepancies automatically.
  
Non-PO invoices (utilities, subscriptions, one-off charges) have nothing to match against.

They rely entirely on your coding rules and approval hierarchy.
  
That's where exception queues balloon and touchless rates stall out.
  
If a demo only shows you clean PO matches, ask to see the non-PO workflow.

That's the part that's actually hard.
  
Tonight's newsletter breaks down the full 6-step process in our updated AP Automation Guide, what to evaluate before you buy, and the mistakes that quietly sink well-funded AP automation projects.

You are prompting Claude Fable 5 like it is Claude 4.

12 prompts from Anthropic's official guide: 

1. Tell it when to act

Fable can burn minutes over-planning a simple job.

"When you have enough information to act, act. Give a recommendation, not a survey."

You get a decision, not a stalled plan.

2. Check its own progress

On long runs it used to report work it never did.

"Audit each claim against a tool result. If it isn't verified, say so."

No more fake "done".

3. Set boundaries

Fable takes action you never asked for, like an email.

"When I'm thinking out loud, the deliverable is your assessment. Report and stop."

It reports, then waits for you.

4. Only pause when needed

Left alone, it checks in far more than the work needs.

"Pause only when the work truly needs you: a destructive action or your input."

Fewer interruptions, more finished work.

5. Keep it running on long jobs

Deep in a session it stops and just states the plan.

"Before ending your turn, check your last paragraph. If it's a promise, do it now."

It finishes instead of describing.

6. Give it a memory

Without notes, it repeats mistakes it already made.

"Store one lesson per file. Record why it mattered. Update, don't duplicate."

It compounds what it learns.

7. Give it the reason

With no purpose, it guesses at what you actually want.

"I'm working on [TASK] for [WHO]. They need [OUTCOME]. With that: [REQUEST]."

Ten words of context, far sharper output.

8. Spin up parallel subagents

It spins up parallel workers more readily than old models.

"Delegate independent subtasks to subagents and keep working while they run."

Three jobs at once instead of one.

9. Lead with the outcome

Left alone, it buries the point under build-up.

"Lead with the outcome. Your first line is what happened, the detail comes after."

You get the answer first.

10. Write for the absent reader

After a long run its shorthand gets dense.

"Your summary is for someone who wasn't watching. Open with the outcome, no arrow chains."

The summary makes sense to anyone.

11. Don't over-engineer

On high effort it tidies and refactors past the task.

"Don't add features, refactor, or add abstractions beyond what the task requires."

It builds what you asked for, nothing more.

12. Verify with a fresh subagent

Self-review misses what a fresh agent catches.

"Every so often, have a fresh subagent check your work against the spec."

A real check before you ship.

I've hired 100s of people across 4 8-figure businesses.

My best hires did not have the most experience...

Scaling Verb Brands, I brought in people with big agency names. 
They had the impressive titles and strong references...

But time after time, those credentials let me down.

It took more than a few fumbles to learn that experience ≠ impact. 

Nearly any role can be taught with the right training and culture.
What I really needed to find was drive, hunger, and resilience. 

(The skills that can't be taught !)  

So I created a framework to bypass hiring mistakes and wasted time.

I call it ALIGN: 

A — Anchor the Role in Business Reality
↳ Every hire should tie to a strategic goal.
↳ Don't hire a marketing manager. Hire to increase qualified leads by 30%.

L — Look for Cognitive Diversity
↳ How someone processes a problem matters more than what they know.
↳ Pose a real scenario in the interview and watch how they solve it. 

I — Institutionalise Role Intelligence
↳ Most hiring failures come from unclear expectations.
↳ If you can't describe the function of the role, you're not ready to hire.

G — Generate the Right Environment
↳ Have the infrastructure ready before they arrive.
↳ Without it, you'll lose people before they've even really started.

N — Nail the Economic Case
↳ Every hire should pay for itself. Have their direct impact in mind.  
↳ This stops over-hiring and helps you say no to the wrong candidates.

Beyond the framework, there are 4 things I do in every interview:

1️⃣ Design questions around behaviour
↳ "Your top client is about to churn. You have 48 hours. Walk me through what you'd do."

This helps me see how they think, not just the answer they prepared. 

2️⃣ Look for pattern recognition and pace
↳ "What's a system you built or fixed in a past role, and how did you know it needed fixing?"

If they can't answer this one, they might not be used to taking initiative. 

3️⃣ Test for care
↳ Watch how they follow up. You can't fake it, and you can't train for it. 

A thoughtful note or reflection on the conversation goes a long way.

4️⃣ Hire for where the business is going
↳ Hiring reactively to fill a gap meant I replaced the role months later.

Now I hire someone who can grow into the business in 12 months.

An A-player will run circles around B-players any day. 

I learned that over more than a decade of hiring, 
But you can get out ahead of it with the framework above.

5,192 distilled spirits permits filed reports with TTB in 2024. Of those, 2,746 reported zero taxable removals for the year. Another 2,002 moved less than 10,000 proof gallons, roughly 60,000 bottles or under, at any reasonable price point.

The math: 53% of permitted US distilleries did no commercial business in 2024. Another 39% operated at a scale most CPG operators would not consider commercially relevant.

The "thousands of craft distilleries" headline carries a long tail of dormant operations, hobby projects, and sub scale producers most consumers will never encounter on shelf.

The actual competitive set for any commercial spirit is much smaller than the permit count suggests. 

444 producers moved more than 10,000 proof gallons in 2024. 120 produced at over 100,000 proof gallons, the rough threshold where producer revenue clears $10M. 50 produced at over 750,000 proof gallons, which is essentially the major industry players.

Read "craft boom" as a long tail with a small commercial head. The head is who actually competes for shelf.

Landed Cost: The True Cost of Buying
The purchase price is not the real cost.
A supplier may offer a cheaper unit price, but by the time the product reaches your warehouse, the total cost may be much higher.
Why?
Because the final cost includes:
🚚 Freight
🛃 Duty
🛡️ Insurance
📦 Handling
💰 Taxes
⏱️ Demurrage or detention
🏭 Inland transport
📄 Documentation and clearance charges
That is why Landed Cost is a critical supply chain finance metric.
Formula:
Landed Cost = Product Cost + Freight + Duty + Insurance + Handling + Taxes
Supporting formulas:
📌 Landed Cost per Unit = Total Landed Cost / Units Purchased
📌 Freight % of Landed Cost = Freight Cost / Landed Cost × 100
Simple Example:
Supplier price per unit = $20
After freight, duty, insurance, handling, and taxes:
True landed cost per unit = $28
That means the real cost is 40% higher than the supplier price.
This is why the cheapest supplier is not always the cheapest supply chain option.
A supplier with a higher unit price may still be better if the total landed cost is lower.
Purchase price shows what you pay the supplier.
Landed cost shows what the product really costs your business.
A strong procurement decision is not based only on the lowest quotation.
It is based on the lowest reliable total cost.

When demand moves, the first question should not be “who was wrong?”

That sounds obvious, but it happens more often than people admit.

The team explains the variance, the baseline was too high, a promotion did not lift the way it was expected to, orders moved between weeks, a customer pulled back.

All of that is useful, but it is still only the diagnostic layer.

The real value starts when the team asks what the miss changes.
Does inventory need to move? Does capacity need to shift? Does supply need to be expedited, delayed, or rebalanced? Does the customer promise still hold?

This is where demand planning becomes more than a forecast review. The forecast is an input, but the demand plan is the operating commitment the business chooses to make after looking at the signal, the assumption, the risk, and the trade-off.

A stronger demand review separates four things very clearly:
• what signal changed
• where the forecast missed
• which assumption needs to be tested
• which decision changes next

And if the same miss keeps coming back, the answer is not always to tune the model harder. Sometimes the team needs to update the assumption the model is built around.

That is the idea behind this decision lens: read the miss, test the assumption, and then change the decision with discipline.

If actual demand moved away from the forecast tomorrow, which decision would your team change first?

Cyber-attacks 💻 are becoming frighteningly common place, and this is getting corporate buyers understandably twitchy. 

No buyer wants to declare to their business that production may be affected if / when their supplier gets hacked. So, what cyber-security credentials do SME Manufacturers need to prove to their customers buyers to stay in the supply chain?
.
.
.
Now, please note that I am not cyber security expert, but whilst I was working for a client, I needed to spend some time talking with IT professionals and insurance companies after some big brand names were effectively closed down for a period of time. 

During this process I learned a few things that you may wish to consider:

1.	Ensure your IT asset register 📒 is up to date: Most failed supplier assessments begin with poor knowledge of what kit and systems exist, what version software they have installed, who uses them and what data they hold.
2.	Be clear on where your buyer-sensitive data is held 🔏 : this demonstrates you have control and clarity over commercially sensitive information. This is especially important where you as an SME handles customer drawings, prototypes, schedules, financial data or personal data.
3.	Create a “Supplier Cyber Evidence pack” 📦 : In here you need to have the latest records of policies, training records, an incident action plan, insurance policy documents etc.
4.	Implement the five “Cyber Essential” control areas: this consists of evidence covering firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection and patch management. If you have a third-party IT provider, I recommend you verify they have all of this in hand.
5.	Enable Multi Factor Authentication 📲 : this can be a challenge when some business data and systems are accessible on staff personal phones. I had quite a difficulty finding a solution when some didn’t want to lock their own phone!
6.	Train your staff and retain the records 📜 : there are many online courses now that have a test at the end and create a certificate and a training record.
7.	Consider cyber insurance: this is not necessarily a cheap option but the cover and peace of mind, in case of business interruption, is a relief. I must say that the insurance broker I selected was extremely helpful and supportive here.

There are many more actions to consider but I’m sure you get the idea. 

If you really want to get serious, take a look at ISO 27001 certification for example, the standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS). 

Also talk to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and IASME. They are very helpful. 

It can be surprising what procurement / operational professionals get involved in.

The shortest route is not always the best route!!
In logistics, route optimization is not only about reducing kilometers.
It is about balancing:
✅ Delivery time
✅ Fuel cost
✅ Vehicle capacity
✅ Customer priority
✅ Time windows
✅ Driver availability
✅ Service commitment
Many teams plan routes based only on geography.
But a route can look efficient on the map and still fail in real operations.
A short route can become expensive if it creates:
❌ Missed delivery windows
❌ Late priority orders
❌ Driver overtime
❌ Low truck utilization
❌ Failed deliveries
❌ Customer complaints
Smart Route Planning Asks:
🔹 Which customers must be served first?
🔹 Are there fixed delivery time windows?
🔹 Is the truck capacity properly used?
🔹 Can stops be grouped more efficiently?
🔹 Does the sequence reduce waiting time?
🔹 What is the cost per successful delivery?
🔹 What service risk exists if the route fails?
Simple Decision Rule
✅ Stable routes + predictable customers
➡ Standard route planning may work.
✅ High stop count + complex delivery windows
➡ Use route optimization tools.
✅ Urgent orders + strict time windows
➡ Prioritize service impact over distance.
✅ Low utilization + frequent empty miles
➡ Redesign route grouping and delivery frequency.
Route optimization is not about choosing the shortest road.
It is about choosing the route that protects:
✅ Cost
✅ Speed
✅ Capacity
✅ Service level
✅ Customer priority
Because a route that saves 10 kilometers but misses one important delivery may not be optimized.
It may be expensive.

While KPIs and metrics are important, leaders build genuine relationships. They make the effort to know the person behind the role. Understanding their aspirations, their concerns, and what motivates them beyond the numbers.

2. Distribute Decision-Making Power Across All Levels
Leaders trust their team enough to let them make their own decisions. I've repeatedly found that empowering your people builds their confidence, inspires them to be creative, and makes them accountable.

3. Come Down to Their Level
Leaders adapt to each team member's unique needs. Flexible work, personalized feedback, whatever it is… meet people where they are if you want them to thrive.

4. There is Power in Vulnerability
Leaders are transparent about struggles and uncertainties. I've learned that being open about my own challenges and seeking help when I need it builds trust. You share, you grow.

5. Identify And Celebrate Diversity
A high-performing team is also a well-rounded team. Identify and nurture each member’s strengths and create a space where they feel safe to contribute. Their varied perspectives and skills will only help you thrive.

6. Create Purpose-Driven Work
Your people are inspired when they understand how their contributions shape the bigger picture. Help them find meaning in their work and they will champion your business.

Yes, outcomes matter. Hitting your targets matters. But leadership is more than that. It’s enriching the lives of those you lead. And that can only happen by leading with
compassion, kindness, and empathy.

S - Show Up Consistently: People trust what they see often.
E - Educate Your Audience: Give away insight, frameworks and shortcuts.
R - Reinforce With Proof: Use clear case studies, outcomes and testimonials.
V - Validate Their Problems: Make it clear you understand their pain.
E - Extend The Offer: Invite them into a solution when they are ready.

It's about selling at the right time, with the right offer.

The system below is the one I used to scale Searchable to $85 million, 
Not to mention 3 other businesses to 8-figures.

📣 ATTRACT

Around 3% of your audience is ready to buy at any given time.
Your only job is to be the most visible, credible option.

Personal Brand and Content:

Your feed should be where people come to learn for free. 
Don't start pitching in your content until you've built real trust. 

Lead Magnets:
↳ Give away a resource people would happily pay for

Email Sequences:

↳ Prompt a follow-up while intent is still high

✅ Conversion rate
✅ Response time
✅ Lead-to-customer ratio

✅ Reach and impressions

Sales and supply chain think differently.

Sales thinks about:
↳ Quota to hit
↳ Bonus to earn
↳ Inventory to have
↳ Forecast to submit

Supply Chain thinks about:
↳ Which forecast is the real one

↳ Inventory explanations for Finance
↳ Market inputs to pull from Sales
↳ When Sales will own the forecast (if ever)

Neither side is wrong.

↳ Forecast ownership belongs to demand planning only

↳ Frustrated customers

Think back to the last time you had to take charge of a floundering effort. Something important was falling apart. Nobody was going to fix it except you.
Was it because you were the only one with the horsepower? Did someone misunderstand your intent and go sideways? Was the team not ready for the responsibility?
Here's the hard part: as leaders, we need to be able to delegate. If we can't trust our team with critical work, we're burning ourselves out.
But when you do step in — and sometimes you will — the question isn't just "how do I fix this." It's "what went wrong that forced me to step in."
Did the team identify the root cause of the failure? Or did everyone just rush to fix the symptom and move on?
Did you take time to put systems in place to ensure you could hand it off next time and know it would work? Or are you setting up the same failure to happen again?
Here's what I've learned: taking time to ensure everyone has the knowledge, authority, and clarity for the tasks they're responsible for is a force multiplier. It keeps you from having to jump in. And when you do jump in, it gives you a clear picture of what actually broke.
The best leaders I've worked with don't minimize the number of times they have to take over a project. They minimize the second time the same thing happens.

When a forecast misses and the product has a long lead time, organizations reach for the magic word…”EXPEDITE”.

Here’s what that actually costs.

I had a sterilization queue I could push a SKU through faster when we needed it. It worked. The product showed up. What wasn’t immediately apparent is that every other product sitting in that queue got delayed to make room.

Expediting feels like a safety valve. In reality, it’s an exchange. The disruption doesn’t disappear, it moves to someone else’s product line, and almost nobody traces it back to the original forecasting miss that caused it.

This is why “we can always expedite” is one of the most expensive sentences in supply chain. It’s true in isolation and false in aggregate. The capacity to expedite is finite, shared, and invisible until you’re the one waiting behind someone else’s emergency.

If your SIOP process treats expediting as a free recovery option instead of a cost with a real budget, you’re not planning…you’re borrowing against the future.

#SIOP #SupplyChain #ForecastAccuracy

Planning complexity (in real life) tends to evolve like this:

1) Early-stage (single channel, lean SKU count) → Demand is easier to read. Supply is more direct. Fewer moving parts.

2) Growing multichannel (DTC + wholesale, expanding SKUs) → Demand signals multiply. Fulfillment gets more complex. Forecasting becomes a cross-functional sport.

3) Mass wholesale (broad network, high SKU count) → Supply networks layer. SKU velocity behaves wildly differently across the catalog. Retailer behavior starts driving the forecast (POs, chargebacks, replenishment cycles).


The constants — regardless of stage:
-Your model is only as good as the data you trust

-Planning is only as good as the alignment conversations around it

-Cadence beats sophistication (re-forecasting + scenario planning)


When a client works through this framework, they can immediately spot where they’re overbuilt (wasting time) or underbuilt (risking bigger problems later).

And if you’re waiting for “enterprise tools” before you plan well — you can stop waiting. 

Get the basics right, keep them consistent, and scale them as complexity shows up.

Most predictive maintenance projects in mid-size shops follow the same arc. Sensors get installed. Dashboards get built. Alerts fire. 18 months later, nothing on the floor runs differently.

Ten failure modes I keep seeing. Almost never the model.

1. No standard work, no baseline to predict from. A model needs to know what "normal" looks like. If two operators run it two ways, the baseline is fiction. The prediction looks confident anyway.

2. Sensor data without process context. Vibration spike at 03:14. Was the machine cutting, idling, or in test mode? The sensor doesn't know. Neither does the model. The alert fires regardless.

3. Digital twin drifts, nobody validates. Built six months ago. The line has changed - new fixture, new feed rate, swapped servo. Decisions get made against a snapshot the floor has already walked past.

4. Model trained on bearing X, deployed on bearing Y. Maintenance swapped the part. Different vibration signature, different failure curve. The model was never retrained. It predicts failures that can't happen and misses the ones that can.

5. No feedback loop. The fix never returns to the model. Technician replaces the seal. The machine runs fine for nine months. That's the most valuable data the model could get. It stays in a notebook in someone's truck.

6. Tribal knowledge walks out the door. Lost a press brake operator last year. He was also the die maker. A drawer full of custom small dies - he knew which one was for which job because he'd made them. The day he left, the toolbox became a guessing game. No graph captured that.

7. Knowledge graph populated once, then abandoned. A consultant ran a workshop. Filled the schema. Got paid. Machines kept changing. The graph stayed frozen. Two years on, it documents a plant that no longer exists.

8. Alert into a vacuum. Dashboard wired into a shared Slack channel. The channel had no owner. The operator who saw the alert wasn't trained for it. By the time anyone figured out the next move, the bearing was gone. The alert worked as designed. The receiving end was never built.

9. Prediction without authority to act. The system says shut down for inspection. The plant manager has a shipment due Friday. Production wins. The prediction becomes a record of an action that didn't happen.

10. Reactive culture eats the predictive tool. Bonuses get paid for fixing things fast. Preventing the breakdown pays nothing. Operators learn what the org actually rewards.

Every one of these is a workflow problem in tech-shaped packaging. The standard. The context. The owner. The authority. The loop back. The incentive. AI amplifies what's already there - when the workflow's missing, it amplifies the absence.

Without standard work, AI only accelerates chaos. Before you automate the work, understand the work

Fable is Anthropic's most powerful AI model (and also most expensive). Here's how to get it to train cheaper AI models and save $$

Not because the expensive model isn't worth it. But because they're using it wrong.

Here's the framework AI companies use internally, called model distillation, and how you can apply it yourself.

What AI labs do:
They train an expensive model on a specific task until it's really good at that task. Then they use that expensive model to generate the data for a cheaper model needs to do the same job.

Expensive model builds the playbook. Cheap model runs it.

You can do the exact same thing.

When I'm building a new AI workflow, I always start with the most capable model I have access to. I use it to develop and refine the playbook for that process. I have it critique the playbook. Update it. Run it. Improve it.

Once the playbook is solid, I test it on a cheaper model.

Nine times out of ten, a well-written playbook runs just fine on a cheaper model. The expensive model did the hard thinking. The cheap model executes.

You keep the expensive model in your back pocket for genuinely novel problems. But your day-to-day workflows? Those can run cheap.

So if you're experimenting with Fable right now, use it to build the playbook. Not just to run tasks.

The goal isn't to use the most powerful model for everything. The goal is to use it once, well, so everything else gets cheaper.

Why the sentence "can you just change the plan?" is rarely as simple as it sounds? 

Sales may see demand, finance may see revenue, customer service may see a promise date. 

But operations has to translate that into lines, people, materials, tooling, changeovers, quality checks, supplier arrivals, and all the smaller constraints that do not show up neatly when the number first changes.

That is where the production plan sits.

It is the translation layer between demand ambition and factory commitment, it takes the demand signal and asks a more grounded set of questions:
• Do we have the capacity?
• Do we have the material?
• Do we have the labor and skills?
• What does the sequence do to changeover?
• What gets delayed if we pull this forward?
• Is this still a plan, or has it become a fire drill?

The factory schedule is more detailed. It says what runs on which line, in which sequence, and when.

The production plan comes before that. It decides what the factory should commit to build across the planning horizon after the constraints have been checked.

Sometimes the answer is yes. Sometimes the answer is yes, but with a service, cost, overtime, inventory, or changeover trade-off. And sometimes the honest answer is no, because the constraint moved faster than the plan could absorb.

A good production plan does not make the factory rigid. It makes the trade-offs visible early enough for the business to make a better decision.

When demand changes, which constraint changes the plan first in your 
environment?

As leaders, we love asking:

Excel is rarely the real problem in Supply Chain Planning.
It is usually the place where the real problem becomes visible.

The system has a number.
The planner knows the number cannot be trusted yet.
The meeting needs a decision.
The business still needs a compromise between service, inventory, cost and capacity.

So the spreadsheet appears.

Not because people love manual work.

Often because the operating model has not answered basic questions.

Who can override the plan?
Which data is trusted enough to act from?
Which exception needs escalation?
Which KPI wins when service and inventory conflict?
Who owns the outcome after the manual adjustment?

If those answers are unclear, a new tool will not remove the spreadsheet.

It will sit next to it.

That is why I do not like the sentence "we need to get rid of Excel."

I would rather ask:
What job is this spreadsheet doing for the organization?

Once you know that, you can decide whether the logic belongs in the system, in the process, in the governance, or in the management rhythm.

Excel is not always the enemy.
Sometimes it is the evidence.

Which spreadsheet in your organization would be dangerous to delete tomorrow?

“Never become the Godfather of your organization.”

Many leaders unknowingly become exactly that.

Everyone comes to them for:
* Every decision.
* Every approval.
* Every problem.
* Every conflict.

At first, it feels like leadership.

In reality, it’s a bottleneck.

If every road leads to one office, you don’t have a management system you have dependency.

Lean asks leaders to build systems that solve problems without needing “the Godfather.”



Other powerful metaphors include:

🤝 Loyalty vs. Capability

The Godfather values loyalty above almost everything.

Lean values capability first.

Loyal people who cannot solve problems will never build a great organization.

Develop people so they can think, not just obey.



🤫 Information is Power

In The Godfather, information is closely guarded.

In Lean, information is visual, transparent, and shared.

Visual Management exists so everyone can see reality not just senior leaders.



👀 Respect Over Fear

Many obey the Godfather because they fear him.

Lean organizations improve because people feel safe enough to speak up.

Fear hides problems.

Respect reveals them.



🔥 Solving the Symptom

In the film, many conflicts are “solved” by removing people.

Lean removes the process that created the problem.

People are rarely the root cause.

Systems usually are.



👑 Succession

The Godfather worries constantly about who comes next.

Lean builds successors every day.

A great leader creates more leaders not more followers.



My private message:

If your organization cannot function without you, you’ve built dependence not leadership.

That’s one of the deepest Lean lessons.

The ultimate goal of Lean leadership isn’t to become indispensable.

It’s to build people and systems that no longer depend on you.

That is when you know you’ve truly succeeded.
🌱🎲🎳

A member of my TRIBE community reached out last week. His DMs weren't getting any responses.
"Send them over" I said. He's making a mistake most of us make.
 
He was putting in real effort, thoughtful, well-intended messages. But without realizing it, every one of them was a statement about himself. His work, his offer, his value. Not one left room for the other person to say anything back.
 
That's not a copywriting problem but more a psychology problem.
 
Let me tell you what's actually happening in someone's head when they open a DM:
 
→ If the message asks them to justify their own behavior ("why did you view my profile?"), most people have no real answer, what do they reply? Right. Nothing! 
 
→ If the message describes you instead of them, there's nothing in it for their brain to react to.
 
→ If the message ends in a soft, open-ended CTA ("I'm just a DM away"), you've handed them all the work of deciding what happens next. Most people won't do that work. They'll just scroll on.
 
The fix isn't "be more salesy" or "be more casual." 

It's actually much more simple:
 
Every message should end in something answerable in under 10 seconds. 
A specific question. A fork. A light provocation instead of a statement.
 
I broke this down into the 3 moments that matter most:

1. Profile View
2. Connection request accepted
3. 48 Hours later

Everyone wants to be "AI-first."

Most companies aren't even process-first.

John Kloetzing and I got on a call that was supposed to last 15 minutes. It turned into an hour of comparing scars — two people who've walked into 400+ factories between us, across pharma and manufacturing supply chains.

What we kept landing on had almost nothing to do with AI:

→ In most companies the "process" isn't written down anywhere. It lives inside one or two experienced people. The day they leave, the real logic walks out the door.
→ You can't put an agent on top of that. There's nothing underneath to put it on top of.
→ And nearly every "data quality" problem turns out to be a decision problem in disguise.

So we wrote it down — the version from the battlefield, not the webinar. Where agents actually create value (it's boring on purpose), where they quietly break, and why the bottleneck is almost never the software.

The average GTM engineer is about to get wiped out. The best one is about to get rich.

This role is going through exactly what software engineering went through in the 2010s.

Back then Silicon Valley had the 10x engineer: one person who did the work of ten. The same gap is opening in GTM right now.

A GTM engineer builds the systems that find leads and run a sales team's outreach. The routine half of that already runs on its own. AI researches the accounts, drafts the outreach, and keeps the follow-ups moving overnight.

So the job is splitting into two.

One version just runs the tools. Anyone with the same setup gets the same output, which means an agent gets there too. Most of those people will end up running their agents inside Claude Code or Codex, and whoever only operates the stack gets cheaper every year.

The other version builds the tools: the agents and the internal systems the rest of the team runs on. That's the person doing the work of ten, and you can't buy it off the shelf. Those roles already pay $40 to $60K above an equivalent RevOps hire, and that gap only widens.

People keep telling me this role is about to dissolve into every other seat. I don't buy it, and 9 in 10 people doing the work don't either. It doesn't disappear. It concentrates: fewer engineers, each one worth far more.

If I were hiring for this today, I'd stop counting the tools someone has used and start looking at the systems they've built.

HOW MANY SHOULD WE ORDER?
It's one of the toughest questions every buyer or merchandiser faces when launching a completely new item.
There are no sales records to review, no historical demand to analyze, and no previous orders to compare. Yet, a decision still has to be made.
The good news is that you don't have to guess.

Instead, make your decision based on a few practical factors:
📌 Compare it with the closest existing product in terms of price, quality, purpose, and target customers.
📌 Research the market. Is demand growing? Are competitors offering similar products? Is it seasonal or an everyday item?
📌 Understand your supplier's requirements, such as lead time, minimum order quantity (MOQ), and packaging.
📌 Consider your own capacity your available budget, warehouse space, and how quickly you expect the product to sell.

A simple way to estimate your first order is:
Initial Order Quantity = Estimated Monthly Demand × Inventory Coverage (Months)
For example, if you believe the item can sell 40 units per month and you want enough stock for 2 months, your initial order would be:
40 × 2 = 80 units

Of course, this is only a starting point.
The first order isn't about getting it perfect it's about collecting real market data. Once customers start buying, you'll gain valuable insights that allow you to adjust future orders with much greater confidence.
The best buyers don't rely on luck. They make informed decisions, monitor results, and continuously improve their planning. Every new product starts with an estimate, but every reorder should be backed by data.
Every successful product today was once a new item with no sales history. The key is not to eliminate uncertainty but to manage it wisely.

Every buyer has faced this challenge at least once:
"How many units should I order when it's a completely new item from a new supplier?"
Without historical sales data, determining the right order quantity can feel like guesswork. But it doesn't have to be. The key is to make data-informed assumptions instead of relying on intuition alone.

Here's a simple approach beginners can follow:
✅ Identify the closest comparable product in your current assortment based on category, price range, target customer, and product function.
✅ Estimate expected monthly demand using the sales performance of those comparable items.
✅ Consider the supplier's lead time, Minimum Order Quantity (MOQ), and your desired safety stock.
✅ Start with a controlled trial order rather than placing a large purchase immediately.
✅ Monitor sales closely during the first few weeks, then adjust future orders based on actual demand.

Remember, your first purchase is not about achieving perfect accuracy it's about reducing risk while collecting valuable sales data. Every replenishment becomes more accurate because your decisions are supported by real customer demand.
Successful buying isn't about predicting the future perfectly. It's about making informed decisions, measuring the results, and continuously improving your forecasts.

If you're new to procurement, merchandising, or demand planning, mastering this simple process will help you minimize overstock, reduce stockouts, and build confidence in your purchasing decisions.

S&OP does NOT mean IBP (integrated business planning).

This infographic shows 6 areas IBP integrates that traditional S&OP does not:

1. Volume Plan → P&L
↳ S&OP: balances units
↳ IBP: shows what those units do to revenue, margin, and working capital
↳ The gap: a plan approved without anyone seeing its cost 

2. Plan → Financial Forecast
↳ S&OP: runs two numbers, ops and Finance
↳ IBP: runs one; same demand signal drives both
↳ The gap: every review becomes a debate about whose number is right
 
3. Decision → Downstream Consequence
↳ S&OP: weighs decisions one at a time
↳ IBP: traces what each one sets in motion
↳ The gap: problems no one traces back to the choice that caused them; no traceability; no learning path

4. Scenarios → Decisions
↳ S&OP: plans one baseline
↳ IBP: plans a range, with the response to each agreed in advance
↳ The gap: every deviation becomes a crisis, and reality deviates 99.9% of the time

5. Functions → One Set of Assumptions
↳ S&OP: gets functions in the same room
↳ IBP: gets them on the same model
↳ The gap: consensus that holds in the meeting and falls apart between them

6. Plan → Strategy
↳ S&OP: answers "can we execute?" 
↳ IBP: answers "should we, and where do we invest?"
↳ The gap: the monthly cycle stays operational instead of becoming where strategy gets made

She'd been a supply chain planner for 11 years.
Good at it. Really good. 

The kind who caught problems before the system did, knew every supplier quirk, and read a situation faster than anyone on the floor.

Last month she moved into marketing.

She told me she was tired of spending 70% of her week reacting to problems the system should have prevented.

"I used to love this job," she said. "Now I spend Monday firefighting last week's problems. Tuesday planning Friday's expedites. Wednesday justifying to procurement why I need stock we haven't forecast. By Friday I'm just hoping nothing explodes over the weekend."

She wasn't failing. Her system was doing exactly what it was designed to do.

MRP was built for a stable, predictable world. It optimises for efficiency in conditions that haven't existed for 20 years. Run it in a volatile environment and it amplifies every disturbance, turning small uncertainties into constant crises.

Here's what the numbers show:
→ 60-80% of a planner's week in a forecast-driven environment is reactive work
→ In a flow-based environment: under 20%

Same intelligence. Same experience. Different system.

She didn't burn out. Her system burned her out.

What percentage of your planning team's week is spent planning versus reacting?

𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘞𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘛𝘢𝘪𝘪𝘤𝘩𝘪 𝘖𝘩𝘯𝘰 𝘛𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘩 𝘜𝘴 𝘛𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘺?

I recently watched an old interview with Taiichi Ohno.

No PowerPoint.
No AI.
No digital dashboards.
No fancy Lean vocabulary.

Just clear thinking.

And while watching it, I kept asking myself one question:

𝘐𝘧 𝘛𝘢𝘪𝘪𝘤𝘩𝘪 𝘖𝘩𝘯𝘰 𝘸𝘢𝘭𝘬𝘦𝘥 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘰 𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘺… 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘩 𝘶𝘴?

Probably not another Lean tool.
Probably not another certification.
Probably not another workshop.

He would ask uncomfortable questions.

⁉️Why are managers discussing problems in meeting rooms instead of at the Gemba?
⁉️Why do we measure activity instead of customer value?
⁉️Why do we celebrate busy people instead of improving processes?
⁉️Why do we build reports instead of solving problems?
⁉️Why do we automate waste before eliminating it?

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘐 𝘭𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘥, 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘐 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘦𝘥 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘵.
𝘔𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘰𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦𝘯’𝘵 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯.
𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺’𝘷𝘦 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺’𝘷𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨.

Today we have AI.
Real-time dashboards.
Predictive analytics.
Digital twins.
Automated workflows.

Yet many organizations still struggle with the same problems Toyota was solving more than 50 years ago.

Why?

Because technology never fixes poor thinking.

Taiichi Ohno never started with software.

He started with observation.

He didn’t ask,
“What system should we buy?”

He asked,
“Why does this waste exist?”

He didn’t build Lean around tools.
He built it around curiosity.
He didn’t ask people to work faster.
He designed systems where working smarter became natural.

⚠️Perhaps the biggest lesson from the video is this:
Lean was never about manufacturing.
It was about leadership.

🎯Leaders who go and see.
🎯Leaders who challenge assumptions.
🎯Leaders who develop people instead of creating dependence.
🎯Leaders who understand that every inventory pile, every delay, every workaround and every defect is simply a symptom of a deeper problem waiting to be understood.

Today many companies invest millions in digital transformation.

But imagine if they invested the same energy in teaching leaders how to observe.

How to ask better questions.
How to think scientifically.
How to solve problems at the root.

That would be a transformation no software could replace.

If Taiichi Ohno walked into your organization today…

I don’t think he would ask to see your dashboards.

I think he would ask one simple question:
“Show me where the work happens.”

Because that’s where improvement has always started.

Not in the boardroom.
Not in PowerPoint.
Not in AI.

At the Gemba.
And perhaps that lesson is more relevant today than ever.

Pharma and fine-chemical manufacturers spend years perfecting a formulation — then leave 15-20% of capacity on the table through changeover delays, batch-to-batch variability, and reactive quality checks.

Finance wasn’t in the room when the decision was made. But they owned the consequences six weeks later.

A few weeks ago, I sat in a planning review with a pharma company. Finance and Supply Chain each had their own systems, their own numbers, and ultimately their own version of the truth.

During the meeting, Supply Chain shifted production priorities between two products to protect a critical customer commitment. Given the information available in the room, it was a reasonable decision.

Six weeks later, Finance saw the consequences during month end close. Margins were lower. Working capital was higher.

No one in the planning meeting had been able to see either impact before the decision was made. That wasn’t a poor decision. It was a system that could only reveal the consequences after they had already happened.

So we tried something simple. Before locking in a scenario, we added one question to the discussion.

What does this option do to margin? What does it do to cash? Not after the fact. Not in the monthly review. Right there, before the decision was made.

We didn’t build a sophisticated model. We simply introduced a rough estimate at the right moment. That alone changed two decisions during the first pilot.

I’ve seen the same pattern across many organisations. Operational decisions are made in one room. Financial consequences become visible in another.

By the time both perspectives come together, the decision has already become history.

Gianni Infantino and the FIFA just gave every leader on this platform a live case study in how NOT to use power.
 
One phone call from the Oval Office. One suspended red card. One World Cup match reshaped in real time.
 
In case you didn't got the message.
 
Trump called Infantino. Asked him to review Balogun's suspension. Days later, FIFA suspended the automatic ban for a one-year probation. Belgium's appeal got thrown out on a technicality: apparently they weren't even a "party" to their own protest. The US played Belgium anyway.
 
Result? USA lost 4-1. Eliminated. Every ounce of "special treatment" backfired spectacularly.
 
But the damage was already done before kickoff.
 
UEFA called it "unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable." Belgium's federation said it was "astonished." Infantino kept insisting the judicial bodies are independent, while confirming on the record that a sitting head of state got a rule bent in his direction.
 
The leadership lesson hiding behind all of this?
 
Infantino's entire mandate after the Blatter scandals was one word: TRUST Show the world FIFA plays it straight, every time, for everyone.
 
He broke it in one weekend. In front of the biggest audience football has ever had.
 
Now let's bring this to LinkedIn.
 
You also have power. Reach. Authority. Followers who take your word more seriously than they probably should.
 
The temptation is the same one Infantino faced. Bend a rule. Make an exception. Protect someone close to you when you think nobody's watching.
 
Except on LinkedIn, everybody's watching.
 
Three rules I never break with influence, and what they look like on LinkedIn:
 
1. Protect fair process. 
   Don't quietly delete a critical comment on your own post because it makes you look bad. Leave it up, or reply to it in public.
   
2. Share the spotlight. 
   Don't claim your success when it's a joint effort like "I built this." Tag the people who actually did the work, in the post, not buried in a comment.
   
3. Set the standard higher. 
   Don't write a glowing recommendation for someone in your circle that you wouldn't write for a stranger with the same track record.
 
Infantino had one shot to prove FIFA earned trust back. 
He ruined it on a single phone call.
 
You get hundreds of those "one phone calls" a year, in comments, in promotions, in decisions nobody will ever audit.
 
What's the one rule you'd never bend, even for your favorite person in the room?

1. AUDIT. Read the current CLAUDE.md in full, then read enough of the actual project (folder structure, key files, recent commits, how I work here) to judge whether the file matches reality. List every gap: anything vague, contradictory, outdated, missing, or that only works because I fill it in from my head.

2. UPGRADE. Rewrite CLAUDE.md so it is complete, unambiguous and self-sufficient. State the project's purpose, stack and the standards I hold in plain, testable language. Make the implicit explicit: capture the conventions and how I like things done a new model would otherwise get wrong. Remove contradictions and dead instructions. Add a short definition of done and the checks to run before calling work finished. Preserve my voice, my existing rules and anything marked as a hard rule. Do not invent preferences I have not stated, and where unsure, ask me.

3. SHOW YOUR WORK. Give me a before and after diff of every change with one line of reasoning each, and list any open questions.

Only output the improved CLAUDE.md and your change summary. Do not touch other files."

Prompt #2 Audit and rebuild your skills

"You are my AI systems analyst. Study how I actually use Claude, then turn my repeated work into a clean, reusable system a cheaper model can run.

1. STUDY. Look across my recent projects, my chat and session history, my CLAUDE.md files, my saved prompts and my skills folder. Work out what I use Claude for most and find the tasks I repeat by hand.

2. AUDIT MY SKILLS. Go through every existing skill and workflow. Flag the redundant, outdated, duplicated or broken ones. For each, tell me keep, fix, merge or delete, with one line of reasoning.

3. IMPROVE AND CREATE. Rewrite my top repeated workflows as clean reusable skills, each with a clear trigger, inputs, steps and output. Spot the gaps and build the strongest two.

4. CAPTURE MY STANDARDS. Write a systems-instruction block I can drop into my CLAUDE.md so Opus or Sonnet gives me close to Fable 5 quality.

5. REPORT. List what you audited, what you fixed, what you created and where you saved it.

Ask me before deleting anything."

Fable does the thinking once.

Cheaper models run the result for months.

Anthropic has released the perfect prompt guide.

Here's the full structure:

1. Task context
↳ Vague context produces vague output.
↳ Set the scene properly before you ask for anything.

2. Tone context
↳ Tell it exactly how to communicate.
↳ Every output should be specific to a team member.

3. Background data, documents, and images
↳ Feed it everything relevant (URLs, existing content, rankings)
↳ The more context it has, the sharper the output.

4. Detailed task description and rules
↳ Be specific about what you want it to focus on and what the rules are.
↳ Tell it exactly what matters and what to ignore.

5. Examples
↳ Paste in an example of the output format you want.
↳ Claude follows examples better than instructions alone.

6. Conversation history
↳ If there's previous work or feedback from earlier sessions, include it.
↳ Claude has no memory between conversations unless you give it one.

7. Immediate task description
↳ After all the context, tell it exactly what you need today.
↳ Specific, scoped, with one clear request.

8. Think step by step
↳ Ask it to reason before it responds. 
↳ This step alone dramatically improves output quality.

9. Output formatting
↳ Tell it how to structure the response before it writes anything.
↳ Summary, top priority fixes, secondary recommendations, and quick wins.

Keep this handy for your next Claude prompt. ✨

Holy sh*t, there's 40,000 of you. Best year of my career, easily. So why the hell am I losing all my friends?

Between 7K and 40K, this is my "success story":

- Friends building families while I build my brand.
- I go to concerts feeling Thrivecart buzz in my bag
- I'm the last to arrive, first to leave at every gathering

The more I grow, the more my circle keeps shrinking.

My wedding invitation list gets shorter every year.

I used to think "becoming successful" meant everyone would finally get it. Finally stop side-eyeing my choices.

Nope. Success just made the contrast louder.

The people who knew me before? Some couldn't handle the version I stopped hiding.

The AuDHD brain on full display. The unfiltered takes. The labrador energy that doesn't have an off switch.

I'm not mad at them. Okay, maybe a little. Mostly we just outgrew each other.

But man, nobody warned me that 40,000 strangers cheering would feel lonelier than 7,000 and a full dinner table.

Anyone else?

I look pro on stage, but I felt like an imposter all day...

Even after building three businesses.
Even after getting into Forbes 30u30
Even after speaking on international stages

I'm scared, 99% of the time. 

And I don't talk about it enough, I'm sorry. 

Before recording videos I get nervous.
Before speaking on stages I get anxious.
Before posting on LinkedIn I get stressed...

I feel the exact same way you do. 

How I deal with it? I don't. I crave it actually.

Discomfort means growth. Seek it everywhere you go. 

Remember:

You're not bad at things, you're just new at it. 

From LinkedIn, to work, to a stage... keep going.

You counted your warehouse last year.
You'll find the same errors this year.
And you'll blame the same people.

Because the count was never the problem.

Warehouses mostly treat counting like a correction exercise.

Find the gap.
Adjust the system.
Move on.

Nobody asks why the gap exists.

So next month:
same location, same SKU, same variance.
Different person gets blamed.

Counting finds the number.
Only investigating fixes the process.

Two methods exist.
They do two different jobs:

→ Physical count: 
Full shutdown, count everything, reconcile the books. 
For audits and year-end.

→ Cycle count: 
Small ongoing counts during operations. 
Catches errors early. No shutdown.

But both are useless
if you skip the real step:

→ A variance shows up. Why?
→ Same bin, third month in a row. Why?
→ Messy location, mixed stock. Why?
→ Adjustment made, no approval trail. Why?

The count didn't fail.
The follow-up never happened.

Start correcting what caused the gap.

Your warehouse doesn't need more counts.
It needs fewer reasons to be wrong.

P.S. What's the most common variance you keep finding in your operation?

Except…

Operations lives in reality, not in PowerPoint.

Looking busy is not the same as understanding the work.

The model is doing its job. 
You've just asked it to do 5 other jobs at the same time.

Every tool in the AI stack got good at solving one specific job.

But when you layer the right ones together... 

You've got a system that does more than any single model can on its own.

Here's the stack I use to run LinkedIn, broken down by the job each tool does:

1/ Business & Comms

The admin layer no one talks about. 
Get this right and everything above it moves twice as fast.

Zapier, Loom, Fireflies, Slack, Gusto and Wispr Flow are what keep my business ticking day to day.

2/ Research

One of the most important steps that so many people rush past. 
Do it properly here, and the writing gets way easier later.

Perplexity, Gemini, Saywhat and Claude Cowork are where I go to pressure-test ideas and find stronger angles.

3/ Design

Where the idea becomes something people want to save and screenshot.

Figma, Saywhat, Nano Banana, Opus Clip and Gamma all give you output you'd be happy to post.

4/ Writing

The drafting layer. 
This is where so many people lean on one tool and end up sounding like everyone else.

5/ Systems

The layer that stops you from doing the same manual job 40 times a month.

The feedback loop.

No single tool sits in every layer, and that's the point.

The trick is knowing which tool to use for which job.

Build the stack once, and you stop guessing what to post next, because the system tells you.

In the past 6 months I’ve grown from $15k/mo to $45k/mo.

Your list has 50 things on it. 1 moves the business more than the other 49.

AIS - the Automatic Identification System that ships use to broadcast information about their identity, location, and destination - was first envisioned in the 1960s by Swedish seaman Benny Pettersson.

Today, it is an essential part of maritime safety... but it is under attack.

AIS is based on the premise of mutual benefit. That vessels can operate more safely when they know who is around them and where they are going.

The stakes are higher than ever in the Strait of Hormuz, and it is taking a toll on AIS. Ships are spoofing, trolling, turning off their AIS signals, and using them as a means of communication. 

We're watching as trust in the system slowly but surely erodes...

In this week's Art of Supply, I share the history of AIS, how it is supposed to work, and why it became so successful, and speculate about whether it will survive the current challenges.

Not long ago, ~6% of commercial Google searches returned AI Overviews. 

That figure is now above 90%, and no SEO is not dead...

I don't think anyone, including Google, expected it to move this fast.

We are witnessing the category get rewritten every week. 
It’s been a wild ride watching this play out in real time !

And it matters especially because of the type of searches these are. 

Low-intent, navigational queries rarely trigger an AI Overview. 
The ones that almost always do are commercial, high-intent searches. 

That's the exact moment a buyer is deciding about your brand or business,  
And whether they trust you enough to opt in. 

They can't trust you if they can't see you... 
And if your search strategy ignores AI search, they never will. 

So the traffic that you're losing now isn't random at all. 
That's all the traffic that was about to convert and didn't. 

But that doesn't mean SEO is dead. It means the moment worth optimising for has moved.

Google still handles over 13 billion searches a day. 
Most people are still searching the way they always have. 

But the foundations you built for SEO, structure, authority, clarity, are now what get you cited in the Overview too.

I always wanted my career to be a ladder. 

Thank God, it didn’t happen that way. 

It became a jungle gym, instead.

That may be one of the best things that happened to me.

For the first few years, it looked like one.

Perform well.
Move up.
Take the next role.
Climb the next rung.

Then life interrupted the ladder.

I moved into an international assignment.

It gave me cultural understanding, team leadership, and humility that no straight-line career path could have taught me.

Then I moved into a role that looked similar to something I had done before.

At that point, I needed space.

My family was going through major personal transitions, and that role gave me the stability to keep growing without breaking.

Then I tried a broadening assignment in marketing.

It lasted only a few months.

But it gave me something extremely valuable:

Clarity.

I learned what energizes me.
I learned what drains me.
I learned where I can create the most value.

Then came the move to the US.

I thought it would be a short assignment.

Six years later, I am still here.

In that time, I have bought core packaging, led responsible sourcing and sustainability, and now I am in a broadening role focused on building ecosystems and external partnerships.

None of this would have happened if I had only chased the next rung.

The ladder would have given me progression.

The jungle gym gave me perspective.

It gave me range.
It gave me resilience.
It gave me stories.
It gave me skills I did not even know I needed.

I am grateful to the leaders who saw possibilities I could not see yet.

I am grateful to my family, who stayed flexible through every turn.

And I am grateful that my career did not follow the perfect plan I once wanted.

A ladder can take you up.

But a jungle gym can make you broader, stronger, and more ready for the work that actually matters.

If you lead others, do not only design career ladders.

Design career experiences.

If you are leading your own career, remember this:

Your ideal next move may not always look like the next rung.

Sometimes the sideways move is the one that prepares you for your biggest leap.
#CareersOfTheFuture

The fastest way to kill a SIOP process isn't in a bad forecast.

It's one sentence: "I'm not sure that data is right."

Here's how it plays out.  the SIOP numbers get compiled manually.  Usually one person, one spreadsheet, every month.  Then a function walks into the meeting with their own dashboard that slices the data differently.  Something appears they don't like.  So they challenge the data itself.

No refuting data.  No alternative number.  Just doubt.

And it works...because doubt is asymmetric.  The challenge takes five seconds.  Proving the data was right takes two weeks, and by then the meeting has moved on and the decision didn't get made.  A manager told me years ago: everyone reads the headline, no one reads the retraction on page 6.

The damage isn't that one number got questioned.  It's that the process itself is now suspect.  Next month, every uncomfortable finding gets the same treatment...because the precedent is set that data you don't like can be dismissed instead of disproven.

The fix isn't a better spreadsheet.  It's a rule: challenges to the data require data.  If you can't bring a number, the number on the screen stands.

#SIOP #SupplyChain #SalesAndOperations #DataDriven

Well, well, well... Every major S2P platform now has an AI Agent Studio.
  
Zip, Coupa, Oracle, Ivalua, Jaggaer, Zycus, GEP, SAP Ariba. All of them.
  
Quick level-set: For me, an AI agent is just an automated business process that supports ambiguity.

The only different with past workflow tools? Supporting ambiguity via LLMs.
  
An "AI agent" can use an LLM to "figure things out" when the inputs aren't clean or the path isn't fixed.
  
An Agent Studio is the workbench that lets you configure, govern and deploy those agents inside your platform, instead of waiting on the vendor's roadmap.
  
I mapped the press release date for every studio on the right-hand side of the Gartner Magic Quadrant for S2P Suites.

Full timeline is in the graphic.
  
But does that mean they're all created equal?
  
God no.
  
→ Some let you Bring-Your-Own-LLM
→ Others lock you into a frontier model like ChatGPT, take it or leave it

→ Some come with lots of pre-packaged agents for procurement
→ Others come with the toolbox and you need to start from scratch

→ Some let your team build and deploy freely
→ Others require the vendor to vet and approve every agent first

→ Some are true low-code studios for business users
→ Others still need a technical admin in the loop
  
None of that shows up in the press release.

You only find it in the demo, the contract fine print, the implementation roadblocks.

(There's also a ton of great "non-Gartner MQ" options out there depending on your context. Happy to point you toward a few via DM if useful)
  
Those nuances are important to see the differences between options.

Those differences can make or break your business case.

But there's another important bit with these AI Studios:
  
They are just the new generation of workflow builder, with LLMs as one more tool in the workflow.
  
And the value was never in the tool.

It's in the work underneath it:

→ Defining the problem precisely,
→ Mapping the process steps,
→ Deciding where an LLM actually earns its place,
→ Configuring the workflow and governance to hold up at scale.
  
Buy the studio for the flexibility.

Win with it through the strategy work most teams skip.

(There are no silver bullets)

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce got married last Friday, and while everyone was wondering about her dress, my supply chain brain went straight to the loading dock 😅

The wedding lasted one night.
But the load-in took a week.

We saw countless trucks at Madison Square Garden. Crates wrapped in plastic. Handwritten labels on boxes. Streets closed. 

Crews carrying in rigging, lighting, and apparently an entire garden - every piece under packing blankets so nobody outside knew what was happening inside.

By Friday night, you couldn't see any of it. A thousand guests walked into a secret garden.

But that's the whole job, isn't it?

➡️ Somebody figured out how to build all of that in an arena with other events on the calendar
➡️ Somebody sourced flowers at a volume that doesn't exist on a normal week
➡️ Somebody stood on a sidewalk at 5AM directing trucks nobody will ever thank them for

Listen, I've spent almost twenty years in supply chain and logistics. The pattern never changes. 

When it goes right, it looks like it was always going to ... but when it goes wrong, suddenly everyone learns your name.

The people who make the impossible look effortless are almost never the ones in the photos.

---

What part of this are you still thinking about?

The build? The flowers? Or the demand spike about to hit every couture bridal shop?

The delay email hit—and my stomach dropped.


Earlier this year, I was managing a PO for a co-manufacturer that needed to feed directly into a display build for a client, timed to help their team get ahead of their busy season.

Then the timeline started slipping. Once… then again… then again. Weeks of delays.

People assume that’s where you go into full firefighting mode.

And I get it. The stress was real. Each update felt like a gut punch.

But I didn’t want stress making the decisions for me, so I forced one small reset: get calm, get specific, and look for what we could actually move.

That’s when the solution got obvious.

Sitting in our warehouse was returns inventory that hadn’t been touched. We QC-ed it, re-packed it, and repurposed it for the display.

The client’s team stayed on track for their busy season. No drama. No scramble.

That moment reminded me: operations rewards steadiness. 

When you stay calm, you see the puzzle—not just the pressure.

What’s a moment where staying calm unlocked a solution you wouldn’t have found otherwise?

What do you call this wee guy? 

He was on my wall here in Mauritius, I‘ve known him as a forky taily my whole life.

Apparently he’s an earwig to the rest of the world 😂

Trustworthy - when you have all of the above, your data becomes trustworthy, reliable, and AI ready.
