Knowing what to post on LinkedIn can seem complicated. 

But the content system behind it is simple: 

There are 4 buckets you need to choose from…

1. Your story

→ Share what happened 
→ What worked and what didn't
→ The moment everything changed
→ What you'd do differently next time 

💜 People love following journeys 

2. Your client's world

→ Describe their problem better than they can
→ The frustration they can't articulate
→ What they stress about late at night 
→ The outcome they actually want

💜 When someone reads your post and thinks "that's me" you've won

3. Your industry

→ Say the things others are too polite to say
→ The advice everyone gives that doesn't work
→ Why the conventional wisdom is wrong
→ What's broken in your space

💜 Conviction builds authority faster than expertise

4. Your skills

→ Teach others how to do what you do
→ Show what you know in a way that's useful
→ Show your clients why they need you to do it
→ Frameworks, processes, and systems that worked

💜 Teaching builds more trust than telling

Don't know what to write…

Use this structure:

→ Here's the problem your reader has
→ Here's why it's costing them
→ Here's what they actually want instead
→ Here's what to do about it
→ Here's what changes when they do
→ Here's the line that makes them act

Before you publish run it through this checklist:

✅ Does it use language your clients actually use?
✅ Is the main point something they can act on today?
✅ Does it come from a real story or real experience?
✅ Is it simple enough to understand in one read?
✅ Does it describe their pain and their desired outcome?
✅ Would you be proud of it in six months?

Score it out of six → if it gets four or more, publish it.

Perfectionism kills more content than bad writing ever will.

Power BI can show you the error, but Claude can help turn it into the questions the planner needs on the table.

That is where a lot of planning meetings quietly lose momentum.

A variance table can tell you actual demand moved away from forecast. It can show the product family, the order movement, the customer pullback, or the promotion that behaved differently than expected.

But the factory still needs the next layer.

Which family is exposed? Which material check changed? Which line is now tighter? Which customer promise are we protecting? Which sequence creates the least unnecessary changeover?

This is where Claude becomes useful if we stop treating it like a summarizer and start using it to build the first draft of the operating artifact.

Give it the actual planning context: forecast vs actual by product family, open orders, current production plan, frozen window, line constraints, changeover rules, material status, service priority, and planner comments.

Then ask Claude for a demand-to-sequence board.

The useful output is not a generic paragraph, it is a meeting artifact:
• what demand miss matters
• which root cause looks most likely
• which family, line, or customer promise is affected
• which material, capacity, service, or changeover check moved
• which 2-3 sequence options are worth discussing 

This is the capability that's makes claude shine. It can take scattered planning inputs and turn them into a structured board that the planner can challenge, improve, and use to focus the conversation.

For me, that is a much stronger AI use case than asking for another dashboard summary. The value is the team starting the meeting with the miss, the assumption, the affected family, the constraint check, and the sequence options already visible.

If demand moved tomorrow, would your review show which production sequence decision changes first?

📊 Excel for Industrial Engineers – 10 Excel Functions Every IE Should Master

Industrial Engineering is all about analyzing data, solving problems, and making smarter decisions. While advanced software is helpful, Microsoft Excel remains one of the most powerful tools every Industrial Engineer should master.

Whether you're analyzing production, calculating efficiency, or preparing reports, these Excel functions can save hours of work.

🔟 Essential Excel Functions for Industrial Engineers

✅ SUM() – Calculate total production, output, or defects.

✅ AVERAGE() – Find average SMV, efficiency, or cycle time.

✅ IF() – Automate decisions based on production conditions.

✅ COUNTIF() – Count defects, delays, or operators meeting targets.

✅ SUMIF() – Sum production or defects based on specific criteria.

✅ VLOOKUP() / XLOOKUP() – Retrieve SMVs, operator details, or style information instantly.

✅ INDEX() + MATCH() – A more flexible alternative to VLOOKUP for accurate data retrieval.

✅ ROUND() – Standardize efficiency percentages and production calculations.

✅ TEXT() – Format reports, dates, and production summaries professionally.

✅ Pivot Tables – Transform thousands of production records into meaningful insights within seconds.

👖 Garment Industry Example

Imagine managing 20 sewing lines with daily data on production, efficiency, defects, and absenteeism.

Instead of spending hours calculating manually, Excel can:

📈 Generate efficiency reports automatically
📊 Highlight bottlenecks instantly
🎯 Identify low-performing lines
📉 Track defects and rework trends
📋 Create professional dashboards for management

💡 Key Takeaway

Excel isn't just a spreadsheet—it's one of the most valuable productivity tools for Industrial Engineers.

Mastering these functions will help you analyze faster, make better decisions, and improve factory performance.

💬 Which Excel function do you use most often in your Industrial Engineering work? Share your favorite in the comments!

Planning debt.
That's what I call it.

It compounds like financial debt, but you pay the interest in emergency freight, planner attrition, and customer failures that could have been caught six weeks earlier.

I spoke to a planning team last week paying north of R20M a year in expedite fees alone. Two planners had left in 18 months. When I asked their lead planner what a normal Tuesday looked like, she had to think about it.

"Honestly? I don't know what normal is anymore. Every Tuesday is different. But every Tuesday is the same kind of different. Something's on fire, and by end of day we're already worried about Wednesday."

Nine years in supply chain. Brilliant at the job. The system won't let her do it.

MRP generates exceptions faster than any team can clear them, so they triage instead of plan. The debt accumulates quietly. "I'll get to proper planning next week" stops being said out loud, because everyone knows it won't happen next week either.

Change the priority system and the triage stops. 12 real signals instead of 400 noise events. Planning becomes possible again.

How deep is the planning debt in your organisation?

Building a product is now the easy part.
Getting anyone to use it is the hard part.
 
Before AI, a few people had the idea, some built it, and a massive crowd used it. Usage was the wide end of the funnel. Distribution was mostly free: a good product sold itself. Ship something decent and people found you.
 
After AI, that funnel is upside down.
 
ChatGPT makes everyone's idea sound worth building. Anyone can ship it in a weekend. And almost none of it gets used.
 
Ideas went from scarce to infinite. Code went from months to an afternoon. The one thing that stayed brutally hard: getting a real human to pick you, pay you, and stay.
 
This is why I keep saying GTM is the new MVP.
 
We ran outbound for 275+ companies. The pattern was consistent, and a little painful to admit: the winners had the sharpest motion: right list, right offer, relevant enough that the reply felt obvious. Product quality barely predicted who made it.
 
Frontal is at ~$350k/mo, and the software is not the reason. Someone could clone your tech stack. Nobody clones 100 meetings a month, or the distribution engine that prints them.
 
So here is the uncomfortable math for founders:
 
Your product is a commodity the day after you launch.
Your distribution is the only thing that compounds.
 
Spend the next month on the motion, not the roadmap.

Your AI agent keeps failing for 1 reason.

It's not the model. It's the harness around it.

AI agents have moved through three eras.

Here is how you actually build one:

Context Engineering

An agent only acts on the context you give it.

1. Pick one narrow, repeatable job.
2. List the exact inputs and outputs.
3. Define what "done" looks like.
4. Set clear stop conditions.

Harness Engineering

A model is not an agent. Wrap it in a harness.

1. Connect it to 9,000+ tools with Zapier MCP.
2. Give it memory and context.
3. Set guardrails and rules.
4. Add a human check before it acts.

Loop Engineering

Prove it on real work before you trust it.

1. Test on real cases with clear pass/fail metrics.
2. Ship to a small, low-risk group first.
3. Monitor the logs and error rate.
4. Fix what breaks, then scale up.

What separates agents is the harness you build.

The Financially Conflicted Middle [Consumer Sentiment Series] 5 of 5

The Squeeze + the Splurge. This is where it all lands from this series and evaluating the underlying mechanics of cosumer spending. 

The household in the middle is usually mid-40s to mid-50s which are now peak earning years. 

But they’re also still raising kids (they started late) and starting to help aging parents. Gen X is now the biggest-spending generation, and more than half of them are supporting a kid, a parent, or both. 

Peak income and peak obligations at the same time, with inflation widening the gap between them. This is basically the squeeze.

The response is fairly predictable: trade down on everyday things, then spend on one small treat. The “lipstick effect.” About 3 in 4 consumers traded down in at least one category last year, but most still planned to splurge somewhere. 

And the splurging skews young now with roughly 63% being high-income millennials. When the big goals feel out of reach, the small wins are the small reassuring indulgences. And these are not investments in assets but guilty pleasures. 

That’s also what’s behind the vibecession. 

Sentiment is down about 30% year over year, but spending rose 5–6%. Strip out inflation and real spending grew only about 2% — most of that “resilient consumer” is just people paying more for the same stuff. (Kyla Scanlon  coined “vibecession,” though she now says it’s more than just vibes.)


Data: Empower , McKinsey & Company , University of Michigan , Bureau of Economic Analysis

All B2B growth problems are messaging problems (and AI exposed it brutally!)

Because AI made reach cheaper...so weak messaging now leaks into every buyer touchpoint and confuses people at 10x the volume

These are the messaging problems that keep showing up when a B2B SaaS company thinks growth is stuck somewhere else:

1/ The team internally uses different wording for the same product across the website, sales calls, ads and emails, so buyers never get the same story twice and every touchpoint makes them rebuild context from scratch (which is already too much work for a buyer who barely cares yet!)

2/ Sales calls start too far back because the website did not do enough explaining before the buyer booked, so the first part of the demo gets wasted on basic education... and then everyone acts like the demo flow is the problem

3/ Paid traffic gets blamed too fast because the ad is reaching the right buyer just fine. The page (and the rest of the funnel) tells a completely different narrative 

4/ The pricing page explains plans before the buyer understands value, so the decision becomes about cost too early and the product ends up feeling expensive instead of necessary (this is usually one of the first fixes that needs to be done!)

5/ The product onboarding has to carry confusion from the website, because users sign up with a rough idea of what the product does... but not a clear idea of what they should do first or why (some product adoption can be done on the website before they sign up)

6/ AI just exposed all of this, because now you can distribute at 10x more speed and quantity, which means you can share untested, unclear messaging into the ether much faster

So even though we know AI switches context easily and hallucinates, it needs to be heavily edited and guided with strict guardrails to keep the same messaging consistent across channels and GTM motions 

I’d bet an enormous amount of conversion drop-off is just buyers needing too much time to understand the product (this keeps showing up in my recent projects and you can literally see it in the numbers)

In 1997, Apple had 90 days of cash left.

The company that saved it was Microsoft.

Steve Jobs stood on a stage in Boston, put Bill Gates on a giant screen behind him, and told a room full of Apple loyalists that their sworn enemy had just wired $150 million.

The room booed.
The deal had some wild terms.

What Apple agreed to:
↳ Internet Explorer shipped as the default browser on Mac for 5 years
↳ A 5 year commitment to keep the Mac compatible with Microsoft Office
↳ Every open patent lawsuit against Microsoft, dropped
↳ A 5 year cross-licence on both companies' patents
↳ Joint work with Microsoft on Java and QuickTime streaming

What Microsoft agreed to:
↳ 5 more years of building Office for Mac
↳ A 3 year lock-up on its $150m of non-voting Apple stock
↳ Mac versions of its software shipped the same day as the Windows versions

Join me in a conversation on the meaning of supply chain orchestration at Cleo Connect in Chicago on September 2nd-3rd. I love dialogue. Let's plan to meet up.

Excel can calculate EOQ, but ChatGPT can help turn the calculation into a planner-reviewable decision board.

That matters because batch size can look like a clean calculation from the outside.

But in a real planning conversation, that number is only the first draft.

If the batch gets smaller, the business may carry less inventory and respond faster, but it may also create more setups, more changeovers, and more planning noise.

If the batch gets larger, the production run can look efficient because setup frequency drops, but the cost can come back later through trapped cash, shelf-life risk, slower response, or capacity used on the wrong product.

This is where ChatGPT becomes useful if we stop treating it like a calculator and start using it to build the first version of the decision artifact.

Give it the actual planning context: demand rate by SKU or family, setup or changeover cost, holding cost, current batch size, MOQ or pack-size rule, production rate, shelf life, capacity calendar, service priority, demand variability, and planner comments.

Then ask for a batch-size decision board.

The useful output is a review table that shows:
• first-pass EOQ
• smaller, current, and larger batch options
• setup or changeover burden
• inventory exposure
• capacity fit
• service risk
• assumptions that need to be verified 

Batch size decisions often hide behind the word efficiency. Bigger runs feel efficient because setup drops, but the planner still has to ask what the business is choosing to carry in return.

The value of AI here is not that it decides the perfect batch, the value is that it makes the trade-off visible before the planner changes the plan or master data.

If demand changed next week, would your team know which batch size is still carrying the right trade-off?

How are you going to successfully deploy AI Agents if you can't define them in one sentence?

Most procurement leaders can't.

They just know AI agents are supposed to fix everything.

Here's the definition we use at Pure Procurement:

An AI agent (big or small) is a trigger-driven business process that navigates ambiguity to produce a defined outcome inside policy guardrails (guides), using connected systems, data and stakeholders (enablers).

Here are the 5 parts:

→ Trigger — what starts it (a request, a document, a scheduled job)
→ Outcome — the defined result it's working toward
→ Guides — the policy layer constraining behavior
→ Enablers — the systems and data it can call on
→ Process — the reasoning path between trigger and outcome (not a fixed flowchart)

Once you have that, ask 3 questions before you deploy:

1️⃣ Is the path to the outcome ambiguous? If every rule is explicit, use traditional automation, not an LLM agent.

2️⃣ Is a "directionally correct" output recoverable? If a wrong output is catastrophic, raise the bar significantly.

3️⃣ Are the guides clearly defined? An agent without guardrails isn't an agent. It's chaos with a chatbot interface.

Can't answer all 3? It's not ready for production.

We go deeper on this framework (and the AI Agent Studio arms race across S2P platforms) in episode 5 of the ProcureTech Unpacked podcast, out today

Most MSME owners think Lean Six Sigma is a "large factory" thing — for the Tatas and the Boschs of the world, not for a 40-machine unit running on tight margins and a lean (pun intended) team.

A large plant with a 2% defect rate absorbs it. An MSME with the same 2% defect rate might be looking at the difference between profit and loss that quarter.

One of the best things about traveling is coming home to a whole list of new AI playbooks I want to write.

GOOD NEWS: You think you missed the AI Bus. 
GREAT NEWS: You can leap frog using these 10 steps

1. Find the smallest pain 
Look for that annoying, repetitive task you cannot stand. Data entry. Sifting emails. Chasing down updates. Stay humble, pick one thing.

2. Grab a basic tool 
Find an off-the-shelf AI tool meant for that pain point. Minimum setup. Forget custom anything. Speed beats perfection.

3. Test it in the wild 
Put it in the hands of a small group that feels the problem. No big project teams. No endless planning. Let them use it for real work.

4. Measure something real 
Pick a metric nobody can ignore. Time saved per week. Issues avoided. Workflow speed. Keep it so simple nobody can argue with the number.

5. Show off 
Share the before and after with your boss, your peers, and anyone else who will listen. No fluff. One slide, one stat. Real work done faster.

6. Take a bigger bite 
Now you have credibility. Tackle a process that nags at multiple teams. Maybe it is customer response times, invoice approvals, or onboarding. Same process: pick the pain, pick the tool, test, measure, share.

7. Recruit an ally 
Look outside your team. Find someone in another function who hates a similar grind. Give them access to your tool or share what worked. Let them ride your coattails.

8. Teach your sharpest people 
Do not boil the ocean. Pick a handful of the most curious, action-oriented folks. Get them trained up fast, let them experiment and report back.

9. Build your win list 
For every single improvement, capture what changed: What was the pain? What did you try? What changed? Stack these stories. They become your movement's proof.

10. Pitch something bold 
Now you are armed. Use those real-world results to propose a larger AI project. You are not pitching theory, you are pitching momentum. The business case writes itself.

Everyone is busy "transforming." Most get stuck in endless meetings, pilots that never scale, slides that gather dust.

Skipping the AI bus means you are not on someone else's failed roadmap. You get to jump straight to what matters: solving problems, stacking wins, building a reputation for delivery.

Start small, move fast, go bigger only when you have proof. 
No one cares about ideas. They care about results.

So, what are you going to leap frog first?

The smartest thing you can do in your first week on LinkedIn: 

Not post at all.

And I say this as someone who runs a programme telling founders to post every day.

Posting daily is a habit you have to build, and there's no way around it.

But the people who break through faster are the ones who watched the platform before they started shipping.

They spend 1 week learning the game. 
And the second week playing it.

So when they finally start posting, they already know what works in their niche, who to talk to, and which formats get the engagement.

Here's what to do in that first week:

1️⃣ Study 10 creators in your space

Open their last 20 posts and look at how they open their posts, structure them, and what gets reposted.

You'll spot patterns in a couple of hours that take months to figure out on your own.

2️⃣ Start commenting with intent

Pick 5 creators bigger than you and leave an insightful comment on their posts every day.

That's how you get on their radar before they've got any reason to follow you back.

3️⃣ Connect with people in the comment sections

The people commenting on the posts you'd want to write are your future audience.

Send the request before you've posted a single thing. 
You'll have a warm audience ready before your first post goes live.

4️⃣ Save what stops your scroll

Every post that makes you stop becomes a reference for your own content.

Winning the first 10 customers at my first business took months. 

For Searchable, we did it within 24 hours. 

When I launched Verb at 21, I was basically starting from scratch. 
I had to prove myself and my business on every call.

With Searchable, I'd been building in public for 4 years.
Founders turned up pre-sold, having read or watched our content.

Each launch was easier than the last because all that work compounded. 
But it never would have started without those first 10 (hard-won) customers.

Here's the playbook I wish I'd had at the beginning 👇

1️⃣ Get painfully specific

Define your ideal customer profile before you build anything, then use it as a filter for every decision.

Verb went from "marketing agency" to "digital marketing agency for luxury brands." We went from competing with 10,000 agencies to being the only obvious choice in our category.

2️⃣ Talk to 10 real people

Find 10 people who fit your ICP and listen, don't pitch.

[What you do] + [Who you do it for]

A Stanford study tracked 30,000 adults over eight years.

People under high stress had a 43% higher risk of dying.

But only if they believed stress was harmful.

The ones who saw stress as useful? No increased risk at all.

Same pressure. Different response. Different outcome.

That finding changed how Dr. Christian Poensgen and I think about performance.

The goal was never to remove stress. Stress is a fact of life.

Instead, you learn to stop the good kind from tipping into the bad.

8 ways to make that shift:

1/ ACUTE VS. CHRONIC STRESS
→ Acute stress sharpens focus and settles fast
→ Chronic stress scatters it and stays on
→ The difference is duration and recovery

2/ THE STRESS-IS-ENHANCING MINDSET (h/t Alia Crum)
→ Notice the stress, welcome it, then channel it
→ Your beliefs about stress actually change its biology

3/ THE SYNERGISTIC MINDSET (h/t David Yeager)
→ Growth mindset alone stalls at the first failure
→ Pair it with a stress-is-fuel mindset and both compound

4/ STRESS VS. ANXIETY
→ Stress has a clear trigger and a built-in off-ramp

→ Heart rate variability measures your stress-rest flexibility
→ High HRV shifts gears cleanly. Low HRV means you're stuck in high gear

Bad metrics make demand and supply planners fail.

This infographic shows 10 critical calculations for demand and supply planners:

Demand Planners

# 1 - WMAPE (Weighted Mean Absolute Percentage Error)
Provides a more balanced view of forecast accuracy by weighting errors
WMAPE= ∑∣Actual−Forecast∣​/∑Actual  X 100
 
# 2 - Forecast Bias
Identifies whether forecasts consistently overestimate or underestimate demand
Bias=∑(Forecast−Actual)/∑Actual X 100
 
# 3 - FVA (Forecast Value Added)
Measures whether changes to the forecast actually improve or hurt accuracy
FVA=Baseline Forecast Error−New Forecast Error
Where: baseline error = forecast error from a reference method; new forecast error = forecast error from new method

# 4 - Demand Variability (Coefficient of Variation)
Indicates the consistency or volatility of demand
Demand Variability =  σ​/μ X 100 
σ: Standard deviation of demand
μ: Average demand
                                      
# 5 - Promotional Lift Factor
Evaluates the impact of promotions on demand
Lift Factor = Promotional Demand/Baseline Demand​                                                       
Supply Planners

# 6 - OTIF (On Time In Full) 
Shows how many orders are delivered on time in full
OTIF = Number of On Time In Full Deliveries/Total Number of Deliveries X 100

# 7 - Inventory Turnover
Indicates how fast or slow inventory is moving
Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods/Average inventory

# 8-  Safety Stock
Determines the buffer stock needed to handle demand variability
Safety Stock = Z×σ×Lead Time​ 
Where
Z = Z-score (based on the desired service level)
Σ = Standard deviation of demand or lead-time demand

# 9 - Obsolescence Ratio
Tracks the portion of inventory that is no longer usable
 Obsolescence Ratio = Obsolete Inventory/Total Inventory X 100        

# 10 - Capacity Utilization
Tracks how much of available capacity is being used
Utilization  =  Actual Output/Maximum Capacity X 100

Any others to add?

Reorder Point: The Inventory Trigger That Prevents Stockouts
Many stockouts don’t happen because demand is impossible to predict.
They happen because replenishment is triggered too late.
That is where Reorder Point (ROP) becomes important.
ROP answers one simple question:
When should we order again?
The formula:
Reorder Point = Average Daily Demand × Lead Time + Safety Stock
Example:
Average daily demand = 100 units
Lead time = 7 days
Safety stock = 250 units
ROP = 100 × 7 + 250
ROP = 950 units
This means the next order should be placed when inventory reaches 950 units.
Not when stock reaches zero.
Not when the warehouse feels low.
Not when sales starts complaining.
At the calculated trigger point.
A good ROP protects the business from:
✅ Demand during supplier lead time
✅ Supplier delivery delays
✅ Forecast variation
✅ Stockout risk
✅ Service level failure
But ROP is not a one-time setting.
It should change when:
• demand changes
• supplier lead time changes
• safety stock changes
• service level targets change
• supplier reliability changes
The real power of ROP is not only in the formula.
It is in the discipline of reviewing it regularly.
Because an outdated reorder point creates either:
Stockouts  or Excess inventory
Both are costly.
Reorder Point is not just a number.
It is a living inventory control rule.

Most leaders don’t become “part of the solution” overnight. They become it by recognizing they are still somewhere on the left side, and deciding to move.

Almost every leader who sees it will immediately look to the green side.

“Yes, that’s leadership.”
“Absolutely.”
“100% agree.”
And this were feedback.

Very few will willingly point to the red side and say:

“That’s me.”

And that’s completely human.

None of us wake up intending to blame people instead of solving problems.
None of us schedule meetings hoping to avoid reality.
None of us choose assumptions over facts.

Yet many organizations slowly drift there.

Not because leaders are bad.
Because leadership is difficult.


The interesting part isn’t choosing between the left and the right.

It’s understanding that the right side isn’t a destination.
It’s a direction.

Every great leader started somewhere left of it.
The difference is that they were willing to admit it.

Because improvement always begins with one uncomfortable sentence:

“Maybe I am part of this problem.”

That isn’t weakness.
That’s leadership.


The biggest obstacle to becoming better isn’t capability.

It’s believing you’re already there.
If you think you’re already the leader on the green side…

Why would you change?
Why would you ask for feedback?
Why would you go to the Gemba?
Why would you challenge your own decisions?


Toyota never expected perfect leaders.

It expected leaders who learned.
Who observed before judging.
Who listened before deciding.
Who coached instead of controlled.
Who solved problems instead of assigning blame.

Leadership isn’t about never standing on the left.
It’s about spending less and less time there.



So perhaps the real daily leadership question isn’t:

“Am I part of the solution?”

It’s:

“What is one thing I can do today that moves me one step to the right?”

Because better is always an option.
But improvement never starts with agreement.

It starts with honesty.



What was the moment in your leadership journey when you realized you needed to move a little further to the right?

7 Japanese Concepts That Will Change How You Work:

Most people feel like they're drowning in work.

But some people stay calm through chaos.

Sometimes the best answers come from ancient wisdom.
And these timeless principles still work today.

Here are 7 Japanese conacepts you need to know:

1/ Wabi-Sabi: Embrace Imperfection

↳ Chase progress not perfection - ship at 70%.
↳ Share a work-in-progress update, not just polished results. Show the messy middle.

2/ Shoshin: Beginner's Mind

↳ Ask the dumb questions in meetings
↳ Say "I don't know but I'll find out" more

3/ Shokunin: Master Your Craft

↳ Pick the top up and coming skill you need in your industry. Block 30 minutes daily.
↳ DM someone great at it. Ask one question. Learn from real experience.

4/ Kaizen: Get 1% Better Everyday

↳ Every evening, write one tiny thing you'll do better tomorrow.
↳ End projects with: What worked? What didn't? What's next?

5/ Shikata ga nai: Accepting the Unchangeable

↳ Sort concerns: "My control" vs. "Not my control." Act accordingly.
↳ Use the 10-minute rule. Address it briefly, then decide.

6/ Kintsugi: Your Failures Are Your Best Stories

↳ Name three lessons from each setback. Write them down.
↳ Share lessons learned. Prevent repeat mistakes.

7/ Ikigai: Finding Your Purpose

↳ Track what energizes you. Reorganize your calendar around it.
↳ Map skills to market needs. Improve your market value.

I've seen hundreds transform their work with these principles.

Businesses don't just pop up fully formed and error-free. 

You need to notice the flaws and adjust fast... 

Businesses are complex systems with moving parts that can break at any time. 

And with market changes and global trends shifting fast, 
Founders must see the big picture and make improvements accordingly. 

I personally do an audit across 8 key areas every quarter. 

Here are some leaks I caught and how I fixed them ⬇️
(Check out the sheet for more details !) 

1️⃣ Marketing and Personal Brand

❌ Post when you remember to, or only when you're launching something.
✅ Post daily on the platforms your buyers use, build your personal brand, and turn happy clients into case studies. 

2️⃣ Sales

❌ Treat sales as something you'll get to, and give away free calls to anyone who asks.
✅ Treat it as a profession with a weekly rhythm, and sell the transformation before the price.

3️⃣ AI Search and SEO

❌ Optimise for Google the way you did three years ago and hope you show up in AI search.
✅ Optimise for both at once, structure your content to be cited, and track exactly where you appear across ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini.

(Or, even better, have Searchable do that last part for you: https://lnkd.in/epgXyFmi !) 

4️⃣ Product

❌ Keep building features nobody asked for before you know anyone wants them.
✅ Ship the smallest version that delivers real value, then let customer feedback build the roadmap.

5️⃣ Team and Hiring

❌ Hire cheap and defensively, then spend your week managing people who need managing.
✅ Bring in A-players for specific problems. One is worth more than five B-players.

6️⃣ Systems and Delegation

❌ Let every lead, decision, and delivery run through you, and call that being busy.
✅ Protect your 20%, delegate 80%, and document it so the business isn't dependent on you.

7️⃣ Finances

❌ Chase revenue and never look at whether it's actually profit.
✅ Grow profit first, turn one-off work into recurring revenue, and build something that's sellable even if you never plan to sell.

8️⃣ Positioning

❌ Try to be for everyone, and end up competing with everyone.
✅ Niche down until you're the obvious choice, and say what you do and who for in one sentence.

If you want success in all 8 areas of your business, 
Start improving them before there’s a problem to fix. 

Better to make your business leak-proof from the start, 
Than waste time plugging holes later !

85% of your week goes to collaboration.
Meetings, email, group chat.

Rob Cross studied where all that time actually goes.

More than half the overload is self-inflicted.

The good news: 18 to 24% of it is reclaimable.

That's one full day a week you can win back.

When Dr. Christian Poensgen and I were writing Ultraproductive, this was one of the chapters that hit hardest.

The fix comes from an unexpected place. 

Instead of reducing the interactions with people, you change how the teamwork happens.

7 places to start:

1/ THE COLLABORATION CURSE
→ You give 85% of your week to collaboration
→ The overload hides in three places: meetings, email, and group chat

2/ HAVE FEWER MEETINGS
→ Most recurring meetings survive on habit, not value
→ If it's recurring and adds nothing, cut it
→ Protect one no-meeting day a week. At Microsoft, 73% reported better well-being

3/ RUN BETTER MEETINGS
→ 71% of senior managers call their meetings unproductive
→ Before: agenda sent, only essential people, 25 or 50 minutes max
→ During: devices away, cameras on, fully present
→ After: next steps, owners with deadlines, absentees catch up

4/ BEAT ZOOM FATIGUE (h/t Jeremy Bailenson)
→ Hide self-view. You'd never carry a mirror all day
→ Shrink the window so faces aren't oversized
→ On long calls, drop video, stand, stretch

5/ THE 3-2-1 EMAIL METHOD
→ You check your inbox 77 times a day. It's not a to-do list
→ 3 folders: sort every email by what it needs from you
→ 2 labels: flag urgent, separate from what can wait
→ 1 focused hour: process in batches, app closed otherwise

6/ WRITE EMAILS THAT END THE THREAD
→ Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle: conclusion first, support second
→ If you can't say it in three sentences, it shouldn't be an email

7/ USE GROUP CHAT IN BURSTS
→ Jason Fried called it an all-day meeting with no agenda
→ Short sessions are restorative. Too long is draining
→ Notifications off, check at fixed times, move long threads to a call

You don't need to do all seven. Pick one this week and measure what you get back.

Many supply reviews waste everyone's time.

This infographic shows the 10 must-have slides for supply review.

1. Executive Summary
↳ Snapshot of service, inventory & production vs plan; highlight key constraints & improvement actions
↳ Purpose: get leaders aligned on the top 3 issues within the first 5 minutes

2. Demand vs Supply Overview
↳ Chart comparing unconstrained demand vs feasible supply by month or region
↳ Purpose: show the planning gaps, if any; give the good news if everything can be fully supported

3. Capacity Utilization
↳ Plant-wise capacity vs load chart; color code: green (balanced), yellow (tight), red (overloaded)
↳ Purpose: focus on which plants need balancing action or reallocation
 
4. Supply Constraints
↳ List of top bottlenecks, equipment downtime, manpower, supplier shortages; include recovery plans
↳ Purpose: discuss issues that threaten service or production continuity

5. Production Plan Adherence
↳ Planned vs Actual production output trend; highlight misses and reasons (e.g., maintenance, raw material delays)
↳ Purpose: identify recurring efficiency or scheduling issues
 
6. Material Availability & Supplier Performance
↳ Chart showing supplier OTIF or inbound fill rate; mark critical materials and their risk level
↳ Purpose: share potential disruptions outlook before they hit
 
7. Inventory Health
↳ Snapshot of inventory by category: raw, WIP, Finished Goods; add KPIs like DOS (Days of Supply), SLOB%, and working capital impact
↳ Purpose: balance availability vs excess the sweet spot for every planner
 
8. Deployment & Distribution Plan
↳ Share inventory positions and stock movement across regions or DCs; compare planned vs actual dispatch
↳ Purpose: show whether the right stock is in the right place at the right time
 
9. Risks, Scenarios & Contingency Plans
↳ Table: “If X happens → Then Y response”
Example: “If supplier delay > 3 days → Shift to Plant B.”
↳ Purpose: bring structured thinking to issues that can lead to crisis

10. Actions, Owners & Next Steps
↳ Tracker of previous actions closed, pending ones, and new commitments
↳ Purpose: drive accountability and ensure progress is shared month-on-month

Any others to add?

Forklift Safety: Where Warehouse Safety Often Fails First
One forklift accident can stop operations in seconds.
It can injure people, damage inventory, hit racks, delay dispatch, and expose a weak safety system.
The real issue is not only the forklift.
It is the system around the forklift.
Common failures include:
❌ Forklifts and pedestrians sharing the same route
❌ Operators driving too fast in narrow aisles
❌ Loads blocking visibility
❌ Skipped daily pre-use checks
❌ Blind corners without mirrors or warning lights
❌ Forklift entry into trailers without dock checks
❌ Near misses ignored because “nothing happened”
Forklift safety should never depend only on the operator being careful.
It should be controlled through:
✅ Authorized operators
✅ Daily inspection checks
✅ Pedestrian separation
✅ Speed limits
✅ Clear visibility controls
✅ Safe load handling
✅ Dock entry discipline
✅ Near-miss reporting
Simple framework:
Forklift Safety = Operator Competency + Traffic Design + Daily Control
A safe warehouse does not depend on experience alone.
It depends on training, layout, visibility, speed discipline, load control, supervision, and daily safety routines.
Because in warehouse operations:
A forklift is not just equipment.
It is a moving risk that must be managed every shift.

22+years. 1 company. Some say Lazy. Some say Loyal.

Today, I reveal the 6 reasons why it’s been a great deal.

When people hear I’ve spent more than two decades at P&G, they usually make one of two assumptions.

“You must really love stability.”

Or worse...

“You got comfortable.”

I don’t blame them.

A résumé tells you where someone worked.

It rarely tells you why they stayed.

Looking back, I don’t think I’ve stayed because of the company alone.

I’ve stayed because, time and again, P&G has fulfilled six fundamental human needs that all of us are searching for in our careers.

1. Certainty
Knowing I was part of a company whose values I trusted, even when the business around me was changing.

2. Variety
Moving across India, Thailand, and the U.S. From media to packaging. From sustainability to AI. From procurement transformation to ecosystem partnerships. The company stayed the same. My career never did.

3. Significance
Being trusted with problems that mattered. Not just reducing costs, but building partnerships, driving business growth, advancing responsible sourcing, and helping shape what I believe is the Procurement of the Future.

4. Connection
Working alongside mentors, leaders, teammates, suppliers, and partners who shaped not only my career, but who I became as a person.

5. Growth
Every few years, I found myself in a role where I felt like a beginner again. New countries. New industries. New technologies. New challenges. Those moments of discomfort became my greatest teachers.

6. Contribution
Realizing that the most meaningful work isn’t what you accomplish while you’re there. It’s what continues after you’ve moved on—leaders you’ve developed, capabilities you’ve built, partnerships you’ve strengthened, and systems that continue creating value long after you’ve left.

Has every one of those 22 years been easy?

Not even close.

There were failures.

There was difficult feedback.

There were moments when leaving would have been the easier choice.

But I’ve come to believe something.

A great career isn’t built by changing companies every few years.

Nor is it built by staying for decades.

It’s built by continuously becoming a better version of yourself.

For me, P&G has simply been the place that kept giving me reasons to become that next version.

Maybe that’s what real loyalty is.

Not staying because nothing changes.

Staying because you never stop changing.

Which of these six human needs has had the biggest influence on your own career?

We talk a lot about resilience.

“Never give up.”
“Keep pushing.”
“Try harder.”
“Find a way.”

It sounds inspiring.

Until it isn’t.

⁉️What we rarely talk about is where the boundary is.

At what point does perseverance stop being a strength and become waste?
How long should someone keep giving 110% when the system keeps taking 120%?

In Lean, we are taught to eliminate waste.

Yet 𝘸𝘦 𝘰𝘧𝘵𝘦𝘯 𝘤𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘣𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘣𝘪𝘨𝘨𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘸𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘢𝘭𝘭:

𝘞𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘩𝘶𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘱𝘰𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘭.

Not because people don’t try.
Because they keep trying in systems that refuse to change.

There is a difference between persistence and stubbornness.
Between commitment and self-sacrifice.
Between solving problems and repeatedly absorbing them.

A great leader doesn’t ask people to keep compensating for broken systems.
A great leader fixes the system.

Sometimes the bravest decision isn’t to push harder.

It’s to stop.

To say:
“This process is broken.”
“This expectation is unrealistic.”
“This is no longer creating value.”

Respect for People isn’t asking someone to give more.
It’s knowing when they have already given enough.

⁉️So here’s my question to leaders:

𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘰𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦… 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘣𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘵𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺’𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘷𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨?

Because burnout is not commitment.

Constant firefighting is not Operational Excellence.

And endless effort is not a strategy.

🚨💥Helping or Hiding the Problem?

I recently listened to an interesting podcast by Cole DaSilva, and one sentence stayed with me:

“𝘠𝘰𝘶’𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘰𝘸𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘱𝘪𝘤𝘬 𝘶𝘱 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘬 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘤𝘰-𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘦𝘳𝘴. 𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘬𝘦𝘦𝘱 𝘥𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘦𝘭𝘴𝘦’𝘴 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬, 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘸𝘦 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘺 𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦?”

At first, it sounds harsh.

However the more I thought about it…

The more I realized how often this happens in organizations.
There is almost always that one employee.
The one everyone depends on.
The one who stays late.
The one who fixes mistakes.
The one who quietly finishes work that someone else left behind.

⚡️Leadership calls them a high performer.
⚡️Their colleagues call them helpful.

But here’s the uncomfortable question:
Are they helping… or are they hiding the problem?

Every time a strong employee compensates for poor performance, the organization loses visibility.

The KPIs look acceptable.
Customers receive their orders.
The shift finishes on time.
Managers think everything is under control.

But it isn’t.

The system isn’t working.

One person is simply carrying the weight of everyone else.

Lean teaches us to make problems visible.

Yet many organizations unknowingly reward the people who make problems invisible.

Helping each other is essential.

That is teamwork.

But there is a difference between supporting your team and permanently covering for a broken system or repeated poor performance.

If someone occasionally needs help, great teams step in.
If someone constantly needs saving, leaders need to ask why.

Is it training?
Is it unclear expectations?
Is it poor leadership?
Or is it simply the wrong fit for the role?

Respect for People doesn’t mean lowering standards.

It means giving everyone the opportunity to succeed, and having the courage to address performance when they don’t.

Because the strongest team isn’t built around one hero.
It’s built around people who can all be trusted to do their part.
A great organization doesn’t need one person carrying ten others.

It builds ten people who are capable of carrying themselves and helping each other when it truly matters.

Helping should strengthen the team.

Not hide the problems leadership needs to solve.

Cole DaSilva 💜🌱🙏🏻 

#Leadership #Lean #OperationalExcellence #RespectForPeople #Accountability #Culture #ContinuousImprovement #LeanLeadership #Gemba #Management

🎭🎪Lean Theatre vs. Real Lean

Walk into almost any company today and you’ll find Lean.

There are boards.
There are KPIs.
There are daily meetings.
There are audits.
There are improvement projects.

On paper, everything looks impressive.

Yet somehow…

The same problems return every week.
The same leaders make the same decisions.
The same firefighting continues.
The same people become the heroes who keep saving broken systems.

That’s not Lean.

That’s Lean theatre.

Real Lean isn’t measured by how many tools you implement.

It’s measured by how few problems depend on one person.

A real Lean organization looks different:

✅ Leaders start their day at the Gemba, not in PowerPoint.
✅ Problems become visible immediately instead of being hidden.
✅ Standards help people succeed instead of collecting dust in folders.
✅ KPIs trigger action, not discussions.
✅ Managers develop people instead of becoming the solution to every problem.
✅ Decisions are based on facts from the Gemba, not opinions from meeting rooms.

And there is one simple test that reveals everything.

Go on holiday.

If your phone never stops ringing…
If every decision waits for your approval…
If improvement stops until you return…

You haven’t built a Lean system.

You’ve built dependency.

The purpose of Lean has never been to make one person indispensable.

Its purpose is exactly the opposite.

To build people.
To build capability.
To build systems that continue improving even when the leader isn’t there.

Because the greatest Lean achievement isn’t becoming the hero.

It’s creating an organization that no longer needs one.


Question for leaders:

If you disappeared for two weeks tomorrow…

Would your operation survive… or continue to improve?

#Lean #Leadership #OperationalExcellence #ContinuousImprovement #Gemba #LeanManagement #DailyManagement #RespectForPeople #ProblemSolving #LeanCulture

Claude Code or Codex is the wrong question.

You can (actually) run both.

Ask these 4 questions instead:

Both read your repo, edit files and run commands.
The defaults are what actually separate them.

1. Where do you want to work?

Claude Code centres on the terminal.
Codex spans app, IDE, cloud and GitHub by default.

Pick the surface you already work in.

2. How do you split up the work?

Both can run agents in parallel.

Claude Code delegates to subagents in one session.
Codex fans work out to threads you supervise.

One nests the work. One lines it up for you.

3. How do you encode your workflow?

Claude Code defaults to CLAUDE.md.
Codex defaults to AGENTS.md.

Both read MCP.

Write the rules your team will maintain.

4. Where should long-running work happen?

Claude Code runs headless in your shell and CI.
Codex leans on cloud jobs and a review queue.

Codex runs headless too. I use codex exec.

Send the long job to CI or the cloud, not your laptop.

Then pick:

✦ If you live in the terminal, run Claude Code.
✦ If you want more surfaces, run Codex.
✦ If you want pairing plus background runs, run both.

I run both. Claude Code builds, Codex attacks it.

OpenAI shipped Codex as a Claude Code plugin.

The integration only runs one way.

Install it inside Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add openai/codex-plugin-cc
/plugin install codex@openai-codex

Then run /codex:adversarial-review

’Go viral’, ‘Chase reach’, that’s all you hear when it comes to marketing.

Yet one of the greatest marketers alive did the exact opposite...

While everyone else was chasing reach, he was proving a different theory entirely:

The smaller the audience, the bigger the impact.

Along the way, he built ideas like permission marketing and finding your smallest viable audience.

These concepts are still shaping how good marketers think today.
And that's the same game LinkedIn plays. 

Say something worth hearing, to the right person, and stop trying to convince everyone at once.

So here are 12 lessons from Godin, and what they mean for your content:

1. Do the strategy before you do the work.

Get clear on your ICP, your one goal, and the outcome you're chasing before you plan a single post.

Skip that step, and you'll spend hours creating content that doesn't do anything for you.

2. Create tension.

People stay comfortable until you show them the cost of staying the same.
Name the thing they're missing out on by not acting.

3. Pick a narrow audience.

Trying to please a broad audience waters everything down.
Build for your actual ICP and let everyone else scroll past.

4. People act for status, affiliation, or fear of missing out.

Know which one you're using before you hit publish.
If you can't name it, don't expect your audience to act on it.

5. Tell a story.

The tale as old as time: Data tells, stories sell.
Save the numbers for backup and let the story do the convincing.

6. Make it visible.

The best strategies live somewhere visible.
If nobody can see it, nobody can act on it.

7. Talk to real people.

Message 3 customers this week and ask them why they bought.
Then use their answers in your marketing. 

8. Treat every failure as data.

People who talk openly about what failed build more trust than the ones who only show wins. 

Try it once this month, and watch what happens to how people respond to you.

9. Be generous.

Every post should solve something real for someone specific.
If it doesn't solve anything, it's just you talking about yourself.

10. Do the work that scares you.

If posting it doesn't feel a bit exposing, it's probably too safe to be remarkable.

11. Find the right audience for you.

Write for the person who actually needs to hear it. 
Let everyone else scroll on.

12. Confidence comes after you start.

Waiting to feel ready is how people never post. 
Starting is what builds confidence.

Seth never built his career chasing followers.

He built it by saying the true thing clearly, to the people who needed to hear it.

That's the whole game.

What's stopping you from posting the thing that scares you a bit?
Drop it below.

💾 Save this, you'll want to read it again before your next post.
♻️ Repost to help someone in your network market smarter.

Total vodka volume bottled for domestic use across the same period: 123.6 million wine gallons in 2012, 125.9 million in 2024. Flat.

Average bottled output per vodka producer fell from roughly 710,000 wine gallons in 2012 to about 121,000 in 2024. An 83% drop in per-producer scale.

That average distorts because the top of the distribution carries enormous weight. Strip out the few real giants like Tito's, Smirnoff (Diageo), and the multinational portfolios, and the median craft vodka producer is operating at sub-scale economics in a category that has not grown in volume for over a decade.

Vodka's volume has been held together by premiumization on the dollar side. Super-premium share of spirits revenue roughly doubled across the same period. 

On the volume side, the math is the same problem playing out across every traditional spirits category: producer count grew, category volume held flat.

Every B2B buyer looks for 5 answers before your product feels worth trying 

...even when they come from a referral or with high buying intent!

Because high buying intent does not remove buyer uncertainty. Someone can arrive already interested, understand that they have a problem and still leave because the homepage makes them interpret too much on their own

So the homepage has to answer 5 questions in roughly the same order they appear in the buyer’s head:

1/ What is it for?
Buyers need to place the product first. They want to know what it is, who gets the clearest value from it, where it fits into their current workflow and what it helps them do

2/ What does it solve?
The problem needs to feel close to their actual work. Broad pain points make almost everyone sound relevant, while specific moments of friction help the right buyer recognize themselves

3/ How does it work?
Buyers need enough detail to picture the path from their current problem to the promised value. This usually means a simple process, clear capabilities and the key features behind each step

4/ Why should I trust it?
Claims become easier to believe when the page supports them with customer proof, examples, integrations, security details, FAQs and a realistic explanation of what setup requires

5/ Why try it now?
The CTA works better once buyers know what happens after the click, who the next step is for and why that step deserves their time

When these answers are missing, buyers can leave without ever forming a fair opinion of the product (which hurts when you know how good the product is...and hurts conversions even more because they never really gave it a chance)

So they judge the incomplete version created by the homepage because that is the only version they have seen.

That is why I separate the page into 5 zones:

Orientation: Help buyers place the product and understand whether it fits them

Relevance: Describe the problem through the work situation they already recognize

Adoption: Make the product easy to picture before they open it

Trust: Put proof and answers beside the claims that need support

Capture: Ask for action once the page has made the next step feel reasonable

Across 50+ B2B SaaS messaging projects, I have found that CTA problems often start much earlier on the page. Buyers rarely need a louder promise before clicking

Usually they just need enough clarity and proof to believe the click could be worth their time

Safety Stock: The Buffer That Protects Service Level
Safety stock is not simply “extra inventory.”
It is the buffer that protects a business when demand and supply do not behave as expected.
Stockouts can happen because of:
📈 Demand fluctuations
🚚 Supplier delays
📊 Forecast errors
⏱️ Lead-time variation
📦 Urgent customer orders
🌐 Transportation disruptions
A commonly used formula is:
Safety Stock = Z × Demand Standard Deviation × √Lead Time
Where:
• Z = target service-level factor
• Demand Standard Deviation = demand variability
• Lead Time = replenishment time
However, when both demand and supplier lead time vary, a more practical formula is:
Safety Stock = Z × √[(Average Lead Time × Demand Std Dev²) + (Average Demand² × Lead Time Std Dev²)]
This difference matters.
The basic method protects mainly against demand variation.
The advanced method protects against both:
✅ Demand uncertainty
✅ Supplier lead-time uncertainty
High safety stock may indicate more than just strong service protection.
It may also reveal:
• poor forecast accuracy
• unstable supplier lead times
• inconsistent replenishment
• weak demand planning
• low supplier reliability
• poor S&OP alignment
The goal is not to carry more inventory.
The goal is to reduce uncertainty so the business can operate with the right buffer.
Because safety stock is often the visible cost of invisible process variation.

I have made a few Career-Limiting Moves (CLMs).

This time, the 10-10-10 rule saved me.

We were locked in, voices raised, both trying to get the last word. The room was silent except for us. It felt like the meeting was about to go off the rails.

I was ready to dig in. Make my case stronger. Prove I was right.

But I forced myself to pause. I went back to a trick I picked up years ago, the 10-10-10-10 filter. Four ruthless questions:

Will this fight even matter in 10 minutes?
Will it matter in 10 days?
In 10 months?
What about 10 years?

Most conflicts crumble right away. The ego hit? Fades in under an hour. The bad meeting? Forgotten by Friday. Some things stick around for a month, but even those lose power quickly.

In reality, I can only remember a handful of moments from my career that really mattered for 10 years. Things like owning a tough decision. Backing a team member when it was unpopular. Pivoting when the data demanded it.

Arguments rarely make the list.

That day, I realized the fight was pure ego. Nothing strategic. Not worth losing trust or credibility.

So, I took a breath. I reset the conversation. I asked, What problem are we actually trying to solve here?

Everything shifted. Suddenly, it wasn't about being right. It was about moving forward.

The executive lowered his guard. We found common ground. The team left with a real solution, not just a winner and loser.

Without the 10-10-10-10 rule, I might have torched a key relationship over nothing. And that's the trap most leaders walk right into. They pick up battles that vanish in the rearview mirror, while missing the ones that change the course of their team.

The 10-10-10-10 rule isn't soft. It's ruthless. It forces you to cut through your own drama and see what actually deserves your attention.

Use it. Most fires burn out on their own. Save your energy for the rare ones that matter years from now.

What argument did you regret spending energy on? Would it pass the 10-year test?

When you treat procurement as a process, you lose every strategic advantage it could give you.

Let's be honest.

Every business says procurement is "a strategic partner."

But most procurement teams would tell a different story.

The truth?

Procurement's status isn't what leadership says it is.

It's what procurement experiences daily.

6 green flags that separate great procurement teams from the rest:

1/ Procurement is in the room before decisions are made.

The business doesn't bring you in to rubber-stamp a supplier they've already chosen. Early involvement is the clearest signal that procurement is trusted. Not just processed.

2/ The CPO has a seat at the leadership table.

Not buried in Finance. Not three layers removed from the CEO. Where procurement sits in the org chart tells you exactly how seriously the business takes it.

3/ Procurement is measured on value. Not just savings.

Risk reduced. Supplier innovation unlocked. Business outcomes delivered. A business that only measures procurement on cost reduction is asking it to stay tactical forever.

4/ Stakeholders come to procurement voluntarily.

They don't ask "do I have to involve procurement?" They ask "can procurement help with this?" When the business comes to you before it has to, you've become a partner. Not a process.

5/ Procurement has a real development budget.

Tools. Training. Headcount. Career development that reflects strategic importance. A business serious about procurement invests in it. Lip service doesn't come with a budget line.

6/ The business understands what bypassing procurement costs them.

Not as a policy threat. As a shared understanding. When stakeholders self-police maverick spend, procurement has genuinely changed the culture.

Most procurement leaders overestimate where they stand.

They look at the policies. The job titles. The "strategic" label on the org chart.

But none of that matters if the business still treats procurement as the team you go to last.
Status isn't built in policy documents.

It's built in the small moments. The early invites. The unsolicited "can you help us with this?" The maverick spend that doesn't happen.

Your business is showing you everything.

What are you seeing?

A small engineering change in one location can create a big supply chain problem everywhere else.

One BOM update.
One supplier change.
One design revision.
One process adjustment.

If it is not managed properly, it can affect production, quality, compliance, inventory, cost, and delivery timelines.

That is why global engineering change needs a structured lifecycle.

Here are the 8 steps:

𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝘆 & 𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲
Capture the engineering change request, define the problem, identify affected products, and assign a clear owner.

𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗔𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻
Review BOMs, manufacturing impact, supplier readiness, logistics, cost, timelines, risks, and dependencies.

𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 & 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲
Run cross-functional review, validate feasibility, check business alignment, and approve through governance.

𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Create the rollout strategy, action plan, responsibilities, milestones, communication plan, and training needs.

𝗨𝗽𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲 & 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗔𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸
Update engineering data, BOMs, documents, suppliers, plants, partners, and change instructions.

𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲
Execute the approved change across systems, production processes, tooling, templates, and work instructions.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘆 & 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲
Check quality, compliance, documentation accuracy, supplier implementation, and process performance.

𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿, 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 & 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲
Track KPIs, collect lessons learned, solve post-implementation issues, and improve future change workflows.

The real goal is not just to approve a change.

It is to implement it without breaking the global supply chain.

Done well, engineering change management reduces risk, lowers rework, improves quality, strengthens supplier collaboration, and keeps the business moving.

A 6-figure creator just called me a h00ker. He's right. After seducing 8 million, here are my favorite buyer psych triggers ↓

LinkedIn coaches treat hooks like neurosurgery. Babes, it's patterns with a potty mouth.

I use PLACE to make my hooks stupidly specific. But on top of that? I rotate these 5 buyer psychology triggers to get y'all to do whatever the f*ck I want:

1/ Garden-path effect creates instant investment

Write a first line that reads one way, then flip the meaning with the next.

"[A line that means one thing]. [The turn that reveals you meant another]."

The flip forces a re-read. Someone who just caught the twist feels smart = they keep scrolling.

I use this when I'm about to get vulnerable and need a soft way in. Lures them past their defenses before they realize they're about to feel something.

2/ Expectation subversion gets them in the comments

Name the advice everyone parrots, break it, show the receipts.

"[The rule everyone repeats]. [Your proof it's wrong]. [What you did instead]."

You're picking a fight with a belief they hold. They'll comment to argue or to cheer. 

This one's my chaos gremlin for when I want smoke.

3/ Self-disclosure reciprocity builds trust

Show the win everyone sees, then admit the private cost behind it.

"[The public flex]. [The thing behind it you don't say out loud]."

You go first with something real. They drop their guard because you dropped yours.

FYI, people don't connect with your wins. They connect with what your wins cost you.

4/ Time contrast makes them believe in you

Put two moments side by side. Same you, different chapter.

"At [then], I [low point]. At [now], I [where you are]. [The line that ties them]."

Two timestamps do the selling. The distance you covered is proof it's possible for them too.

Comeback fuel, baby. 

5/ Pratfall effect makes them want to buy

Drop a real number to flex, then pair it with a flaw you're not hiding.

"[Real result with a specific number]. [The messy, human detail right next to it]."

A flex on its own reads like bragging. A flex with a visible crack reads like a person. Competence plus one honest flaw makes you look human.

That instinct is high agency. It's the only thing on my scorecard that predicts who works out.
 
So I stopped asking about strengths and weaknesses. I ask one question:
 
"Tell me about a time you wanted to accomplish something, but you didn't have the resources, the authority, or the support you needed. What did you do?"
 
Then I listen for how the story ends.
 
If it ends in a reason it wasn't their fault, I'm out.
"I didn't have the resources."
"It wasn't my call."
"Nobody would help me."
A story that ends at a closed door is a person who stops at closed doors.

2nd: when that didn't work, what did you try next? One attempt is luck, three is agency.
 
The best hire I ever made never applied. He came inbound from my content, not the résumé I'd have written the job spec for. But he had the trait, and today he's the most valuable person on my team: he returns roughly 6-7x what he costs.
 
Agency, not pedigree.
 
Steal the question. Ask it in your next interview, then stay quiet and listen for the pronoun.

I used to wear 14-hour days like a badge of honor.

Your body needs seven different types of breaks.

Each one has a specific window where it works best.

Skip them and the hours keep going but the output drops.

7 breaks that protect your performance:

1/ THE MICRO-REST
→ Focus fades after 60 to 90 minutes of deep work
→ That dip is a signal, not a failure
→ Step away before it hits. Look at the horizon. Walk for 10 to 20 minutes

2/ THE BREATHING RESET
→ When stress spikes mid-task, you may not have 10 minutes
→ One breathing cycle takes about 10 seconds
→ Long inhale through the nose, short second inhale, long exhale

3/ THE POWER BREAK
→ The afternoon slump is real and predictable
→ A 10 to 20 minute nap or eyes-closed rest gives you a second wind
→ Finish well before evening so night sleep stays intact

4/ THE LUNCH BREAK
→ Midday is your best shot at a true reset
→ Eat away from your desk, leave your phone behind
→ Skip the work talk for 30 to 60 minutes

5/ THE SHUTDOWN RITUAL
→ A workday without a clear ending never really ends
→ Signal "work is over" the same way each day
→ Phone away for the evening. Takes 10 to 15 minutes

6/ THE WEEKEND RECOVERY
→ Not all time off restores you
→ Real recovery means stepping fully out of work mode
→ Spend time in nature, build a skill, take one full day off screens

7/ THE STRATEGIC VACATION
→ Recovery follows a curve. It peaks around day 7, then fades
→ Frequent planned breaks beat one long trip you save up for
→ Take one week off every three months. Book it non-refundable

Three out of four people experience burnout at work.

Your post died at 500 impressions again.

(LinkedIn's engineers explained why)

I've spent 5 months studying 3+ technical documents LinkedIn published on the new algorithm: the engineering blog, the retrieval paper, and their VP of Engineering's feed breakdown.

Reach jail is a real mechanism. So is the way out.

LinkedIn's A/B tests showed +3.29% revenue and +1.17% more professional interactions for members with fewer connections. The rebuild favors small accounts. You just have to give it something to work with.

How you get in:

→ You're posting to the wrong room.

Your followers are old colleagues, peers, and connections from 2019. They follow you. They don't buy from you. They're the audience your content gets judged by first. When they shrug, it never travels past them.

→ Buyers never see it.

Your post lives in two places: your connections' feeds by default, and a suggested content pool where the system matches it to strangers by meaning. Both run from minute one. And both can fail. A vague post gives the system nothing to match. A shrugging network gives it no confidence signal, so the wider push never comes.

→ Reach jail.

The system converts engagement into percentile buckets: "71st percentile" instead of raw view counts. Flop with the wrong first audience and you sit in a low bucket the model won't push wider. Embeddings update within 30 minutes, so the burial happens fast.

How you get out:

→ Fix the profile first.

Five author fields travel with every post: your name, headline, company, industry, and title. Your headline is telling the algorithm what you're qualified to talk about before anyone reads a word.

→ Post growth + authority.

The suggested content system retrieves 2,000 candidates from hundreds of millions, and it matches on meaning. Growth content is how you enter that pool: hot takes, trends. Its job is reach: strangers finding you. Authority content is what those strangers find when they click your profile: frameworks, client results, how you actually run things. Its job is trust.

→ Go where your buyers are.

A sharp comment on a post with 50K impressions puts your name in front of every buyer reading it, and the good ones click your profile. Reciprocity is real: the people you show up for show up for your posts, and their engagement lifts your percentile out of jail.

→ Build the relationship.

Connect, DM, coffee chat. The algorithm decides who sees your post. It can't follow up with the CMO who read your case study and said nothing. That part is still manual. It's the part that compounds: posts have a lifespan of days, relationships keep paying out quarters later.

→ Pull them off-platform.

LinkedIn rents you the audience and can change the terms whenever it wants. Your newsletter is the part you own.

Save this for the next time a post flatlines and you want to blame the algorithm.

Our clients set that bar. We work with 2 public companies, several billion dollar companies, and some of the top VCs in the world.

On Friday, I was in a meeting with a client had to had to pop out for a sec because “that might be Sam Altman calling." 😅 These are people driving the future of technology forward. They don't clock out at 5pm. And when you're their trusted partner, you move, and learn, at their pace.

On top of that, everyone here is learning the dark arts of social media. That takes real work too.

So I'm upfront with everyone - this involves a lot of work and if you want a 9 to 5, you won't find it here.

The people who hear all of that and still want in know exactly what they're walking into.

Combine clear expectations with interesting work and good pay, and the result is a team that works hard and enjoys it.

Sugarcoat the interview and the mismatch doesn't go away. It just shows up a few months later, when it costs everyone more.

solid starting points.

Watching how the best teams actually work:

Use the tool built for the outcome you want.

The closer a requirement gets to the factory, the more expensive a casual change becomes.

That is why I find it useful to think about the Master Production Schedule as the line between planning intent and factory commitment.

At forecast level, a new signal is information. Inside the near-term production horizon, the same signal may require material checks, rough-cut capacity review, changes to planned or released orders, and a decision about which customer commitment the team is still protecting.

A stronger MPS review makes four things explicit:
• which item is affected
• what quantity is moving
• which period changes
• whether the line is planned, firm, or already released 
And then it applies a different level of control depending on where the change sits.

Firming converts planned orders into actual production or purchase orders. The exact configuration will vary between systems and businesses, but the operating principle is the same: the closer the plan gets to execution, the more deliberate the change needs to become.

The MPS is not the detailed production sequence either, it does not decide every machine slot or changeover. It creates the item-time commitment that material planning, capacity checks, production orders, and detailed scheduling can work from.

So when demand moves, the useful conversation is not only “can we change the plan?”
It is:
• What exactly are we changing?
• What has already been protected or firmed?
• Which material, capacity, order, or customer commitment moves with it?
• Who owns the exception? 

Protected does not mean impossible to change, it means the business understands that responsiveness has a cost, and the trade-off should be visible before the schedule moves.

When demand changes inside your near-term horizon, who owns the decision to change the MPS?

If your ERP is “the source of truth,” why does everyone still live in Excel?


I used to think it was only a legacy-system problem.

But I’ve seen it in plenty of modern environments too—across industries and company sizes.

Here’s the pattern I keep running into:

Spreadsheets don’t show up because teams love spreadsheets. They show up because teams are trying to solve one of three gaps:

Trust gap (the ERP data is wrong or inconsistent)

Fit gap (the ERP can’t flex to how the business actually runs)

Visibility gap (people can’t validate what’s behind the number)


And once a spreadsheet becomes the “real” planning file, it quietly changes how decisions get made.


Curious where you land: in your world, is Excel mostly filling a trust, fit, or visibility gap?

I analyzed 98,611 LinkedIn posts that I’ve helped write. 

The top performers have this in common: 

1. They use a visual

🌠 Image posts outperform text-only by 1.6x
🌠 Carousels and text get shared more
🌠 Polls and articles are bottom of the list

2. Write longer posts

✍️ The sweet spot is 1,200 to 1,800 characters
✍️ 2.7x the engagement of posts under 200 chars
✍️ Longer posts earn longer dwell time

3. Format for scanning

✅ 41+ line breaks vs 1-5 line breaks = 5x gap in engagement
✅ White space is not wasted space
✅ One idea per line

4. Keep the hook short

🪝 Your hook should fit on one line
🪝 Under 60 characters outperforms by 2x
🪝 First line hooks, second line rehooks

5. Ask questions

❓ End every post with a question
❓ Make it easy to answer in one or two words
❓ 4+ questions pull 60% more comments than posts with 0

6. Drop the hashtags
# No hashtags vs 7+ hashtags = 39% higher engagement
# Hashtags do not increase your reach
# They make your post look spammy

7. Never put links in the post

🔗 The algo punishes you for sending people away
🔗 One link in the post = 43% engagement drop
🔗 Always put the link in the first comment

8. Time it right

🕐 Engagement drops 1.6x by 10pm
🕐 Weekday mornings peak at 6 to 7am local time
🕐 Weekends run 17% below the weekday median

The biggest finding:

Nail all five fundamentals and you get 8x the engagement of someone who nails none.

They stack.

Every habit adds up.

We launched a strategic project to improve delivery performance.

First finding: nobody could say what our delivery performance actually was.

Every site self-reports.  No metric standard.  One site measures against request date.  Another measures against promise date...and gives itself a 7-day grace period after the promise.  Same company, same metric name, multiple different definitions.  Every number in every review deck was true by its own rules and comparable to nothing.

So we collected the data manually across a subset of plants.  Two things became obvious fast: the volume can't be managed by someone on top of their day job, and Excel can't hold it.

Here's the part that should sound familiar.  The data exists.  Every order, every promise date, every ship date is sitting in our systems right now.  It's not a data problem, it's an access problem.  And the IT investment to fix access has been sitting in approval for months, while the strategic project that depends on it moves forward anyway.

That's the pattern: companies fund the initiative because initiatives are visible.  The data plumbing underneath is invisible...right up until you discover your sites have been grading their own homework with different answer keys.

You can't improve what you measure six different ways.

💜🎯🌱The Best Leadership Lesson I’ve Seen in a Long Time

I watched a short video today.

Less than a minute.

Yet it contained more leadership wisdom than many full-day conferences.

It reminded me of something we’ve forgotten in many organizations:

Leadership isn’t about explaining why something can’t be done. It’s about taking responsibility for making it happen.

Too often I see leaders who:

* own meetings instead of problems,
* own presentations instead of results,
* own opinions instead of decisions.

Real leaders do something different.

They don’t ask:
“Whose fault is this?”

They ask:
“What do we do next?”

They don’t wait for another report.
They go to the Gemba.

They don’t blame the system.
They improve it.

They don’t ask employees to be accountable for things they themselves avoid.
That’s why people follow leaders not because of their title, but because of their behavior.

Every employee watches what a leader tolerates.
Every employee notices which standards are ignored.
Every employee learns what is truly important not from PowerPoint slides, but from daily actions.

The strongest leadership message is never spoken.

It is demonstrated.

Sometimes, one minute of truth is worth more than one hundred hours of corporate training.

Question for leaders:

If your team copied everything you did this week, would your organization become better… or just busier?

Lean starts with leaders who lead by example not by exception.

— Agnes

Almost every week, I run my work past my 10Y daughter, Ira.

Not because I want her to go into procurement.

She's not a future buyer in training.

She couldn't care less about suppliers, contracts, or any of the stuff I obsess over.

But honestly, she's my best test.

If I can explain my work in a way that makes her actually pay attention, I know I'm onto something.

If she starts zoning out or hits me with a "wait, what does that mean?", I know I've lost her.

That's when I realize I'm just hiding behind big words and business talk.

Adults will smile and nod through anything.

You toss in a few fancy terms, maybe a framework or two, and everyone acts like it all makes sense.

Kids do not play that game.
They want it simple, clear, and real.

So I'll take a complicated project and try to break it down for her.

If she's still listening by the end, I know I've actually figured it out myself.
If not? Back to the drawing board.

The point isn't to turn Ira into a mini version of me.
She'll find her own thing, and that's exactly what I want.

This is about testing myself.

Can I take all this complicated stuff and make it so clear, so obvious, that even a 10-year-old can explain it to someone else?

The real kicker: the stuff that finally lands for her is always what lands for everyone else too.

If a kid can repeat your main point, you've stripped away all the nonsense.

Try it.

Pick a kid in your life and see if you can get through to them about what you do or what you care about.

You'll get honest feedback. You'll spot the parts where you're faking it or relying on jargon.

It's tough, but you end up with something that actually sticks in people's heads.

So yeah, my secret weapon for clarity is a 10-year-old who couldn't care less about procurement.

Maybe give it a shot yourself.

You'll be surprised how much better you get at your own job.

Every time someone waves the Gartner Magic Quadrant to justify their arguments, here's my systematic playbook:
  
This week I was in a multi-function, multi-stakeholder meeting.

→ "Leader" status measures market presence and vision, not fit for your stack

→ The same weighting applies to a 200-person company and a 50,000-person company

→ Change management capacity isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your existing tech debt isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your internal champions and political capital aren't a criteria on the chart

→ Your industry isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your strategy isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your budget isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your spend profile isn't a criteria on the chart
  
The "Best" solution in a box does NOT mean it's the right solution for you.
  
Analyst reports are a starting point for market awareness.

→ Map your objectives and the capabilities you need to get there (not a requirements wish list)

→ Weight vendors against YOUR constraints
→ Test drive with YOUR data, YOUR team, YOUR workflows
→ Reference-check with companies YOUR size and complexity
