Do you think AI research is just about giving ChatGPT a prompt?

If yes, you’re wrong.
That is how people get confident nonsense with clean formatting.

The best researchers use AI like a research team.

In 2023, 
“Using AI for research” felt like cheating.

Now refusing AI feels like the bigger risk.

It was this:
• too many papers
• too many tabs
• too many citations
• too many conflicting claims
• too much time wasted before thinking starts

I have seen people spend hours just trying to find the right sources.

That is where AI becomes powerful.
It removes friction before your brain can work.

But here is the trap:
Most people use AI for research like this:
“Write me a report on this topic.”
And then they trust the answer.
That is outsourcing judgement to a machine that can still hallucinate.

The smarter workflow is:

✅ Use Perplexity for fast orientation
→ What is happening?
→ What are the major angles?

✅ Use Elicit for paper discovery
→ Find studies.
→ Extract methods.
→ Compare outcomes.

✅ Use Consensus for evidence checking
→ What does peer-reviewed literature say?
→ Is the evidence mixed?

✅ Use Scite or Semantic Scholar for citation context
→ Who cited this?
→ Was it supported?

✅ Use Claude or NotebookLM for synthesis
→ Summarise your PDFs.
→ Find gaps.
→ Turn notes into insight.

✅ Use ChatGPT for reasoning
→ Build outlines.
→ Stress-test arguments.
→ Create counterpoints.

The big shift is this:
AI is a huge part of the research lifecycle now.

• Search faster
• Read smarter
• Extract cleaner
• Compare better
• Verify harder
• Write clearer
But the final judgement still belongs to you.

The researchers who win in 2026 will use the right tool at the right stage.

𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐛𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐩𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥.

I recently watched a podcast that shared an interesting way of looking at organizational performance.

Imagine your company has 200 employees.

The square root of 200 is roughly 14–15 people (often rounded in examples to around 16).

The idea is that this surprisingly small group generates a disproportionately large share of the company’s value. Whether or not the exact numbers hold for every organization, the underlying leadership lesson is powerful.

Then think about the Pareto Principle.

Roughly 20% of your people often contribute to a large share of the results.

These are not just your top performers.

They are the people who:
✔️solve problems before they become crises,
✔️influence others without asking for authority,
✔️improve standards instead of working around them,
✔️carry the culture when no one is watching,
✔️make everyone around them better.

Yet where do many organizations spend most of their leadership time?

🔻On poor performers.
🔻On constant firefighting.
🔻On fixing the same problems.
🔻On endless performance conversations with people who have already decided not to improve.

⚠️ Meanwhile, the people carrying the business quietly continue doing exactly that… carrying the business.

Without recognition.
Without mentoring.
Without investment.
Without a clear development path.

Eventually someone else notices them.

And they leave.

As a Lean leader, I believe this is one of the biggest strategic mistakes organizations make.

„𝘠𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘩𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘢𝘵𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘣𝘪𝘨𝘨𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴.”

That doesn’t mean ignoring underperformance.

It means understanding where your greatest return on leadership investment truly is.

Find your emerging leaders.

Coach them.

Challenge them.

Give them difficult projects.

Invest in their development.

Teach them how to lead others.

Protect them from burnout.

Because the future performance of your organization will not be determined by how much time you spend managing your weakest employees.

It will be determined by how well you develop the people capable of building the next generation of leaders.

Don’t only ask:
“Who needs fixing?”

Start asking:
“Who deserves more investment?”

That question may change the future of your company.


⁉️Leadership Challenge

If tomorrow your five strongest people accepted offers somewhere else…

Would your organization continue improving?

Or would it simply continue holding more meetings?

CAMERON HEROLD 💎🌱🙏🏻

I wrote about why 5S isn't just for big factories.
Today, let's go deeper. Part 2 of the series: the first S — Sort.
Most shop floors have three kinds of items lying around: things you use every day, things you used once six months ago "just in case," and things nobody even remembers buying.
Sort means one thing only — separate what's needed from what isn't, and remove the second pile from the work area. Not "organize it neatly in a corner." Remove it.
Here's the exercise I ask every MSME owner to try, this week:
→ Pick one workstation or tool crib → Red-tag anything not used in the last 30 days → Give red-tagged items 7 days to be claimed — by anyone, for any active job → Anything unclaimed gets moved out, sold, scrapped, or stored off the floor → Measure the walking distance an operator covers at that station before and after
The result is almost always the same: less searching, less double-handling, fewer "where did that go" conversations, and — this surprises people every time — fewer defects, because operators stop grabbing the wrong tool or the wrong batch of material by mistake.
Sort feels like the easiest of the five S's. It's actually the one most units get wrong, because "we might need it someday" is a very hard habit to break — for owners as much as operators.
One red-tag exercise. One station. Seven days. That's the whole ask.
What's sitting in your shop floor right now that hasn't been touched in months?

If I wanted to become a Negotiation Ninja in 2026...

I'd follow this 7-step program for the next 90 days

1. One uncomfortable conversation every day 
Most people hide behind emails, decks, and "circling back." I'd force at least one real, uncomfortable conversation daily. Face-to-face or phone only. No written excuses. The more direct, the better. If it makes my stomach flip, it's the right conversation.

2. Break down real-life deals, not theory 
Books are fine, but the real gold's in the deals we close (and lose). I'd sit down with my team and dissect recent negotiations. What worked? Where did we fold too soon? Where did the other side outplay us? What warning signs did we ignore? Patterns hide in plain sight.

3. Train silence like a skill 
I'd use the ten-second rule after every major offer or request. No talking. Let the silence do the work. Most people jump in and fumble their leverage. With practice, that dead air becomes an advantage.

4. Make one bold ask per week 
Nothing reckless. Just one meaningful ask that stretches my comfort zone. Maybe it's a bigger price, tighter deadline, or extra concession. Even if it gets shot down, the learning's in the attempt.

5. Log every negotiation 
Not just the outcome. The moves. The emotions. The triggers. What did I fear? Where did I hesitate? After ninety days, this log becomes a playbook of my own weaknesses and edge.

6. Get feedback from the "no's" 
Every "no" comes with intel. Instead of chasing the win, I'd ask lost deals for feedback. Their objections, doubts, and friction points are where your blind spots are hiding.

7. Operate like every move is public 
Assume every conversation will end up on the front page of your company's website or CEO's desk. Would I be proud of how I treated the other side? Would I want my team to copy my approach? That's the standard.

You don't become a world-class negotiator by reading more books or finding the perfect script. 
You get there by practicing deliberate discomfort, over and over, until hard conversations feel normal.

Anyone can negotiate when it's easy. 
But the ones who keep leveling up? They run toward the friction.

Don't overcomplicate it. 
One habit, one day at a time. That's how you vault past everyone still playing it safe.

PLM migration fails before go-live.

The biggest risk is not moving the data. It is moving inaccurate, incomplete, or poorly structured information into a new system.

A successful PLM migration depends on five disciplines.

First, audit existing data. Identify every source, remove duplicates, archive obsolete records, standardize naming, confirm ownership, and assess overall quality.

Second, map data correctly. Define source-to-target mappings, validate attributes, align BOM structures, preserve CAD relationships, maintain document links, and keep metadata consistent.

Third, validate data integrity. Check completeness, references, revision history, version control, traceability, and relationship accuracy before prioritizing migration speed.

Fourth, test before go-live. Run pilot migrations, compare source and target records, validate workflows, complete user acceptance testing, measure performance, and resolve errors early.

Fifth, establish post-migration governance. Assign ownership, define policies, monitor data quality, train users, schedule audits, and document the complete migration process.

Poor preparation creates duplicate records, broken CAD references, missing BOM links, incorrect revisions, weak metadata, and low user adoption.

Key takeaway: 
A successful PLM migration is not a data-transfer project. It is a business-continuity project that must preserve product context, engineering relationships, and operational trust.

Complaint Analysis Using Pareto + RCA
🚨Customer complaints are not just issues to close. They are signals that a process failed somewhere.
A late delivery.
A short shipment.
A wrong item.
A damaged package.
Customer service receives the complaint—but the root cause may sit in planning, warehousing, logistics, sales, finance, or the ERP workflow.
That is why complaint analysis should start with data, not assumptions.
📊 Step 1: Use Pareto Analysis
Pareto helps identify the few issues causing most customer pain.
Example:
• Late delivery - 38%
• Short shipment - 24%
• Wrong item - 17%
• Damaged goods - 9%
• Invoice mismatch - 7%
• Poor communication - 5%
The top three causes represent 79% of all complaints.
Instead of treating every issue equally, the team can focus improvement efforts where they will create the greatest impact.
🔍 Step 2: Run Root Cause Analysis
Suppose late delivery is the biggest complaint.
A 5 Whys review may reveal:
• Orders were delivered late
• Because dispatch was delayed
• Because picking finished after cut-off
• Because priority orders were released late
• Because release depended on manual approval
• Because the ERP workflow was not automated
The real root cause was not simply “warehouse delay.”
It was a slow order approval process.
✅ Step 3: Prevent recurrence
Possible corrective actions:
• Automate order release approvals
• Define clear order cut-off times
• Create priority-order alerts
• Track repeat complaint rates
• Review major complaints in S&OP
• Verify corrective-action closure
Pareto shows where to focus.
RCA shows why the problem happened.
Corrective action prevents it from happening again.
The best companies do not only respond to complaints.
They study them, learn from them, and convert them into better processes and stronger customer trust.

Even the smallest choices impact your long-term success. 

World-class founders know this better than ANYONE.  

Genuinely, if you want to master or build anything, 
You cannot leave your progress up to willpower alone. 

Habits become a routine, and a routine becomes an identity.
Eventually, being a high-performer just becomes who you are.

If I had to list the top 12 I see in the top 1% founders, this would be it:

➡️ Systemise everything 

You can only go so far with sheer willpower alone. Instead, build systems. Anything I do more than twice I turn into a checklist or a template for it.

➡️ Protect your zone of genius

There is a small set of work that only you can do and will actually help you scale. Find your top 3 tasks and protect them at all costs.

➡️ Run a monthly 80/20 audit

Once a month, go through your calendar, the month behind you and month ahead of you. Then, mark the 20% of tasks that drove the most results. 

➡️ Eat the frog

I do the hardest task of the day first, before other priorities land on my plate. Decide tonight what your frog is, then eat it before you open your inbox.

➡️ Turn your phone off for deep work

It goes off and into another room. The jump in quality of work when it's out of reach is something you have to feel for yourself to believe. Try doing that yourself in your next deep work block.

➡️ Set delegation triggers

I don't decide what to hand off in the moment, I set rules that decide for me... Write 2 or 3 delegation rules of your own and hold yourself to them.

➡️ Build your calendar around energy

I build my week around when I'm at my best for a given type of work. Map your own energy for a week, then move your hardest work into your peak window.

➡️ Write tomorrow's top 3 each evening

I set my priorities when I'm calm, so I'm not picking them when I'm tired and reactive first thing. 

➡️ Close open loops ASAP

Open-ended tasks can stay in your mind for a very long time. Give every task on your list a date today.

➡️ Set deadlines on everything

The moment a task has a hard finish line, it gets done properly and on time.

➡️ Review your numbers daily

You can't fix what you're not watching. Pick your core metrics and put them somewhere you'll see them daily.

➡️ Move your body every day

Even if it's only 20 minutes, it doesn't have to be extreme. But movement is good for your body AND mind. 

You won't find quick fixes here, because that doesn't build routines. 
Habits are unglamorous and often boring, but they work. 

That’s how I’ve built 4 8-figure businesses, 
While still showing up for myself and the people I love.

I see the procurement spend funnel a bit differently than others...

Here's how I break down procurement's spend influence:

→ Total Company Spend
This is everything your company spends money on. Salaries, rent, utilities, software, materials - everything.

→ Addressable Spend
All spend where procurement CAN have an influence. Non-addressable = spend where procurement involvement is useless.

→ Spend Under Management
How much of addressable spend is currently formally under procurement's purview (e.g. via your procurement policy's RACI). This varies and depends on your function's maturity, responsibilities and organizational influence.

→ Spend Under Contract/Strategy
Spend that's actively managed from a strategic procurement standpoint. Where competitive negotiation and value creation happens. How much spend are you running through your classic "7-step procurement process"?

→ Fully Governed Spend
Where procurement can link strategy to realized savings through clear purchasing channels (P2P). Very hard to measure without a spend cube and purposeful mapping of your purchasing channels to your spend category (e.g. commodity codes).

You need Procurement, Accounting, Operations and IT fully aligned to get "Fully Governed Spend"

(You also need a good handle on this to make Intake & Orchestration work, by the way...)

Yet, this is where the magic happens.

Key Insights:

→ Addressable comes BEFORE spend under management scope
→ Just because spend is "addressable" doesn't mean you have jurisdiction/influence over it
→ Procurement's job is moving spend down the funnel systematically to generate value
→ Full governance = strategy linked to realized savings in procure-to-pay processes

The biggest gap?

Most procurement teams measure success on "spend under management" but can't prove value creation.

The real question isn't "how much spend touches procurement?"

It's "how much spend can we prove we're optimizing?"

What does your spend funnel look like?

Doesn't matter if it's different...

What matters is that you have clear/coherent definitions...

And aligned stakeholders 😅

Preparing for a major product launch? Easy.

Just do these 5 simple steps:

Line up your co-manufacturer months in advance ✅

Nail down every component of your BOM ✅

Execute a flawless tech transfer from your old co-man to your new one ✅

Watch a key component get stuck in your new co-man’s supply chain and threaten your entire launch timeline ✅

Panic.

Simple! See you at launch day! 🎉

Okay, jokes aside.

We were mid-tech transfer—moving to a turnkey model with a new co-manufacturer—when they hit trouble sourcing a critical component in time for our launch window. 

The clock was ticking, and my first thought was, “Are we really about to delay this over one part?”

The obvious options were to scramble for a new supplier or push the launch.
Instead, we paused and took stock of what we actually had. 

Sitting at our old co-manufacturer? The exact raw material needed.

We sold the component directly to the new co-man, kept the timeline intact, and launched without a hitch.

My manager kept giving me extra unnecessary work.

Years later, I discovered his hidden agenda.

Message 5/22: To the Nikhil who kept asking, "Why do I have to do this?"

Message in short: 

Do not optimize your early career for less work. 

Optimize it for more capability.

My first manager, Ravishanker Begari, had a phrase I still remember:

"Your skills are your passport to success. You can only travel as far as your skills allow you."

And he practiced what he preached.

If company policy required a contract only above a certain spend, Ravi would sometimes ask us to write one for much smaller projects.

If a sourcing strategy was not technically required, we might still create one.

At the time, I found it frustrating.

Why do extra work when the policy does not require it?

Years later, I understood his hidden agenda.

He was not trying to get more work out of me.

He was trying to build more capability into me.

Every extra contract was practice.

Every extra sourcing strategy was practice.

And that practice compounded.

I eventually became qualified at advanced levels in those skills.

Today, I teach many of them as a Master Trainer.

The work I once questioned became part of the expertise I am known for.

So, to the younger me:

Stop asking:

"Do I have to do this?"

Start asking:

"What capability could this build in me?"

Because the best time to build a skill is not when your career finally demands it.

It is years before.

When the business is profitable, why is the owner regularly stressed?
.
.
.
I often see businesses that are growing, with orders increasing, and enjoying a good reputation with high performance, however the owner / senior leader is emersed in day-to-day firefighting.

The trouble is that everything has become dependent on the MD. Their work ethic. Their drive. Their foresight. Their decision making.

The team and structure surrounding them is not delivering the performance and support needed to allow growth and reduce the pressure. 

At a networking meeting I attended recently a common theme of "my biggest problem is my people" raced to the front of the list.

Aside from wrong people, wrong roles, wrong structure, I often find that the strategy, procedures, systems, checks and balances are also missing or no longer suitable. There is such a lack of clarity and direction everyone is floundering.

Sometimes it takes an experienced outsider to see what is occurring from an objective and neutral position, identify the infection and recommend the medicine.

Image generate by AI.

Wir schauen oft auf den Bestand, wenn das eigentliche Problem längst sechs Wochen alt ist.

Der Bestand steigt. Die Lieferfähigkeit wird schlechter. Nach einer Störung braucht die Supply Chain erstaunlich lange, um wieder in einen stabilen Zustand zu kommen.

Dann beginnt die Suche.

War der Forecast falsch? Sind unsere Sicherheitsbestände zu hoch? Stimmen die Planungsparameter noch? Brauchen wir ein besseres System?

Alles berechtigte Fragen.

Aber ich frage mich zunehmend, ob wir damit nicht häufig zu spät ansetzen.
Denn die eigentliche Ursache liegt manchmal in einem Planungsmeeting Wochen zuvor.

Der Vertrieb sieht eine Chance im Markt. Supply hat Bedenken wegen Kapazitäten oder Lieferzeiten. Finance schaut auf Cash und Working Capital.
Jede Perspektive ist für sich nachvollziehbar.

Die Zahlen werden diskutiert, der Plan wird angepasst und irgendwann ein Forecast verabschiedet.

Was dabei erstaunlich oft unsichtbar bleibt, ist der Trade-off, den wir gerade akzeptiert haben.

Wenn wir diese zusätzliche Nachfrage absichern, was bedeutet das für unseren Bestand?

Wenn wir die Produktion heute reduzieren, wie schnell können wir bei einer Veränderung wieder reagieren?

Wenn wir die Lieferfähigkeit schützen, was passiert in den nächsten Wochen mit Cash und Marge?

Gerade in mittelständischen Pharmaunternehmen halte ich das für einen wichtigen Punkt.

Nicht jedes Planungsproblem braucht sofort Kinaxis. Und nicht jede Organisation muss erst ein dreijähriges SAP-Projekt durchlaufen, bevor bessere Entscheidungen möglich sind.

Vielleicht beginnt es an einer viel einfacheren Stelle:
Die Konsequenzen einer Planungsentscheidung sichtbar zu machen, solange man noch anders entscheiden kann.

Denn der Bestand ist nicht immer das Problem.
Manchmal ist er nur der Ort, an dem eine frühere Entscheidung endlich sichtbar wird.

#SupplyChain #IBP #Pharma #Mittelstand #DecisionMaking

How to shift procurement to strategic. Free Guide 🎁 

Perception is built on evidence. But the evidence the business sees every day is tactical.

Let's look at the transformation step by step:

1️⃣ Signs the business sees you as tactical

↳ They only involve you AFTER a supplier has been chosen 
↳ Stakeholders treat procurement as a box-ticking exercise 
↳ You're only measured on cost savings 
↳ You spend more time on POs than influencing decisions 
↳ Nobody invites you to early planning conversations 
↳ Your reports go to Finance, not the boardroom 
↳ The business regularly goes around procurement entirely

If 3+ are true, you're seen as purchasing. Not procurement.


2️⃣ The 5 shifts to close the gap

(i) From Price to Value 
↳ Stop leading with "we got 10% off" 
↳ Start showing total cost of ownership, risk reduction, supplier reliability

(ii) From Reactive to Proactive 
↳ Stop waiting to be briefed after decisions are made 
↳ Start building relationships that get you upstream

(iii) From Process Enforcer to Business Partner 
↳ Stop saying "you need to follow the procurement process" 
↳ Start saying "let's figure out how to get you the outcome you need"

(iv) From Tactical KPIs to Strategic Metrics 
↳ Stop reporting PO cycle times and savings vs budget 
↳ Start reporting supplier risk, value delivered, market benchmarks

(v) From Departmental to Cross-Functional 
↳ Stop talking only to direct budget holders 
↳ Start building relationships with Finance, Legal, Operations, and the C-suite


3️⃣ Change how you speak

Instead of: "You should have involved us earlier" ❌ 
Try: "At what point did the supplier conversation start?" ✅ 

Instead of: "That's not the procurement process" ❌ 
Try: "Let's see how we can make this work safely" ✅ 

Instead of: "We need 3 quotes" ❌ 
Try: "Here's what the market looks like. Let me show you the options" ✅ 

Instead of: "I can't approve that supplier" ❌ 
Try: "There are some risks here. Let's talk through them" ✅ 

Instead of: "We saved £200K this quarter" ❌ 
Try: "We reduced cost AND improved delivery reliability by 15%" ✅ 


4️⃣ The perception checklist

↳ Do stakeholders involve you before supplier decisions? 
↳ Do you have relationships with senior leaders beyond direct contacts? 
↳ Can you articulate procurement's value beyond savings? 
↳ Do you bring market intelligence, not just process? 
↳ Does the business know what it costs to bypass procurement? 
↳ Are your KPIs linked to business strategy? 
↳ Does procurement have a voice in supplier innovation?

The gap isn't about capability. It's about visibility, language & how procurement shows up.

The BOM is becoming a sustainability system.

A traditional Bill of Materials tracks parts, quantities, suppliers, costs, and lead times.

𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮

Track ESG ratings, sustainability certifications, ethical sourcing, and country of origin.

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲
Monitor RoHS, REACH, conflict minerals, and other regulatory requirements directly within the BOM.

𝗘𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁

I've seen these 10 mistakes in almost every S&OP / IBP implementation I've worked on.
Some are obvious. Some are sneaky. All of them quietly kill the process.

1. No common objectives or aligned bonuses
If sales and supply chain are rewarded for different things, don't expect alignment.
2. Lack of commitment from CEO and senior management
If leadership doesn't show up, neither will anyone else, eventually.
3. Lack of clarity on responsibilities
"Who owns this decision?" should never be a mystery in the room.
4. An overly complex process
The more steps you add, the less people follow them.
5. Data not centralized or standardized
Three teams, three spreadsheets, three versions of the truth.
6. No action plan or follow-up of responsibilities
Decisions without follow-up are just nice conversations.
7. Lack of focus on essentials
If everything is a priority, nothing is.
8. Vision too short term
S&OP / IBP is not about firefighting next week. It's about steering the next 3 to 18 months.
9. Too much online, not enough human
Dashboards don't build trust. Conversations do.
10. No official S&OP / IBP process facilitator

Without a clear owner driving the process, it slowly dies on its own.
If I had to pick the one that kills the most processes: #2 and #10. Without leadership commitment and a real facilitator, everything else collapses eventually.

Which one resonates the most with what you're seeing in your organization?

Everything you learned about cold email in 2019 is now the best way to go to spam.
 
Instantly.ai analyzed billions of emails. Average reply rate in 2026 is 3.43%. Some other teams are closer to 15%.
I've run outbound for 275+ companies. I've understood what makes the gap massive.
 
Here are the 6 things the gap comes down to.
 
1. Start with one buyer and one outcome.
 
Your ICP isn't a job title and a headcount range. It's the outcome they're chasing and the exact words they use for the problem.
Stay vague here and it costs you twice: you lose the deal, and the low engagement drags your inbox placement down with it.
 
2. Send when something changes, not off a scraped list.
 
A funding round. A new AE hire. A visit to your pricing page.
Signal-triggered lists reply at 15%, versus 3.43% for a cold scrape.
Build small and clean: 500 to 1,000 verified contacts, bounce under 2%.
 
3. Open on something real.
 
"Hope you're doing well" gets deleted. "Saw you're hiring 3 AEs after your Series B" gets a reply.
Keep it under 80 words and make one point. First-name merge tags stopped counting as personalization.
Context is what earns the open.
 
4. Fix deliverability or none of the rest matters.
 
SPF, DKIM and DMARC aren't optional anymore. Google rejects non-compliant mail outright.
The volume math changed too: 15 to 25 sends per inbox per day, not 30 to 50, and warm every new domain for two to four weeks before it sends anything.
You scale by adding inboxes, not by squeezing more out of each one.
 
5. The follow-ups are half your pipeline.
 
58% of replies come off the first email.
The other 42% come from the follow-ups, so skipping them throws away nearly half your results.
Run 4 to 7 touches, keep each short, reference the last one, add something new every time.
 
6. Treat it like a pipeline.
 
You're not trying to close someone today. You're trying to be in their inbox the week they're ready to buy.
Reply rates keep going down for everyone still running the old playbook.

Pixar has built a $30B+ empire on stories people can't stop thinking about.

These are the 22 rules they live by 👇

Shout out to Tara Vracevic for this sick visual!

Storytelling is the most valuable skill you can build right now.

It doesn't matter what industry you're in or what you sell. 
In a world where everyone has access to the same AI tools, the storyteller wins every time.

Don't get me wrong, a lot of these rules were written for screenwriters and novelists.

But the thinking behind them works for any type of writing you're doing, LinkedIn posts included.

Here's a few that hit hardest for me:
(You can see all 22 in the visual ! XD)

1️⃣ What's interesting to you as an audience isn't always what you'd choose to write.

The version of you that reads and the version of you that writes want different things.

Listen to the reader more often.

2️⃣ You won't find your theme until the end. Then rewrite for it.

Your first draft is you working out what you're trying to say.
Your second draft is where you finally say it.

3️⃣ Simplify → Focus → Combine

Cramming in more ideas doesn't make writing stronger.
Take one idea and push it as far as it can go.

4️⃣ Finish your writing. Let it go even if it's not perfect.

The post that goes live will outperform the draft sitting in your notes app.
Perfect is a fantasy, whereas done is a habit.

5️⃣ Give your reader a reason to care about the outcome.

If nothing's on the line, nobody's reading to the end.
Stakes are what keep eyes on the page, so set up what your reader stands to gain or lose in the first three lines.

6️⃣ Come up with your ending before you figure out your middle.

Know where you're taking the reader before you start the journey.

Write the last line first, then build the post backwards from there. 
You'll waste less time, and the writing will feel smoother.

7️⃣ What is your story about, at its most essential level?

If you can't say it in one sentence, you don't know what you're writing yet.
Get the one sentence right, and the rest gets easier.

8️⃣ Putting it on paper only allows you to start fixing it.

The first draft is supposed to be rough; that's where you're building the idea.
Write the messy version first, then edit it into the version you're proud of.

9️⃣ Discount the first thing that comes to mind. Surprise yourself.

The first idea is the one everyone else has too.
The second or third idea is where the post gets interesting and unique to you.

🔟 Why must YOU tell this story?

Readers can tell when you mean it and when you don't.
The writing that travels is the writing that came from somewhere real.

Pixar built a $30B empire on one thing:
Making people feel something.

Carry that into whatever you're writing next, and the rest follows.

What's a story that's stuck with you for years? 

💾 Save this for the next time the writing feels flat.

Everybody says "build a personal brand."
Nobody tells you where to actually start.

Most people do 1 of 2 things. They either post random thoughts and hope something sticks, or they never start at all.

Both get you to the same place…nowhere.

In reality, the whole thing comes down to 7 steps:

Step 1: Fix your profile

Your banner, photo, headline, About and Featured sections should tell one story. who you help, what you help them do, and where to go next.

If a stranger can't work that out in 5 seconds, they bounce.

Step 2: Pick your niche

One person, one problem. Fill in this line: "I help [who] do [what] so they can [outcome]."

Saywhat started because I was spending too much time on LinkedIn instead of my actual work. I solved my own problem first, then found the people who shared it.

Step 3: Build a topic bank

Keep a running list of the real problems your audience complains about, the outlier posts in your niche, and the stories only you can tell. That list alone is months of content.

Step 4: Adapt what already works

Find posts in your niche that performed 2x better than average. Then adapt the topic, format or design for your audience.

ADAPT is the important word here. Don't copy. Make it your own!

Step 5: Write posts people save

Lead with proof. Name the pain and make it sting a little. Then give people 1-3 things they can do tomorrow. Useful posts get saved… and saved posts get you remembered.

Step 6: Set your content mix

Every post has ONE job. Post to grow your audience most days, post to build trust twice a week, post to convert once a week.

Step 7: Turn attention into relationships

Reply to every comment in the first hour. DM the people who keep showing up. Comment on other people's posts like a human, not a lead-gen bot.

You don't need all 7 on day one. Start with your profile this week and work down the list.

In a few months, you'll have what most people never build: a brand that works while you sleep.

YES or NO???

One interesting cultural nuance:

In Italy, conversations are often highly interactive. It's common to end a statement with "no?" as a way of directly inviting confirmation or agreement.

In many Chinese business conversations, it's less interactive and silence is often comfortable and shows consideration and they need to be asked directly for confirmation. But many times, "yes" often means "I hear you" rather than "I agree with you." It's an acknowledgment before it's an agreement.

Now imagine these cultures and colleagues working together.

That could be the beginning of perfect communication... or one of the biggest misunderstandings in global business.

Culture is fascinating.

Sales has two forecasts.

The one they commit to their leadership.  And the one they hand to SIOP.

The number they give sales leadership is conservative because that number has consequences.  Miss it and there's no bonus, no high fives, no place to hide.

The number they give SIOP is inflated because that number has none.  If supply chain builds to it and demand doesn't show, the disappointment lands on the SIOP team, the inventory lands on ops metrics, and sales absorbs exactly nothing.

I've sat in leadership meetings and heard it said out loud: "We're driving to X, but think we'll hit Y."

Here's what that tells you: sales can forecast just fine.  They forecast precisely as accurately as each audience can hold them accountable.  The inflated SIOP number isn't a skill problem, it's a rational response to a process with no teeth.  Infinite inventory means never missing a potential sale, and there's no downside charged to the people asking for it.

So before you buy forecasting software or run another accuracy workshop, ask one question: what happens to sales when the SIOP number misses?

If the answer is "nothing", you don't have a forecast.

You have a wish list.

A faster forecast cycle can create more planner activity without creating a better decision.

You can use Claude to build it, to test whether a fresh signal exists, whether the response window is still open, and whether an operating decision can actually move.

For each SKU-location, the workflow reads demand history alongside recent order, POS, promotion, inventory, lead-time, service, lifecycle, and planner context. It then tests regularity, variability, volume and value, signal freshness, and the remaining response window.

From there, it recommends one of three lanes:
• SENSE FREQUENTLY when a fresh signal can still change replenishment, deployment, allocation, or production
• PLAN MONTHLY when the baseline cadence still fits the decision horizon
• SPECIAL METHOD / REVIEW when intermittent demand, lifecycle status, or weak evidence makes the choice less straightforward 

Claude becomes useful here because the method does not need to be reconstructed in every conversation.

One worker profiles the demand, one applies the routing policy. A third tries to reject the recommendation when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or disconnected from an open decision.

• the current routing board
• a route-change log showing what moved and why
• data-quality and validation exceptions
• a demand-review brief focused on the decisions still open
• a run manifest showing which evidence and policy produced the output 

The planner still approves the method, cadence, master data, and every system-of-record change. But the meeting can start with the SKUs that changed lanes, failed a check, or still have a decision worth discussing.

Last week's post on Sort got the most comments yet — a lot of you asked the same question: "we removed the clutter, so what now?"

Now comes Part 3: the second S — Set in Order.

Sort answers "do we need this?" Set in Order answers a different question: "does this have a home?" Every tool, file, and material that survived the red-tag exercise needs one fixed, visible, obvious place — not a drawer, not "wherever there's space."

Here's the exercise I ask every MSME owner to try this week:

→ Take the same station you sorted last week → Outline each tool's spot with tape, paint, or a shadow board → Label it — so a new operator finds it without asking anyone → Put the most-used items at arm's reach, rare ones further away → Time how long it takes to find and return a tool, before and after

The payoff isn't cosmetic. A missing tool means a stopped machine, a supervisor hunting the floor, and a changeover that runs long. A shadow board means anyone — including a substitute operator — puts their hand on the right tool in seconds and puts it back just as fast.

Here's the harder truth: Set in Order fails wherever putting things back is harder than leaving them out. If the return step takes longer than grabbing a new one off the shelf, operators will skip it — no matter how good the labels look on day one.

A place for everything, and everything back in its place within seconds. That's Set in Order.

Where in your shop floor would a missing tool cost you the most time right now?

Trade Update | Before You Assume Your Brazilian Imports Just Got 25% More Expensive... Read This.

Most headlines are saying the same thing: "The US imposed a 25% tariff on imports from Brazil."

That's true. But if you are responsible for sourcing, procurement, logistics, finance, or customs, the headline alone isn't enough.

The Executive Order applies a 25% additional tariff to many Brazilian imports beginning July 22, 2026.

However, it also includes an extensive list of product-specific exemptions.

Some of Brazil's largest exports to the US remain excluded from the additional tariff, including:
• Coffee
• Orange juice
• Crude oil
• Iron ore
• Civil aircraft and aircraft parts
• Pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients
• Fertilizers
• Certain wood products

For Supply Chain teams, this should trigger an immediate review of:
→ HTS classifications
→ Product-specific exclusions
→ Purchase orders already on order or in transit
→ Landed cost impacts
→ Customer pricing commitments

There is also a limited transition period.

Certain shipments loaded before the effective date may qualify for the in-transit exception if they meet the required entry deadlines.

One more observation.
This reinforces a broader trend that Supply Chain leaders should be watching closely: The continued expansion of Section 301 as a strategic trade policy tool.

𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘢 𝘱𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘵 𝘪𝘯 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶’𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘰 𝘭𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘦𝘳 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴, 𝘺𝘰𝘶’𝘷𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘢𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘬𝘦𝘦𝘱𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘷𝘦.

I’ve seen organizations where talented people work harder every quarter, attend more meetings, produce more reports, and implement more processes. Yet somehow, nothing really improves.

The system isn’t underperforming because people aren’t trying hard enough.

♨️The system is broken.

Too often, leadership responds by asking individuals to compensate:
* Work longer.
* Be more resilient.
* Communicate better.
* Take more ownership.

But 𝘢𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘹𝘤𝘦𝘱𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘺 𝘥𝘺𝘴𝘧𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘴𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘱. 𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘴𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵.

High performers eventually burn out.
Average performers adapt.
Innovation disappears.

The uncomfortable truth is this:

𝘈 𝘣𝘳𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯 𝘴𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘮 𝘳𝘦𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘴 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯, 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘪𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘰𝘴𝘪𝘵𝘺.

You cannot coach your way out of bad incentives.
You cannot motivate people past conflicting priorities.
And you certainly cannot automate broken thinking.

Technology—including AI—doesn’t solve dysfunctional organizations.

It scales them.

If your processes are inefficient, AI makes inefficient processes faster.
If your decisions are biased, AI amplifies those biases.
If your culture discourages questioning, technology simply accelerates silence.

Real transformation begins somewhere far less exciting than a new tool or a new strategy.

It begins with asking difficult questions:
* Why do we do this?
* Who actually benefits?
* What would we design if we started today?
* Which rules are protecting value and which are protecting comfort?

Sometimes the bravest thing a leader can say isn’t “Let’s optimize this.”

🚨It’s:
“Let’s stop doing it.”

The future doesn’t belong to organizations that work the hardest.

It belongs to those willing to redesign the system instead of asking people to survive it.

I no longer aspire to fix broken systems.
I aspire to build better ones.

Because people deserve systems that help them succeed, not systems that require them to sacrifice themselves just to keep them running.

The same product has three different truths.

Engineering defines what the product should be.

Manufacturing defines how it should be built.

Production records what was actually built.

That is why EBOM, MBOM, and As-Built BOM are not interchangeable.

They are three connected views of the same product lifecycle.

𝗘𝗕𝗢𝗠: 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗕𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹𝘀
EBOM represents the product as designed by engineering.

It includes CAD models, drawings, part numbers, design specifications, material specifications, revisions, functional assemblies, and product structure.

Its purpose is to create a complete engineering definition before manufacturing begins.

𝗠𝗕𝗢𝗠: 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗕𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹𝘀
MBOM converts the engineering design into a manufacturing-ready structure.

It includes production parts, manufacturing assemblies, assembly sequence, work instructions, packaging materials, tooling requirements, production routing, and manufacturing resources.

Its purpose is to help factory teams build the product consistently, efficiently, and cost-effectively.

𝗔𝘀-𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗕𝗢𝗠
As-Built BOM captures the exact product configuration that was actually manufactured.

It includes installed components, serial numbers, lot and batch numbers, supplier information, production records, inspection results, manufacturing dates, and traceability records.

Its purpose is to support quality, compliance, service, warranty, and field support.

The flow is simple:

EBOM answers: What should be built?
MBOM answers: How should it be built?
As-Built BOM answers: What was actually built?

Together, they create the digital thread:

Customer requirements → product design → EBOM → manufacturing planning → MBOM → production execution → As-Built BOM → quality, service, warranty, and compliance.

When these BOM views are connected properly, companies reduce errors, improve collaboration, speed up root-cause analysis, and build a stronger lifecycle record.

Which BOM view is hardest to manage in your organization?

Most procurement teams are managing spend wrong. 

(And don't know which category costs the most.)

The challenge: 

Every pound leaving your business falls into one of four buckets. And each one demands a different approach.

DIRECT SPEND - "Cost of Production" 
↳ Raw materials, components, packaging
↳ The spend that directly builds what you sell 
↳ Miss this? Your gross margin disappears overnight

INDIRECT SPEND - "Cost of Running the Business" 
↳ IT, facilities, marketing, travel and office supplies 
↳ Spread across every department, often completely unmanaged 
↳ Ignore this? Maverick spend quietly drains your EBITDA

SERVICES SPEND - "Cost of Expertise" 
↳ Consulting firms, legal, IT partners, interim contractors 
↳ Bought for outcomes, usually paid for activity 
↳ No clear scope? Watch invoices spiral out of control

CAPEX SPEND - "Cost of Assets & Investment" 
↳ Manufacturing equipment, facilities, major tech platforms 
↳ Capitalised on the balance sheet, depreciated over time 
↳ Get the supplier wrong? You're locked into that mistake for years

Let's look at 2 examples:

Manufacturing Business:
• Direct: £2M/year (steel, components, packaging)
• Indirect: £500K/year (IT software, facilities management)
• Services: £300K/year (engineering consultants, legal)
• CapEx: £1.5M once (new production line)

Professional Services Firm:
• Direct: Minimal (people are the product)
• Indirect: £800K/year (office space, technology, HR)
• Services: £200K/year (specialist subcontractors, legal)
• CapEx: £400K once (proprietary software platform)

Most procurement teams lump everything into one "spend" bucket. Then wonder why they can't find savings.

But when you separate them?

Direct → Conduct should-cost analysis & protect gross margin 
Indirect → Consolidate suppliers & drive contract compliance 
Services → Define scope clearly & link payment to outcomes 
CapEx → Evaluate total lifecycle cost, not just purchase price

Crucial insights: 

✓ High Direct Spend? Strategic sourcing & supplier partnerships are non-negotiable 
✓ Unmanaged Indirect? Maverick spend is quietly killing your EBITDA 
✓ Rising Services costs? You've got scope creep & weak governance 
✓ Poor CapEx decisions? You'll feel the pain on the balance sheet for years

Common traps: 

❌ Focusing on price rather than total cost 
❌ Applying the same strategy to every spend category 
❌ Weak stakeholder engagement across business functions 
❌ No spend visibility to even know where the real problem is

When you finally understand your spend categories?

You negotiate with confidence.

A 150% BOM is not 50% more product.

It is a complete product-family structure that contains every possible part, option, alternative, and variant that could be used across multiple configurations.

Think of a vehicle family.

The 150% BOM may include petrol, diesel, hybrid, manual, automatic, different interiors, trims, and sunroof options. It represents the full range of possibilities, not one buildable vehicle.

A 100% BOM is the resolved version.

It contains only the exact components required for one specific configuration, such as a hybrid engine, automatic transmission, black interior, and no sunroof.

This distinction matters across the product lifecycle.

The 150% BOM helps engineering teams manage reuse, standardization, product complexity, configuration rules, and dependencies inside PLM.

The 100% BOM supports execution. Manufacturing knows what to build, procurement knows what to purchase, and operations can trace the exact product or order.

The biggest risk with a 150% BOM is unmanaged complexity.

The biggest risk with a 100% BOM is incorrect configuration or missing components.

In simple terms:

150% BOM = every valid possibility
100% BOM = one finalized configuration

How does your organization manage product variants between PLM, ERP, and manufacturing?

A former Apple engineer texted a colleague right after he quit:
 
"LOL, I found out I can still access the servers. So funny."
 
That text is now Exhibit A in the biggest tech lawsuit of the year.
 
Last week Apple sued OpenAI. The claim: OpenAI didn't just recruit Apple's people, it recruited what was in their heads, their laptops, and in one case their still-active server login.
 
The filing is wild:
400+ former Apple employees now work at OpenAI.
Its hardware chief allegedly told Apple candidates to bring "actual parts" and prototypes to interviews for "show and tell."
One engineer allegedly kept his Apple laptop and pulled dozens of files on unreleased products after his last day.
OpenAI allegedly passed around an internal Apple guide on how to dodge Apple's own exit-security check.
 
OpenAI denies all of it. A court will decide.
 
But strip the names off and this is a story every founder is living in miniature.
 
I run a business whose entire product is know-how. Clay builds, signal stacks, the whole system on outbounds, ads and content. All of it is, in theory, stealable. People see it, learn it, and some of them leave.
 
For a while I thought the fix was locking it down hard with tighter contracts, more NDAs, guard the playbook.
 
It doesn't work. Apple has the best lawyers on earth, and its unreleased roadmap still allegedly walked out on a personal laptop.
 
Here's what I believe after 3 years of this:
 
The secret was never the moat, the moat is how fast you can make today's secret irrelevant.
 
Apple's edge was never one metal-finishing trick. It was decades of compounding execution that outruns whatever leaks. One AI release can dissolve a "protected" advantage overnight. Speed can't be poached.
 
In our case, we stopped trying to own information and started trying to out-run the copy.
Publish the playbook. Give away the signals. Move faster than anyone who screenshots them.
 
What are you still trying to protect that you'd be better off just giving away?
 
P.S. Flashback to 2024, when Apple and OpenAI shook hands on the partnership Elon Musk immediately mocked. Two years later, they're in court.

Most “authentic” posts on LinkedIn are completely useless.
There’s an easy fix to make sure yours aren’t.

If your personal posts are falling flat, it's likely because they're giving nothing.

Personal stories are a great tool for your personal brand - they can build trust quickly.

They show people what shaped you, how you think, and what you have learned along the way.

But the story still needs to give the reader a lesson, a takeaway, or a change they can make today. 

Here’s how to do it without being cringe:

1/ Start with the moment

Choose one specific event, conversation, or result that changed how you think. Give people the details they need to understand it, but cut anything that does not move the story forward.

Earlier this year, I met with a founder who runs a recruiting business for AI startups. Eight years in, his business is doing $65M a year, completely bootstrapped.

I was telling him how I'm the bottleneck in my business, because I can't find anyone as good at creating content as me.

He was polite, but said one thing that made me rethink everything: "You've got an imaginary scarcity mindset.” 

2/ Name the lesson

Explain what the experience taught you. The best lesson is usually something you now do differently because of what happened.

In my case, the lesson was simple. The talent wasn't missing...my willingness to actually go look for it was.

3/ Make it useful

Be clear with your readers how they can apply the lesson to their own work or life. Give them a question to ask themselves, common mistakes to avoid, or one action they can take.

To avoid imaginary scarcity, find someone a few years ahead of you. Tell them what you think is holding you back, and let them tell you which parts are real and which parts you made up.

An authentic, personal story earns the reader's attention when it teaches them something they can use.

→ Overly perfect grammar

→ Words like "leverage, "foster" and "synergy"
→ Generic takes that could have been written by anyone

You need to add your voice. 

Here's how to make sure your content sounds like you:

Step 1: Read everything out loud before you publish
↳ If it doesn't sound like something you'd actually say…
↳ Rewrite it. Remove any words that feel unnatural 

Step 2: Find your own vocabulary
↳ The words you use when you're excited or annoyed
↳ Write down 10 to 15 phrases you use in real conversation
↳ Add those words to your LinkedIn posts 

Step 3: Build a voice bank
↳ Record yourself talking about your content ideas
↳ Ask AI (or me) to convert that into a post 
↳ Include the phrases you repeat 

Step 4: Write like you text 
↳ Include abbreviations you use in text
↳ Include emojis that you’d add to texts 
↳ Keep it short, simple and concise 

Step 5: Never publish the first draft
↳ The first draft is what AI gives you
↳ The second draft is where your voice comes back
↳ Edit until it sounds like you then publish

AI is not there to replace your voice. 

It’s there to amplify it.

ECR. ECO. ECN.

Three acronyms that confuse 90% of engineers, manufacturers, and PLM professionals every single day.

Get them mixed up and you'll launch a product change with the wrong approval, the wrong stakeholders, and the wrong consequences.

Here's the difference, decoded simply:

𝗘𝗖𝗥 (𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁)
The "We need this change" stage.
Identifies a required product change. Triggered by a problem, defect, or improvement idea.
Owned by engineering or quality teams. Beginning of the change lifecycle.

𝗘𝗖𝗢 (𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿)
The "We approved and executed it" stage.
Approves and implements the change. Triggered by an approved ECR.
Owned by change control or engineering management. The execution phase.

𝗘𝗖𝗡 (𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗡𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲)
The "The updated change is now live" stage.
Notifies stakeholders about the released change. Triggered by a completed ECO.
Owned by operations or document control. Final communication phase.

𝗘𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿:
ECR asks: "What should change?"
ECO answers: "How will we execute it?"
ECN announces: "What has officially changed?"

The brutal truth:
Most product launches don't fail because of bad design.
They fail because someone confused an ECR with an ECN and made a million-dollar decision based on the wrong document.

The engineers who master change management aren't paid more because they design better.
They're paid more because their changes don't break production.

Which one trips up your team the most?

Both under-planning AND over-planning kill businesses.

Success lies in mastering 3 types of plans 👇

Founders love to hide behind over-planning because it feels productive.  
But “refining strategy” is not a good use of an entire quarter ! 

Planning can also keep you from the clarity that comes with taking action and adjusting. 

To be clear, I’m not saying “plan less”...
But I am saying “plan smarter.” 

While building my first business, Verb Brands (Adjust Media at the time), 
I had loads of ambition and passion, but no real structure. 

I knew roughly where I wanted to go, and we did move forward, 
But we were all over the road with no clear direction. 

This is how I wish I had been taught to plan my business back then 👇

🔭 Strategic Planning

This is where you decide what the business is actually trying to become. You need to look at the bigger picture, around 3-5 years out, and create specific goals.  

The hardest part of strategic planning is deciding what you won't do. Clarifying the direction and being specific will help you know when to say yes and when to step away. 

Review your strategy annually to make sure you’re on track ! 

📋 Tactical Planning

This is where strategy becomes projects the team can actually execute. Tactical planning bridges the gap between the vision and the daily work. 

You’ll need to allocate resources properly at this stage. 

The most common mistake here is spending 3 months planning and 1 month executing. You want to do the exact opposite. 

You really want to plan 1 to 3 years out and break deadlines down into quarterly milestones.

⚡ Operational Planning

This is your daily and weekly planning that will get adjusted most often. You’ll probably revisit this plan every week. 

Even with a brilliant strategy and a solid quarter mapped out, things can start to fall apart if you don’t have tangible operational plans. 

Keep your KPIs realistic here; there’s nothing less productive than overloading your team with unrealistic expectations. That’s where frequent adjustments can help. 

Nothing slows momentum like building with unclear intent.

And this 3-tier breakdown is by far the best way to clarify where you’re business is headed. 

The layers feed into each other, so you can’t realistically skimp on any of them. 

✅ Strategic planning is your destination. 
✅ Tactical planning maps the route. 
✅ Operational planning is how you actually drive.

A business is a complex ecosystem and there are 1000s of factors to success.

But proper planning is how good businesses become excellent.

Most companies are bleeding cash in 4 spots.

(And don't even know which wound to fix first.)

The brutal reality:

Every dollar leaving your business falls into one of these buckets:

OPERATIONS (OpEx) - The Daily Bleed
↳ Your rent, salaries, software subscriptions
↳ The money that vanishes every month
↳ Cut too deep? Your business stops tomorrow

ASSETS (CapEx) - The Big Bets
↳ That $50K machine, new warehouse, custom software
↳ Spend once, use for years
↳ Get it wrong? You're stuck with expensive mistakes

SALES (RevEx) - The Revenue Tax
↳ Every sale costs you something
↳ Materials, commissions, shipping, processing fees
↳ Ignore this? Profit margins turn into losses

MONEY (FinEx) - The Hidden Killer
↳ Interest on loans, bank fees, credit charges
↳ The cost of using other people's money
↳ Let it grow? It eats your profits alive

Let's look at 2 examples:

Coffee Shop Reality:
• OpEx: $15K/month (rent, barista wages, utilities)
• CapEx: $80K once (espresso machine, renovation)
• RevEx: $3 per cup sold (beans, cup, lid)
• FinEx: $500/month (equipment loan interest)

SaaS Startup Truth:
• OpEx: $50K/month (team, AWS, office)
• CapEx: $200K once (custom platform build)
• RevEx: $20 per customer (payment fees, onboarding)
• FinEx: $2K/month (venture debt interest)

Most founders lump all expenses together.
Then wonder why they can't scale.

But when you separate them?

OpEx → Find your true burn rate
CapEx → Time investments perfectly
RevEx → Price products profitably
FinEx → Optimize capital structure

Crucial insights:

✓ High OpEx? You're not scalable yet
✓ No CapEx? You're not building moats
✓ Rising RevEx? Your unit economics are broken
✓ Climbing FinEx? You're overleveraged

Common traps:

❌ Treating CapEx like OpEx (and vice versa)
❌ Ignoring RevEx when setting prices
❌ Letting FinEx compound silently
❌ Not tracking any of them separately

Watch what happens when you finally see where your money really goes.

Your future self will thank you.
Your investors will respect you.
Your business will actually scale.

Stop managing "expenses."
Start managing OpEx, CapEx, RevEx, and FinEx.

That's how you build something that lasts.

Our Mondays need love on Saturdays and Sundays. 

Here are 6 suggestions for a Miracle Monday Morning.

Most people treat the weekend as a time to check out. Binge, scroll, or simply drift. Then wonder why Monday hits like a truck.

But building a better Monday isn't about Sunday night panic. It's about how you set yourself up, before the week even starts.

Here's how I get ahead, without burning out:

1. Plan your upcoming week. Review your calendar. Don't just accept what's there, edit it like you mean it. Remove anything that's just noise. Add what deserves your attention. Make space for what actually moves you forward.

2. Identify one big thing you want to accomplish next week. Not just at work. Pick one for work, one for family, and one for yourself. When you wake up with a purpose, Monday isn't just another grind.

3. Give yourself a gift. Not for hitting a target or checking a box. Just for being you. Massage, movie, walk, a silent cup of coffee, something that feels like a reward from you to you.

4. Find time to truly connect. Weekdays are a blur, calls, emails, constant interruptions. Weekends give you back some control. Use it. Sit down for dinner, no screens. Break out a board game. Ask a real question and actually listen.

5. Catch up on sleep the right way. Not by sleeping in and feeling groggy, but by winding down and getting to bed early. Your Monday morning will feel completely different when you wake up rested, no bonus hours needed.

6. Journal the wins from last week. Take inventory of every role you play, parent, partner, leader, friend. Write down the small stuff. It all adds up. You'll realize you're building momentum, not just running in circles.

Nobody gets a Miracle Monday by accident. 
They're built on purpose, habit by habit, long before the alarm rings.

You can wait for motivation to show up, or you can make Monday yours, before anyone else even starts.

Welcome to the first-ever supply-driven freight market cycle

In a recent article, InTek Intermodal Logistics CEO Rick LaGore offers some interesting thoughts about the current freight market cycle. 

Unlike past market cycles, we're in a supply (v. demand) -led cycle. Although demand has largely remained flat, significant capacity has left the market: UPS restructured, FedEx Freight rationalized their network, and small/regional carriers simply shut down their businesses.

This cycle will require shippers to revisit their assumptions about capacity and cost. Most importantly, they shouldn't expect the market to self-correct as quickly as a demand-led cycle would. It takes a lot more time (and investment) to stand up new freight capacity than to 'unpark' existing equipment. Driver recruitment will play a role here as well.

I am often asked what did I gain/lose after moving to the US.

I gained a lifelong lesson. I lost my superhero cape.

For years, I thought working late was commitment.

Being the last person to leave was dedication.

Being available whenever someone needed me was leadership.

Then I moved to the US.

The change wasn't my choice. It was forced.

Most evenings, I had somewhere I needed to be.

Ira's Taekwondo.

Anaya's tennis.

Groceries to pick up.

A family commitment.

I couldn't rely on staying late to get everything done anymore.
And I didn't have house help or a support system.

So I had to change how I worked.

Prioritize harder.

Delegate more.

Trust people more.

Say no more often.

And focus my time where only I could add value.

Something unexpected happened.

I didn't become less effective.

I became more effective.

It made me question something I'd believed for years:

Sometimes, working long hours isn't commitment.

It's a sign we haven't built a system that works without our heroics.

I still work late when it truly matters.

But I don't wear it as a badge of honor.

Leadership isn't about being the hero.

It's about building a team that doesn't need one.

Leadership isn’t just what you do who you *become* in the process. It's about condintually developing yourself.

One month after IBF & ASCM's Best of the Best S&OP Conference in Chicago, one message continues to stand out:

S&OP is not just a process, it is a leadership capability.

My biggest takeaway: S&OP is far more than a monthly process for balancing demand and supply.

At its best, it is a business management capability that connects strategy to execution, aligns commercial, operations, finance and supply chain teams around shared assumptions, and enables faster, better-informed decisions.

From a supply chain consulting perspective, four themes stood out for me:

Technology and AI improve visibility, scenario modelling and decision-making speed, but they cannot compensate for poor data quality, unclear governance or weak collaboration.
- Technology and AI improve visibility, scenario modelling and decision-making speed, but they cannot compensate for poor data quality, unclear governance or weak collaboration.
- Resilience is built before disruption occurs. It requires scenario thinking, clear decision rights and a planning cadence that turns insight into action.
- The "one-number" mindset is not about forcing consensus; it is about fostering transparency, constructive challenge and accountability.
- Executive ownership is the difference between S&OP being a reporting exercise and becoming a true value-creation engine.

Thank you to Institute of Business Forecasting & Planning, ASCM, Eric Wilson, Abe Eshkenazi and all the speakers for sharing valuable insights and practical experiences across industries and maturity levels.

The question is no longer whether organisations need S&OP/IBP. The real question is: Does your process help leaders make better decisions when uncertainty increases?

Where do you see the biggest barrier to S&OP maturity today: data, process, technology or leadership alignment?

How to master Claude Fable 5 in only 15 steps:

(Send it to your team. They're burning credits)

1. Pick one super hard, expensive problem.
"Rewrite this email" is shooting a bird with a bazooka. Bring Fable a hard decision, a research report, a mess only a genius untangles.

2. Open a new Claude chat.
Fable re-reads the entire thread with every message - and you pay for every re-read. 
New task, new chat. No exceptions.

3. Select Fable 5 → Effort High.
Save "Max" effort for the truly brutal jobs. 
Thinking time costs credits too.

4. Paste your "about-me" doc.
AI is average by default - trained on everyone, so it answers like everyone. Keep one Google Doc: who you are, what you do, how you write. Paste it first.

5. Give it your goal, not a task.
The template: "I need [task] for [goal]. I expect [goal] achieved once we hit [specific targets]."

6. Add to the first prompt: "Ask me questions first."
Exact Prompt: "Start by asking me questions about the task, goal & targets to fully understand the context."

7. Add this to a prompt: "Answer first, explain after."
Now the first sentence of every follow up prompt is the bottom line. No more scrolling through methodology to find your answer.

8. Add: "Don't say done. Prove it."
Exact prompt: "Only report work you can point to evidence for. If something is not verified, say so."
This removes the fake "all done!" reports. Same standard you'd hold a new hire to.

9. Add: "Pick one option. Commit."
Exact prompt: "When you have enough information to act, act. Give me a recommendation, not a survey of options." You want a verdict, not a menu.

10. Send it. Answer its questions.
It asks 3-4 sharp ones. This 2-minute interview decides the quality of everything after.

11. Let it work. Don't interrupt.
Every "oh wait, also-" makes it re-read the whole thread. I paid $14 for one chat learning this.

12. Stop after 2 messages.
Fable's job is the genius part: the plan, the strategy, the hard call. That's it.

13. Switch to Opus 4.8 (High). Same chat.
Model menu → switch. Opus is included in your plan & it reads everything Fable just planned.
(Cowork can't switch mid-chat. Annoying, I know)

14. Finish everything there.
Drafts, edits, the 20-message back-and-forth: all on Opus. That's the free part.

15. Save it all in a Project.
Your files and instructions live there permanently. Tomorrow's session starts warm, not from zero.

Fable 5 thinks for 2 prompts. Opus 4.8 does the rest

----

One last thing.

I built a Skill that writes these prompts FOR you.
It's called /fable-prompter. You hand it a lazy idea. 
It gives you an optimised prompt.

Here's how to get it (takes 3 minutes):

1. Subscribe to my free newsletter: how-to-ai.guide.
2. You will receive an email. 
3. Click the Notion Library link mentioned inside. 
4. The /fable-prompter file is inside.
5. Go to Claude settings → Skills ("Capabilities").
6. Click + and upload the file. Toggle it on.
7. Open a chat. Type /fable-prompter + your idea.

PLM is the spine of the entire product lifecycle.

When PLM is weak, everything downstream breaks:
BOMs drift.
Manufacturing improvises.
Quality reacts late.
Costs spiral silently.

PLM isn’t a tool.
It’s a system of record + system of flow.

Here’s what a real end-to-end PLM architecture actually looks like:

At the center sits the 𝗣𝗟𝗠 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺
→ the single source of product truth.

- 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 & 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲
Parts, BOMs, CAD, documents, metadata, variants, lifecycle states - all structured, versioned, and classified.

- 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 & 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹
Change management, approvals, audit trails, access control, compliance.
This is what keeps engineering sane at scale.

- 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗣𝗟𝗠 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀
Versioning, ECO/ECR workflows, validation, digital signatures - the plumbing nobody sees until it’s missing.

- 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀
PLM doesn’t work alone:
ERP, MES, CRM, SCM, QMS, ALM, Simulation, BI - all feed in and out.

- 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄
Engineering → Manufacturing → Operations
EBOM → MBOM → Process plans → Shopfloor data → Quality → Service.

- 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀
Master data for structure
Transactional data for execution
Analytics for decisions.

This is how products stay consistent from design to field usage.
This is how changes stop becoming disasters.
This is how scale actually works.

PLM done right isn’t overhead.
It’s leverage.

I wrote these 6 Claude formulas for my team.

Nobody's allowed to skip them (including you):

FORMULA 1. Delete your "about-me" text file.

I asked you to create the text file, but later I realised Claude re-read it before every single task.

Turn it into a skill instead:

→ Open a Claude chat. Upload your old file.
→ Prompt: "Turn this into a skill I invoke with /about-me. Trim it under 2,000 words. Ask me questions"
→ Save. Now it loads only when you call it.

Download my file from here: how-to-ai.guide to get started (the link in the email after subscribing)

FORMULA 2. Skills + Projects. Nothing else.

The test my team runs on every workflow:

You can teach it to someone → Skill.
It's a client or a campaign → Project.

The move nobody does: combine them.

/contract skill, inside the client's Project, with Gmail connected. Claude drafts the contract in your style, with the client's real context, quoting the actual email thread.

FORMULA 3. No settings are the best settings.

Turn off Memory. Leave Global Instructions empty. Keep Connectors on. Done.

Too much context sends Claude in circles. Same answer, every time. Fine when you draft the same contract weekly. Death when you brainstorm.

FORMULA 4. Make Claude ask YOU.

"I want [task] to [success criteria]. Ask me questions using AskUserQuestion before you start."

The part most people miss: this trick is infinite. When Claude hallucinates mid-chat, say "ask more questions." It keeps asking until failing is impossible.

FORMULA 5. Fable on Low. Opus on High.

Fable-5 runs on usage credits: $0.15 for a question, $14 if you let a session run long. I tested. I paid.

So: Fable on Low effort, your 2 hardest turns only. Then switch the model mid-chat to Opus 4.8 on High. It's included in your plan.

FORMULA 6. Edit. Don't follow up.

Message 30 costs 31x more than message 1. Claude re-reads everything, every turn.

So never type "no, I meant..."

Click Edit on your prompt. Everything after it disappears. Or click "Restart the conversation from here" and go as high up as you can.

BONUS: 3 formulas that didn't fit on the image.

FORMULA 7. Batch your tasks. 
3 prompts = 3 full re-reads. 
"Summarize this, list the main points, suggest a headline" = 1 message, 1 read, better answer.

FORMULA 8. Speak. Don't type. 
You type 60 words a minute. You talk 150. 
Dictate your prompts using wispr .ai and Claude gets double the context in one shot.

FORMULA 9. Chat. Code. Cowork. 
A quick question → Chat. 
Software → Code. 
Anything document-shaped → Cowork.

Every LinkedIn poster's enemy: staring at a blank page. 

Here are 9 ways to trick your brain into posting anyway: 

You promise yourself you'll get to it later, then later turns into next week.
Then next week turns into a month of silence on a feed you said you'd take seriously this year.

I've been there. 

I've spent years posting on LinkedIn every single day. 
And I've had plenty of days where I've stared at the cursor for an hour and walked away with nothing.

So I put together the 10 things I do when nothing is coming. 
Tiered by effort so you know what you're scrolling into:

🟢 Easy (30-second warm-ups)

1. Look at your camera roll

The last 20 photos on your phone are 20 post ideas. 
Pick the most random one and write what was going on.

2. Go back to the last DM that made you think

The answer you typed out at 11 pm is already the content.
Paste it as the body, write a hook that sets up the question someone asked you, and you've got a post in 10 minutes.

3. Steal a line from one of your favourite books

Grab your favourite book and pull a line you've underlined or gone back to more than once.
Use it as your opening, then write the post as if the idea were yours.

You'll end up somewhere different from where the line started.

🟡 Medium (a bit more thinking):

4. Use your industry's most talked about topics and reports

Find the report, survey, or stat everyone in your space is already sharing.
Skip the recap and give your own take on what it means for your ICP.

5. Borrow a line from a post that stopped your scroll

Use it as the starting point for your own version.
Take the angle, rewrite it in your own words, and add the example or framework the original was missing.

6. Write the follow-up to your best post last month

Your audience already told you what they want more of.
Take the same theme and go a layer deeper. 

Add the tactical breakdown, a case study, or the thing you didn't have space for the first time.

🔴 Hard (deeper work, higher reward):

7. Write the post you wish existed when you started

Think back to a specific problem you couldn't solve in year 1.
Write the post that past-you would have screenshotted.

8. Find a stat from your business and write backwards

Pick a number or an outcome, then unpack what led to it.
Be honest about the mess behind it, and you'll get the comments and saves.

9. Answer the objection you hear most

Write the pushback you get the most often, then write the answer you always give back.
It's a post and a script at the same time.

Pick one and try it the next time you open the app with nothing.

What do you do when you can't think of anything to post?

💾 Save this for the next blank page moment.

And follow me, Josh S., for more.

I dreaded negotiations early in my career.

Then I realized:

You don’t have to be confrontational
to be a strong negotiator.

All it takes is using the right frameworks.

Here are 5 proven approaches to negotiate
every deal more effectively:

🤝 The 4 Phases Framework
(h/t: Roy Lewicki)

Great negotiators don’t jump straight to bargaining. 
They follow a structured process:

• Preparation (lay the groundwork)
• Information Exchange (build mutual understanding)
• Bargaining (explore potential solutions)
• Commitment (secure the agreement)

💪 The BATNA Strategy
(h/t: Roger Fisher & William Ury)

Your power in any negotiation comes from knowing 
your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement (BATNA).

It’s your safety net, your source of confidence. 
Always define it before you start.

🎯 The Negotiation Matrix
(h/t: Lewicki & Hiam)

Different situations call for different strategies:

• High stakes? Compete.
• Building a long-term relationship? Collaborate.
• Minor issue? Avoidance might be best.
• The relationship is too critical? Accommodate.
• Both matter equally? Compromise.

🤔 The Harvard Principled Negotiation Method
(h/t: Fisher, Ury & Patton)

This is a game-changer:
Focus on interests, not positions.

Instead of asking what they want, ask why they want it.

That’s where real value creation happens.

🎯 The ZOPA Framework
(h/t: Fisher & Ury)

The Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA) is where deals get made.

Understanding both sides’ limits helps you identify common ground. 

Everything else? It's just noise.

Key takeaway:

The best deals happen when both sides feel heard.

And the most successful negotiators aren’t the most aggressive.

They’re simply the most prepared.

Most people are using AI more. 
They're not using it better.

That's the gap nobody talks about.

You open ChatGPT or Claude, type something vague, get something generic, and assume that's just how it works.

You copy-paste the output without a second read.

You trust a confident answer that turns out to be completely wrong.

You hand over sensitive data without thinking twice.

And then you wonder why AI isn't saving you as much time as everyone says it should.

Here's what I've seen after 16 years in marketing: 
The tool is rarely the problem.

The habits around the tool are.

Running marketing, 
We went through this exact learning curve as a team.

The people getting the most out of AI weren't the most technical.

They were the ones who treated it like a skilled junior colleague: useful, fast, but needing clear direction and a final check.

30 mistakes I'd tell every marketer and operator to eliminate right now:

→ Trusting AI blindly instead of verifying important claims 

→ Skipping fact checks on AI-generated answers 

→ Writing vague prompts and expecting specific outputs 

→ Giving AI no context about your goal or audience 

→ Accepting hallucinations as facts 

→ Sharing passwords or confidential business data with AI tools 

→ Ignoring sources and assuming claims are verified 

→ Treating AI as an expert instead of a powerful assistant 

→ Replacing search engines entirely with AI for factual research 

→ Mistaking a well-written answer for a correct one 

→ Publishing AI content without a human review pass 

→ Not asking AI to explain its reasoning or show its sources 

→ Stopping after one prompt instead of iterating 

→ Giving broad instructions when specific ones get far better results 

→ Ignoring what AI genuinely cannot do 

→ Copy-pasting AI output directly without editing for your voice 

→ Expecting perfection from a tool that still needs human oversight 

→ Using outdated data without checking whether it's still current 

→ Ignoring the audience when prompting, and getting generic content 

→ Bundling too many tasks into one prompt 

→ Automating AI outputs without testing or reviewing them 

→ Assuming AI knows what you want without telling it clearly 

→ Ignoring bias baked into training data 

→ Using AI to replace your thinking instead of sharpen it 

→ Not asking for structured outputs like frameworks or checklists 

→ Failing to define what a good result actually looks like 

→ Trusting AI citations without checking the actual source 

Use AI as a copilot that accelerates your work, not an autopilot that replaces your responsibility.
