🎭 Lean Theatre vs. Real Lean — Part 2
Last week I wrote about Lean Theatre.

𝘔𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘴𝘢𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨:

“𝘐 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘸𝘦’𝘳𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘳𝘦… 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘥𝘰 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘱?”

The answer isn’t another tool.

It’s changing the questions leaders ask.

Most organizations are full of leaders who ask:
❌ Is the KPI green?
❌ Did everyone attend the meeting?
❌ Was the audit completed?
❌ Is the action plan finished?

Those questions create compliance.
Lean leaders ask different questions.

Instead of asking:
“Who made the mistake?”

they ask:
“What in the process allowed this to happen?”

Instead of:
“Did we complete the improvement project?”

they ask:
“What capability did we build?”

Instead of:
“Who owns this problem?”

they ask:
“Who learned to solve it?”

Because Lean isn’t about fixing today’s issue.
It’s about making tomorrow’s problem easier to solve.

𝘛𝘩𝘢𝘵’𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘺 𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘭𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘨𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘴…
…𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴.

Not because they don’t know the answer.
Because every answer they give creates dependency.

Every good question builds capability.
The real measure of leadership isn’t:

“How many problems did I solve today?”

It’s:
“How many problems can my team solve tomorrow without me?”

That shift changes everything.
Meetings become coaching sessions.
KPIs become learning tools.
Gemba becomes a classroom.
Managers become teachers.

And improvement stops being an event…
…and becomes the way people think.

Lean has never been about creating experts.
It’s about creating thousands of expert problem solvers.

That’s how organizations become resilient.

Not because leaders are always present.

But because capability is.

Question for leaders:
Think about the last problem your team brought to you.

Did you give them the answer…
…or did you help them discover it?

The difference is where Lean begins.

#Lean #Leadership #OperationalExcellence #ContinuousImprovement #Gemba #LeanManagement #Coaching #ProblemSolving #RespectForPeople #LeanCulture

⭐️1️⃣0️⃣ Qualities That Define an Exceptional Lean Manager!

Lean is often misunderstood as a collection of tools to reduce waste or improve efficiency. In reality, Lean is a way of thinking. The best Lean managers don’t simply implement processes they build cultures where people continuously solve problems, improve performance, and create value for customers.

🎯🌱Here are the 10 qualities that separate great Lean managers from the rest.

 1️⃣ They Lead by Example

A Lean manager never asks others to do what they wouldn’t do themselves. They demonstrate discipline, respect, accountability, and a commitment to continuous improvement through their own actions every day.

2️⃣ They Focus on Customer Value

Every decision starts with one question: Does this create value for the customer? Lean managers eliminate activities that don’t add value and ensure teams stay focused on what truly matters.

3️⃣ They Respect People

Lean is built on respect. Successful Lean leaders listen actively, empower employees, encourage ideas, and create an environment where everyone feels responsible for improvement.

4️⃣ They Embrace CI

The journey is never finished. Lean managers understand that every process can be improved, regardless of how well it performs today. Small, consistent improvements often lead to extraordinary results over time.

5️⃣ They Solve Problems at the Root Cause

Instead of treating symptoms, Lean managers investigate the real causes behind issues. They use structured problem-solving methods to prevent problems from recurring rather than repeatedly fixing the same mistakes.

6️⃣ They Make Decisions Based on Facts

Data guides decisions not assumptions. Effective Lean managers spend time observing processes, gathering evidence, and understanding reality before implementing solutions.

7️⃣ They Develop People

One of the greatest responsibilities of a Lean manager is coaching others. They invest in developing skills, encouraging learning, and helping employees become confident problem solvers.

8️⃣ They Communicate Clearly

Transparency builds trust. Lean managers share goals, expectations, performance metrics, and challenges openly, ensuring everyone understands priorities and how their work contributes to success.

9️⃣ They Think Systemically

Lean managers recognize that optimizing one department while hurting another is not improvement. They understand how processes connect across the entire value stream and focus on improving the whole system.

🔟 They Stay Humble and Curious

The best Lean leaders know they don’t have all the answers. They ask questions, seek feedback, learn from failures, and remain open to new ideas. Their curiosity drives innovation and continuous learning.

🔔 Lesson learned 

Lean management is not about achieving perfection, it’s about pursuing it every single day. The most effective Lean managers combine technical knowledge with strong leadership, empathy, and a genuine passion for developing people.

🔔The Biggest Mistake Many Organizations Keep Making

I’ve seen it too many times, and it still surprises me.

A company is struggling with poor quality, customer complaints, and rising operational costs. The cost of poor quality reaches millions every year.

So what does management do?

They decide to reduce costs by letting go of their most experienced experts the very people who understand the processes, know the customers, and have spent years solving complex problems.

Why?

Because they are “too expensive.”
Instead, they hire less experienced people simply because they cost less.
On paper, it looks like a smart financial decision.

💥In reality, it’s often one of the most expensive decisions an organization can make.

𝘌𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘢 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵.
𝘐𝘵 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵.

𝘞𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘭𝘬𝘴 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘰𝘳, 𝘴𝘰 𝘥𝘰 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘭𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘥, 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮-𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘴, 𝘤𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘳 𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺. 𝘛𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨𝘴 𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘣𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵.

Unfortunately, I see the same pattern with Lean.

Leadership announces a Lean transformation because they want better performance and lower costs.

But instead of investing in experienced Lean professionals who can build a sustainable culture, they hire the cheapest option just to show that “something is happening.”

Lean is not about ticking a box.
Lean is not about hiring the lowest bidder.

𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬𝘴, 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘰𝘶𝘴𝘭𝘺 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘴. 𝘛𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘲𝘶𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘴 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦, 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦, 𝘤𝘰𝘢𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺.

Choosing someone simply because they are cheaper may save money today but it often creates much bigger costs tomorrow:
♨️More quality issues.
♨️More customer complaints.
♨️More rework.
♨️More firefighting.
♨️Lower employee engagement.
♨️Lost customer trust.

The irony?

𝘖𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘧𝘪𝘹𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘺 𝘬𝘦𝘦𝘱𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘰𝘳 𝘩𝘪𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘦.


𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘲𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴, 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘴𝘦 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯.

𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘧𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨.

And eventually, the bill always arrives.

The question is:

LinkedIn creators aren’t fighting the algorithm. 
They’re fighting 4 much bigger challenges.

If you’re posting consistently and still feel invisible, it’s probably not your “content quality”. 
Nope, I think it's the system you’re trying to win in.

4 Real challenges most LinkedIn creators are facing right now👇

1. Reach is collapsing while effort is exploding 
   You post more, you engage more… and your impressions still go down. The feed is overcrowded, attention is fragmented, and LinkedIn quietly prioritises formats that keep people scrolling and clicking, not thinking. Result: High‑effort posts get the same reach as low‑effort “engagement bait” and creators burn out.
   
2. The platform wants creators, but isn’t built for them 
   LinkedIn talks about “supporting creators”, but most tools still serve recruiters, advertisers and B2B sales teams first. External links are punished (don't tell me they aren't because some person at LinkedIn says they aren't), analytics are still pretty basic, and there’s no real creator‑centric infrastructure for audience ownership or monetisation. You’re building a brand on rented land, with very limited control over what gets seen and by whom.
   
3. Format shift is happening faster than skill shift 
   Carousel posts are no longer the default power format. Text only, video, visual storytelling and “multi‑touch” content loops win. In the meantime most creators still operate like it’s 2024. The gap between “I can write a post” and “I can architect a content system” is where a lot of reach and revenue is currently dying.
   
4. Engagement doesn’t equal business outcomes anymore 
   It’s now very possible to have big numbers and small pipelines. The feed rewards emotional stories, but most creators don’t have a clear path from post → profile → product → pipeline Likes, comments and followers feel good… until you realise they’re not paying your invoices.

If you’re creating content on LinkedIn please keep this in mind:
You don’t need more content. You need a better content economy around you:

• Clear positioning instead of random topics
• A portfolio of formats, not just text posts
• A distribution & relationship strategy beyond the feed
• A monetisation path that turns attention into opportunity
  
I’m curious: Which of these 4 challenges is hitting you the hardest right now—1, 2, 3 or 4?

Drop the number in the comments and I’ll reply with one practical fix you can implement this week.

Many say the RFP process is "used to get the best possible price". 

I'm sorry. It’s not. Even Wikipedia is wrong.

I don’t like semantic battles

And I know many in Procurement are being tasked with cutting costs for Q3 of 2026

Particularly with the continued bleak economic forecasts and widely held viewpoint that AI can drive efficiency savings. 

But if you employ that approach to assess outcomes, the most likely long term one for your business is failure.

So, what exactly is an RFP used for? 

RFP is short for “Request for Proposal.” 

But perhaps it should be rebadged as “Request for Partnership”.

The goal of an RFP is to evaluate multiple options and get the maximum return on any investment your business makes.

It's about learning what’s available as efficiently and objectively as possible. 

Maximising value while minimising risk. 

Not creating a low cost MVP solution for your business.

The evaluation stages of an RFP often cause greatest confusion. 

Once the RFP has been sent to suppliers, many evaluate the responses based on pre conceived criteria of ‘what good looks like’.

And the worst go on to over inflate the importance of cost while completely dismissing the significance of value.

In a Vendr interview here https://lnkd.in/g9S86SKH

re-evaluation of key performance indicators (KPIs) is discussed, particularly the shift away from focusing solely on cost savings.

Dr. Elouise Epstein advocates for using revenue as a more effective guiding metric and turning cost centres into profit centres where possible. 

Another approach I heard recently and loved is using the term "solutions workshops," rather than supplier or product demos when it comes to the presentations in an RFP.

The emphasis being on collaborating with suppliers to learn and develop understanding

Rather than pitching suppliers against each other in a race of doom to the bottom.

The executive meeting does not rescue a weak S&OP cycle. It exposes where the hand-offs stopped.

Once Operations reopens the capacity assumptions, Finance starts rebuilding the gap to plan, and Commercial explains what moved, the meeting is no longer choosing between prepared options. It is reconstructing the pre-work with the executive team already in the room.

Where I think the process often breaks is in the hand-off between reviews. A review can happen on time, use the right template, and still leave the next team with work it cannot use.

The data can be accurate, but the exceptions may have no owner. Demand can agree a number that has not been tested against supply. Supply can produce feasible options without showing the service or financial consequence. Integrated reconciliation can quantify the gap and still arrive without a recommendation.

In each case, the review happened but the actual hand-off did not.

The exact review names and ownership will vary between businesses, but the operating test is useful: each review should remove avoidable uncertainty from the next decision.

Before an unresolved issue enters the meeting, I would want four things visible:

• Evidence: what changed, and what do we trust?
• Owner: who is accountable for moving it?
• Options: what can the business genuinely choose?
• Ask: what decision requires executive authority?

Think about your last executive S&OP: which discussion arrived with a well-described problem, but no choice the room could actually make?

Excess, Obsolete & Dead Stock: When Inventory Stops Creating Value
Not all inventory is an asset.
When products sit too long without demand, they consume space, tie up cash, and quietly reduce profitability.
📊 Key Metrics
 Excess Inventory = Inventory On Hand − Expected Demand
Obsolete Inventory (%)  = (Obsolete Inventory Value ÷ Total Inventory Value) × 100
Dead Stock (%) = (Dead Stock Value ÷ Total Inventory Value) × 100
Why It Matters:
💰 Increases carrying costs
🏢 Occupies valuable warehouse space
📉 Reduces inventory turnover
🔒 Locks up working capital
🗑️ Leads to write-offs and losses
🎯 How to Reduce It
✅ Improve demand forecasting
✅ Review slow-moving SKUs regularly
✅ Optimize reorder parameters
✅ Run promotions for aging inventory
✅ Rationalize low-performing products
Inventory creates value only when it moves.
The longer stock sits idle, the more it transforms from an asset into a liability.

"Women are too emotional for business", my last boss said to my face. So I sent him the most emotional exit email of his life:

In 2024, this man hired me to run marketing for his company. He wanted me as his cofounder.

On paper, a dream. In reality, he:

- Called me greedy for asking to split the equity fairly
- Mocked our female stakeholders behind their backs
- Asked me to disclose my autism diagnosis live on a client call, as proof I "overreact"

The last one I still feel in my chest. Him, smiling like he'd made a joke. Me, swallowing every word so I wouldn't prove him right.

The money never added up either. Figures I couldn't reconcile, questions he waved away. 

Every time I pushed, he shrank it. So I shrank myself to match.

That's what gaslighting does, right? You stop trusting your gut and start believing you're the problem.

So I did for months. Until the day he said it again. Then I did get emotional. Very. I sent an email saying:

- Keep your stinking shares. I don't want a cent of 'em
- You still owe me $21K on an unpaid invoice
- I learned a lot from you, but f*ck, I'm out

This unemotional man blocked me everywhere within the hour. Said he wouldn't pay. Waved off $83K of unpaid labor like it was pocket change.

That week, I posted my first emotional LinkedIn piece.

Today, I've made 20x what he still refuses to pay me. I did it by being a very emotional woman.

Highly profitable, these female instincts. ✌️

I run my entire business from a 14-inch laptop.

My small screen opened up a big world.

This year alone I've been flown out to Serbia, a mastermind in Guangzhou, China, and a conference in Amsterdam. End of the month, London, for something exciting with the Kleo team.

My team is spread across 4 countries. Most of them are friends from school, university, or family. Remote since day 1. And the business has tripled while I've been on the road this year.

And none of it would exist without the same technology we all complain about.

We all love to complain about this new reality. Phones glued to our hands, brains fried by notifications, can't sit through a meal without checking something.

But sometimes I forget how insane it is that this is even possible.

20 years ago, a girl from Medellín, Colombia with no network, no money, and no connections in the rooms that matter would have been stuck. You either knew the right people or you didn't.

Today you can land in a country where you know nobody, open your laptop, post on LinkedIn, and 6 months later be on stage at a conference on the other side of the world.

I don't think we're grateful enough for how insane this is.

The internet is the most level playing field that's ever existed. Your zip code doesn't decide your ceiling anymore. Your content does.

If you've been sitting on the idea of starting, posting, building something online, this is your sign. The window has never been more open.

I'm building a community of people doing exactly this inside The LinkedIn Engine → https://lnkd.in/ecb5awAT

PS: yes, my screen is orange. It's flux, a blue light filter app. 10/10 recommend for better sleep.

Most marketers are using AI to write content.

The ones pulling ahead are using it to think.

There's a difference. 
A big one.

Writing is output. 
Thinking is the thing that shapes the output.

And most of us never got trained to think systematically. 
We got trained to move fast, react, and trust our gut.

I spent 16 years in marketing rooms doing exactly that. 
And honestly? 
The gut was right a lot of the time.

But there were also moments where I'd spend three meetings going in circles on a problem that had a clear answer. 
We just weren't asking the right questions.

That's what this infographic is about.

Not prompts for creating a caption or a campaign brief. 
Prompts for breaking down the actual problems that slow your team down.

These are the 20 I keep coming back to:

→ Root Cause Analysis: Stop treating symptoms. 
Use the Five Whys and fix what's actually broken. 

→ Stuck Problem Reframe: When you've been spinning on something for weeks, this forces you to ask if you're solving the wrong problem entirely. 

→ Decision Framework: Two options, unclear answer. 
This one structures the trade-offs so you can actually pick. 

→ Constraint Solver: When resources are limited, this finds what's possible inside those limits instead of assuming they're walls. 

→ Scenario Planning: Best case, worst case, most likely case. 
Right response to each. 

→ Expert Perspective Simulation: Get three expert lenses on one problem. 
Synthesised into one recommendation. 

→ Trade-off Navigator: Stops you from pretending all your priorities are equal. 

→ Information Gap Identifier: Know what you don't know. 
Rank it by impact. 
Decide anyway. 

→ Failure Mode Mapping: Map how a plan breaks before it breaks. 
Not after. 

→ First Principles Breakdown: Question the assumption the whole approach is built on. 

→ Prioritization Under Pressure: When the list is long and time isn't, this forces the call. 
→ Feedback Loop Diagnosis: Your process keeps producing the same bad result. 
This finds why. 

→ Complexity Reduction: When a problem feels too big to start, this gives you a model and a first step. 

→ Second-Order Thinking: What happens after the thing you planned happens? 

→ Post-Mortem for Future Prevention: Not just what went wrong. 
Why it'll happen again if you don't change something now.

Running marketing, 
I wish I'd had these structured prompts earlier. 
Not because we lacked brainpower. 
Because we lacked a consistent way to apply it.

"If we forecast per product, we won't be able to use the forecasts we receive from our customers!"

Customers' forecasts are often trusted blindly and rarely measured. 
Their Forecast Value Added (FVA) should be tracked like any other input. 

Each time we measure their FVA for our clients we realize that, 
1. Customers' forecasts are less accurate than our ML model (and barely more than a moving average).
2. They are highly variable (2-3x more than our model)
3. It takes a lot of (manual) processing time to collect and format these forecasts (which are often inconsistent)

So, why bother? 

If you really think these customers' forecasts can help, measure their added value.

I analyzed 98,611 LinkedIn posts (I’ve helped write).  

The top performers have this in common: 

1. They use a visual

🌠 Image posts outperform text-only by 1.6x
🌠 Carousels and text get shared more
🌠 Polls and articles are bottom of the list

2. Write longer posts

✍️ The sweet spot is 1,200 to 1,800 characters
✍️ 2.7x the engagement of posts under 200 chars
✍️ Longer posts earn longer dwell time

3. Format for scanning

✅ 41+ line breaks vs 1-5 line breaks = 5x gap in engagement
✅ White space is not wasted space
✅ One idea per line

4. Keep the hook short

🪝 Your hook should fit on one line
🪝 Under 60 characters outperforms by 2x
🪝 First line hooks, second line rehooks

5. Ask questions

❓ End every post with a question
❓ Make it easy to answer in one or two words
❓ 4+ questions pull 60% more comments than posts with 0

6. Drop the hashtags
# No hashtags vs 7+ hashtags = 39% higher engagement
# Hashtags do not increase your reach
# They make your post look spammy

7. Never put links in the post

🔗 The algo punishes you for sending people away
🔗 One link in the post = 43% engagement drop
🔗 Always put the link in the first comment

8. Time it right

🕐 Engagement drops 1.6x by 10pm
🕐 Weekday mornings peak at 6 to 7am local time
🕐 Weekends run 17% below the weekday median

The biggest finding:

Nail all eight fundamentals and you get 8x the engagement of someone who nails none.

They stack.

Every habit adds up.

eAuctions are the most misused tool in the sourcing toolkit... Here's what you need to know.

Most teams reach for eAuctions to "squeeze suppliers"...
  
Then wonder why the savings vanish and the relationship sours.

The same failures play out over and over again:

→ Fuzzy specs, so nobody can bid apples-to-apples
→ Launch day arrives... and nobody shows up (or hates you for it)
→ A strategic partner treated like an interchangeable vendor
→ Weeks of work... Trust quietly torched... Swearing off eAuctions forever.

The tool isn't broken. It's pointed at the wrong target.

The real question isn't "can we auction this?"

For beginners, it's "does this category fit an auction, and did we run the RFP first?"

Here's the shift most teams miss:

Yes, you can run an eAuction instead of an RFP...

For truly commoditized spot buys with decent volumes, it's a fast, repeatable play.

(If "one-off widgets", just use a marketplace!)

But if that's the only way you use them, you're capping the value you can pull out.

Or worse, you'll use them in situations where you're hurting things rather than improving them...
  
The bigger, safer unlock on your learning journey: run the RFP first, and let the eAuction replace the best-and-final-offer process that comes after it.
  
That way you keep a backup position, protect the relationship, and true-up bids before anyone races to the bottom.

My response was that I always classify based on what you’re buying from the supplier. So, if the parts/spares are included as part of the service or maintenance, then I would classify it as a service.

Output quality drops as the context window fills up.

The second or third is almost always what you actually needed.

“Dress for the role you want, not the one you have.”

Great advice then. I’m less sure now. 

A mentor gave me this advice years ago.

Maybe today, I would change just one word.

Don’t DRESS for the role you want.

BEHAVE for the role you want.

And by “behave,” I don’t mean acting important.

I mean demonstrating the behaviors the next role demands.

If you want a bigger role:

Stop waiting to be told what to do.
Start spotting problems before they reach you.

Stop optimizing only for your function.
Start thinking about what is best for the enterprise.

Stop escalating every difficult decision.
Start making thoughtful calls with incomplete information.

Stop measuring success only by your own results.
Start making the people around you more successful.

Stop building relationships only when you need something.
Start investing in trust before you need it.

Stop asking, “Is this my responsibility?”
Start asking, “What does the business need from me?”

Because promotions rarely make you ready for bigger roles.

More often, you demonstrate readiness first.

The title catches up later.

Maybe the new career advice is:

Behave for the role you want, not the one you have.

The White House announced three new Executive Orders using Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a trade authority that has rarely been used.

Here's what supply chain leaders need to know:
- A new 50% tariff will apply to certain Canadian goods.
- The tariffs apply even if the product qualifies under USMCA.
- Effective August 19, 2026
- 3 proclamations cover products ranging from wine and spirits to sporting goods, building materials, and other Canadian imports.

Important exclusions include:
- Energy products
- Potash
- Products already subject to Section 232 tariffs
- Certain fish products
- Certain critical minerals

The Administration says the action is intended to respond to what it considers discriminatory Canadian treatment of US exports, particularly involving:
→ Automobiles
→ Alcoholic beverages
→ Dairy

One final highlight: Section 338 does not have a built-in expiration date. Once these tariffs take effect, they remain in force until they are modified or revoked.

Last week we talked about Set in Order — giving everything a fixed home so anyone can find anything in seconds. This week: Shine.
Most MSME owners hear "Shine (Seiso)" and think it's just a cleaning schedule. It isn't. Shine is inspection disguised as cleaning — the moment you wipe down a machine is the moment you're close enough to spot the leak, the loose bolt, the hairline crack that a walk-by glance would miss.
Here's the exercise I ask every MSME owner to try: → Pick one machine or workstation and assign a single owner to it → Have them clean it thoroughly for 15 minutes today — and log every abnormality they find: leaks, loose fasteners, unusual noise, wear marks → Photograph the "before" state → Repeat in 7 days, and count how many issues were caught before they became breakdowns
The payoff shows up fast. Teams that run this consistently catch small failures weeks before they'd otherwise cause unplanned downtime — and the cost of a 15-minute inspection is nothing next to an emergency repair.
Here's the harder truth: in most shops, cleaning is treated as the junior-most task on the floor — something you hand off, not something you own. Flip that, and your operators become your earliest warning system, not just your cleanup crew.
Sort removes what doesn't belong. Set in Order gives what's left a home. Shine turns your equipment into something that tells you when it's about to fail — before it does.

People sometimes ask me where I normally find the biggest opportunities to improve a manufacturing business.

It's an interesting question because, after more than four decades in industry, the answer is almost never what people expect.

Many imagine I arrive with a checklist of supplier costs to reduce or contracts to renegotiate. Those things certainly have their place, but they rarely tell the whole story. More often than not, the clues appear long before I've looked at a single purchase order.

I remember walking around a factory with a Managing Director who was understandably proud of what he'd built. The order book was healthy, the machines were busy and there was an obvious sense of commitment from the people working there. If you'd driven past the building, you would probably have assumed everything was running exactly as it should.

As we talked, I noticed a forklift driver making the same journey backwards and forwards between two departments. Nobody seemed particularly concerned because it had become part of the daily routine. A little later, I watched a supervisor leave a production meeting because someone needed a decision that only he could make. Then an operator stopped work for a few minutes while waiting for clarification about the next job.

None of those moments lasted very long and none of them would have appeared on the monthly management report but they all had something in common: They represented tiny interruptions that had quietly become accepted as normal.

That's the thing about manufacturing businesses. They rarely lose significant profit because of one catastrophic mistake. More often, profit disappears through hundreds of perfectly ordinary habits that nobody has questioned for years.

When you've worked in the same business every day, it's remarkably easy to stop seeing what is right in front of you. We all do it. Familiarity has a way of disguising inefficiency.

That is one of the reasons I enjoy carrying out Business Performance Reviews. The most rewarding moment isn't producing the report. It's the owner's reaction when they suddenly notice something they've walked past every day for years.

Those moments often become the beginning of meaningful change.

From my own experience, one lesson my career has taught me is that factories rarely need heroes. They need systems that make it easier for good people to do good work. Once those systems improve, profitability usually follows.

Image generate by AI.

The planning system had all the data. Just not in a way anyone could use.

I worked on a supply chain project for a medical device business in North America. Three production sites. Components arriving from Europe and Asia. Everything maintained in SAP. But when the planning team needed to understand where parts were, when they would arrive, and in what quantity, SAP couldn't surface that in any practical way.

So we built a transparency layer in Excel. Not because we wanted to. Because the system wasn't designed for that business model. The SKU complexity, the multisite dependencies, the cross regional flows. SAP handled the transactions. It just couldn't give planners the view they needed to make decisions with confidence.

Once they had that view, things changed. Coordination between the European and North American teams improved. Escalation paths became clearer. Less firefighting, more forward planning. 

Service levels went from around 80 to above 90 percent.

What is the learning for me from that project is not only the result. It is the workaround. A global business running on spreadsheets sitting next to a system that cost tens of millions to implement.

Legacy ERP was built for a different era. Standardized processes, stable portfolios, predictable flows. When the business model gets more complex, the system rarely adapts. The organization does. Usually in Excel.

That gap is still there. In most companies I know, it never really closed.

What is changing now is the cost of closing it. With AI agents and lightweight custom tools, the workaround no longer has to be a spreadsheet. 

It can be something that actually fits the business model, connects to the data that matters, and surfaces the right decision at the right moment.

The technology is not the hard part anymore. Understanding what decision needs to be made, and by whom, still is.

Most people accidentally discover what procurement is really about.

Because nobody tells them.

Universities don’t teach it.
 Job descriptions don’t explain it.
 And most procurement careers are built through trial and error.

The reality?

The job is very different from what most people expect.

7 things nobody tells you about procurement:

1/ It’s a commercial function, not an admin one.

Yet you’ll spend years proving that to people who should already know. The best procurement professionals don’t process requests. They influence business outcomes.

2/ The politics are real.

Supplier decisions get overridden. Stakeholders have favourites. Budget holders have agendas. Technical capability matters, but learning how organisations really work matters just as much.

3/ Soft skills beat technical skills.

You can know every clause in the contract. Every sourcing methodology. Every procurement process.
None of it matters if you can’t build trust, influence decisions and bring people with you.

4/ Your suppliers know more than you think.

They’ve seen your competitors. They’ve seen other industries. They’ve seen what works and what fails.
The smartest procurement professionals treat suppliers as a source of market intelligence.

5/ Speed and compliance pull in opposite directions.

The business wants things faster. Procurement wants things controlled.
Your job is to find the balance.
And somehow you’ll often get blamed from both directions.

6/ The value you create is often invisible.

The crisis that never happened. The supplier failure that was avoided. The cost increase that never materialised.
Nobody celebrates what didn’t go wrong.

7/ The career path is wider than most people realise.

CPO. Consultant. Founder. COO. Commercial leader.

The skills you develop in procurement transfer far beyond procurement itself.

Most procurement professionals spend years learning these lessons the hard way.

The lucky ones learn them early. 

I probably learned many of the lessons too late to save me from some real dips in confidence and episodes of anxiety. 

This is why it’s now my life’s work to help procurement professionals globally to learn these lessons. 

Know you are not alone.

A digital thread can connect everything. It can also expose everything.

The promise is simple: create an uninterrupted flow of product data across engineering, manufacturing, quality, service, and operations.

The implementation is not.

Data silos limit visibility. Legacy systems resist integration. Poor-quality data reduces trust. Different platforms maintain conflicting versions of the same information.

Then the complexity expands.

PLM, ERP, MES, QMS, and IoT systems must exchange data reliably. Part numbers, revisions, configurations, and engineering changes must stay synchronized across every downstream process.

Even when the technology works, organizational challenges remain.

Teams operate independently. Data ownership is unclear. Employees resist unfamiliar workflows. Skilled professionals who understand PLM, APIs, architecture, governance, and manufacturing processes are difficult to find.

Security, compliance, scalability, migration, and implementation costs add another layer of risk.

This is why a digital thread cannot be treated as a one-time integration project.

It requires clear ownership, trusted master data, shared standards, controlled access, change traceability, cross-team collaboration, and continuous governance.

The goal is not merely to connect systems.

It is to ensure that every team can access the correct product information, in the correct context, at the correct time.

42% of startups fail because no one wants the product. 

A successful MVP removes all doubt. Here's how to build one: 

I've launched MVPs across 5 businesses in different niches,  
And the hardest part is never the technical side. 

For me, it's always the discipline of leaving things out.
The founder instinct will always tell you to add more, do more. 

But that's how you end up wasting 6 months on features no one needs. 

When Tom Blomfield, founder of Monzo, agreed to invest £100k in Lottie, 
He gave us one condition: launch in 14 days. 

We basically had to strip everything back and ship. 
And with sheer speed and effort, we did just that. 

The signals we got back were completely different from what we expected.
He saved us months of wasted time with 1 deadline.  

With Searchable, I was more prepared as a founder. 

When it came time to build our MVP, we asked one question: 
What's the single thing we can build that proves this idea works? 

The answer was prompt tracking. 

We kept it insanely simple and opened our waitlist in December. 
The feedback we got built the next version of the product.

This is now the framework I use EVERY time:

1️⃣ Who is your MVP for?
↳ Define your ideal customer before you build anything.
↳ What single problem are you solving, and how does it provide immediate value?

2️⃣ Validate the problem first
↳ Would people actually pay for a solution to this?
↳ If nobody is eager, rethink before you write a line of code.

3️⃣ The Core MVP Rules

✅ Solve one specific problem in the simplest way possible.
✅ Be usable without extensive training.
✅ Provide immediate value.
✅ Be built in 4 to 8 weeks maximum.
❌ Don't build the full product vision from day one.
❌ Don't pack in features nobody asked for.

4️⃣ Get Your First Users
↳ Social media, early access deals, direct email outreach.
↳ Your first users are your best product team. Treat them that way.

5️⃣ The Feedback Loop
↳ Launch. Get feedback. Iterate. Relaunch.
↳ Remove what isn't working before you add anything new.

6️⃣ Signs Your MVP Is Ready to Scale: 

✅ Strong retention and repeat users.
✅ Users asking for more features.
✅ Customers willing to pay without being pushed.

If in doubt, aim to remove as many things as you can.

The simplest version that delivers real value will always teach you more than the most complete version you could imagine.

A machine can be running... and still be losing money!!
Many manufacturers measure output.
But output alone doesn't tell you:
❌ How much time was lost
❌ How much speed was reduced
❌ How many defects were produced
❌ How much capacity was wasted
This is why OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness) matters.
📊 OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality
Consider this example:
🔹 Availability = 80%
🔹 Performance = 90%
🔹 Quality = 95%
➡️ OEE = 68.4%
That means 31.6% of planned production capacity is being lost.
Where does the loss come from?
⚙️ Equipment breakdowns
⏳ Changeover delays
🛑 Minor stops
🐢 Reduced operating speed
♻️ Rework and scrap
❌ Quality defects
These losses don't just affect production.
They create a ripple effect across the supply chain:
📉 Low OEE
→ 📦 Inventory shortages
→ 🚚 Expedited shipments
→ ⏰ Late deliveries
→ 💰 Higher costs
→ 😟 Customer dissatisfaction
Before investing in new equipment, ask:
Are we fully utilizing the capacity we already have?
Because improving OEE isn't just about machines.
It's about improving the entire supply chain.

Joe had an offer in hand, ready to resign.

One career conversation changed what happened next.

Joe is fictional.

But I have seen versions of his story many times.

He was a strong performer.

Respected by his colleagues.

Successful in his role.

But something was missing.

Before informing his manager, he reached out to a mentor.

Out of courtesy.

Maybe for perspective.

I appreciated the trust.

So instead of asking him why he wanted to leave, we explored something deeper.

His six fundamental human needs.

Certainty.

Was he looking for more stability?

No.

Variety.

Was he bored and looking for something different?

Not really.

Connection.

Did he feel disconnected from his team?

No.

Then we got to significance.

And something clicked.

Joe wanted to feel that he mattered.

He wanted his leadership to be recognized.

The bigger title in the new company represented that.

Then we explored growth.

He felt he had stopped learning.

The new role promised a bigger challenge.

Finally, contribution.

Joe wanted to make a bigger impact.

He believed the new company would give him that opportunity.

Suddenly, the problem became clearer.

Joe was not simply leaving for a bigger title.

Three important needs were not being met:

Significance.

Growth.

Contribution.

So I asked him one more question.

“Is leaving the only way to meet them?”

Maybe not.

Joe decided not to resign.

At least, not yet.

Instead, he would have a different career conversation with his manager.

Not:

“When will I get promoted?”

But:

“How can I expand my leadership, keep growing, and contribute at a higher level?”

Maybe there was a bigger role he could play.

A new challenge he could take on.

A team he could lead.

A problem he could own.

Even without an immediate promotion.

Perhaps Joe would still decide to leave.

And that might be the right decision.

But at least he would be solving the real problem.

This fictional story makes me wonder:

How many regrettable losses happen because we start the career conversation only after someone resigns?

By then, the conversation may already be too late.

If you know someone who could benefit from this conversation before it is too late, tag them.

88% of businesses now use AI design tools.

Only 18% say it has reduced their need for designers.

That gap tells you something important.

It is not replacing the designer. 
It is removing the bottleneck around them.

After 16 years in marketing, 
That distinction is the one I wish I had understood earlier.

Recently, we had talented designers and tight campaign timelines. 
The problem was never the design quality. 
It was the wait between the brief and the first draft. 
By the time it came back, 
The window had shifted.

Claude Design is the first tool I have seen that actually addresses that. 
Not by removing the designer from the room. 
By cutting out the part that slows everything else down.

Anthropic launched it in April 2026 as part of their Labs program. 
It is not an image generator. 
It builds clickable prototypes with real typography and real interactions. 
You can iterate on them through conversation.

Here is what this infographic breaks down:

→ What it is: 
A visual design tool that creates prototypes, UI mockups, wireframes, and landing pages. 
Works from text prompts, uploaded files, codebases, or website captures.

→ Who it is built for: 
Founders, PMs, marketers, designers, engineers. 
Pitch decks from rough notes in minutes. 
Wireframes and feature flows in hours. 
Landing pages and campaign visuals without the design queue.

→ How to get better output: 
Context engineering. 
Give Claude an identity file, a voice profile, and an anti-AI file listing what it must never say as you. 
The structure around a task now matters more than how cleverly it is phrased.

→ Which model to use: 
Haiku for speed and simple tasks. 
Sonnet for most daily work. 
Opus for complex, multi-step output. 
Picking wrong costs more time than most people realise.

→ Power user moves: 
Prompt chaining so one output feeds the next. 
Batching independent tasks together for faster output. 
Skill systems so Claude follows the same format and style every time automatically.

→ Common mistakes: 
Treating it like a search engine. 
Vague prompts with no output format specified. 
Repeating context every session instead of building one context file and reusing it.

The prompt templates at the bottom of the infographic are worth saving.

Pitch deck, UI prototype, one-pager, design system. 
Each structured to produce a first draft you can actually use.

This is what changes output speed for marketing teams. 
Not the AI itself. 
The workflow you build around it.

If this is useful, you will find more like it on my feed. 
Worth passing to whoever is still fighting the design bottleneck on their team. 
Curious which part of your workflow you would hand over to this first.

💎📍🕸️The Most Important Team Almost Every Organization Is Missing

After more than 20 years of working across different organizations, I’ve come to a conclusion that may sound controversial:

Most companies don’t have a communication problem.
They don’t even have a silo problem.

They have a missing function.

Every organization has talented specialists. Finance optimizes financial. Operations improve efficiency. IT delivers technology. Sales drive growth. HR focuses on people.

Everyone is doing exactly what they were hired to do.

And that’s where the problem begins.

Every department makes logical decisions from its own perspective. Individually, those decisions make sense. Collectively, they often create conflicting priorities, unnecessary complexity, expensive rework, delays, frustration, and stress.

Why?

Because very few organizations have an independent person or team responsible for looking at the business end-to-end.

Not another management layer.
Not another approval board.
Not another bureaucracy.

An experienced, independent function whose role is to connect the dots, challenge assumptions, identify cross-functional impacts, and ensure that important decisions have been considered from an end-to-end business perspective before they are implemented.

Not to make the decision.

But to ask the questions others often don’t.

1.Who else will this affect?
2.Have all impacted functions been involved?
3.Are we solving one problem while creating new ones somewhere else?
4.Is this decision truly aligned with the organization’s overall objectives?

These are simple questions.

Yet they are often asked only after the damage is done.

The consequences are familiar to all of us: projects redesigned months later, disconnected processes, departments blaming each other, wasted budgets, unnecessary stress.

The cost isn’t just financial.

It weakens trust, slows execution, and makes collaboration harder with every avoidable mistake.

I’m not suggesting someone should know every detail of every process. That’s impossible.

But it is absolutely possible to build an independent capability with broad business knowledge, strong end-to-end understanding, and enough experience to see risks, dependencies, and unintended consequences before they become expensive.

Organizations invest millions in AI, digital transformation, new systems, and consultants.

Yet many still overlook the capability that could significantly increase the success of every one of those investments: independent end-to-end alignment.

After 20 years, I no longer believe organizations fail because they lack smart people.

They fail because smart people make isolated decisions while no one is truly responsible for protecting the whole.

The organizations that will outperform tomorrow won’t just have the best specialists.

They’ll have the people who connect everything together.

End-to-end thinking isn’t a luxury. It’s one of the greatest competitive advantages an organization can build.

🆘🛑We Measure Quality… But Are We Measuring the Right Thing?

Many people know me as a Lean enthusiast. And yes, I am passionate about Lean.

However Lean is much more than flow, waste, and efficiency. One of its strongest foundations is quality.

I’ve spent as many years working with quality as I have with Lean, and one thing has always surprised me.

Every organization measures quality in some way:
* Defects
* Errors
* Rework
* Customer complaints
* Scrap
* Cost of poor quality

We create dashboards, KPIs, Pareto charts, and monthly reports.

But 𝘐 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘴𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳, 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘳, 𝘦𝘯𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘳, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘲𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘧𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭:

𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘰𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘮𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘴?

𝘕𝘰𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘵𝘢𝘭 𝘯𝘶𝘮𝘣𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘧 𝘥𝘦𝘧𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘴.
𝘕𝘰𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘵 𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦.
𝘉𝘶𝘵 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘺’𝘴 𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘶𝘦𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢𝘭𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘺 𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘦.

Because that’s where the real story begins.

A defect that happens once might be an accident.
A defect that happens twice is a warning.
A defect that keeps returning is no longer a quality issue, it is a failure to learn.

If the same complaint appears every month, the problem isn’t the operator.
It isn’t the customer.
It isn’t bad luck.

The problem is that the organization solved the symptom instead of eliminating the root cause.

Reducing defects is good.

Preventing the same defect from ever happening again is what world-class organizations do.

So here’s my challenge to my network:

Do you measure repeat mistakes, repeat rework, and repeat complaints?
Because if you don’t know how many of your quality problems are recurring…

How can you honestly say your organization is improving?

𝘘𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘪𝘴𝘯’𝘵 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘧𝘪𝘹𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴.
𝘘𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮 𝘯𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘣𝘢𝘤𝘬.

A loaded truck is not always an optimized truck.
Sometimes the floor is full…

but the cube is still half-empty.

That means you are not just moving product.

You are also moving air.

And unplanned empty space increases cost per shipped unit.

Good pallet loading is not only about fitting more boxes.

It is about balancing:

→ stacking pattern
→ weight distribution
→ pallet stability
→ vehicle height
→ route sequence
→ product compatibility
→ safety limits

Column stacking may give strength.

Interlocking may give stability.

Pinwheel may reduce shifting.

Split row may help mixed-SKU deliveries.

But none of them should be used blindly.

The right loading plan depends on the product, pallet, vehicle, route, and handling conditions.

Before maximizing cube, always check:

→ Weight limit
→ Stack height
→ Product fragility
→ Route sequence
→ Compatibility

Because the goal is not just a full truck.
The goal is a safe, stable, cost-efficient load.

Save this cheatsheet for your next dispatch or loading review.

Two types of LinkedIn creators. Only one builds a brand that survives.
The Hype Guy vs. The Doom Guy. 

You probably know a Hype Guy. Every post is a win. 
Every client is thrilled. LinkedIn "loves" him.
 
Then we have the The Doom Guy. LinkedIn is broken. Reach is dead. 
He's burned out and telling you about it daily.
 
Both work short-term. Both quietly damage your brand long-term.
 
𝗟𝗲𝘁'𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝘀𝘆𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆, 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲:
 
1. Our feeds are already biased toward positivity. Across major platforms, 80–90% of posts lean positive, even when people are not that happy offline. Result: your "always winning" narrative stops feeling inspiring and starts feeling fake.
2. Vulnerability does create connection, but only in a specific form. Recent studies show people trust you most when you share past, mild vulnerabilities plus current competence. "I struggled with X, here is how I solved it, here is the system" beats both "I never struggle" and "I'm still drowning."
3. Extremes drive engagement, not authority. One large LinkedIn analysis found neutral or mixed-tone posts can drive up to 9x more meaningful engagement than overly positive ones, and negative posts often spark more comments than hype posts. But if all you post is outrage, people see you as entertaining, not as someone they'd pay.
 
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱:
 
Live in "everything is a success" mode, and short-term you get more likes, less friction, easier sponsor deals. Long-term you get less perceived authenticity and an audience that quietly doubts your numbers and your advice.
 
Live in "LinkedIn is evil, I struggle every day" mode, and short-term you get more comments, more debate, more "finally someone says it." Long-term you brand yourself as the system's victim, not the operator who can navigate it and help others win.
 
People follow success with scars. 
Not success without cracks. 
Not struggle without solutions. 
 
My recommendation: show wins with receipts. Show struggles with constraints. Stop performing at the extremes, and let your feed show competence and honesty instead of hype and drama.

Now! Audit your last 30 posts. Which extreme are you closer to, and what is that doing to how people trust your brand?

Note to myself: let's balance it a bit more okay Mr. Critical Guy?

It's a question I've been asked quite a few times by customers considering moving to Business Central SaaS.

The answer is update windows.

For our customers, we configure maintenance windows so Microsoft knows when updates can be applied with the least disruption to the business.

One of our customers was due to receive a production update last night. The update started as planned, but something interesting happened.

The monitoring systems determined that the update wasn't going to complete within the agreed update window. Rather than overrunning into business hours and causing potential disruption, Microsoft automatically stopped the update and rolled everything back.

This morning the system was fully available and the customer could carry on working as normal.

It's one of those behind-the-scenes features that most people never see, but it highlights the amount of engineering that goes into running a modern SaaS service.

When people think about Business Central SaaS, they often focus on new features, automatic upgrades and not having to manage servers.

For me, it's also about things like this. The safeguards that make sure updates happen at the right time, in the right way, and don't get in the way of the business.

Not the most glamorous feature, but definitely one of the most important. 👍

Every half-empty truck is a missed opportunity!
Many logistics teams focus on freight rates, but the bigger savings often come from improving truck utilization.
Load consolidation is the practice of combining orders, shipments, or delivery points to maximize vehicle capacity and reduce transport costs.
Done well, it can:
✅ Reduce freight cost per unit
✅ Improve truck utilization
✅ Lower fuel consumption
✅ Reduce carbon emissions
✅ Decrease empty miles
✅ Improve overall transport efficiency
But consolidation also comes with trade-offs.
Waiting to fill a truck may reduce cost, but it can also:
❌ Increase lead time
❌ Delay customer deliveries
❌ Impact service levels
❌ Create inventory holding costs
Smart Consolidation Asks:
🔹 Can shipments to the same region be combined?
🔹 What is the cost of waiting vs shipping now?
🔹 Will service levels be affected?
🔹 Is truck utilization meeting targets?
🔹 Are we creating unnecessary urgent shipments later?
Simple Decision Rule
✅ Stable demand + flexible delivery windows
➡ Maximize consolidation.
✅ Urgent demand + critical orders
➡ Prioritize service over consolidation.
✅ Mixed demand profiles
➡ Use planned consolidation days by region.
The goal is not to fill every truck.
The goal is to find the right balance between cost, utilization, and customer service.
A full truck delivered too late is a problem.
A half-empty truck delivered too often is also a problem.
The best logistics teams know when to consolidate and when not to.

How to shift procurement to strategic. Free Guide 🎁 

Perception is built on evidence. But the evidence the business sees every day is tactical.

Let's look at the transformation step by step:

1️⃣ Signs the business sees you as tactical

↳ They only involve you AFTER a supplier has been chosen 
↳ Stakeholders treat procurement as a box-ticking exercise 
↳ You're only measured on cost savings 
↳ You spend more time on POs than influencing decisions 
↳ Nobody invites you to early planning conversations 
↳ Your reports go to Finance, not the boardroom 
↳ The business regularly goes around procurement entirely

If 3+ are true, you're seen as purchasing. Not procurement.


2️⃣ The 5 shifts to close the gap

(i) From Price to Value 
↳ Stop leading with "we got 10% off" 
↳ Start showing total cost of ownership, risk reduction, supplier reliability

(ii) From Reactive to Proactive 
↳ Stop waiting to be briefed after decisions are made 
↳ Start building relationships that get you upstream

(iii) From Process Enforcer to Business Partner 
↳ Stop saying "you need to follow the procurement process" 
↳ Start saying "let's figure out how to get you the outcome you need"

(iv) From Tactical KPIs to Strategic Metrics 
↳ Stop reporting PO cycle times and savings vs budget 
↳ Start reporting supplier risk, value delivered, market benchmarks

(v) From Departmental to Cross-Functional 
↳ Stop talking only to direct budget holders 
↳ Start building relationships with Finance, Legal, Operations, and the C-suite


3️⃣ Change how you speak

Instead of: "You should have involved us earlier" ❌ 
Try: "At what point did the supplier conversation start?" ✅ 

Instead of: "That's not the procurement process" ❌ 
Try: "Let's see how we can make this work safely" ✅ 

Instead of: "We need 3 quotes" ❌ 
Try: "Here's what the market looks like. Let me show you the options" ✅ 

Instead of: "I can't approve that supplier" ❌ 
Try: "There are some risks here. Let's talk through them" ✅ 

Instead of: "We saved £200K this quarter" ❌ 
Try: "We reduced cost AND improved delivery reliability by 15%" ✅ 


4️⃣ The perception checklist

↳ Do stakeholders involve you before supplier decisions? 
↳ Do you have relationships with senior leaders beyond direct contacts? 
↳ Can you articulate procurement's value beyond savings? 
↳ Do you bring market intelligence, not just process? 
↳ Does the business know what it costs to bypass procurement? 
↳ Are your KPIs linked to business strategy? 
↳ Does procurement have a voice in supplier innovation?

The gap isn't about capability. It's about visibility, language & how procurement shows up.

A company I backed 15 years ago just sold for $3.6 billion.

And honestly? I couldn't fully explain what they build today.

Sounds crazy for an investor to admit.

But it's the whole reason I made the bet in the first place.

See, everyone thinks investing is about spotting the right idea.

I've never once bet on an idea.

Rewind to 2011. I'd just moved to San Francisco.

Met this founder at an event - Eoghan McCabe. Irish guy who'd packed up his whole life and moved across the world to build his thing.

He came by the office and showed me a prototype.

I understood maybe half of it.

Didn't matter. Because I wasn't looking at the prototype.

I was looking at him.

"Bro, you're smart. This is awesome. I'm in."

On the spot.

The company? Intercom.

Over the next decade, they raised a small fortune. Tens of millions. Maybe a hundred plus.

And every so often, an email would land in my inbox:

"Dan, want to sell your shares?"

Every time, I'd fire off one message to Eoghan.

"You still in?"

"Yep."

That's all I needed. I held.

Now here's the wild part.

The company I backed in 2011 barely resembles the one that exists today.

The product changed. The market changed. The whole business flipped when AI hit and Eoghan bet everything on it.

The one thing that never changed?

Him.

Fast forward to last month: Salesforce agreed to buy them for $3.6 billion.

When the wire lands, it'll be an incredible payday.

But I want you to catch what actually made it work.

Bet on the person. Not the pitch.

Ideas are fragile. Markets shift. The "sure thing" you back today can look like a disaster three years from now.

People who refuse to lose? They just… figure it out.

They pivot. They rebuild. They bet the whole company on a technology that didn't even exist when they started.

That's what I actually invested in.

Not a chat widget. Not an AI agent.

A guy who was never going to walk away.

So when people ask me for my big "investment thesis," here it is:

Find someone who'd run through a wall for their vision. Back them. Then get out of the way.

Oh, and one more thing.

This works whether you ever write a check or not.

The best bet you'll ever make isn't on a company.

It's on becoming the kind of person someone would back without blinking.

The one who doesn't flinch when it gets ugly.

The one who's still standing - still building - long after everyone else moved on.

Be that person.

The rest has a funny way of working itself out.

HYPOTHESIS: Speaking about pain points alone doesn’t give B2B buyers enough reason to sign up (even when it's something they literally said on the call!)

Because action comes from friction + motivation. And keep in mind that messaging has to mirror how decisions are made (especially the WHY to act now part):

-First, they recognize themselves (relevant pain points)
-Then, they recognize the fit (alignment with their job-to-be-done)
-Finally, they feel ready to act (driven by internal motivators!)

Seems like motivation is what they’re already under pressure to fix, speed up or prove is the tipping point.

Here are 4 core ICP motivators I look for + the specific friction that actually drives action:

1/ CONTROL (e.g. Ops, Product, RevOps need this)
 Responsible for building systems that hold under pressure.
 – Friction: workarounds, inconsistency, siloed data, misalignment
 – Motivation: restore structure with a process that scales without daily involvement (and stess)

2/ SPEED (e.g. Founders, Growth, Sales need this)
 Under pressure to hit goals faster than the market moves.
 – Friction: slow handoffs, inconsistent leads, delayed cycles
 – Motivation: shorten loops and move faster than the market

3/ CERTAINTY (e.g. Finance, Procurement, Strategy need this)
 Needs to make confident decisions with clear data trails.
 – Friction: unclear attribution, scattered metrics, guesswork
 – Motivation: justify spend and de-risk decisions under pressure

4/ RECOGNITION (e.g. Marketing, Enablement, ICs need this)
 Crave visibility, so their work to be seen, valued and defended.
 – Friction: work disappears into the void, no clear impact
 – Motivation: prove influence and earn trust, not just praise

Yes, start with pain... but tie it to what’s at stake for them (your ICP). 

Pain point needs to be connected to a real threat + expected outcome to make them believe your offer enough to act now and go start a trial or book a demo.

Christopher Nolan is the last great director of this century. But not because The Odyssey made $264 million opening weekend.

Because he found a method to irresistible storytelling:

Nolan uses the Plot Map Technique to visualize his storyline.

He doesn’t want “constraints” to hold him back when writing the story (especially if it's complex).

So he uses this technique to help his production team:

1. Visualize the plot arc(s)
2. Create it on screen

Let's take Inception as an example (since I haven't gotten a chance to see The Odyssey yet).

The intricate plot is a journey around dreams within dreams, jumping between layers of reality.

Nolan's Plot Map for Inception resembles Kurt Vonnegut's "Man in Hole" story shape.

This is where the main character:

1. Faces a problem
2. Gets out of it
3. Grows from the experience

But Nolan added an interesting twist:

In Inception, as Cobb (played by DiCaprio) moves closer to the dream world of Limbo, he travels "down" the plot map toward problems.

Then, he must fight his way "up" to reality.

This not only mirrors Cobb's journey but also the movie's core concept of nested dreams.

By using the Plot Map, Nolan keeps the story focused despite the movie's:

• Multiple “dream” storylines
• Competing character arcs
• And ever-increasing stakes

Without the Plot Map, the story would have become unfocused and hard to follow.

Nolan planned the entire 2.5-hour Inception movie on a single page.

Other notable writers have similar practices:

• Norman Mailer (in Harlot's Ghost)
• Henry Miller (in Tropic of Capricorn)
• JK Rowling (in the Harry Potter series)

Want to use this technique for yourself?

Try this:

• Make a Visual Outline (shapes, arrows, visuals)
• Emphasize Key Points (incident, climax, resolution)
• Map Character Development (impact of events/themes)

This will help you keep your story focused while writing.

I was tasked with modeling how much warehouse space a client would need during peak season.

On paper, it sounds straightforward.

In reality, the pressure is that if your inputs are messy, your “answer” looks confident… and still leads you straight into a capacity problem.

So I started with the unglamorous part:

1️⃣ I made sure all logistics specs for their SKUs were documented and up to date. Simple, but everything downstream depends on it.

2️⃣ I built a more detailed inventory model with a week-over-week view, so we could see where inventory swelled and dipped throughout the month.

3️⃣ We aligned on the “rules” for ordering by category (because different categories created very different outcomes).

4️⃣ Then I pulled it all into one model that summed weekly pallet-position needs by storage area against current warehouse capacity constraints.


The result: transparency on what storage needs to prioritize, plus a clear map of which weeks were close to (or over) capacity so we could build a solid gameplan for the next several months.

If you’re heading into peak, what’s the one piece that feels hardest to get clean right now: the data, the rules, or the model?

Most people use AI. 
Almost nobody is actually getting good at it.

There's a difference between using AI and mastering it.

Most people are stuck at level 1 or 2.

They open ChatGPT, type a prompt, get a mediocre output, and call it a day.

They wonder why AI isn't changing their output.

They assume the tool is the problem.

It isn't.

The gap isn't the model. 
It's the level you're operating at.

After 16 years in marketing, 
I've watched this pattern repeat.

The people who get real results from AI aren't just using it differently.

They're operating at a completely different level of understanding.

I've been mapping this for a while.

There are 9 distinct levels of AI mastery.

Most marketers I speak to are sitting between level 2 and level 3 without realising it.

Here's what the full picture looks like, 
And where you probably are right now:

Level 1: 
AI Awareness 
You understand what AI is, how LLMs work, and where the limits are. 
Tools: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity.

Level 2: 
AI User 
You know how to prompt, research, summarise, and write with AI. 
Outcome: you save time and increase your output.

Level 3: 
AI Power User 
You've moved into few-shot prompting, prompt chaining, and structured outputs. 
You're building repeatable systems, not just one-off generations.

Level 4: AI Creator 
You're working across text, image, video, and audio. 
Articles, graphics, shorts, voiceovers, you're producing AI assets end to end.

Level 5: AI Automation Builder 
You're connecting AI to workflows using Zapier, Make, or n8n. 
APIs, triggers, logic flows. Your work is running while you sleep.

Level 6: AI Agent Builder 
RAG, memory systems, tool calling, agent planning. 
You're building AI that acts, not just answers.

Level 7: AI Engineer 
Python, databases, deployment, evaluation. 
You're shipping production AI: apps, chat systems, SaaS tools.

Level 8: AI Architect 
Security, governance, monitoring, scaling, cost control. 
You're designing enterprise AI infrastructure.

Level 9: AI Researcher 
Transformers, RLHF, alignment, fine-tuning, safety. 
You're pushing what's possible.

Most marketing directors I talk to are operating at levels 2 to 3.

The ones pulling away from the field are at levels 4 and 5.

That gap is only going to widen.

I was listening to a podcast discussing Millennials, Gen Z, Gen X, Boomers… and it made me wonder:

𝘏𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘸𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘰 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘦 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘭𝘢𝘣𝘦𝘭𝘴?

Not just generations.

Cultures too.

How often do we hear:
⚠️“That’s just how Gen Z is.”
⚠️“Millennials expect too much.”
⚠️“It’s their culture.”
⚠️“That’s how people from that country work.”
⚠️“It’s a cultural difference.”

Sometimes these observations are valid.

But too often, they become convenient excuses.

🔻An excuse for poor leadership.
🔻An excuse for weak communication.
🔻An excuse for avoiding uncomfortable conversations.
🔻An excuse for not adapting.
🔻An excuse for accepting behavior that should simply be addressed.

Yes, every generation is shaped by different experiences.

Yes, every culture has its own values and traditions.

However integrity, accountability, curiosity, respect, kindness, and professionalism don’t belong to one generation or one culture.

I’ve met young people with extraordinary discipline and older people with incredible openness to change. 
I’ve worked with people from cultures that were supposedly “direct” who were incredibly empathetic, and with people from “relationship-focused” cultures who were exceptionally results-driven.

⁉️Maybe we’re asking the wrong question.

Instead of asking:
“What generation are you?”
or
“Where are you from?”

Maybe we should ask:

⁉️Are you willing to learn?
⁉️Can you adapt?
⁉️Do you take ownership?
⁉️Do you treat others with respect?
⁉️Can you work with people who think differently?

Labels can help us understand patterns.

They should never become excuses or limits.

What do you think?

Have we reached a point where we use generations and cultures as explanations for almost everything, when many of our challenges are really about leadership, accountability, communication, and individual choices?

I’d love to hear your perspective.

I learned this the hard way. I do not want you to.

What made me a manager didn’t make me a leader.

Message #6/22: To the Nikhil managing his first direct report...

I was a newly promoted manager.

My first direct report, Ketan, was significantly more experienced than me.

And I had a rough start.

Until then, I had built my career on things I was good at.

My intelligence.

My skills.

My ability to get things done.

Those strengths had helped me become a manager.

So naturally, I tried to use the same strengths to lead.

That was my mistake.

I was too focused on my ideas and my way of doing things.

I did not appreciate enough that Ketan had years of experience, his own perspective, and a different way of working.

Fortunately, he gave me something every new manager needs.

Patience.

And honest feedback.

I was equally fortunate to have Ravi, a senior leader who saw me stumbling and coached me through it.

Together, they taught me one of my earliest leadership lessons:

Your team does not need you to prove that you are smarter than them.

They need you to listen to them.

Respect them.

And create the conditions for them to succeed.

Years later, I became known as a strong coach and eventually a Master Trainer in people management.

The irony is not lost on me.

Something I eventually became good at started with something I initially struggled with.

So, to the younger me:

Stop trying to prove you deserve to be the manager.

You already have the title.

Now earn the trust.

Because becoming someone’s manager can happen overnight.

Becoming their leader takes much longer.

22 years. 22 messages to younger versions of me.

Looking at your business through someone else's eyes 👀.
.
.
.
"If you bought your own business tomorrow, what would frustrate you first?"

I've asked that question of several Managing Directors and almost every time the response is the same. There's a pause, followed by a smile 🙂 , and then a thoughtful conversation.

I remember one owner beginning the factory tour with enormous pride, and rightly so. He'd spent years building the business from the ground up. He knew every customer by name, every supplier, every machine and every member of staff.

Towards the end of the tour, I asked him that question. He looked at me for a moment before saying, "I've never thought about it like that."

What followed wasn't criticism of his business. Quite the opposite. It was a fascinating discussion about all the little compromises that had accumulated over the years. Processes that only existed in people's memories. Supplier agreements that had simply rolled on from one year to the next. Reports that nobody entirely trusted but everyone continued producing because they'd always done so.

There was nothing unusual about any of it, in fact, that's precisely why it interests me. Businesses evolve, they adapt, they respond to customers, markets and opportunities. Along the way they also collect habits, workarounds and assumptions that eventually become invisible or frustrating to the people closest to them.

Stepping back and looking at your own business as though you were a potential buyer 💷 , can be an unexpectedly revealing exercise.

Sometimes the greatest opportunity isn't changing the business, it's simply seeing it differently 👓.

From my own experience, whether I've been working in quality management, procurement or operations, I've found that asking thoughtful questions ❓ nearly always reveals more than arriving with ready-made answers.

“𝘞𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯?”

It’s probably the question I’m asked most often.

Not:

“What is Lean?”

But:

“Which Lean tools should we implement first?”

My answer usually surprises people.

None.

At least not yet.

Because Lean is not a toolbox.

It’s a way of thinking.

Too many organizations start with 5S, Value Stream Mapping, Kanban, A3s, Kaizen boards, or visual management… hoping the tools will magically transform the business.

Months later they conclude:
“Lean doesn’t work here.”

The reality?

The tools weren’t the problem.

The mindset was.

Lean starts by understanding three simple questions:

✔️ What problem are we trying to solve?
✔️ What creates value for our customer?
✔️ What prevents us from delivering that value consistently?

Only then should we think about tools.

So where would I start?

Not with a tool.

I’d start by going to the place where the work happens.

Observe.
Listen.
Ask questions.

Talk to the people doing the work every day.

They usually know where the waste is.

If I had to choose only a few tools to begin with, they would be:

1. Gemba Walks
Go and see.
Don’t manage from PowerPoint.

2. Process Mapping
Understand the current reality before designing the future.

3. 5 Whys
Don’t fix symptoms.
Find the root cause.

4. Visual Management
Make problems visible instead of hiding them.

5. PDCA
Improve through small experiments, not big assumptions.

Notice something?

None of these tools are complicated.

Because Lean has never been about complexity.

It’s about developing a culture where people solve problems every day.

The biggest mistake isn’t choosing the wrong Lean tool.

It’s believing the tool will create the culture.

𝘊𝘶𝘭𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘶𝘭𝘵𝘴.
𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘰𝘭𝘴 𝘴𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘺 𝘴𝘶𝘱𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵 𝘪𝘵.

So next time someone asks,

“Which Lean tool should we start with?”

Maybe the better question is:
“𝘈𝘳𝘦 𝘸𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘸𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬?”

I’d love to hear your experience.

If you were starting a Lean transformation tomorrow, what would be the very first thing you’d do?

Most IBP processes were designed to create alignment. What they often create instead is a very expensive consensus ritual.

Forecasts get negotiated. Numbers get smoothed. The uncomfortable scenarios disappear before they reach the meeting. And four weeks later, the market moves in exactly the direction nobody wanted to discuss.

I have been thinking about what it would mean to design IBP differently. Not lighter. Not faster. But genuinely built around decisions rather than around agreement.

CAD collaboration breaks when teams work from different versions.

A reliable design process needs more than shared folders and frequent meetings. It requires clear controls for product data, ownership, approvals, engineering changes, and downstream integration.

The foundation starts with disciplined data management:

↳ Store every CAD model in one controlled repository
↳ Use check-in and check-out to prevent editing conflicts
↳ Separate working versions from approved revisions
↳ Apply role-based access permissions

Collaboration improves when teams conduct structured design reviews, capture comments directly on models, assign clear assembly ownership, and involve manufacturing, quality, and procurement before release.

Change management is equally important.

Every modification should move through a formal engineering change workflow with impact analysis, automatic notifications, release gates, and complete traceability. This prevents unapproved updates from reaching downstream teams.

Finally, CAD must connect with the wider product ecosystem:

↳ Synchronize CAD data with PLM
↳ Keep BOM structures aligned
↳ Standardize file names and numbering
↳ Reuse approved components
↳ Maintain a connected digital thread

The goal is not simply faster design.

It is controlled collaboration that reduces duplication, prevents errors, and keeps engineering, manufacturing, procurement, and quality working from the same trusted product data.

➡️ Operations is waiting for Finance.
➡️ Finance is waiting for Leadership.
➡️ Leadership is waiting for more information.

The result?

📉 Frustrated teams
That's why decision frameworks like RAPID and DACI incredibly practical.
🔹 RAPID
• Recommend – Propose the best solution
• Agree – Align key stakeholders
• Perform – Execute the decision
• Input – Provide expertise and data
• Decide – Own the final call
🔹 DACI
• Driver – Moves the decision forward
• Approver – Has final authority
• Contributors – Provide expertise
• Informed – Stay updated
A simple supplier approval example:
Without clear roles:
❌ Procurement waits → Operations waits → Finance waits → Leadership waits
With DACI:
✅ Driver: Procurement Manager
✅ Approver: Supply Chain Director
✅ Contributors: Quality, Finance, Operations & Planning
✅ Informed: Warehouse, Sales & Customer Service
The conversation changes from:
"Who's responsible?"
to
"Let's execute."
Leadership isn't about making every decision. It's about ensuring every decision has a clear owner.
Clear decision ownership converts discussion into execution.

At Frontal AI, the one thing we don't let AI run on its own is content. And it's our single biggest source of pipeline: 50+ inbound meetings a month.

I watched this happen to cold email first.

The moment everyone got the same AI, our inbox filled with the same message. Reply rates were under pressure from a dozen directions, and sounding like everyone else was the accelerant. The cost of blending in went up, and it never came back down.

Content is next. Type a prompt, get something clean, and it reads like the 100 other LinkedIn creators who prompted the same thing that same hour.

Running content for one profile, you can wing it. Running it for dozens without them all blurring into the same voice takes a system.

This is the exact content system we run, top to bottom 👇

1/ Profile
Before a single post goes out, we rebuild the profile to convert a visitor into a lead. Banner, headline, About, and a Featured section that leads with proof (a lead magnet works very well here), then one clear CTA.

2/ Strategy
5 sources feed every idea:
→ Real call transcripts, the highest-signal source we have
→ Competitor and viral posts pulled through Apify
→ Live research across Reddit, YouTube, X 
→ Performance data from what already worked
→ A swipe file of the account's own best posts

3/ The engine
Everything runs in one terminal on Claude Code. The brain is a Client OS: one folder per person, 3 foundation docs.
→ Voice profile: a real conversation that captures how you actually talk, before AI writes a word
→ ICP: 3 buyer tiers and the words each one uses
→ Pillars: 5-6 themes every post traces back to

4/ Content mix
Every week balances 3 jobs: reach at the top, authority in the middle, pipeline at the bottom. 
We hold it near 40/20/40, so the account grows and books meetings at the same time.

5/ Development
59 hook templates, 20+ openings per idea. A full draft in the documented voice. 
Then 4 gates every post clears: a de-AI pass, a quality score out of 50 (under 38 goes back), a check against the account's own feedback log, and a final sign-off. Visuals built in AI, finished by human judgment.

6/ Calendar
Posts scheduled and balanced by job, so no week leans too hard one way.

7/ Learning loop
Every session logs itself. Every 5 sessions the system flags what keeps getting rewritten and where a voice is drifting. Once a quarter we re-check the pillars against the market and refresh the voice from fresh transcripts.

That's how content made it to our #1 acquisition channel on the way from $0 to $7M ARR, with our employees's brand (170K+ combined followers) out-pulling the company page many times over.

A well-built folder remembers who you are. So the model never gets to fill that in for you.
