At 16, I was in a rehabilitation facility.

At 35, I had built and sold 3 companies.

Those 19 years taught me that the hard way is rarely the only one.

Yet I see founders grinding endlessly long before they ever question their approach.

Nowhere is that more true than in how they sell.

People buy from people they trust.

And there's more than one way to earn that trust.

This is the playbook everyone defaults to:

Cold calls → Discovery calls → Proposals → Follow ups → Demos

Burning hours on people who were never going to buy.

So I built an 8-figure business doing the exact opposite.

$6M+ sold through DMs.
On Instagram, between meetings, on my boat, at the gym.

Here's the system behind it:

1. Build trust before you sell.
Your buyer needs to feel like they already know you before they hear an offer.
↳ Share your process, not just your results.
2. Don't rely on one way to find customers.
Outbound, inbound, partners.
↳ If you're starting from zero, outbound gets you moving fast. But inbound is what scales, so build it in the background from day one.
3. Open with personalization.
Generic openers get ignored.
↳ Reference something specific to them before you ask for anything.
4. Qualify with the A-B method.
Don't pitch until you know exactly where they are and where they want to go.
↳ The gap between A and B is where your offer lives.
5. Make the offer fast.
Momentum dies in the gap between qualified and offered.
↳ Speed is everything once someone is ready.
6. Follow up shamelessly.
Time kills momentum.
↳ The longer a conversation sits, the colder it gets.
↳ Don't go quiet because they did.

Save this for next time you are reviewing your sales strategy.

Remember, people don't want to be sold.

They want to be understood.

And there's more than one way to get there. 

-DM

They're looking at ChatGPT, then over to Pinterest, then Instagram...etc !

Most businesses haven't responded accordingly, 
And are only showing up in a couple of places. 

Which means they're invisible everywhere else...

This is what marketing actually involves in 2026 👇

☑️ Google Search
- Target conversational queries, not just short-tail keywords.
- Strengthen your E-E-A-T signals by adding and updating content regularly.
- Answer questions directly in the first paragraph to capture featured snippet positions.

☑️ AI Search (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude)
- Structure content with clear definitions, FAQ sections, and schema markup.
- Write in natural language that answers specific questions directly.
- Get mentioned on third-party sites, forums, and trusted publications.

☑️ Social Search (LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, X)
- Participate in genuine conversations in your niche.
- Share original educational content that gets saved and reshared.
- Publish consistently so the algorithm associates your profile with your topic.

☑️ Video Search (YouTube, TikTok)
- Write video titles as questions people actually ask.
- Add full transcripts to every video so AI crawlers can parse the content.
- Create short summaries of longer content and publish as Shorts or Reels.

☑️ Community and Trust Platforms (Reddit, Quora, G2, Trustpilot)
- Seed value-driven answers on Reddit threads relevant to your category.
- Encourage customers to leave detailed reviews that mention specific use cases.
- Monitor and respond to mentions so AI platforms see active brand engagement.

☑️ Traditional Search (Bing)
- Don't ignore Bing. ChatGPT pulls heavily from Bing's index.
- Optimise with clean structure, fast load times, and schema markup.

☑️ Voice Search (Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant)
- Write in natural, conversational language that mirrors how people speak.
- Answer "near me" and "best for" queries explicitly in your content.
- Format key pages as direct question-and-answer pairs.

All these touchpoints form one connected system.

Your buyers aren't staying in one place by any means.

The biggest Claude mistake is sticking with a workflow that worked six months ago.
It slows you down and costs more tokens.

10 of them have simpler replacements now.

Here's where to start:

1/ Taking Claude's first draft as final

The first output is rarely the best one. Tell it exactly what's off, like "too formal" or "cut this by 30%". The next version gets much closer, and Claude gets smarter on what you want over time.

2/ Prompting without an audience in mind

Claude guesses when it doesn't know who will read the output. Spell out who it's for, what format it should be, and what it needs to achieve.

3/ Trusting every answer blindly

AI still gets things wrong with total confidence. Ask for sources or have it flag anything it's unsure about, then verify the claims that actually matter.

4/ Leaving Claude without a role

A generic assistant gives generic answers. Give it a persona to work from, like a sharp editor or a skeptical analyst, and the quality jumps immediately.

5/ Explaining your data in the prompt

Summarizing a spreadsheet by hand wastes time and loses detail. Drop the actual file in and let Claude run the numbers itself.

6/ Making charts and documents manually

Production work is exactly what Claude is good at. Describe what the finished piece should look like and it builds the file, chart, or doc for you.

7/ Treating one search as research

A single search answers small questions, and big ones need more. Research mode pulls from multiple sources and gives you a cited report.

8/ Ignoring Extended Thinking

The default setting is built for speed. Turn it on when a problem needs proper reasoning and you can see the logic behind every answer.

9/ Digging through old chats by hand

That conversation from three weeks ago is findable in seconds. Ask Claude to search your past chats and it pulls up the exact thread.

10/ Losing your best outputs in dead threads

Great work shouldn't vanish when the chat ends. Save the final version into the Project and Claude learns from it on the next run.

Most people are using ChatGPT like a search engine.

They open it, type a question, read the answer, close the tab.

That's not wrong. 
But it's leaving so much on the table.

I spent 16 years in marketing before AI existed at this level.

And even I underestimated how deep this tool actually goes when you use it properly.

The basics everyone knows: 
Ask questions, write content, do research.

The reality: 
ChatGPT is a full workspace if you treat it like one.

I kept watching smart marketers get mediocre outputs and blame the tool.

The tool wasn't the problem.

The approach was.

After digging into what actually changes results, 
It came down to a few things nobody talks about clearly.

The model matters more than people realise.

GPT-5.5 Instant is fast and great for writing and everyday questions.

GPT-5.5 Thinking spends more time reasoning, which is better for strategy, analysis, and complex tasks.

GPT-5.5 Pro is the most powerful, built for deep research, long reports, and high-stakes decisions.

Most people are on Instant for everything.

That alone is costing them quality.

Then there's the prompt itself.

Here's the framework that changed how I use it:

→ Role: tell it who to be 

→ Task: tell it exactly what to do 

→ Context: give it the information it needs 

→ Constraints: set the rules it should follow 

→ Output format: tell it how to structure the response

Five elements. Every strong prompt has all five.

One example: "Act as a marketing strategist. Write a LinkedIn post for B2B founders. Use a direct tone. Keep it under 200 words. Structure it with a hook, three points, and a close."

That one prompt gets a different result than "Write me a LinkedIn post."

Beyond prompting, the features most people ignore:

→ Projects: organise your chats, files, and instructions by client or campaign 

→ Memory: enable it so ChatGPT learns your preferences over time 

→ Deep Research: use it for multi-step research tasks, not just a quick web search 

→ Agentic Workflows: let it plan and execute multi-step tasks without hand-holding

The common mistakes I see constantly:

→ Vague prompts with no context 

→ Expecting perfect output first time without refining 

→ Not uploading relevant files to give it full context 

→ Restarting from scratch instead of iterating

The marketers getting serious results aren't smarter.

They just treat it like a workspace, not a search box.

What would you do if management asked you to reduce your purchase order?

This is a situation that almost every procurement and supply chain professional will face at some point.

The first instinct might be to simply reduce the order and move on. But every decision has consequences. A smaller order may improve cash flow today, but it can also increase the risk of stockouts, lost sales, emergency purchases, higher freight costs, and dissatisfied customers tomorrow.

Procurement should never rely on assumptions it should rely on data.

Before recommending any order reduction, always ask a few key questions:
• Is the demand forecast still accurate?
• Do we have enough inventory to maintain our target service level?
• Which SKUs are business-critical and should be protected?
• What are the supplier's lead time, MOQ, and reliability?
• What is the financial impact versus the operational risk?

Sometimes reducing the order is the right decision. Sometimes negotiating staggered deliveries or partial shipments is a much better solution. And in some cases, maintaining the original order is the smartest choice.

The goal isn't simply to reduce inventory it's to find the right balance between customer service, inventory investment, profitability, and business risk.

The infographic I've shared outlines a practical framework that procurement, demand planning, and supply chain teams can use to evaluate order reduction requests with confidence and make decisions backed by facts rather than opinions.

Great supply chain decisions aren't measured by how much inventory we cut. They're measured by how well we protect the business while using capital wisely.

How do you evaluate order reduction requests in your organization? I'd love to hear your approach and learn from your experience.

#SupplyChain #Procurement #DemandPlanning #InventoryManagement #SupplyChainManagement #Operations #Purchasing #Forecasting #ABCAnalysis #InventoryOptimization #Leadership #ContinuousImprovement #DataDrivenDecisionMaking

Are you giving every SKU the same attention? That could be one of the biggest inventory mistakes.

One of the most effective tools in inventory management and demand planning is ABC-XYZ Analysis. It's simple to understand, yet incredibly powerful when applied correctly.

Think of it this way:

🔹 ABC Analysis helps you identify which products matter most financially. Not every item contributes equally to your inventory investment, so why manage them the same way?

🔹 XYZ Analysis looks at how predictable demand is. Some products sell consistently every month, while others fluctuate significantly. Knowing the difference helps you decide how much inventory you should actually carry.

When you combine these two methods, you gain a much clearer picture of where to focus your time, inventory investment, and planning efforts.

For example: 
✅ AX items deserve your highest attention because they are high-value products with stable demand. 
⚠️ AZ items are high-value but unpredictable, requiring frequent reviews and more agile replenishment. 
📦 CZ items usually need the least investment and may even be candidates for reduction or discontinuation.

The result?

✔ Better service levels
✔ Lower inventory costs
✔ Fewer stockouts and excess inventory
✔ Improved cash flow
✔ Smarter purchasing decisions backed by data

The goal isn't to have more inventory it's to have the right inventory, in the right quantity, at the right time.

In today's competitive supply chain environment, data-driven decisions are no longer optional—they're essential.

How does your organization prioritize inventory? Are you using ABC, XYZ, or the combined ABC-XYZ approach? I'd love to hear your experience.

⛑️🧰Have you ever noticed something interesting?

We spend a lot of time talking about how to onboard new employees. We create welcome packages, training plans, buddy systems, and first-90-day roadmaps. But we rarely ask an equally important question:

How do you onboard a Lean Specialist?

The answer isn’t as obvious as it seems.

A Lean expert can become one of the biggest drivers of improvement or one of the fastest ways to create resistance. The difference often has little to do with technical knowledge and everything to do with how the organization introduces the role.

📍Scenario 1: Lean doesn’t exist yet

This is both the easiest and the hardest situation.

There are no previous failures to overcome, but there are also no success stories. Expectations can quickly become unrealistic. Many leaders expect the new Lean Specialist to “fix the company” within a few months.

The reality is different.

The first responsibility is not to launch dozens of improvement projects. It is to understand the business.

A Lean Specialist should spend time on the shop floor, talk with operators, engineers, supervisors, maintenance teams, logistics, and office functions. Observe before proposing. Learn before teaching.

Only after understanding the culture, challenges, and daily work should the first improvement initiatives begin.

The first wins should be small, visible, and solve real problems for employees not just improve KPIs on a dashboard.

📍Scenario 2: Lean already exists

This is often more challenging.

The new Lean Specialist doesn’t start with a blank page. They inherit existing standards, projects, successes, failures, and, most importantly, opinions.

Before changing anything, it’s worth asking:

* Why do we work this way?
* What has already been tried?
* What worked?
* What failed?
* What frustrates people about Lean today?

Many organizations make the mistake of expecting every new Lean expert to introduce their own tools immediately.

But Lean is not about leaving your personal signature everywhere.

Sometimes the biggest improvement is continuing what already works while helping people improve it further.

Respect for people also means respecting the organization’s history.

The first 90 days matter

Whether Lean is new or already established, I believe the first months should focus on:

✅ Building relationships before driving change.
✅ Listening more than presenting.
✅ Understanding the business before selecting tools.
✅ Finding quick wins that matter to employees.
✅ Creating trust instead of pushing methodologies.

Lean tools are relatively easy to learn.

Building credibility takes much longer.

The biggest misconception

Companies often hire a Lean Specialist expecting immediate transformation.

But Lean transformation is never the responsibility of one person.

The Lean Specialist facilitates, coaches, and develops problem-solving capabilities.

Real improvement happens only when leaders and employees own the change together.

OpenAI's AI went rogue.  How is that for clickbait.

But I think many people are taking away the wrong lesson.

OpenAI wasn't asking the AI to be a helpful chatbot and make you happy. It was intentionally testing an AI agent designed to find vulnerabilities and achieve a cybersecurity objective while solving for a test. During that evaluation, the system aggressively pursued its assigned goal in ways the researchers did not anticipate.

The important question isn't... "Why did AI become evil?" It's... "Did we define the objective correctly?"

This is a lesson supply chain professionals, planners, and executives need to be careful of.

Goodhart's Law states: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

AI doesn't understand your business objective. It optimizes the reward function you give it. Reward functions are proxies, not perfect representations of success. AI eventually exploits the proxy rather than achieving the true objective

If your reward is "solve this problem," or “reduce forecast error” don't be surprised when it finds a shortcut you never intended that doesn’t solve the problem you actually intended.

That's not AI "going rogue." That's AI doing exactly what it was optimized to do.

Most AI today is highly specialized and capable within its objective. 

The lesson from this week's incident isn't that machines have become self-aware. It's that as AI becomes more capable, defining the right objective becomes just as important as building a better model. The biggest risk isn't AI thinking for itself. It's humans asking AI to optimize the wrong thing.

Tell it exactly who it is before it writes a single word

→ Constraint Prompting: 
Set hard rules upfront, word limits, banned phrases, required angles

→ Prompt Chaining: 
Use the output of one prompt as the direct input to the next

→ Iterative Refinement: 
Treat the first output as a draft, then give it specific critique instructions

→ Meta-Prompting: 
Ask it to write the ideal prompt for your task first, then use that

→ Least-to-Most: 
Break the hard problem into its smallest parts and solve each in sequence

→ Skeleton-of-Thought: 
Get the outline first, expand each section separately

→ Retrieval-Augmented: 
Paste in your own docs so it responds from your knowledge, not its defaults

Trade Update | Before You Assume This Is "Just Another Tariff"... Read This.
 
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) has finalized new Section 301 tariffs on imports from 60 trading partners.

Key Takeaways
➝ Scope: Applies to 60 economies representing approximately 99.4% of US imports covered by the investigation. 
➝ Legal Authority: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. 
➝ Reason: USTR concluded these countries' failure to prohibit imports made with forced labor is an unreasonable trade practice that burdens US commerce. 
➝ Effective Action: Additional tariffs of 10% or 12.5%, depending on each country's actions regarding forced labor import prohibitions. 
 
Tariff Breakdown
 
➝10% Tariff
Applies to countries that: 
Already have a forced labor import prohibition. 
Have committed to adopt one through a Reciprocal Trade Agreement. 
Have implemented a partial regime restricting forced labor imports. 

Countries include:
- Canada 
- Mexico 
- United Kingdom 
- India 
- Malaysia 
- Indonesia 
- Bangladesh 
- Argentina 
- Pakistan 
- Sri Lanka 
- Cambodia 
- Ecuador 
- El Salvador 
- Guatemala 
- Honduras 
- Jordan 
- Trinidad and Tobago 
 
➝ 10% or 12.5% (Net of MFN Rate)
Applies to certain products from:
- European Union 
- Japan 
- South Korea 
- Taiwan 
- Switzerland 
 
➝ 12.5% Tariff
Applies to the remaining investigated economies that have not adopted comparable forced labor import prohibitions.
 
Important Exemptions
The tariffs do not apply to:
- Products already subject to Section 232 tariffs 
- Informational materials, donations, and accompanied baggage 
- Certain critical raw materials 
- Products where tariffs could disrupt the US economy 
- Products unavailable from US or alternative sources 
 
➜ Why This Matters for Supply Chains
These new Section 301 tariffs replace the temporary Section 122 tariffs that were scheduled to expire tonight.

Sort cleared the clutter. Set in Order gave everything a home. Shine turned cleaning into inspection. Here's the problem: without the next S, all three quietly slide back to where they started within a few months.
Part 5 of the series: Standardize — the S that stops the first three from becoming a one-time cleanup drive.
Standardize isn't a thick SOP nobody reads. It's turning "how this should look" into something anyone can check in seconds, without asking a supervisor.
Here's the exercise I ask every MSME owner to try this week:
→ Photograph the station at its best — right after Sort, Set in Order and Shine
 → Turn that photo into a one-page visual standard, pinned at the station
 → Add a 2-minute daily checklist: does the floor match the photo, yes or no
 → Assign a rotating audit — any operator, any shift, no advance notice
 → Track how many "no" answers show up week over week, and why
The checklist itself isn't the point. What it exposes is: which shifts are slipping, which stations need a rethink, and where the standard was unrealistic to begin with.
Here's the harder truth: most standardization efforts die because they're written by management and enforced on operators. The ones that stick are built with the same people who'll live inside them every shift.
A standard that only exists on paper isn't a standard — it's a wish.
Does your shop floor look the same on Monday morning as it did the Friday you cleaned it?

What do Procurement and Emi Martinez have in common?

More than you think.

Martinez blocked 12 shots in the final against Spain. Including that miracle save with seconds left.

Nobody talks about those. All anyone remembers is the one shot that got past him. Even though it wasn't his fault.

Procurement works the same way.

The metrics always focus on what goes wrong, never what you quietly fix in the background.

One miss overshadows a dozen saves.

That's the reality.

Your team can't win without you.

You won't hear the cheers. You won't see your name in lights. But every smooth handoff, every avoided disaster, every quiet save, those are your fingerprints.

The crowd only sees the scoreboard. They miss the work behind the scenes.

Your wins might be invisible, but they're what keeps the business moving.

Spent the last few weeks running experiments for the October Algorithm Report update. Three things stood out. All three surprised me.
 
1. "Celebrate an Occasion" posts get an algorithm boost
 
Bigger creators are quietly shifting their announcement content. Not "here's my new offer" but "I hit 25,000 followers." "I signed client #1,000." "I just became an ambassador for [tool]."
 
I was skeptical. Then I tested it myself. My own celebration post outperformed my regular announcement posts by 2.3x impressions.
 
Across 800 posts we analyzed, the average lift sits between 1.6x and 2.1x.
 
How to use it:
 
• Attach the milestone to a number, not a feeling. "25,000 followers" beats "grateful for this community."
• Pair the win with one specific lesson, not a thank-you list.
• Use it sparingly. This works because it's rare. Every week and it reads as humble-bragging, not milestone-marking.
 
2. Infographics are in freefall, especially AI-made ones
 
2024 was the year of the infographic. Dense visual, one scroll-stop, multiplier between 5x and 7x. Everyone piled in.
 
That era is over. Across more than 6,000 infographics we analyzed, the format now sits between 0.9x and 1.4x. Some underperform a plain text post. Fully AI-designed ones drop further, to 0.6x-1.1x.
 
My read: infographic fatigue plus a growing "this smells like plagiarism/AI" instinct from the audience.
 
What to do instead:
 
• Swap the single dense infographic for a document post (carousel/PDF). Underused, and it outperforms infographics at the moment
• One clear insight per visual, not ten data points crammed into one frame.
• Hand-drawn or clearly human-annotated visuals are currently beating polished AI graphics. Imperfection reads as authenticity.
 
3. Popular topics can pull you outside your own topic cluster
 
Your distribution is built mostly on topic fit now, not network size. Which normally means: stay in your lane, post your 2-3 core themes, let the algorithm learn where you belong.
 
But there's an exception. Tie a trending, seasonal topic to a genuine personal experience, and it temporarily pulls your post into interest clusters you don't normally reach. Summer is here, so climate and sustainability content is a live example. Across 1,200+ posts in this category, a post connecting that theme to a personal experience outperformed regular posts by up to 3.5x impressions.

How to use this: 

Treat it as an occasional excursion, not a new content pillar. The topic gets you the temporary reach into new clusters. Your usual 2-3 themes are what get you remembered once people arrive.
 
None of these samples come close to the 1.3 million posts behind the Algorithm Insights Report itself, but 800 to 6,000+ posts is still a solid early signal. Full breakdown lands in the October update.

A digital thread succeeds only when the entire product lifecycle stays connected.

Integrating PLM, ERP, MES, and QMS is an important step, but technology alone is not enough. Teams also need trusted data, consistent processes, clear ownership, and complete traceability.

Nine factors create a reliable digital thread:

↳ Unified Data Foundation
Establish one trusted product data source, eliminate duplicates, and standardize data models.

↳ Seamless System Integration
Connect enterprise platforms through secure APIs and remove manual data transfers.

↳ Strong Data Governance
Define ownership, manage revisions consistently, and maintain complete audit trails.

↳ End-to-End Traceability
Link requirements to delivered products and preserve the history of every engineering change.

↳ Standardized Processes
Align engineering workflows, approvals, and release procedures across departments.

↳ Cross-Functional Collaboration
Share product information in real time across engineering, manufacturing, quality, and procurement.

↳ Change Management Excellence
Evaluate downstream impact, automate approvals, and synchronize revisions across systems.

↳ Scalable Architecture
Support new products, platforms, and business growth without reducing performance.

↳ Continuous Monitoring
Track adoption, data quality, synchronization health, and improvement through clear KPIs.

A digital thread is not a one-time integration project.

It is a connected operating model that improves decisions, accelerates changes, and strengthens product delivery.

Aravind Srinivas is beating Google at its own game, without a marketing budget.

Google had more models, more data, more engineers, more money. But Aravind won on the one thing many founders still treat as a second priority: distribution.

Here's what happened.

A few years ago he was a research intern. 4 months at OpenAI, 5 months at DeepMind, a year at Google. He was brilliant at building models but had never sold anything.

In August 2022 he started a search engine to take on Google. Everyone called it suicide. Seven days after ChatGPT launched, Perplexity went live.

Then he did the part nobody expects from a researcher.

He made himself the channel. Nonstop interviews, building the story in public every day.
He turned the product into the ad. Shipped a browser, gave it away free to the whole world. Reach over revenue.
He rented other people's audiences. One telecom deal added 640% more users in a single quarter.
He let word of mouth carry the rest. Around 80% of Perplexity's growth is organic.

Just distribution, engineered.

What it got him:

3,000 searches a day at launch, to nearly 100 million a day now
Roughly $0 to a $20B+ valuation in about 3 years

A guy who wrote research papers out-distributed the most powerful distribution machine ever built.

The best product almost never wins. The best go-to-market does.

Your model is table stakes. Everyone has access to good models now. What decides the winner is how you get in front of people, and what they feel when you do.

That's the entire reason Frontal AI exists: helping companies run their GTM as one flywheel. It's how you take on a bigger competitor with a fraction of its budget.

Aravind is the proof that this works.

my favorite events are the ones where nobody is networking.

no pitching. no scanning the room for someone more important. no "so what do you do" before they've even learned your name.

just people talking like friends.

my friend Ryan threw an event two days ago and it was genuinely one of the most fun events i've ever been to.

the wildest part? he pulled it together in 24 hours. in collaboration with Stanley.
24 hours. did i say 24 hours? crazy work.

i run events for a living and i can tell you that most people spend six weeks planning something that ends up feeling like a networking obligation with a coat check. maybe even 2 weeks if they're really rushing it. 

ryan pulled something together in a day that people are still talking about.

because he didn't optimize for the flyer. he optimized for the vibe.

that's the thing nobody gets.

the venue doesn't make the room. the guest list on paper doesn't make the room. the panel definitely doesn't make the room.

the room is made by whether people actually want to be there.

and you can feel that within 30 seconds of walking in.

the best events don't feel like events.

they feel like a really good hang that happens to be full of interesting people.

that's the whole bar.

what's the last event you went to where you actually forgot you were networking?

Don't post (obvious) AI-written content.

Here are 12 tells to delete & the 11 skills that fix it:

(all 11 skills are free here → how-to-ai.guide)

Delete these from your writing today-

1. "Delve." You've never said it out loud. Once.
2. "Crucial/pivotal." Nothing is that pivotal.
3. "Tapestry." No human speaks like this.
4. "Here's the thing." There is no thing.
5. "Hope this helps." It doesn't. It outs you.
6. "After careful consideration." without considering
7. "to provide a quick update." Just give the update.
8. "Most people…" The lazy oversimplification.
9. "Robust / seamless / realm." The corporate AI.
10. Adverb abuse. "X quietly runs Y." Nothing runs.
11. "It's not X, it's Y." The famous AI sentence alive.
12. 'This isn't a budget. It's a statement of intent' No

Now my personally used 11 Claude skills that fix it:

1. /writer
Writes the first draft in your structure, not Claude's.
Good draft in = nothing to clean up later.

2. /editor
Cuts the fluff and the filler.
Every sentence earns its place or dies.

3. /fact-checker
Kills invented stats and fake-sounding quotes.
One hallucinated number and nobody trusts you again.

4. /anti-AI style
The base rewrite. Breaks the robotic rhythm 
where every sentence is the same 18 words.

5. /ban-the-AI-words
Auto-blocks "delve," "crucial," "tapestry"
& the entire red list above.

6. /ban-the-AI-patterns
Kills "It's not X, it's Y" and the fake-deep endings.
The patterns out you faster than the words do.

7. /sound like your posts
Feed it 5 of your old posts. It writes like YOU, not like Claude. This one replaces every "humanizer" tool you've paid for.

8. /humanizer
Strips whatever AI smell is left.
Contractions in, em dashes out.

9. /red-pen
Flags your weak lines before your readers do.

10. /self-critique
Claude critiquing Claude beats Claude on the first try. It loops until the text reads clean.

11. /auto-block-banned-words

Your AI output is only as good as the prompt you're too lazy to write.

Blame the tool all you want... that won't fix the content.

I see people typing "make this better" into Claude 
And wondering why the post flops.

The real issue is what you're typing into it.
Without specifics, Claude is just guessing too.

And then you get generic content that sounds like everyone else's AI slop on the feed.

Here are 12 swaps that'll change what you get back, starting today:

1. When you want to make something more professional:

❌ "Make it more professional"
✅ "Rewrite so my ICP, [describe them], finds it clear within 5 seconds"

2. When you want to improve the output:

❌ "Improve it"
✅ "Tighten it using 3 filters: clarity, rhythm, and one clear CTA"

3. When your post needs to be reduced:

❌ "Make it shorter"
✅ "Cut 30% without losing the core point or the hook"

4. When the post doesn't sound like you:

❌ "Make it sound natural"
✅ "Rewrite in the way I'd say it out loud, no LinkedIn jargon. Ask me if you need clarity on this"

5. When you want small fixes without changing your voice:

❌ "Fix this"
✅ "Fix the rhythm and spelling, leave the voice exactly as it is"

6. When you want the post to hit harder:

❌ "Make it more persuasive"
✅ "Rebuild around this objection my reader has: [objection]"

7. When you want options to choose from:

❌ "Give me 3 versions"
✅ "Give me 3 versions with different hook angles and tell me which one you'd publish and why"

8. When you're starting from a blank page:

❌ "Write me a LinkedIn post about X"
✅ "Write a LinkedIn post for a founder building [company] selling to [ICP], with a hook that names a specific pain in line one"

9. When you need a better hook format: 

❌ "Make the hook better"
✅ "Give me 5 hook variations: One stat-led, one contrarian, one personal, one question-led, one story-led"

10. When you want a tailored carousel:

❌ "Write a carousel about X"
✅ "Write a 7-slide carousel: Slide 1 is the hook, slides 2-6 are one tactic each with an example, slide 7 is the CTA pushing to X"

11. When you need specific content ideas:

❌ "Give me content ideas"
✅ "Give me 10 post ideas a [founder type] would screenshot, based on this list of pain points: [paste pains]"

12. When you need a powerful CTA: 

❌ "Write the CTA"
✅ "Write 3 CTA options: One for saves, one for comments, one for DMs. Tell me which fits this post best"

None of these are complicated.

They're just specific.

And specific is the entire difference between AI output that sounds like everyone else's and AI output that sounds like you.

Stop wasting energy on the wrong people.

Focus on the ones who WANT to grow.

After coaching 650+ CEOs, I keep seeing the same pattern.

The leaders with the strongest teams refuse to manage everyone the same way. They diagnose each person individually and adjust their approach to fit.

One of the simplest tools for this is the Skill/Will Matrix, created by Max Landsberg.

It plots every team member on two axes: skill (their ability and experience) and will (their motivation and drive).

The result is four very different types of people, each needing a very different leadership response.

🟡 Top Performers sit in the high-skill, high-will quadrant. They deliver, they push themselves, and they raise the bar for everyone around them.

These are the people you build the future of the company around. Give them ownership. Ask for their input. Raise expectations over time. Recognize them often.

The mistake is overloading them just because they can handle it. Stretch them, but invest in them too.

🟢 High Potentials have the will but not yet the skill. They are eager, hungry, and ready to grow. They just need reps.

Coach them. Break their work into small wins. Celebrate progress over perfection. Pair them with a mentor. These are your future Top Performers if you develop them well.

🔵 Disengaged Experts are the trickiest group. They have the skill, but the motivation has gone. They might be bored, burnt out, or quietly outgrowing the role.

Ask what's behind the disconnect. Reconnect them to the mission. Adjust their goals or responsibilities. Set a clear timeline for change. If nothing changes, you have your answer.

🔴 Low Performers drain energy from the rest of the team. They lack the skill and the drive to build it.

Set clear expectations, give one chance to improve, and exit respectfully if nothing changes. Keeping them in place tells everyone else that your standards are negotiable.

People will not always fit neatly into one box, and skill and will both shift over time.

The point of the matrix is to lead each person according to where they are right now. That's where your energy compounds.

A demand planner is NOT a supply planner.

This infographic compares both roles:

Focus
↳ Demand planner: prediction of the future demand
↳ Supply planner: optimization to accomplish demand plan

Key activities
↳ Demand planner: identify anomalies in data and refine forecasts
↳ Supply planner: plan capacity and inventory to align with demand

Stakeholders
↳ Demand planner: CEO, marketing, sales, new product introductions, finance, supply planning
↳ Supply planner: manufacturing/operations/production, materials, procurement, finance, demand planning

Negotiation skills
↳ Demand planner: to navigate internal politics and communicate gaps against the plan
↳ Supply planner: to secure favorable terms with demand planners, production managers and suppliers

Data
↳ Demand planner: uses models to predict demand; POS data, shipments, orders
↳ Supply planner: uses models to optimize capacity, resources, inventory 

Demand
↳ Demand planner: unconstrained demand
↳ Supply planner: turns unconstrained demand into constrained demand

Metrics
↳ Demand planner: FVA (forecast value added), MAPE, WMAPE, bias
↳ Supply planner: OTIF (on time in full), fill rate, lost sales, inventory turnover

Technology
↳ Demand planner: advanced forecasting and data representation tools
↳ Supply planner: ERP, planning systems and inventory management tools

Impact on financials
↳ Demand planner: revenue (top line)
↳ Supply planner: cost (bottom line)
Note: late shipments or shortages can also impact the top line

Any others to add?

This is me speaking to Wispr Flow because it’s Friday and I’m tired.

But I needed to share something about how B2B buyers make decisions.

I think whatever marketing tactics come next or whatever new AI tool, these parts stay pretty much the same. And B2B messaging should focus on leveraging these behaviours as main marketing pull.

Because messaging should help your best-fit buyers to make a better decision faster and not regret it later. That’s it. 

So these are parts of human nature I think will probably never change:

1. People usually notice symptoms before they know what the real problem is, so to make something relevant fast, start with symptoms.

2. They protect how they already understand the situation, so when something is missing, they fill it with what they already know and feel comfortable with.

3. Also, they avoid change because the broken process they know still feels safer than one new thing they don’t understand yet.

4. They look for proof when a decision could affect their budget, reputation, job, relationship with the team, boss or whomever they have this accountability to prove themselves to.

5. Finally, after they want something, they look for a logical reason they can repeat to themselves, but which reason feels logical still depends on how they feel.

B2B buyers don’t stop being human when they want to find some solution and go and research and explore your marketing/sales material. 

And whenever I used behavioral psychology instead of another sleazy marketing tactic, results were better because people felt seen, because the messaging mirrored how they already felt.

I have yet to see a single demand/supply planning team improve on accuracy, service levels, or inventory obsolescence by increasing bonuses.

So why do we use them in the first place?

Most content is boring for 1 simple reason:


The writer takes too long to explain why anyone should care.

Most people write LinkedIn posts like they're telling a story at a dinner party.

But at a dinner party, people know who you are. They've agreed to spend the evening with you, and walking away halfway through a story would be a little rude. 

So you can take your time and give all the context you need.

On LinkedIn you get none of that. Strangers owe you nothing, and they can keep scrolling without giving you a second thought.

Your posts have to earn their attention.

Here's how anyone can do this:

1/ Open with proof

Start with a result, a number, or a real example. "I analyzed 200,000 posts" earns more attention than "Here are 5 LinkedIn tips" because the proof does the convincing before anyone even gets to the advice.

2/ Give people a reason to listen

Name the exact thing that earns the right to give this advice. I lean on my time at Goldman and my journey from 3,000 to 436K followers. That background is the one thing nobody can copy, even if they copy my content.

3/ Lead with the most surprising point

I write the full post before I write the hook. The strongest opening is usually buried halfway down the first draft, so I pull it to the top and build the rest of the post around it.

Most content is boring because it makes people wait to find out why it matters. 

Give them the reason first, and make it something they can check. A number, a result, a date, a name. Then they'll stay.

Toyota started 2026 with 33 days of new-vehicle supply.

Volkswagen started 2026 with 143.

Same country. Same year. Same tariffs.

That 110-day gap is not a demand story. It's a planning story.

Two groups of OEMs faced the same conditions. One ran lean buffers tied to actual consumption. The other planned multi-year capital deployment against an EV adoption forecast that did not materialize.

The results are in the filings:

→ EV days-of-supply hit 168 days in January 2026. ICE sat at 97. The widest gap on record (Cox Automotive).
→ Ford booked $19.5 billion in charges in December 2025, including an $8.5 billion Model E write-down.
→ Stellantis reported negative €6 billion in FY2024 industrial free cash flow, citing "temporarily elevated working capital."

That's CFO language for "the inventory plan was wrong."

The supplier base is paying the bill the OEMs forecast:

→ Marelli filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 with $4.9 billion in funded debt.
→ First Brands (FRAM, Raybestos) filed in September 2025 with $6 billion in debt and $4 billion off-balance-sheet.

They didn't fail because tariffs hit 25%. They failed because OEM demand collapsed against the forecast they had built capacity to serve.

AlixPartners 2025 revised the US EV forecast down 46%. When you plan multi-year capital deployment against a forecast, the forecast becomes a single point of failure for your balance sheet.

Toyota didn't dodge the EV trap by predicting better.

Toyota dodged it by carrying less forecast risk.

For those trying to make sense of the latest tariffs (as I am) -> quick update

The Supreme Court struck down the tariffs in February. But we have new tariffs that went up this morning. 

The Court never said tariffs were illegal. It said IEEPA was the wrong statute. So as the The Wall Street Journal reported today, the administration will use an obscure law from the 1930’s to implement this next round.  

Section 122 was capped at 15% and 150 days. The clock ran out July 24. Section 301 is the replacement. 

So here we go again. Below and in the attached charts, are where the pain points are. 

Who walked away: Mexico and Canada, where USMCA-qualifying product stays exempt. Tequila and Canadian whisky untouched. Scotch got its own carve-out this morning.

Who eats the tariff: Ireland, France, Italy and Spain at 10%. Irish whiskey, Cognac, Champagne, Aperol and Campari, and the entire wine bench. New Zealand, Australia and Chile at 12.5%. Japanese whisky at 12.5%.

3 of the four largest single-origin spirits categories are now exempt and the fourth is Cognac. 

France and Italy alone are 70.5% of US spend on imported wine. Both pay in full, because the "net of MFN" softener is worth nothing when spirits already enter at a zero base rate.

This is now the 4th legal regime in five months and this one may be a “stickier” tariff


Credit where it belongs. Park Street  had the supplier notice out before the Federal Register text was digestible. Distilled Spirits Council of the United States and Chris Swonger were on record within hours pushing for EU relief. Scotch Whisky Association  got the outcome everyone else in this thread wants.

The Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America  and the US Wine Trade Alliance  are carrying the wine side, which got no carve-out, no state visit and no champion! At a time when wine needs extra love and attention.

BOM failures begin long before production.

They usually start with duplicate records, uncontrolled revisions, unclear ownership, disconnected systems, and changes made outside formal approval processes.

Strong BOM governance creates one trusted product definition across engineering, manufacturing, procurement, quality, and service.

The foundation includes:

↳ Maintain one authoritative BOM in PLM
↳ Control every revision without overwriting history
↳ Standardize part numbers and naming conventions
↳ Route modifications through approved ECO workflows
↳ Synchronize PLM, ERP, MES, and QMS
↳ Assign clear ownership for EBOM and MBOM

Governance must also protect every release:

↳ Trace each modification from request to implementation
↳ Validate structures, quantities, references, and dependencies
↳ Apply consistent approval workflows
↳ Control product variants through configuration rules
↳ Restrict editing rights through role-based access
↳ Link approved drawings, specifications, and documents

The work does not end after release.

Teams must continuously remove obsolete or duplicate records, monitor BOM accuracy, measure revision cycle time, track approval delays, and update governance standards based on recurring issues.

A governed BOM improves more than data quality.

It reduces incorrect purchases, production delays, duplicate parts, rework, compliance gaps, and downstream confusion.

They say don't believe everything you see on social media, and posts from my last holiday were the perfect example of that.

You all saw the lovely beaches, nice pools and fun activities, and fake smiles, trying to convince myself I was having a good time, but you didn't see what was really going on.

I've raised complaints with the travel agent and fed back to the hotel, but I'm still waiting to hear back.  Here's what happened:

On my first evening, around 20–30 flies appeared in the toilet area, crawling up the walls and across the floor. I was aware there could be flies and had prepared for a few, but this was far more than that.

When I reported it to reception, I was told it was normal, they looked as though they were dying anyway, and it was “just the way it is”. I felt dismissed and as though I was overreacting. After a long journey, as a solo female traveller in an unfamiliar hotel and country, I didn’t have the energy to push further. I simply wanted someone to acknowledge my concerns and remove the flies.

When I returned from dinner, there were even more, crawling beneath the toilet door into the open-plan sink and bedroom area. I killed as many as I could with towels and blocked the bottom of the door with another towel.

Throughout the week, I also experienced poor customer service in the bars and one restaurant, alongside several housekeeping issues. These included a stained duvet and dead flies being left for two days until I cleaned them myself.  And then there were the stray dogs...

I tried to explain at checkout how the initial response had made me feel and how it had set the tone for my holiday. Once again, I was met with comments such as “they’re common here”, “we all have them in our homes” 

Unfortunately, the flies, housekeeping problems, and most importantly, the dismissive way my concerns were handled significantly affected my experience. Not what I expected from a supposedly 4* hotel.

I didn't complain more because, as a solo female traveller, while I felt completely safe there, I didn't want to make myself vulnerable by complaining too much, and I hope this is taken into consideration when they review my complaint.

It also raises a great point around how important customer service and experience are, how you treat people, and how you make them feel.  If you're running a business, this is one of the most powerful things you leverage if you're doing it right.

Most marketers still can't tell their own writing from AI.

That's not an insult. 
It's what happens when you use a tool without knowing what it's actually doing to your output.

The AI writing problem isn't that it sounds bad.

It's that it sounds the same.

Every piece follows the same rhythm. 
Same structure. 
Same words. 
"Pivotal." 
"Groundbreaking." 
"Serves as".
The sentences are clean. 
The logic holds. 
But there's no texture. 
No friction. 
No evidence that a real person sat down and thought about this.

And readers feel it before they can name it.

I spent the first part of my career at a global beauty brand running campaigns at scale. 
We had writers. 
Good ones. 
When AI arrived, the first drafts coming back were faster, but something felt off. 
The content passed spell-check and logic-check.
But it failed the gut check every time.

It took me longer than I'd like to admit to figure out why.

AI doesn't write badly. 
It writes predictably.

There are 29 patterns it falls back on. 
This infographic maps all of them.

The ones that keep showing up in my own drafts:

→ Significance inflation: 
"Pivotal moment." 
"Testament to"
Just say what happened.

→ Vague attributions: 
"Experts say." 
"Research shows." 
Name the source or cut the claim.

→ Em dash overuse: 
One comma. 
One full stop. 
Done.

→ Sycophantic openers: 
"Great question!" 
Just answer it.

→ Filler phrases: 
"Worth noting." 
"Important to remember." 
Start after the filler.

→ Excessive hedging: 
"Could potentially." 
"Might possibly." 
Make a call.

→ AI sign-offs: 
"Hope this helps." 
"Let me know." 
End with a next step or nothing.

→ Generic conclusions: 
"The future looks bright." 
State your actual conclusion in one sentence.

→ Rule of three: 
"Innovation, inspiration, and integrity." 
Pick two. 
Or one.

→ Copula avoidance: 
"Serves as".
"Functions as". 
Just use "is".

The fix for most of these is the same: say less and say it directly.

After 16 years in marketing, 
The discipline I've found most valuable has nothing to do with tools. 
It's the willingness to cut the line that sounds good but means nothing.

AI gives you a first draft. 
Your job is still to say something real.

The infographic attached walks through all 29 tells plus the fixes. 
Worth a proper read if you're editing AI output regularly.

If this kind of practical marketing thinking is useful, 
There's more of it on my page every week.

Pass this on to a teammate who's been cleaning up AI drafts and wondering why it always feels like so much work.

Genuinely curious where you land on this: 
Which of these patterns do you find hardest to catch in your own writing?

Claude launched a new model yesterday (Opus 5).
Now there are 4 to choose from. Here’s what to use when:

A quick email, a deep research project, and an end to end workflow shouldn't start with the same model.

Yet most people pick whichever one is on default and hope for the best.

Here's the simple guide I use instead:

1/ What They’e Built For

I think of them like four different hires. I wouldn't give the same task to a designer and a content strategist, so I don't send every task to the same model.

Haiku is built for fast, one-off tasks. Sonnet is the everyday model. Opus is made for complex enterprise work, and Fable is built for end to end workflows.

2/ Writing

Sonnet covers day to day emails and quick drafts. Fable is my pick when the draft has to follow my voice, specific instructions, and rules.

I use it for complex content where one missed detail makes the whole thing sound like generic AI copy.

3/ Research

Fable is what I reach for when I need deep research with sources, context, and different points of view.

Sonnet is faster when I have one clear question and need an answer I can use right away.

4/ Doc Analysis

Fable is best when the file is dense and every detail matters, like a contract or a filing.

For a normal spreadsheet or short document, Sonnet usually gives me what I need without making the task more complex.

5/ Skip It When

Every model has a wrong job too.

Skip Opus when the task is really simple. Skip Haiku when it's long and complex. Skip Sonnet when it's genuinely hard. And skip Fable when Sonnet can handle it.

6/ Brainstorming

I work with Sonnet to talk through an idea and push back and forth in real time. Haiku is enough for quick lists and captions.

Once the idea needs a proper strategy, more detail, or several angles, I move it into Fable.

7/ Context Window

Opus, Sonnet, and Fable can each hold 1M tokens of context. Haiku holds 200K.

That matters when I'm working with large docs, transcripts, examples, and feedback across a recurring project - the bigger the context window, the more the model can hold in its head at once.

The smartest model can be a waste on a simple job. And the fastest one can fall short on a hard one.

Spend five seconds choosing the right model before you spend twenty minutes fixing the answer - or get an invoice you regret later!

🌱🪴From Lean Practitioner to Lean Manager: It’s More Than a Job Title

I’ve noticed that organizations often use Lean titles replaceable:
Lean Practitioner
Lean Specialist
Lean Expert
Lean Manager
Yet these roles represent very different levels of responsibility, influence, and leadership.

A Lean career isn’t simply about learning more tools. It’s about expanding your impact from improving your own work to shaping an organization’s culture and business performance.

Here’s a practical way to distinguish these roles.

1️⃣Lean Practitioner – Applying Lean

Purpose: Improve your own work and contribute to continuous improvement.

Key responsibilities
• Apply Lean principles and standard work
• Identify waste and solve problems using PDCA or A3 thinking
• Participate in Kaizen activities
• Collect basic process data
• Sustain improvements and share ideas

Mandate
Improve the processes you own or work within while actively supporting your team’s improvement efforts.


2️⃣Lean Specialist – Facilitating Improvement

Purpose: Enable teams to improve.

Key responsibilities
• Lead Kaizen workshops
• Coach teams on Lean methods
• Train employees in Lean fundamentals
• Facilitate VSM and problem solving
• Develop visual management and monitor improvement metrics

Mandate
Lead improvement initiatives through facilitation, coaching, and influence rather than formal authority.


3️⃣Lean Expert – Driving Transformation

Purpose: Design Lean systems that support long-term business success.

Key responsibilities
• Develop Lean deployment strategies
• Coach leaders and managers
• Build Lean governance and operating systems
• Mentor Lean Specialists
• Align Lean initiatives with business strategy
• Remove systemic barriers to improvement

Mandate
Shape how Lean is implemented across functions and ensure improvements deliver sustainable business value.


4️⃣Lean Manager – Leading Through Lean

Purpose: Deliver business results by developing people and embedding Lean into daily leadership.

Key responsibilities
• Build high-performing teams
• Align improvement with strategic priorities
• Develop future Lean leaders
• Allocate resources effectively
• Create a culture of accountability, learning, and CI

Mandate
Lead people, make business decisions, and ensure Lean becomes the organization’s way of working, not just a collection of improvement projects.


⏩️The Progression

Lean Practitioner➡️ Specialist➡️ Expert➡️ Lean Manager

Apply➡️ Facilitate➡️ Transform➡️ Lead

The biggest shift is not technical expertise, it’s leadership.

* Practitioners improve their own work.
* Specialists improve processes with and through teams.
* Experts improve organizational systems.
* Managers improve business performance by developing people and creating the conditions for continuous improvement to thrive.

Lean is not a toolbox; it’s a leadership system. 

Organizations that clearly define these roles create stronger capabilities, clearer career paths, and more sustainable results.

🌱🪴🎯From Lean Practitioner to Lean Manager: What Skills Should Each Level Have?

In my previous article, I shared the different roles and responsibilities of a Lean Practitioner, Lean Specialist, Lean Expert, and Lean Manager.

A question followed naturally:
What are the minimum skills expected at each level?

While every organization has its own competency framework, I believe the progression should look something like this.

1️⃣Lean Practitioner – Learn and Apply

A Lean Practitioner doesn’t need to know every Lean tool. They need to understand why Lean exists and consistently apply its principles.

Minimum skills
• Understanding of Lean principles and the 8 wastes
• 5S, Visual Management and Standard Work
• Basic problem solving (PDCA, 5 Why)
• Ability to identify improvement opportunities
• Teamwork and willingness to learn
• Basic data collection and interpretation

At this level, curiosity and discipline are often more valuable than technical expertise.


2️⃣Lean Specialist – Coach and Facilitate

The Specialist’s role shifts from improving their own work to helping others improve.

Minimum skills
• Kaizen facilitation
• Value Stream Mapping
• Root Cause Analysis
• A3 thinking
• Training and coaching techniques
• Change management fundamentals
• Presentation and facilitation skills
• Basic project management

A great Specialist develops people, not just processes.


3️⃣Lean Expert – Design the System

A Lean Expert sees the organization as an interconnected system rather than isolated processes.

Minimum skills
• Lean deployment strategy
• Daily Management Systems
• Hoshin Kanri
• Leadership coaching
• Advanced problem solving
• Performance management and KPI design
• Organizational diagnosis
• Mentoring Lean Specialists

At this stage, technical expertise is expected, however influencing leaders becomes even more important.


4️⃣Lean Manager – Lead Through Lean

The Lean Manager is accountable for business performance, people development, and culture.

Minimum skills
• Strategic thinking
• Leadership and coaching
• Decision making
• Financial and business acumen
• Stakeholder management
• Talent development
• Conflict resolution
• Building a culture of continuous improvement

A Lean Manager isn’t measured by the number of Kaizen events delivered, but by the capability of the people they lead.


📈The Skill Evolution

The progression isn’t about learning more Lean tools.

It’s about expanding your capability:

Know the tools ⏩️ Teach the tools ⏩️ Design the system ⏩️ Develop people and deliver business results.

💥The higher you grow in Lean, the less your success depends on being the smartest problem solver in the room and the more it depends on enabling others to solve problems without you.

That’s when Lean stops being a methodology and becomes leadership.

Which of these four levels best describes where you are today? And what skill are you intentionally developing to reach the next level?

~Agnes

Andon System: Making Problems Visible Before They Become Failures!
Most operational problems do not become expensive immediately.
They become expensive because they remain hidden, unreported, or unresolved for too long.
A minor machine abnormality becomes downtime.
A picking error becomes a customer return.
A material shortage becomes a missed production plan.
A quality deviation becomes a rejected batch.
This is where Andon becomes powerful.
Andon is a Lean visual management and escalation system that makes abnormal conditions visible in real time—so the right people can respond before the issue spreads.
It may use:
🚦 Signal tower lights
🔔 Audible alarms
📺 Visual performance boards
📱 Digital escalation alerts
🖥️ Warehouse or production dashboards
But Andon is not simply a light or alarm.
A complete Andon system connects five actions:
Detect → Signal → Respond → Contain → Solve
Consider a warehouse picking process.
If a picker scans the wrong SKU, the system can:
✅ Block shipment confirmation
✅ Highlight the mismatch
✅ Alert the team leader
✅ Require correction before dispatch
✅ Record the issue for root-cause analysis
The immediate benefit is preventing the wrong shipment.
The greater benefit is learning from repeated alerts:
• Are similar products stored too closely?
• Are labels or barcodes unclear?
• Is the storage location incorrect?
• Is additional training required?
• Is the system master data accurate?
This is when Andon becomes more than visual management.
It becomes a source of operational intelligence.
However, Andon systems fail when:
❌ Alerts have no clear owner
❌ Response is too slow
❌ Employees fear escalation
❌ Teams reset signals without solving causes
❌ Alert data is collected but never reviewed
A strong Andon culture does not blame the person who exposes the problem.
It recognizes that person for protecting the process.
A hidden problem grows.
A visible problem can be managed.
A solved problem improves the system.

There are countless articles about Lean.

Here are my Top 10 reasons why I love working in Lean.

1️⃣ Every day is an opportunity to make something better.

No process is ever perfect, and that’s exciting—not frustrating.

2️⃣ Small improvements create extraordinary results.

A 1% improvement repeated every day becomes a significant competitive advantage over time.

3️⃣ Lean gives everyone a voice.

The best ideas rarely come from the boardroom. They come from the people doing the work every day.

4️⃣ Problems become opportunities.

Instead of asking, “Who’s responsible?” Lean encourages us to ask, “What can we learn?”

5️⃣ Data replaces opinions.

Good decisions are based on facts, observation, and understanding—not assumptions.

6️⃣ Leadership means serving others.

The best Lean leaders remove obstacles, coach their teams, and help people succeed.

7️⃣ Improvement is never finished.

Reaching today’s target simply creates tomorrow’s opportunity.

8️⃣ Lean develops people, not just processes.

The greatest return on any improvement initiative is a team that has learned how to solve problems independently.

9️⃣ Simplicity wins.

The best solutions are often the simplest ones—clear standards, visual management, and disciplined daily habits.

🔟 Lean creates a culture, not just results.

Better quality, lower costs, and higher productivity are outcomes. The real achievement is building an environment where people continuously improve together.

You know your personal brand can be personal right?? It’s called personal for a reason!!! 

Share what you feel comfortable with. The people saying LinkedIn isn’t Facebook just wish they were you.

AI can write your next LinkedIn post in 10 seconds.

That's why almost every post on this platform sounds the same.

You'll hit publish, get a few likes, and feel like you've cracked it.

Here's the thing though...

Taste is what AI can't shortcut for you. 
It comes from reading widely, studying what works, and knowing your POV well enough to defend it in the comments.

After 5 years in the industry, I know this for certain:

Good writing is built on a handful of habits.
Boring and repetitive, but anyone can build them without any AI tools.

Here are 10, built for anyone trying to grow on LinkedIn 👇

1️⃣ Copy the greats

Someone's already solved the formula you're stuck on. 
Borrow it and then make it yours.

Action: Find a post that performed. Break down its hook and structure, then rewrite your own post using that skeleton.

2️⃣ Cut 30% of every draft 

Every sentence that doesn't earn its place loses you readers.
First drafts are full of them.

Action: Write the post, walk away, then come back and cut a third before you publish.

3️⃣ Write every day, even badly

Post every day, even when you don't feel like it.
That's how you build the reps that make you better.

Action: Block the slot, ship the post. The bad ones teach you more than the good ones.

4️⃣ Read more books

People who read widely write differently.
If the only thing you're consuming is LinkedIn, your posts will sound like LinkedIn.

Action: Pick 1 book a month outside your industry and note the lines that stop you.

5️⃣ Build a brief before you write

The best posts answer 3 questions:
What am I trying to achieve, who's this for, and what do I want them to do next?

If it doesn't sound like you talking to a friend, it won't resonate.
Action: Read every post out loud and cut anything that sounds scripted.

8️⃣ Write for 1 specific person

Every post should be for 1 person with 1 specific problem.
Pick the exact person who's stuck on the problem you're solving.

Action: Finish this sentence before you write, "This is for [name] who is dealing with [problem]."

Anyone can post.

500 likes and no inbound is meaningless.
You need proof it moved someone to act.

Prompt engineering is dead

According to Nvidia's co-founder and the Head of Claude Code

We should write in loops and not prompts.

A prompt gives you one answer.

A loop gives you a system that can repeat the work, check the result, fix mistakes, and stop only when the goal is met.

That is the shift.

The future is not about asking AI better questions.

It is about designing better instructions for how AI should work through a task.

A good loop has 7 parts:

1. Goal: What should be achieved.
2. Work Source: Where the task comes from.
3. Rules: How the AI should behave.
4. Process: The steps it should follow.
5. Verification Checklist: How it checks the work.
6. Stop Condition: When the loop should end.
7. Escalation: When the AI should ask for human review.

This is how AI becomes more useful.

You stop babysitting every single response.
You give it a structure.
You give it a checklist.
You give it a stopping point.

That is how you move from prompting to building systems.

Trust isn't a decision your audience makes on purpose. It's a shortcut their brain takes to avoid risk. Understand this and you'll grow your impact.

Most people treat LinkedIn trust like a light switch.
 
Post → hope people believe you.
 
Unfortunately that's not how it works. The shortcut to avoid bad decisions fires in milliseconds, long before anyone reads your value proposition.
 
A few things happening in your reader's head, whether you're aware of it or not:
 
1. The halo effect.
   means they judge your credibility before they've read a single line, based purely on how your profile looks.
 
2. Specificity beats vagueness, every time. 
   Vague claims trigger skepticism. Specific claims (even small ones) trigger belief, because the brain trusts receipts more than promises.
 
3. Loss aversion is why a single thoughtful comment does more for your pipeline than five posts. 
   Rare reads as valuable, and most engagement on this platform is not rare.
 
4. And the mere-exposure effect explains why the fifth touchpoint lands and the first one doesn't. 
   Your reader isn't more convinced by then. They're just less afraid.
 
None of this happens by accident. It happens because trust is an integrated system with four moving parts, working in sequence, not in isolation.
 
I've been on the platform since 2005 and honestly over 95% of people over-invest in just one signle part of that system, ignore the rest, then wonder why visibility never turns into pipeline.

Most teams jump to solutions too quickly.
A supplier delivery is late.
A warehouse order is picked wrongly.
A customer complaint repeats.
The first reaction is usually:
👉 “Who made the mistake?”
But Lean asks a better question:
👉 “What caused the problem?”
That is where the Fishbone Diagram helps.
A Fishbone Diagram, also called an Ishikawa Diagram, helps teams organize possible causes before deciding on a solution.
The fish head = the problem
The bones = possible causes
Example: Supplier deliveries are repeatedly delayed 
Possible causes may include:
🔹 People
• No clear follow-up owner
• Team overloaded
🔹 Process
• PO released late
• No escalation rule
🔹 System
• Wrong ERP lead time
• No automated reminder
🔹 Material
• Supplier input shortage
• Quality issue
🔹 Data
• Poor KPI visibility
• Inaccurate records
🔹 External
• Transport delay
• Customs issue
• Demand changes
The value of Fishbone is simple:
✅ Stop blaming
✅ See all possible causes
✅ Structure the investigation
✅ Validate with facts
✅ Fix the real problem
But remember:
A Fishbone Diagram does not give the final answer.
It shows what needs to be investigated.
Practical rule:
❌ Don’t ask: “Who made the mistake?”
✅ Ask: “What process condition allowed this to happen?”
Because in Lean, the goal is not blame.
The goal is better process thinking.

In the past 6 weeks, I've gained nearly 1,000 followers on LinkedIn.

And I've maybe spent 3 hours per week on this platform.

Truthfully? I've been inconsistent in all of the things I know work.

And I still almost doubled my follower count.

For 2 years, I've been working behind the scenes of creators. I always saw myself as the behind-the-scenes person.

This year I committed to becoming visible. I started posting on TikTok, then Instagram, then LinkedIn.

And this platform has by far been the easiest to grow on.

No getting ready for video. 
No filming. 
No hour-long editing sessions. 
Just 15 minute drafts.

And it's kinda actually fun?!?

What's actually working:

➡️ Posting at least 4x per week (ideally daily)
➡️ Commenting on other people's posts (which I haven't even been consistent with)
➡️ Tagging creators I know when it's relevant
➡️ Vulnerability and real stories, not corporate lingo

Shoutout to Courtney Johnson 📣 Social Media and Mischa Collins 
for the frameworks and strategic advice from Level up on LinkedIn... 

and Stanley for the AI help.

I think it's time for me to update my profile and take this seriously.

What's stopping you from posting more?

Half the tasks eating your day could be done in a fraction of the time.
The tool you reach for is the problem.

Every common task, from research to note-taking to writing, has a slow way to do it and a faster one that produces something sharper.

The upgrade almost always comes from pairing two tools instead of leaning on one.
A single tool gets you a usable result, and the right second one fills the gap the first leaves behind.

For deep research, Perplexity pulls the sources in seconds while NotebookLM turns them into something you can build an argument from.

For meeting notes, a plain notes app captures what was said, but Granola hands you the summary and the action items before you have left the call.

For writing, Claude lays down the structure while saying it out loud through Wispr Flow keeps the words sounding like you.

Swap one tool on the task that eats your day and watch how much time comes back.

AI is only as good as the system behind it.

And the tool itself is no longer the advantage.

Knowing how to use it is.

Most people open Claude, type a question, get an answer.

The output they get back is a direct reflection of what they put in.

Claude works as well as you feed it, and what you feed it is prompts.

Here's the exact 3-layer system I use across all my companies:

1. The Master Prompt → This is WHO you are.

Most people start every Claude session from zero.
Claude has no idea who they are, what they're building, or how they work.

The master prompt fixes that permanently.
Build it once and every answer comes back built for you instead of for nobody.

1. The System Prompt → This is HOW you WORK.

You already have a process, you've just never written it down.
The system prompt is the recipe.

It tells Claude the steps, the standard, the way you want the job done.

1. Custom Instructions → This is HOW the OUTPUT comes back.

Without this, Claude writes like Claude.
With it, Claude writes like you.

Paste 2-3 examples of how you actually write.
Ask Claude to build your custom instructions from those examples.

The full breakdown of how to build each layer is in the carousel below.

The prompts you build are the most valuable asset your business will own.
And you have to start building that IP now.

Everyone has access to the same tools.
Not everyone has the same instructions behind them.

Save this for the next time you set up Claude to work for you.

Repost this for someone still starting from scratch every time they open Claude.
Follow for more on building a business that runs without you.

If you already knew all 26 hacks, unfollow me.

Almost nobody makes it past Claude hack 8:

(#3 is me deleting my own past advice):

1. Use the Claude Desktop app. The browser is the demo. The app is where Cowork lives.

2. Use Cowork, not the chatbot. If you're typing into a chat box, you're using it like it's 2025.

3. Forget .md files & folders. Folders leak old outputs into your context, and nobody on Earth maintains those files weekly.

4. Skills and Projects. That's the entire system now. A skill is a capability you teach once. A project is a place you go back to.

5. Delete your about-me file. Rebuild it as a skill so it follows you into every single chat.
✦ Don't know how to build one? Take mine:
✦ Go to how-to-ai.guide. Subscribe for free.
✦ Don't pay anything. Open my welcome email.
✦ Hit the automatic reply button inside.
✦ Open the Notion link. Go to "Claude skills".
✦ Download the library. Upload it in Customize.

6. Turn every setting off. Empty your global instructions. Leave Connectors on. That's it.

7. Projects remember between chats. And you can share one with your entire team in two clicks.

8. Here's where most people quit reading. The longer your chat, the dumber it gets. Anthropic's own engineers said it out loud.

9. So stop typing "no, I meant…". Click "Restart the conversation from here" on an earlier message. 

10. A token is roughly one word. Every word you send & receive is money. Message 30 costs you 31 times message 1.

11. Point Fable 5 at your single hardest problem. Two turns. Then switch models. Turns are the most expensive habit you have.

12. Opus 5 High for everything else. High, not Max.

13. Don't give Claude steps. Give it the goal & get out of the way. Steps drag it down to old Claude.

14. Don't paste logins, passwords, or keys. Ever.

15. Skills fire themselves. You don't prompt them. You type /command.

16. It will sound 100% sure when it's dead wrong.

17. Don't trust agreement either. Claude is a sycophant. Pleasing you and being right are two different jobs.

18. Use Research mode (the "+" in the chat box). Almost nobody knows it's in there. Give it something genuinely hard.

19. Add "use AskUserQuestion" to your prompt. Claude interviews you before it answers. It prompts itself better than you ever will.

20. Talk, don't type. Cowork reads 100,000 words in 15 secs, then waits for you at 60 words per minute. You speak at 150.

21. Ask for five very different versions. Then pick one. That part is taste, and taste is the part it can't do for you.

22. Make it audit its own answer before you trust a single line.

23. Feed it too much context and it goes in circles. Same answers every time, zero creativity. Keep the context in the project and the chat clean.

24. The first draft is yours to fix, not to ship. Always.

25. The only rule that matters: outsource the thinking, never the understanding.

Word just quietly became an AI battleground.

Most marketers still think of Word as the place drafts go to get formatted.

They open Copilot once, ask for a paragraph, and move on.

They have no idea two different AI systems are now fighting for control of their documents.

I spent 16 years writing and reviewing marketing docs before any of this existed.

Redlines took forever. 
Every clause, every claim, every compliance line checked by hand.

You're probably still doing version 14 of a doc, 
Chasing changes across three reviewers.

Here's what's actually changed that.

Microsoft Copilot is built straight into Word through Microsoft 365. 
It drafts, rewrites, summarises, 
And can now pull data straight from Excel and PowerPoint into your document.

Claude for Word launched in public beta this April. 
It works inside Word's own Track Changes system, 
So every edit shows up as a tracked, 
Reversible suggestion.

That distinction matters more than people realise.

Copilot can rewrite entire paragraphs without always showing you the exact change.

Claude shows every single edit as a suggestion you accept or reject one by one.

When I ran redlines the old way, a single contract review ate 90 minutes.

With this kind of AI support, that same review is closer to 5 minutes.

Here's what both tools can actually do for you:

→ Draft from a prompt and get a usable first version in minutes 

→ Summarise long reports and pull out the actual decisions buried inside 

→ Import data from Excel or PowerPoint straight into a document 

→ Redline contracts and clauses while keeping your formatting intact 

→ Chat with a document, including footnotes, comments, and tracked changes 

→ Build reusable review checklists your whole team can use

One thing I'd flag from experience: 
Neither tool replaces your judgement.

Copilot is currently missing from Enterprise audit logs and the Compliance API.

If your team lives and dies by compliance, 
That's worth knowing before you roll this out wide.

The marketing directors I talk to every week are past the "should we use AI" question.

They're on to "which parts of our documents should still get a human read before it goes out."

That's the actual skill now.

If this kind of breakdown is useful, 
There's more of it coming.

Pass this along to whoever on your team is still drowning in redlines.

Genuinely curious where you land: 
Copilot, Claude, or still doing it the old way?

US vodka volume in 2012: 123.6 million wine gallons bottled for domestic use. US vodka volume in 2024: 125.9 million wine gallons. Twelve years of essentially zero growth.

US vodka revenue across the same period: up, by a substantial margin.
The mechanism is mix. Super-premium share of total US spirits revenue roughly doubled from 2012 to 2024 (per DISCUS). Volume held at the bottom of the price ladder while dollar growth migrated up.

Premiumization is the only volume-flat story that produced returns. Vodka is the cleanest example because the producer base and the volume math are both well documented, but the same pattern holds across whiskey, tequila, and most established categories.

The practical implication: volume flat is not the same as value flat. The economics of a 2024 super-premium case bear no resemblance to the economics of a 2012 economy case in the same category. Same volume on a P&L, completely different business.

I killed my evening doomscroll habit saving 1-2 hours.

From ONE simple habit:

Switching my phone screen to grayscale.

You don't have to be highly disciplined or have iron willpower to break the doomscroll habit.

Instead, use this simple 30-second habit:

(It's how I consistently stay off my phone after 9pm every single day.)

Go to Settings. Accessibility. Display filters. Turn on grayscale.

That's it. Your phone still works. You just stripped out the color.

This makes the next evening's wind-down effortless for 3 reasons:

1. Color is what makes apps addictive.

Every red notification, every bright thumbnail is engineered to trigger dopamine. Grayscale removes that trigger entirely. The apps look flat. Boring. Easy to ignore.

2. Your brain stops linking your phone to reward.

Repeat this enough nights and the association breaks. Phone in hand no longer means pleasure. It just means a gray screen you don't really want to look at.

3. You put it down sooner because it's less interesting.

No willpower needed. No app blocker. No timer. The phone just stops competing for your attention because it stopped being visually stimulating.

What's one small change you've made that actually stuck?
