Original post:
__________

Claude is everywhere right now.

Every founder loves it.
Every creator loves it.
Every productivity YouTuber has suddenly discovered enlightenment.

And honestly?

I understand why.

But I think most people are learning the wrong lesson.

They think better AI creates better results.

It doesn't.

Better thinking creates better results.

AI just exposes the difference.

A lot of people treat prompting like making a wish.

"Write me a post."
"Build me a strategy."
"Help me grow."

It's the business version of standing in front of a fridge and saying:

"I want food."

Okay.

What food?

For who?
How much?
When?

The fridge is confused.
The AI is confused.
Your life is confused.

The real reason Claude feels so powerful is because it forces you to confront something most people avoid:

Clarity.

And clarity is rare.

Most people don't actually know what they want.

They know what they don't want.
They know what annoys them.
They know what they're afraid of.

But ask them what success looks like in precise detail?

Silence.

The fascinating thing is that AI mirrors this back to us.

A vague mind creates vague prompts.
Vague prompts create vague outputs.

Then people blame the technology.

Imagine giving directions to a taxi driver.

You say:

"Take me somewhere nice."

Good luck.

You might end up at a beach.
You might end up at a shopping mall
You might end up at your ex's wedding.

Technically all three are destinations.

The problem was never the driver.
The destination was unclear.

This is why the best AI users obsess over context.

Because context is how intelligence works.

Humans use context.
Doctors use context.
Lawyers use context.
Investors use context.

Without context, intelligence becomes guessing.

And guessing is expensive.

In business.
In relationships.
In life.

That's why I love the 9 part Claude prompt framework.

Task.
Context.
Reference.
Success brief.
Rules.
Tools.
Conversation.
Plan.
Push.

Notice something?

Almost none of it is about AI.
It's about thinking.
It's a blueprint for communicating clearly.
And clear communication is one of the highest paid skills on earth.

The deeper lesson here has nothing to do with Claude.
Or whatever model gets released next Tuesday.

The lesson is this:

Your results improve dramatically the moment you become specific.

Specific about your goals.
Specific about your standards.
Specific about what success actually means.

Most people spend years trying to find better answers.
Very few spend time asking better questions.
And the people who learn that distinction tend to win everywhere.

Not just with AI.
With everything.

P.S. How many of these 9 sections are actually in your prompts today?

Credit to Arfa Farheen. Follow her for more.

That leaves a lot of leverage unused.
Claude gets better when the request has shape.
Not more words.
Better handles.
Clearer verbs.
Reusable commands.

The useful shift is to stop asking vague questions.
Start giving Claude named jobs.
/summarize turns a wall of text into a clean brief.
/key points pulls out what matters.
/simplify makes messy thinking usable.
/compare creates a decision surface.
/risk check forces the hidden downside into view.

That is why shortcut libraries work.
They reduce the friction between intent and action.
You do not need to invent a prompt from scratch every time.
You choose the right pattern, insert the topic, and tighten the output.

For leadership work, the biggest wins are not novelty prompts.
They are repeatable prompts for repeated judgment.
Briefing.
Prioritising.
Emailing.
Planning.
Reviewing.
Explaining.
Learning.

A good shortcut does three things.
It tells Claude the task.
It gives the input slot.
It defines the kind of answer you want.
That small structure removes a surprising amount of noise.

Use the library like a menu, not a museum.
Pick five commands you actually need this week.
One for explaining.
One for deciding.
One for writing.
One for work admin.
One for learning faster.

Then make them yours.
Add your audience.
Add your constraints.
Add your standard of quality.
Add examples of what good looks like.
Claude is useful by default.
Claude is much better when your operating system is clear.

The real productivity gain is not memorising 100 shortcuts.
It is building a small prompt vocabulary your team can share.
When everyone uses the same verbs, outputs become easier to review.
Decisions move faster.
Drafts need fewer rewrites.
And Claude becomes part of the workflow instead of another blank box.

Start with the commands that remove the most thinking drag.
Keep the ones you reuse.
Delete the clever ones that never leave the notes app.

__________

The debate is framed wrong.
SEO, AEO, GEO, SXO and AIO are not five rival strategies.
They are five layers of the same discovery system.

SEO builds the foundation.
→ Make pages crawlable, technically sound and easy to understand.
→ Target real search intent with useful content and internal links.
→ Without this base, every newer acronym has less to work with.

AEO earns the direct answer.
→ Structure clear responses for snippets, FAQs and voice results.
→ Use schema where it helps machines interpret the page.
→ If the answer is buried, zero-click visibility goes elsewhere.

GEO earns the citation.
→ Create authoritative passages that ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity can reference.
→ Strengthen entities, E-E-A-T signals and topical depth.
→ Check whether AI answers mention your brand, not just your category.

SXO turns attention into action.
→ Improve speed, clarity, navigation and calls to action.
→ Track whether visitors engage, convert or leave confused.
→ Ranking without a useful experience produces traffic, not momentum.

AIO prepares content for AI consumption.
→ Use semantic structure, clean code and reusable content blocks.
→ Make key claims easy to extract without losing context.
→ Design for people first, then make the meaning machine-readable.

The practical sequence matters.
1. Audit technical SEO and indexability.
2. Rewrite weak pages around one clear search intent.
3. Add concise answer blocks for high-value questions.
4. Test citations across ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity.
5. Fix the experience between landing page and next action.

Do not assign every acronym to a separate team.
Create one shared scorecard for visibility, answers, citations, experience and reuse.
Review it monthly against the pages that matter most.

The diagnostic is simple.
❌ Rankings but no clicks: revisit the result and intent.
❌ Clicks but no action: fix SXO friction.
❌ Strong pages but no AI mentions: improve GEO evidence and entity clarity.
❌ Useful content but poor extraction: strengthen AEO and AIO structure.

The winning model is additive.
SEO gets you found.
AEO gets you selected.
GEO gets you cited.
SXO gets users moving.
AIO keeps the content useful in an AI-first interface.

Treat the five layers as one operating system.
The teams that connect them will compound every improvement.
The teams that chase acronyms will keep rebuilding the same foundation.

What if your Lean system is already too slow for AI-driven manufacturing???

That’s the uncomfortable question behind Industry 4.0.

A lot of factories talk about AI, IoT, Big Data, Machine Learning, Cloud Computing, AR, VR and robots.

The diagram looks clean.

But the floor tells a different story.

Machines still wait for decisions.
Supervisors still chase updates.
Operators still ask what’s next.
Maintenance still reacts after the breakdown.
Quality still finds problems too late.

Then we call it “digital transformation.”

But if the basic system is unstable, technology only makes the instability more visible.

AI can read the data.
IoT can collect the signal.
Cloud can connect the plant.
Robots can repeat the motion.
AR can guide the operator.
Big Data can show the pattern.

But someone still needs to define the process.

What is the standard?
Where is the bottleneck?
Who owns the response?
What happens when the signal turns red?
What decision changes on the floor?

That’s where Lean still matters.

Industry 4.0 without Lean becomes expensive noise.

Lean gives the system structure.
AI makes the system visible.

The real opportunity is not replacing the floor with technology.

It is building a floor where people, process and technology finally speak the same language.

Stability first...
Then AI has something worth reading.

Sort cleared the clutter. Set in Order gave everything a home. Shine turned cleaning into inspection. Standardize made "right" something anyone could check in seconds.

Part 6, and the last of the series: Sustain — the S that decides whether the other four were worth doing at all.

Sustain isn't posters, slogans, or a monthly reminder to "maintain 5S discipline." Discipline is what you fall back on when the system is badly designed. Sustain is what you build so the standard survives a rush order, a bad week, and a shift you weren't there to watch.

Here's the exercise I ask every MSME owner to try this week:

→ Block 20 minutes in your own calendar — same day, same time, every week — to walk the floor yourself → Use the same one-page standard your team built, not a separate management checklist → For every "no" you find, ask why the standard failed before asking who failed it → Fix one system-level obstacle each week: a bin in the wrong place, a tool that's too far, a step nobody has time for → Put what you fixed up on the board where the whole shift can see it

The payoff isn't a tidy floor. It's that your team stops treating 5S as your programme and starts treating it as how the floor runs.

Here's the harder truth: 5S dies in the owner's calendar, not on the shop floor. If your walk is the first thing cancelled when things get busy, operators learn exactly what it's worth — faster than any poster can teach them.

Five S's. One habit. That's the whole system.

The wrong way to use Claude is the most common way to use Claude.

And it's the most common way to use other AI tools with similar features.

Like all tools, there are dos and don'ts.

Knowing the difference is what separates a good experience with Claude from a frustrating one.

Start by avoiding these 5 mistakes when using Claude in your content workflow:

1. Don't Type Your Prompts

Typing slows you down and gives Claude less to work with.

Speaking your prompt out loud is much faster and helps Claude understand what you want.

2. Don't Say "Act Like an Expert"

This is too vague and gives you generic responses.

Ask what a specific person would do.

That person could be Warren Buffett, Alex Hormozi, or anyone you take inspiration from for your business.

Specific names get specific answers.

3. Don't Start a New Chat Every Time

You lose all context and have to re-prompt your instructions every session.

Upload a set of instructions with your tone, audience, and offer so every chat has context.

4. Don't Check Claude's Work Yourself First

You'll waste time reviewing Claude's responses when it could have already caught the mistakes itself.

Tell it to review its own response before you read it.

That way, it catches issues on its own and learns from its mistakes.

5. Don't Copy and Paste Everything Manually

Pasting content one piece at a time into Claude wastes time.

Connect Claude directly to tools like Canva and have it read and paste your text into your project for you.

The more intentional you are with how you use Claude, the better your content creation process will get.

Start with these 5 mistakes, and you'll slowly start to notice the difference in your creative output.

Successful AI rollouts run on one counterintuitive rule: the 1% rule.

Find the 1% of work where AI actually compounds. Then stop feeding everything else.

Most companies do the opposite. They fund scattered pilots, chase every use case, buy more tools, and wonder why scale never comes.

After 3 years of enterprise AI, adoption is nearly universal. Enterprise value is still rare. The winners are doing less, on purpose.

Here's how the 1% rule works:

1/ Value Concentrates. Your Budget Should Too
→ ~70% of AI's value sits in core functions like sales, marketing, R&D, supply chain, and IT
→ Most portfolios still fund scattered pilots chasing marginal use cases
Reality: Spreading AI investment evenly is dilution.

2/ Most Pilots Are Already Dead
→ Gartner predicted 30%+ of GenAI projects abandoned after POC by end of 2025
→ Gartner also predicts 40%+ of agentic AI projects canceled by end of 2027
Reality: Zombie pilots drain the work that could compound.

3/ The Gap Is Widening, Not Closing
→ BCG finds only 5% of companies are "future-built" and generating value from AI at scale
→ These companies achieve 5x revenue increases and 3x cost reductions of others
Reality: AI gains compound only when focus does.

4/ Scale Is the Bottleneck, Not Adoption
→ 88% of organizations use AI in at least one business function
→ Only ~one-third have started scaling AI programs
Reality: Using AI everywhere and scaling it nowhere is the default failure mode.

5/ Redesign the Work. Don't Bolt On the Model
→ McKinsey: workflow redesign is one of the strongest contributors to AI business impact
→ AI high performers are ~3x more likely to have fundamentally redesigned workflows
Reality: AI dropped onto a broken process just makes it faster.

6/ Spend 70% of the Effort on People and Process
→ BCG's rule: 10% algorithms, 20% tech and data, 70% people, process, and change
→ Many buy tools before redesigning how people will use them
Reality: The model is easy. The change is the work.

7/ Your Shadow Power Users Already Found the 1%
→ Employees are already using AI to remove friction from repetitive, high-volume work
→ Those unofficial workflows are a map to where value lives
Reality: Look at what your people already try to automate.

8/ Fund the Compounder. Kill the Rest
→ Concentrate budget, talent, data, governance, and executive attention on the workflow that pays back
→ Run it long enough to compound the learning, then expand from strength
Reality: "What do we stop funding?" is the question that scales.

The 1% rule is not about doing less AI. It's about refusing to spread a finite budget across infinite ambition.

Just hold Shift & YAP. Let me show you:

Step 2. Open Settings → General → Shortcuts.
Step 3. Pick your activation key. I use Shift.
Step 4. Open Claude. Hold Shift. Start yapping.

The stories only you can tell.

7 Steps to Master Claude in a Weekend:

(and save hours every week)

You do not need another 20-hour AI course.
You need one weekend.

A few real tasks.
And lots of practice.

Here is your weekend plan for mastering Claude:

1. Pick 3 Real Work Tasks
→ Choose tasks you already complete every week.
→ Try summarising reports, creating training content or analysing feedback.
The Goal: Learn Claude through useful work—not random prompts.

2. Master One Prompt Formula
→ Give Claude a role, context, task, constraints and output format.
→ Clear instructions make strong results easier to repeat.
Try This: “Act as [role]. Using [context], complete [task]. Follow [rules]. Present it as [format].”

3. Show It What ‘Good’ Looks Like
→ Add one or two examples of your ideal output.
→ Ask Claude to identify the patterns before creating something new.
The Goal: Stop describing your standards from scratch every time.

4. Build Your First Project
→ Upload useful policies, reports, templates or learning materials.
→ Add instructions explaining your audience, tone and objectives.
The Goal: Create a focused workspace that understands your work. Projects can contain their own chats, instructions and knowledge base.

5. Learn When To Use Research
→ Use normal chat for quick thinking and drafting.
→ Use Research when you need deeper investigation and checkable sources.
The Goal: Match the tool to the task instead of using maximum power for everything. Claude’s Research mode conducts multiple searches and produces cited findings.

6. Create Something You Can Use
→ Build a quiz, dashboard, decision tool or interactive learning resource.
→ Improve it through several rounds of specific feedback.
The Goal: Move beyond answers and start creating assets. Claude Artifacts can turn instructions into shareable tools, visualisations and content.

7. Save Your Winning Workflows
→ Keep the prompts that consistently produce useful results.
→ Record the task, inputs, prompt and quality checks for each one.
The Goal: Finish Sunday with a repeatable system—not just more AI knowledge.

You will not learn Claude by collecting prompts.
You learn it by solving real problems.

Reviewing the output.
And improving your instructions.

One of the misconceptions about procurement is that it's all about negotiating prices 💷 .
.
.
.
I understand why people think that. After all, procurement professionals spend a great deal of time working with suppliers. But over the years I've learnt that focusing on suppliers too early can mean overlooking the real opportunity.

I remember visiting a manufacturing business that wanted help reducing purchasing costs. Before I arrived, the owner had already assembled files containing supplier quotations, contracts and price histories. He expected we'd spend the day comparing costs. Instead, I asked if we could take a walk around the factory first.

We spent the morning talking to people rather than looking at paperwork. We watched materials arrive, followed jobs through production and listened carefully to the conversations taking place between departments.
Just before lunch the owner looked at me and said, "I thought we were here to talk about suppliers." The truth was that we already were. 

Every delay in production affects purchasing decisions. Every inaccurate stock record influences replenishment. Every unclear production schedule creates unnecessary urgency or lack of action.

None of those issues began with the supplier, yet they all eventually land on the purchasing team's desk.

Strong procurement doesn't necessarily begin with buying. It begins with understanding how the whole business works together. Only then can purchasing become the strategic function it was always intended to be.

Some of the largest commercial improvements I've helped businesses achieve, came not from negotiating harder, but from helping different parts of the business work together more effectively.

Most IBP redesigns add more structure. More meetings, more templates, more review cycles. Agile IBP does the opposite.

The monthly S&OP review stays. But it stops being the place where decisions are made. It becomes the place where decisions are confirmed, challenged, or escalated. The real work happens in smaller, faster loops in between.

What changes in practice:
The demand review stops being a forecast alignment meeting. It becomes a signal review. What has changed since last week, what does it mean for our decisions, and what do we not yet know.

The supply review stops being a capacity utilization report. It becomes a constraint conversation. Where are we exposed, what are the options, and what is the cost of each.

The executive meeting stops being a presentation of agreed numbers. It becomes a decision point for the scenarios that did not resolve themselves at a lower level.

The role of the IBP lead changes too. Less process owner, more decision architect. The job is not to run the meetings. It is to make sure the right tension reaches the right people at the right moment.

This is not a lighter process. It is a more intentional one.

Trust in Procurement isn't built in the boardroom.

I mapped Procurement onto the human heart. 

Every chamber, valve and vessel has a job. So does every habit that earns you trust.

Sinoatrial Node - The Trust Pacemaker 
↳ Sets the rhythm every other beat follows. 
↳ Trust isn't a big gesture. It's showing up on time, replying when you said you would, and doing that on repeat until the rhythm sets itself.

Capillaries - The Micro-Trust Network 
↳ The smallest vessels, where the real exchange happens. 
↳ Not the big meetings. The quick reply. The favour returned. The heads-up given before it was owed.

Miss those two and nothing else in the system works. You can have the strongest negotiation chamber in the business. 

If the rhythm's off and the small exchanges don't happen, stakeholders won't wait around to find out why.

Right Atrium - The Feedback Intake
↳ Supplier complaints, stakeholder frustration, hard feedback lands here first. ↳ The discipline is processing it. Not deflecting it.

Left Atrium - The Empathy Reservoir 
↳ The pause before responding. 
↳ Actually absorbing what someone's telling you before you react to it.

Left Ventricle - The Negotiation Chamber 
↳ The strongest chamber, pumping with the most force. 
↳ Built on preparation, leverage, and knowing your walk-away point before you sit down.

Mitral Valve - The Boundary Valve 
↳ Opens to let the right requests through. Closes to stop scope creep flowing back. 
↳ Saying no cleanly is still a form of trust.

Septum - The Integrity Wall 
↳ Keeps the two sides completely separate so nothing crosses that shouldn't. ↳ The line you don't cross under pressure, even for a good supplier relationship.

Aorta - The Value Artery 
↳ The single channel your value travels through to reach the C-suite. 
↳ Do the work brilliantly and say nothing about it, and it still won't get funded next year.

The muscle, the valves, the arteries all matter. But none of them work without rhythm.

Trust isn't the big win you post about. It's the small thing you did again today.

Traceability turns complexity into control.

A product does not move through manufacturing as isolated files, systems, and processes. Every requirement, design decision, material, inspection, and change must remain connected throughout the lifecycle.

Requirements traceability links customer and business needs to engineering requirements.

↳ Regulatory traceability maps them to applicable standards.
↳ Validation traceability connects them to verification activities and results.
↳ Change impact traceability identifies what is affected when a requirement changes.

Design traceability connects the complete product definition.

↳ CAD files link to parts, assemblies, and revisions.
↳ BOM traceability preserves component relationships.
↳ Documents connect drawings and specifications with product data.
↳ Configuration traceability manages options, variants, and dependencies.

Manufacturing traceability carries this context into execution.

↳ Processes connect routings and work instructions to components.
↳ Materials connect batches and suppliers to finished products.
↳ WIP tracks lots or serial numbers through every operation.
↳ Production orders link BOMs, resources, and schedules.

Quality traceability connects inspections, test results, non-conformances, CAPAs, and calibration records to the correct product records.

Traceability must also continue after shipment through serial numbers, service history, maintenance actions, and audit trails.

End-to-end traceability closes the loop from requirement to design, production, quality, service, and final outcome.

It improves compliance, change control, root-cause analysis, recall readiness, and customer confidence.

Which traceability gap creates the greatest risk in your product lifecycle?

Most AI failures do not start with the model.
They start with the missing governance layer around it.

The risky pattern is easy to spot:
Teams ship pilots before they define ownership.
They connect data before they check data quality.
They add RAG before they control permissions.
They validate outputs after users have already seen them.

That is how AI moves from useful to fragile.

Here are the 4 layers every leader should audit.

→ 1. Governance
Set the rules, roles, accountability, and risk appetite before a model goes live.
Diagnostic check: who owns the final decision when an AI system causes risk?
If the answer is unclear, the governance layer is not real yet.

→ 2. Data Strategy
Own the data layer, not just the AI model.
The source post flags a hard number: 80% of AI project failures trace back to poor data quality.
Action: map data lineage, access controls, structured data, unstructured data, and metadata ownership.

→ 3. Retrieval & Context
Ground every response in verified internal facts.
RAG is not just a search box attached to an LLM.
The mechanism matters: semantic search, permission-aware RAG, knowledge graphs, freshness, and traceability.

→ 4. Model & Output Controls
Build safeguards into the system before deployment.
That means prompt guardrails, output validation, PII detection, content filters, monitoring, and alerts.
The goal is not perfection.
The goal is catching harmful outputs before they reach customers, teams, or executives.

A practical workflow looks like this:
Data sources feed access controls.
Access controls shape context retrieval.
Context retrieval informs the AI model.
The model passes through output controls.
The result becomes a trusted output.

Then the system loops back:
Monitor.
Learn.
Improve.

This is the difference between experimenting with AI and operating AI.
Governance is not the paperwork at the end.
It is the foundation that lets useful AI scale.

Where is your AI governance layer weakest right now?

You don't need Claude Fable 5 for 90% of your work.
Here's how to use it for the other 10% without running out of money:

Most people switched over to Fable 5 the week it launched and never switched back.

That was fine while Anthropic was giving it away…unfortunately, we all need to pay now.

Almost nothing you do in a day needs the power of Fable 6. Emails, quick questions, cleaning up a draft, Opus and Sonnet can all of it and you won't notice the difference.

The 10% that does need it - the deep reasoning, the complex analysis - is worth setting up properly:

1/ Select the model

Open a new chat and pick "Fable 5" from the dropdown. 

Check your plan first, because some have it built in and everyone else is spending credits from the moment they select it.

2/ Choose a problem worth the money

Save it for multi-step work that needs real reasoning. Reviewing a financial report, comparing a bunch of docs, reading charts, PDFs and spreadsheets together in one go.

3/ Tell Claude your goal

Most people describe the task and stop. Add one line before the prompt instead: "When this is done, I need..." Give it a finished deliverable to work backwards from.

4/ Give clear instructions

Every strong Fable 5 prompt has 5 parts. The task, the reason it matters, who it's for, the sources to use, and the rules to follow. 

Miss those and Claude fills the gaps with assumptions, which is the most expensive kind of rewrite.

5/ Add your files

Click the + button in the lower left and upload everything relevant. Then say what each file is for. 

"Use File A for the prices." "Use File B for the customer feedback." Pointed instructions beat a pile of attachments every time.

6/ Set the effort level

This is the dial that actually controls your spend. It sits behind the model name next to the send button and you can change it mid-conversation. 

Keep it low for work that doesn't need a long review, and move it higher when the task has many stages, difficult decisions, large amounts of source material, or numbers that have to be right.

7/ Review the plan

If you're running this in Claude Code, a panel shows exactly what it intends to do before it starts. Glance at it every time. 

Catching a mistake there costs you nothing, and catching it in the finished file costs you the whole run.

8/ Expect auto switching

The model will automatically move over if you're in a certain niche, but don't worry, this happens in ~5% of cases.

For your every day work, Opus and Sonnet are great. But if you are going to use Fable, taking a few minutes to set it up well could save you hundreds.

Every manufacturer I talk to right now is having the reshoring conversation. Most of them are having the wrong one.
The wrong conversation: "Should we move production out of China?" The right conversation: "What's our actual exposure, and how do we reduce it without blowing up the supply chain?"
I've moved 121 SKUs from China. Here's what I've seen go wrong when companies skip the second question:
Panic reshoring is the most expensive version. New tariff gets announced. CEO calls an emergency meeting. Someone gets the mandate to "find domestic suppliers — fast." Three months later, they've moved 10 SKUs at a 30% cost premium, quality isn't dialed in, and they've burned through the engineering team's bandwidth on firefighting instead of qualification. I've seen this happen more than once in the last year.
Here's what the right version looks like:
You start with the math. Map every SKU by tariff exposure, sourcing difficulty, and production criticality. Rank them. That ranked list becomes your project plan.
You build inventory before you move anything. We built 18 months of safety stock before we transferred a single mold. Expensive? Yeah. But it's the decision that lets you move at the right pace instead of urgent pace.
You move the knowledge, not just the contract. Molds, setup notes, first article inspection history — all of it. Most reshoring fails because companies switch suppliers and leave the institutional knowledge with the old vendor.
You do the full cost math. Domestic unit cost is almost always higher. But tariffs, freight, lead time, quality escapes, problem resolution — when you add it all up, the net was 12% cheaper for us.
The manufacturers who are going to come out ahead aren't the ones who move fastest. They're the ones who move most deliberately.
Are you reshoring strategically or reactively?

Bad metrics make demand planners look bad.

This infographic shows the 7 critical metrics for demand planners to track:

# 1 - Forecast Accuracy (at the right level)
↳ How close the forecast is to actual demand at the level where decisions are made (SKU-family, product family, region)
↳ WMAPE = Σ |Actual − Forecast| / Σ Actual

# 2 - Forecast Bias
↳ Whether the forecast is systematically over- or under-stated over time
↳ Bias = Σ (Actual − Forecast) / Σ Forecast

# 3 - Forecast Value Add (FVA)
↳ Whether the demand planning process improves or degrades the forecast compared to a baseline 
↳ FVA = Accuracy_after − Accuracy_before; Positive FVA → planning added value; Negative FVA → planning added noise

# 4 - Demand Volatility (Coefficient of Variation)
↳ How unstable demand is relative to its average
↳ Coefficient of Variation (CoV) = Standard Deviation of Demand / Mean Demand; Higher CoV = more volatile, less predictable demand

# 5 - Consensus Forecast Accuracy
↳ How accurate the final, cross-functional forecast is after Sales, Marketing, and Finance inputs
↳ Consensus Accuracy = |Actual − Consensus Forecast| / Actual
 
# 6 - Forecast Timeliness / Stability
↳ How much the forecast changes after it should be locked
↳ Forecast Stability = |Forecast_t − Forecast_t−1| / Forecast_t−1
Or % Changed Volume = Volume changed after freeze / Total forecast volume

# 7 - Forecast Accuracy vs Inventory Outcome
↳ Whether forecast accuracy actually translates into better inventory and service results
↳ Excess Inventory ≈ Over-forecast × Unit Cost; Stockouts ≈ Under-forecast × Demand Shortfall 

Any others to add?

"Can it be as simple as our current system?"

I had this during a recent Business Central demo. The operations team could immediately see the benefits. Better visibility, more integrated processes and a platform that could support the company's growth plans.

The finance team were less convinced.

Their current system is easier.

And to be fair, they're right.

The challenge is that their current system is a finance system. It does finance really well, but it was never designed to manage the wider business processes that the company now needs.

As businesses grow, processes become more complex. More people. More transactions. More stock. More projects. More reporting. More integration.

There's a common misconception that a modern ERP should be able to handle all of that complexity whilst remaining as simple as an accounting package designed for a much narrower purpose.

Unfortunately, business processes don't become simpler as a company scales.

The real goal isn't to make complex processes look simple. It's to make them manageable, visible and controlled.

Sometimes the easiest system today becomes the biggest constraint tomorrow.

What's interesting, though, is that we're starting to see technology come full circle.

With Copilot, agents and AI becoming increasingly embedded within Business Central, we're getting closer to a world where the complexity remains in the system, but users don't necessarily have to deal with all of it directly.

Instead of learning every process, users can increasingly be guided through tasks, have routine activities automated, and let the system do more of the heavy lifting.

The business still gets the capability it needs to scale. The user gets a simpler experience.

Maybe the question won't be "Can it be as simple as our current system?"

Maybe it'll become "Can it be more powerful without feeling more complicated?"

And that's a much more interesting conversation.

The optimization tool says to cut safety stock.  The risk is low.  The math is sound.

Nobody cuts it.

Not because they disagree with the model.  Because two years ago they took the blame for a stockout, and excess inventory sits in a nebulous bucket on the balance sheet.

That asymmetry is the whole story.  A stockout has a date, a customer, and a name attached to it.  Excess has none of those.  It's a line on a balance sheet that never gets traced back to a person or a decision.  So planners protect against the outcome that gets them called into a room, and the tool becomes something to override, not use.

You see the same instinct on the floor.  A site would rather see material piled in front of a critical machine than trust a number telling them they don't need it.  The pile is visible.  The carrying cost isn't.

What they're buying is protection against variation that would be a historic outlier...insurance against an event that hasn't happened in years, priced at whatever working capital costs.

Optimization doesn't fail on math.  It fails because the pain of the past outweighs the will to optimize.

There are 9 useful patterns to know.
 
Prompt chaining is the assembly line.
Use it when the work has stages: research, outline, draft, edit, final check.
 
Parallelization is the search party.
Use it when many independent checks can run at once: competitors, test cases, content angles, lead research.
 
Orchestrator-worker is the project manager.
Use it when one system should plan the work and assign smaller tasks.
 
Evaluator-optimizer is the editor.
Use it when quality matters enough to create, critique, and improve against a rubric.
 
Routing is the switchboard.
Use it when different inputs need different paths, such as support tickets, sales leads, or internal requests.
 
Autonomous workflow is the machine.
Use it only when the rules are clear, the actions are bounded, and the downside is controlled.
 
Human-in-the-loop is the safety gate.
Use it for legal, finance, hiring, customer promises, medical content, and code deployment.
 
Reflection is the second look.
Use it when the first answer may miss assumptions, edge cases, or weak evidence.
 
Multi-agent debate is the pressure test.
Use it when a decision benefits from opposing views: buyer, operator, CFO, engineer, customer.
 
The mistake is trying to build “an agent” before choosing the pattern.
 
That creates demos.
It does not create dependable workflows.
 
A better build sequence:
Name the task.
Choose the pattern.
Define the inputs.
Define the stopping point.
Add the review rule.
Measure the before-and-after result.
 
One example:
Customer complaint comes in.
Router classifies it.
Retriever pulls account context.
Drafting agent proposes a response.
Evaluator checks policy and tone.
Human approves anything above a risk threshold.
 
That is agentic work you can inspect.
Not magic.
Not a black box.
A workflow with visible joints and owners.
 
The future advantage is not saying “we use agents.”
The advantage is knowing which pattern fits which job.
 
Which workflow in your company needs a pattern before it needs another tool?

Exa and Linkup are search engines built for AI agents rather than for people. 
Limadata reads any page and pulls the whole thing back. 
Claude works all 3 and returns, as in the demo, US companies, VC backed, 50 to 200 employees, funded in the last few months, then digs into what changed after the money landed.

Apollo and ZoomInfo hand every team the same filters, so the same mailboxes get hit by hundreds of reps working the same export. Precision is the only edge left.

The agent conversation has moved past demos.
2025 made agents mainstream.
2026 is about getting them to work reliably inside real businesses.

The first shift is multi-agent orchestration.
One agent is useful.
A coordinated team of specialist agents is where the leverage starts.
Research agents, retriever agents, evaluator agents, and workflow agents can now divide work in real time.

The second shift is context engineering.
Prompt engineering is not enough for production.
Agents need memory, retrieval, knowledge graphs, and structured context.
That is what turns a clever chat into a dependable workflow.

The third shift is guardian agents.
If agents are taking action, something needs to supervise the action.
Guardian systems watch for hallucinations, policy failures, tool errors, and scope drift before they become expensive.

The fourth shift is agentic commerce.
Agents are moving from recommending products to comparing, purchasing, approving, and managing transactions.
Consumer shopping is the visible version.
B2B procurement is the bigger prize.

The fifth shift is coding agents at scale.
Claude Code, Cursor, Devin, Copilot, Replit Agent, and Windsurf are changing the software workflow.
The bottleneck is no longer just writing code.
It is reviewing, governing, and shipping agent-written work safely.

The sixth shift is governance and evals.
Many companies are experimenting with agents.
Far fewer are scaling them.
That gap is not ambition.
It is evaluation, observability, approval, and control.

The messy middle is where most leaders get stuck.
A dashboard full of agents looks impressive,
but production value comes from ownership, limits, and feedback loops.

This is the pattern leaders need to see.
Agents are not one feature.
They are a new operating layer.

The winning teams will not just ask,
which agent should we buy?

They will ask,
which workflow should agents own,
which context do they need,
who supervises them,
and how do we evaluate performance?

That is the difference between agent experiments
and agent infrastructure.

Some of those DMs turned into calls. Some of those calls turned into meeting in person at a conference two years later. A few of them I now work with, travel with, or build products with.

By the time I got fired, I still didn't have clients. What I had was a small group of people who knew my name and knew what I could do.

That group is the reason I have a business now.

Distinctiva exists because of conversations that started as a comment on someone else's post. Every client, every speaking slot, every partnership traces back to a specific person I decided to talk to first.

The ones from this year came the same way the ones from year one did.

Your ceiling has a lot to do with who you're standing next to.

Most people are standing alone on purpose, because sending the first message feels uncomfortable for about ten seconds and then never does again.

Which is why I said yes to the Kleo Mastermind.

I'm speaking in London on August 8, alongside Lara Acosta, Jake Ward and Cam Trew. Three of the people in these photos, which isn't an accident.

You'll get the sessions. You'll also spend a full day next to founders and operators who can change what your next year looks like, and that part never shows up on the agenda.

Every seat is vetted, so it stays a small room.

Details here: kleo.so/mastermind

#ddiinstructor Laurent Vigouroux describes the #AI problem in three simple steps!
#DDMRP #DemandDriven #SupplyChainInnovation #SupplyChainTransformation #SupplyChainResilience

Every new idea in supply chain goes through the same stages.
Nobody cares.

Then people argue with it.

Then a few brave companies try it anyway.

Those companies get results.

And then people stop asking "does it work?" They start asking "why are my competitors doing it?"

One year into building Demand Driven MRP in the US and that's the shift I'm watching happen. It is not new to us as we saw the same shift happen in Europe, APAC, IMEA and LATAM.

We spent the first years explaining what DDMRP is. Then the conversation shifts to how companies are already using it.

Curiosity is replacing scepticism. And that's when markets start to move.

What's the last idea in your industry that went from "that won't work" to "why isn't everyone doing this"?

Original post:
__________

The 7 most interesting tactics to influence what ChatGPT & Claude say about you 👀

1. Put your best customers in the website footer

➡️ Inspiration: Clay, Sundial

Our working theory: LLMs overweight structural prominence, aka what you put in your headers, sub-headers, top nav, and footer.

Research from Josh Blyskal at Profound backs this up. Google AI mode literally extracts your headers, summarizes the text under each one, and only the themes that win across many pages become the bold sections of the final answer.

2. Add a comparison article of your product vs. Claude

➡️ Inspiration: Framer

This is a powerful way to help control the competitive conversation and acknowledge the new world we live in: the majority of SaaS today must be compared against Claude Code.

3. Introduce a 'Summarize with AI' button on your website

➡️ Inspiration: Wispr Flow, Glean, Galileo

Last year we had never seen companies doing this. Now it's popping up everywhere. One of the hottest website changes is to introduce "Summarize with AI" buttons.

Why do it: (a) by controlling the prompt, you control the narrative, (b) LLMs remember what users asked about so you stay with the prospect going fwd.

4. Add tables and screenshots to your FAQs

➡️ Inspiration: Lovable

The question-and-answer style of FAQs seems to be catnip to LLMs, which can easily "borrow" entire chunks of text in response to a user's query.

5. Build your own newsroom

➡️ Inspiration: Rippling

Rippling now gets cited for everything news-related: new features, funding rounds, acquisitions, partnership announcements, you name it.

6. Create a glossary for industry jargon

➡️ Inspiration: HubSpot

HubSpot built out a glossary of every term imaginable around CRM, Marketing and Sales. Each page includes a resource link to related HubSpot blogs/content. Now HubSpot is primed to get cited as new AI jargon pops up -- which, to be honest, feels like it happens every week.

7. Vibecode free micro-tools to expand your product surface area

➡️ Inspiration: Ahrefs

When the LLMs are crawling your site, they see that part of your product offering now includes these tools. Offering them for free increases the chances they'll be mentioned or recommended by other happy users on social media or other websites, which in turn will reinforce LLM visibility.

---

Your website still matters even as buyers get their information from LLMs. It might even matter more now than before.

Huge shoutout to website geek Casey Hill from DoWhatWorks for the collab.

Credit to Kyle Poyar. Follow him for more.

I'm a frequent flyer, so I have a whole system down.

Small bag in the overhead. Laptop in front of me. Headphones on before we take off. And at least a few episodes of Love Island UK downloaded. 
 
What I never think about is what's happening under my feet ...
 
Because underneath the floor of that plane is an entire second operation running: freight, mail, sometimes even parts of a factory.

Most of us never think about it once. Why would we?!
 
That operation essentially runs on its own version of what we deal with at the gate (except it's not $45 to check a bag). 

It's fuel surcharges and accessorial fees that can make or break a shipper's margins overnight.
 
This is what I recently talked about with Marco Ferrara from Delta Air Lines and Ed Burek from SmartKargo.

I asked them: when did surcharges stop being about the actual cost ... and start being a 'lever' companies pull whenever they want more revenue?
 
The answer: "A lot of businesses are built on surcharges. It's become a mechanism to dial up your revenue."
 
Once you see the pattern, you can't unsee it. Because it's not just airlines. 

It's SaaS pricing. Service fees. "Convenience" charges. Almost every industry has a version of the $45 checked bag fee ...
 
Surcharges used to track real costs. Now, they're a revenue driver. And customers (like you and me) can tell the difference, even when we can't name it
 
---

I had fun recording this episode with Marco and Ed at Home Delivery World. 

You can check out our full conversation on YouTube or wherever you listen to podcasts: https://lnkd.in/eGsddGXH
